Overviews

Overview of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a single, undifferentiated whole. Islam as a religion cannot simply be identified with the political idea of the Arab world. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, or Malay Islam, among others.

Readers curious about Iran's archaeology and arts, both before and after the coming of Islam, have a wealth of literature at their disposal. Unfortunately, far fewer books answer the question that confronts anyone who wants to understand the motives of Iranian consciousness—the inner impulses that gave these forms their shape.

From the beginning, the Iranian world has formed a distinctive whole within the wider Islamic community. Its character and calling become clear only when we regard Iran's spiritual universe as a continuous whole, before Islam and after it. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from what it brings to fruition or from its practical consequences. These consequences concern not merely what we today call the social environment, but the whole, concrete world that a person nourishes out of their own being, a world reaching beyond the bounds of earthly life: their spiritual world.

This conviction has guided the author in building the work presented here in seven books. It is the fruit of more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, conducted both in libraries and in the company of Iranian friends, together with the experience of teaching in Paris and Tehran. The method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school of phenomenology. Its aim is to encounter the religious fact by allowing the religious object to show itself as it shows itself to those to whom it appears.

Hence the importance of the book's subtitle: Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects. The very word aspect implies a spectator.

But here the spectator—the phenomenologist—must become a spiritual guest of those to whom the object appears, and must shoulder its weight alongside them. Historical inquiry must therefore remain within the world of the religious object itself, rather than impose some alien category upon it from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise. Only on this condition can the connections suggested throughout this work be drawn across different times, for what we are encountering are variations of one and the same object.

The first two volumes contain Books I and II of the work.

Book I sets out to reveal some of the essential features of Twelver Shiism, also known as Imamism, a tradition firmly rooted in Iran from its earliest days and its official religion since the sixteenth century. These features are identified and studied through what the author has previously called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book”: the way revelation presents itself to those whom the Qur’an calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book,” embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. In every branch of the Abrahamic tradition, interpreters of the Bible and the Qur’an have confronted the same questions and tasks.

All have sought to discover the Book's true meaning. On each side, that search—the search for the spiritual meaning concealed beneath the literal wording—has produced similar ways of disclosing the esoteric, or inner, meaning of divine revelation. The “phenomenon of the Book” is the source of hermeneutics: the art of understanding and interpreting meaning. The interpreters who sought the hidden meanings of the Bible and the Qur’an probably still have much to teach today's philosophers, who are themselves so preoccupied with hermeneutics.

The technical name for this inner interpretation of the Qur’an is ta’wîl, meaning to “lead back” a thing to its origin, its archetype. Shia metaphysics is governed by two ideas: that God's essence is unknowable, inaccessible, and beyond all naming; and that God reveals himself through the pleroma, the complete heavenly assembly, of Fourteen beings of light, manifested on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.

The inner meaning that Shia ta’wîl draws from the literal words of the Qur’an concerns, above all, this assembly of Fourteen. It thereby illustrates the distinctive Shia understanding of prophecy, according to which the future of religion cannot be entirely behind us.

Unlike majority Sunni Islam, in which humanity has nothing further to await after the mission of the final Prophet, Shiism keeps the future open. Even after the coming of the “Seal of the Prophets,” something remains to be awaited: the unveiling of the spiritual meaning of the revelations brought by the great prophets. This was the task of interpretation entrusted to the holy Imams, whose teachings fill many volumes.

Yet this spiritual understanding will become complete only at the end of our age, when the Twelfth Imam—now hidden from sight and the mystical pole of this world—appears again.

Interpretation thus entails a particular experience of time, expressed in the division of sacred history into periods: the age of the prophets' missions is followed by the age of spiritual initiation. Here Shia teachings on prophecy meet the hopes of the movement inspired by Joachim of Fiore in the West, with its proclamation of the coming reign of the Spirit.

Yet this division of time already belongs to metahistory, to a reality beyond ordinary historical succession, because its essential concern with the ultimate end of history breaks through the limits of history itself.

Like the interpretation of scripture, the Shia understanding of the Imams confronted its thinkers with problems comparable to those posed by Christology for Christian thinkers. Yet Shia thinkers consistently tended toward solutions rejected by official Christian Christology. Perhaps it was in this way that Shia spiritual knowledge avoided being secularized into a merely social messianism.

Shia metaphysics and Shia spiritual life are inseparable: each is the very substance of the other. For too long, an understanding of Islam limited almost entirely to the Sunni majority has led people to equate Sufism with the spiritual life of Islam as such. In reality, Shia spirituality reaches beyond Sufism. There certainly are Shia Sufi orders, and the spiritual lineages of most tarîqat—Sufi paths or orders—ultimately lead back to one of the Imams.

But a Shia seeker of inner meaning is already, by that very fact, on the spiritual Path (tarîqat), without needing to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowing the Imam as one's personal guide leads the seeker toward self-knowledge.

Book II is devoted entirely to another equally fundamental feature of the philosophy and spiritual life of Iranian Islam, one that was closely allied from the outset with the Shiism of many Iranian thinkers. Its defining term is ishrâq: sunrise, the coming of dawn (aurora consurgens), the sun's “east.” Just as the philosophy of Ishrâq, understood as a wisdom of Light, is “Oriental” wisdom, so its philosophers—the ishrâqîyân—are “Oriental” philosophers in the metaphysical sense of Orient: the place where light rises. They are also often called “Platonists,” in contrast to the Peripatetic, or Aristotelian, philosophers of Islam.

At the origin of these “Platonists of Persia” stands the heroic resolve of a brilliant young thinker from northwestern Iran: Shihab al-Din Yahya Suhrawardi, who died in Aleppo, Syria, in 1191, at the age of thirty-six, a martyr to his cause. His writings state his purpose plainly: to revive the wisdom of ancient Persia, its philosophy of Light and Darkness; in a sense, to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia. He sought to do so through the very resources of spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) that Islamic spirituality had placed in his hands.

Some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon, this Iranian thinker's work brought together the names of Plato and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, as heralds of a single “Oriental” tradition reaching back to Hermes, the father of the sages. Plato's Ideas were interpreted in terms of Zoroastrian angelology. His interpretation of being made room for a third world whose reality philosophies of abstract concepts had been unable to establish.

Between the intelligible world and the world of the senses lies the mundus imaginalis, a world entirely real—not the merely “imaginary” world to which outward-looking philosophies reduce it, but a world requiring its own name: the imaginal. Suhrawardi understood that by establishing the reality of this “third world,” he was also establishing the objective reality of prophetic revelations, mystical visions, and the events of revelation. This insight would remain alive throughout the centuries of Iranian thought.

It is significant that this metaphysics of Light identifies light's primordial Source with what Zoroastrian wisdom calls Xvarnah, the “Light of Glory.” From that Source flow the hierarchies of archangels. Their order combines Zoroastrian angelology with the celestial hierarchies described by the Neoplatonist Proclus. The theme of Xvarnah itself carries seemingly inexhaustible echoes and implications. Earlier research has identified correspondences between its manifestations and those of the Holy Grail in Western traditions.

Indeed, the Grail itself—the mystical cup that mirrors the world—appears in the heroic epic of ancient Iran, and it is present in Suhrawardi's writings. There it symbolizes the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic, a decisive event in Iran's cultural history. That same passage is announced in a series of brief tales of spiritual initiation, nearly all written in Persian. Their rich symbolism allows Suhrawardi to lead the reader toward the goal of the reader's longing even more effectively than his great systematic works. The author pays particular attention to two such spiritual tales: one rooted in Iran's own mystical epic, the other in the wider epic of Gnosis, the quest for spiritual knowledge.

Suhrawardi's “Oriental” tradition has remained alive in Iran to the present day. It also exercised a powerful influence in India at the time of Emperor Akbar's religious reforms.

Together, the first two books thus reveal two essential sides of Islamic spiritual knowledge as shaped by the spirit of Iranian Islam. At a time when recent discoveries have given fresh momentum to the study of Gnosis—both ancient Gnosticism and Jewish mystical knowledge—these investigations are especially timely.

Overview of Book III

Book III is devoted entirely to Iranian Sufism as it emerges from the writings of a great master, Ruzbihan Baqli Shirazi (1128–1209). He was a contemporary of Suhrawardi, the shaykh al-Ishrâq, or Master of Illumination.

But where Suhrawardi was a man of northern Iran, Ruzbihan belonged to the south: to Fars, the province known in antiquity as Persis, Persia in the strict sense.

His writings and teachings are especially revealing of the spirituality of Iranian Sufism, above all in what distinguishes it from traditional Christian asceticism. The phenomenon of the “unhappy consciousness,” familiar to us from Hegel, belongs specifically to the experience of Christian consciousness—even if today that consciousness increasingly insists on being “present in the world,” ashamed of its unhappiness or hoping thereby to be less unhappy.

Sufism, too, encounters an opposition that must be overcome; but the terms of that opposition differ from those that make, or have made, the Christian's condition so troubled. The Christian has found himself torn between sin and the grace that justifies, belief and knowledge; more crudely, between “mysticism” and “sensuality”; more abstractly, between the truth of historical fact and inward truth, between the object of faith embodied in history and spiritual reality unconditioned by time, between the literal content of revelation and its spiritual meaning, and so forth.

So much so that, as a post-Christian order of things becomes secularized, the illness merely changes its name. Sociology takes theology's place as the ruling authority, with the assistance of psychoanalysis. People speak no longer of sin but of guilt complexes, frustration, and so on.

The Sufi, by contrast, is neither a sinner, nor a patient, nor a frustrated individual. He feels no need to be “justified.” He is a stranger, an exile. Like seekers of spiritual knowledge in every age and place, he longs to find his way home, and therefore to meet the guide who will show him the road back. For him, this is the meaning of prophecy: the religious Law (sharî’at) revealed by the Prophet opens the inner Path (tarîqat) leading to spiritual Truth (haqîqat).

When that Truth is personally experienced and made real, the Sufi becomes a free human being. The mystic’s calling does not stand opposed to prophetic revelation. It fulfills revelation, because it brings to life revelation's hidden truth. Without this inner truth, nothing remains but an abstract monotheism (tawhîd), an assertion of God's oneness that has not become a lived experience. Only the idea—or, better, the actual experience—of theophany, the manifestation of God, can overcome it.

The divine essence is unknowable, yet God's actions are manifestations through which the divine attributes appear. Such a manifestation is not God taking bodily form. To perceive a theophany is to perceive the double meaning (iltibâs) of every manifest being: how it conceals and reveals the invisible at one and the same time. Without the awareness that makes this vision possible, we remain in a world of duality and opposing things. In that condition, both the devout believer and the dogmatic theologian are, at heart, polytheists without knowing it.

Such awareness cannot awaken by turning away from what is visible and perceptible to the senses. The visible must first be recognized as a veil, and then transformed into a mirror. Among all human experiences, one holds a special place: only the experience of human love for a beautiful person can lead us to live through this transformation—the soul's shock and ecstasy before a divine manifestation. Ruzbihan gives Sufism a decisive new direction by distinguishing two kinds of seekers.

There are pious ascetics for whom human love has played no part at the beginning of the spiritual path. And there are those for whom human love is the beginning of divine love, because the two belong to one and the same book, the book of one and the same love—though its text must be learned and read. Only this second group, of which Ruzbihan is the outstanding example, deserves the name Faithful of Love, a name chosen for their kinship with the Fedeli d’amore, Dante's companions in love.

Along this same path, Ruzbihan does not shrink from appearing as a malâmati: one of those who, in order to conceal the purity of their inner face, sometimes deliberately behave in ways that invite public blame. From this point of view he may be considered a forerunner of another celebrated man of Shiraz, the great poet Hafez, whose dîwân, or collected poems, Iranian Sufis have always known how to read as a reminder of the mystical path.

At a friend's request, Ruzbihan composed a “spiritual journal,” an invaluable document in the mystical literature of any age. It calls to mind certain passages from Swedenborg's Memorabilia. This is a record of Ruzbihan's visions and dreams from the age of fifteen. It shows that even as a child he possessed extraordinary emotional intensity and a remarkable gift for visions.

At fifteen, he left his home. A vision revealed his secret rank in the mystical hierarchy. Then came a succession of magnificent visions: angels and beings of beauty, flowering landscapes, crimson dawns... All Ruzbihan's books are written in a highly individual language, alive with an almost unbroken ecstatic lyricism that does not always make for easy reading.

Yet this autobiographical journal gives us the testimony of lived experience from which to trace the stages and trials through which the unfolding drama of love leads, by way of theophanies, to the inner realization of divine oneness (tawhîd).

The first trial is the trial of the Veil. Here Ruzbihan certainly stands within the great Sufi tradition.

But he adds an extraordinary insight of his own, bringing both experiential mysticism and speculative mystical thought to one of their highest points. The “Hidden Treasure” brought the world into existence so that it might be known, and might know itself through its creatures. Spirit is the primordial foundation through which the Holy Spirits endure—the spiritual identities of beings, existing from before all time. Every atom of existence is, no doubt, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it came.

But the Divine Being then experiences jealousy toward himself. By making himself an object to himself, by revealing himself, he is no longer simply his own witness: now there is a witness outside himself, someone other than himself. This is the first Veil.

The Divine Being therefore seeks to regain possession of himself. He turns that Spirit away from contemplating him and directs his creature to contemplate itself. This vision of the self by the self is the second Veil. The trial of the Veil is the very meaning of Creation. The descent of the Holy Spirits into earthly existence has no other purpose than to bring them through this trial to victory.

To pass through it, the mystic must discover that his self-knowledge is the very gaze by which God contemplates himself, that he himself is the witness through whom God bears witness to himself. The veil then becomes a mirror.

But to look for something beyond the Veil, Ruzbihan says, is to fall into the “madness of the unattainable.” Since Creation, God has never looked upon a world other than himself: such a world is abhorrent to him. Those who awaken to their calling as witnesses are the eyes through which God still looks at the world, and through which the world still matters to him. They may be unknown to everyone; nonetheless, it is thanks to them that the world endures.

Far beyond any social role, these mystics fulfill a function of cosmic salvation. Here Ruzbihan's insight comes remarkably close to that of Meister Eckhart. The gaze with which I know God is none other than the gaze with which God knows me. That is the secret of the theophanic visions through which Ruzbihan moves toward the inner experience of divine oneness.

It is the unfolding dialectic of love that makes this progress possible, for love alone reveals the identity of witness and witnessed, contemplator and contemplated. That dialectic fills an entire Persian work, perhaps Ruzbihan's masterpiece: The Jasmine of the Faithful of Love. “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I strove to understand the secret of the Human Form.” The drama of love unveils the secret of divine manifestations because a theophany is, in its essence, the appearance of the divine in beauty.

Our age of “demythologization” has labored so hard to strip beauty of its sacred character that the feeling of the numinous—the presence of the holy—in the face of beauty may now seem strange, even utterly foreign. For all our Iranian Faithful of Love, by contrast, it is a fundamental experience. The same is true of Ibn Arabi, who influenced the whole of Islamic spirituality for eight centuries and remains one of the most distinguished witnesses to this mystical religion of beauty as the supreme divine attribute.

Ruzbihan embraces the Neoplatonic proposition: “Even before the worlds existed, the Divine Being was himself love, lover, and beloved.” He is immediately faced with the great question that had exercised Sufi circles from the beginning: is it fitting to use the word love in speaking of God? Whom does the mystic love when he speaks of his love for God? The whole of The Jasmine answers these questions in a sequence of chapters.

On one side, it explores the prophetic meaning of beauty, contemplating the Prophet of Islam as the prophet of the religion of beauty. On the other, drawing on all the resources of Platonic inspiration, it unveils the eternal source of love, bringing together the great themes of the Eternal Witness and the Eternal Bride. Suhrawardi had already set us on this path toward the transfiguration of Eros.

Here, too, love is not transferred from one object to another, from a human object to a divine one. What takes place instead is a transformation of the person who loves. That transformation finds its emblem in Majnun and Layla—the Tristan and Isolde of the mystical epic, in Persian as in Arabic. At the height of his love, Majnun becomes the “mirror of God.” It is God himself who, in the lover's gaze upon the beloved, contemplates his own eternal face.

This is what it means to attain the vision of vision, the inner realization of oneness through identity, in which there is no longer either I + I or I = I, but I × I = I. Then, in the intoxication of a consciousness that has passed beyond itself, the mystic may utter the celebrated, extravagant cry of al-Hallaj: Anâ’l-Haqq (“I am God”). The case of al-Hallaj occupied Ruzbihan throughout his life. He offered abundant explanations and defenses of that famous “theopathic utterance,” a saying in which the divine speaks through the mystic.

Indeed, it is to Ruzbihan that we owe the preservation of a work by al-Hallaj in his own substantial Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis. We published the Persian text some years ago; it is a veritable compendium of the Sufism of Ruzbihan's time.

Overview of Book IV

Book IV returns to a question first raised in Book I: the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Its four chapters examine the writings of four important authors from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries CE. Unfortunately, the second of these authors remains anonymous.

I. The first chapter is devoted to Sayyed Haydar Amoli (born 720 AH/1320 CE; died after 787 AH/1385–86 CE). His extensive writings, frequently cited by later authors, had until now remained unpublished. We have recently prepared editions of two of his treatises, together forming a true compendium of Shia philosophy. For many of his other works, unfortunately, we have still been unable to locate manuscripts.

Haydar Amoli came from northern Iran. He spent the first half of his life in his native Tabaristan, a province now part of Mazandaran on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea. The works we have so far been able to study supply the materials for a moving spiritual autobiography, particularly characteristic of an Iranian spiritual seeker. Born into a distinguished Shia family of Tabaristan, Sayyed Haydar studied, among other places, in Isfahan.

Until the age of thirty, he enjoyed a brilliant, privileged youth. He even served as his ruler's minister and was briefly caught up in the upheavals of his time. Then a profound spiritual crisis caused him to renounce every worldly ambition and set out upon the roads as a “pilgrim of God,” wearing the poor cloak of a Sufi. He traveled to the Shia holy places of Iraq, where he spent the entire second period of his life producing a body of work on an immense scale.

These writings mark a major moment in the development of Shia philosophy and spirituality. They alone are enough to show that Shia thought, as such, is not—as some modernists would have it—a political invention of the Safavid period. They are also among the works that offer an answer to the difficult question of the original relationship between Shiism and Sufism.

On a matter so decisive for our understanding of Islamic spirituality generally, the student of religion prefers to let those directly concerned speak for themselves and to be guided by their answers. This is why the texts of Haydar Amoli have already played such an important part in Book I.

Haydar confronts the question directly, apparently because it arose with particular urgency for him and those around him. His answer is that of a seeker of inner meaning, for whom Shiism is, in essence, the inward or esoteric dimension of Islam. Any Shia Muslim who confines himself to outward religious forms therefore mutilates the very teaching of the holy Imams. The Sufis, by contrast, affirm the inner meaning of divine revelations and thus show themselves to be the “true Shia.” Unfortunately, they have forgotten their origins and have mutilated their own inner teaching insofar as they have excluded the doctrine of the Imams.

Sayyed Haydar wants to put an end to this situation once and for all. He takes issue equally with Shia who denounce Sufism and Sufis who denounce Shiism. He must therefore contend on several fronts: with the legalistic outlook of Sunni Islam, with Shia who have forgotten the inner meaning of their faith, and with Sufis who have forgotten both their origins and what they fundamentally owe to Shiism. Two centuries later Mulla Sadra Shirazi would face a similar situation. It is, indeed, a tragic situation that spiritual seekers in each of the three branches of the Abrahamic tradition have had to confront in their own ways.

In meeting these challenges, Sayyed Haydar acts as a disciple of Ibn Arabi, to whom he refers repeatedly. Much of his effort goes into tracing the passage from the theological tawhîd—the affirmation of divine oneness to which the prophets called humanity—to the ontological tawhîd, the realization of oneness at the level of being, to which the “Friends of God” invite us in the wake of the holy Imams.

These pages show how fully Shia Iranian thought was able to make Ibn Arabi's spiritual philosophy its own, precisely because it found there something that already belonged to it. Ibn Arabi's Fosûs (The Bezels of Wisdom) could themselves be seen as belonging to the phenomenon of the Holy Book, since their author had received their heavenly inspiration from the Prophet.

Yet, despite his devotion to Ibn Arabi's thought and writings, Haydar Amoli disagrees with him on one point that admits no compromise: the very point that, for a Shia Muslim, determines the meaning of prophecy.

Like all Twelver Shia, Haydar holds that the Seal of walâyat—the inner spiritual reality of prophecy—cannot be a prophet, namely Jesus, as Ibn Arabi maintained. That Seal is, and can only be, the Muhammadan Imamate: in the person of the First Imam as the Seal of universal walâyat, and in the person of the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The entire destiny of Shia sacred history is at stake here—a vision of history whose full significance Book VII will reveal—and Haydar Amoli cannot yield.

Like so many of his fellow mystics, Sayyed Haydar possessed an unusual gift for visions in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. This went hand in hand with his fondness for diagrams. His diagram of a vision beheld in the night sky over Baghdad provides a striking illustration of the structure of the heavenly assembly of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

II. The second chapter studies a treatise from the same period whose author, unfortunately, remains unknown. It offers an extensive commentary on a famous hadith, or saying attributed to the Prophet: “The Qur’an has an outer meaning and an inner meaning; that inner meaning in turn has an inner meaning, and so on through seven depths of hidden meaning.”

In setting out this golden rule of spiritual interpretation—the progressive inward discovery of the meaning of Qur’anic revelation—the hadith returns us to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book,” examined at length in Book I as the very foundation upon which the meaning and calling of Shiism depend. In this respect, the anonymous treatise stands between the great work of scriptural interpretation by Semnani, examined below, and that of Haydar Amoli, who devoted a monumental work in six large volumes to the Shia spiritual interpretation of the Qur’an.

The anonymous author frames the problem in terms familiar to every interpreter of the Abrahamic tradition: what is the relation between a revealed text expressed in a particular language at a particular moment and the eternal truth it proclaims? How are we to understand the passage from the divine Word to its expression in human speech?

The obvious objection is this: if the divine Word is eternal, and if the events it reveals must therefore also be eternal, what becomes of the very idea of an event? The author answers by proposing precisely the idea of an eternal event. For such an event, “before” and “after” cannot be understood in terms of the measurable, irreversible time of chronological history.

If the phenomenon of the Book marks the entry of the divine Word into time, spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) leads that Word back to a time that is not the time of history. Here we see the interpretation of the Book at work: it was this that led our thinkers to confront and master the problem of historical time.

As for the seven depths of inner meaning, each is identified by a name for the Book drawn from the Qur’an itself. Each name corresponds to a level of meaning and, consequently, to the group of people capable of understanding at that level. The interpretation of scripture is thus inseparable from a philosophical understanding of the human being.

We shall see this fundamental connection confirmed twice more below. It is characteristic of a spirituality founded upon the many levels at which the Holy Book can mean something and be understood.

III. The third chapter examines a work of spiritual interpretation by Sa'in al-Din Isfahani (d. 830 AH/1427 CE), a thinker who belonged to an entire family line of Shia philosophers and spiritual teachers. The work interprets a particularly enigmatic Qur’anic verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon was split” (54:1). The author offers, as it were, a practical exercise in interpretation, beautifully illustrating the connection already discussed between our understanding of the human being and our understanding of scripture: between ways of being and ways of understanding, between levels of understanding and the people who inhabit them.

By interpreting this verse on several levels of meaning, he is able to sketch a religious typology embracing all the forms of religious consciousness then found within Islam. In order of increasing penetration into inner meaning, these are: jurists and transmitters of tradition (specialists in hadith); Islamic theologians (here, the scholastic thinkers of kalâm); the Peripatetic philosophers; the Ishrâqîyûn, or Platonists who followed Suhrawardi; Sufis; Hurufis; and Shia.

Once again, through the author's own words, we encounter the serious question: can there truly be a doctrine of prophecy, or an authentic Sufism, without the Shia understanding of the Imams? These philosophical ideas are expressed in a way that makes it appropriate to speak of a doctrine of the Imams that does not dare—or no longer dares—to speak its own name. This is one of the tragic aspects of the history of Shia thought.

IV. The fourth and final chapter of this book is devoted to the writings and teachings of one of the greatest masters of Iranian spirituality, Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 736 AH/1336 CE). By a paradox that is sadly far from unique, his works, in Persian and Arabic, still exist entirely in manuscript. He belonged to the generation before Haydar Amoli.

Like Haydar, he experienced a profound spiritual crisis: once a young page at the court of the Mongol ruler Arghun, he became a Sufi. His teaching stands in the line of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 1221), the great master of Central Asian Sufism who was the first to pay close attention to the colored lights whose aura appears to the spiritual awareness of mystics.

Semnani's teaching is marked by an interpretation of scripture that pushes the inward understanding of Qur’anic revelation to its furthest limit. The relationship discussed above—between scriptural interpretation and the understanding of the human being, between levels of meaning and levels of comprehension—takes on an entirely original form here, joining a theory of colored lights perceived in the mundus imaginalis. At the same time, the succession of the prophets is itself understood in a radically inward way. That succession revives, within Islam, the teaching of the Verus Propheta, the “True Prophet,” found in early Judeo-Christianity.

The inward transformation takes place through a physiology of the subtle organism concealed beneath the human physical body. This subtle physiology has seven centers or organs, called latîfa. They are not, as in Schiller, the “stars of your destiny,” but the “prophets of your being.” Each embodies a prophet, from the “Adam of your being,” through the “Abraham of your being,” to the “Muhammad of your being.” Each latîfa has its own aura, its own colored light. The mystic's perception of that light reveals how far the subtle body has developed—in other words, the body of resurrection.

Every passage of the Qur’an concerning one of the prophets must then be understood as referring to the corresponding subtle organ or center. In Sa'in al-Din Isfahani's typology, levels of understanding were distributed among different groups of people. Here they are brought entirely within the individual: each level corresponds to one of the subtle centers or organs of the spiritual seeker.

Above the seven latîfa of the “prophets of your being” there is another, to which Semnani makes several mysterious allusions. He names it after the very angel of knowledge and revelation: the latîfa jabra’êliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” It is at this summit of mystical understanding of the human being that we glimpse, in Semnani, the secret of a doctrine of the Imams that once again does not dare, or does not wish, to speak its name.

Semnani analyzes and describes in detail the cosmic agents and influences that constitute the seven latîfa. His is a magnificent vision, steeped in tradition yet deeply personal. Semnani the mystic reveals himself as a profound metaphysician, whose system invites comparison on many fronts. His work therefore marks a decisive moment not only in Iran's spiritual culture, but in the wider study of metaphysics and mysticism.

Volume IV will contain Book V (The School of Isfahan), Book VI (The Shaykhi School), and Book VII (The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry), together with a general index.

Book III

Ruzbihan Baqli Shirazi and the Sufism of the Faithful of Love

(522 AH/1128 CE–606 AH/1209 CE)

Chapter I Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The Quranic sura of the Dawn offers this invitation: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, content with Him and pleasing to Him” (89:27–28). Comparing the interpretations given to this verse within Islam brings into focus the different spiritual attitudes that Muslims and Christians have associated with peace of soul. And within Islam itself, the interpretations offered by mystics and spiritual writers reveal another contrast: that between the inward religion of Sufism, with its mystical knowledge, and a religion understood primarily in terms of law, whenever the latter refuses to make room for the esoteric dimension of faith—that is, for the inner life of those whose very souls are turned inward.

The subject of this book is Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz (522/1128–606/1209), one of the most representative figures of Iranian Sufism, though not himself a Shiite Sufi. We have referred to him in the preceding pages, and have already had occasion, as we shall again, to raise the unavoidable question of the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Haydar Amoli will have much to tell us about this (see below, Book IV, Chapter I).

For now, let us recall two fundamental ideas in Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams (see above, Book I): the prophetic mission (nobowwat) and walayat. The latter term, as we have seen, describes the special standing of the Twelve Imams as those whom God loves, the “Friends of God,” and the protective, guiding role they exercise toward their followers. From the followers, in turn, comes a corresponding love for the Imams. At its heart, therefore, the religion of the Imams reveals itself as a religion of love.

We have already observed that, from the standpoint of divine wisdom, one could very briefly express the difference between Shiism and Sunnism in this way: everything that Shiite spiritual knowledge sees centered on the Imam as its pole is, in Sunnism, invested in the Prophet alone. The resulting imbalance is one we have already begun to discern.

One symptom appears in the fate of that central Shiite idea, walayat. Sufism outside Shiism generally speaks instead of wilayat: a state of intimacy with God attained through renunciation of the self. In the West, the customary translation has become “sainthood.”

But to ask about the relative standing of nobowwat and wilayat—whether a prophet is superior to a “saint,” or a “saint” to a prophet—without taking account of the specifically Shiite understanding of the relationship between nobowwat and walayat is to distort the entire teaching about prophecy.

The real question is this: how can wilayat exist without walayat1, or how is it connected to it? Some connection there must be, since at the root of the spiritual lineage of almost every Sufi tariqa, or initiatory path, we eventually find one of the Imams. The result is a situation we shall later describe as “a teaching about the Imams that no longer dares speak its own name” (see below, Book IV, Chapter III).

An ambiguity remains, one that weighs upon tawhid, the affirmation of divine unity, and must continually be overcome. How does the divine Being, beyond words and beyond anything that can be said of it, reveal itself to a human being? Elsewhere, in studying the teachings of Qazi Sa'id Qommi, we have shown how Shiite spiritual philosophy, drawing on the words of the Imams themselves, understands the Face that God turns toward humanity as, by that very fact, the Face humanity turns toward God. That Face is the Imam2.

Without it—as though Christianity were deprived of Christ—the mystic is exposed to the paradox and intoxication that burst forth in the cry Ana'l-Haqq, “I am God.” More fundamentally still, the very practice of Sufism presupposes an answer to this question: can love have a place in the relationship between God and humanity, and between humanity and God? In the religion of the Imams, the Imam as a figure of divine self-revelation provides the mediation that makes the answer possible. As we shall see, this is precisely the central problem Ruzbihan's spiritual life had to confront, together with the related problem of how divine love and human love are connected.

Here we are only pointing to the problem. Other questions will arise later, or will have to be treated elsewhere. There is, for instance, the severity with which Imam Reza spoke of certain Sufis. There is the fact that many Iranian Shiite spiritual teachers use the language of Sufism without being Sufis in any formal sense; strictly speaking, therefore, tasawwuf, or Sufism, does not encompass everything meant by Islamic mysticism.

There is the possibility that the dominant place given to the shaykh, or spiritual master, may amount to an appropriation of the Imam's role. And there is a monistic metaphysics, professed in extreme forms by certain Sufis, which many Shiite spiritual thinkers reject.

We shall leave these issues aside and consider Ruzbihan alone, struggling with his own experiences and his own questions. His case is especially fascinating. Rather than burden it with comparisons or with a history of Sufism from its beginnings, we want simply to allow Ruzbihan's own distinctive voice to reach us: the particular intensity of his mystical feeling, the character of his visions, however formidable the difficulties of his language and style.

In short, we want him to show us, through his own words, why we call his Sufism the way of the “Faithful of Love.” Some pages of his writings may express something unique in the whole literature of mysticism.

Yet whatever the differences between Shiite and non-Shiite Sufism, there is a shared spiritual attitude underlying everything that belongs to Sufism. That same attitude characterizes the inner, esoteric dimension proper to Islam as a prophetic religion3. It helps us recognize both the affinities and the differences between this tradition and what is called “Christian esotericism.” In the Christian world, the Church developed in such a way that every esoteric current took shape on the margins of the official Churches, forming an “inner Church.” Sufism does not stand on the margins: it is the spiritual tradition of Islam.

By Sufism we mean the word in its broadest sense, not merely those outward forms and secondary practices that “modernists” use as an excuse to condemn and reject it, sometimes furiously. It is a tradition that does not even need archives: as we have noted, some Sufi paths have left, or will leave, no visible material trace. Such traces are beside the point. What matters is a spiritual attitude opposed to the will to power—an attitude in which any disturbance of the soul's peace may appear as the supreme paradox.

The phenomenon Hegel taught us to call the “unhappy consciousness” belongs, in a distinctive way, to the inner life of Christianity. It is true that certain forms of Christian consciousness today claim to be increasingly “present in this world,” in the hope of becoming less and less “unhappy.”

But that changes nothing about the place, within Sufism, of a contradiction to be overcome, an absence to be filled, a spiritual struggle to be sustained. What differs profoundly is the nature of the opposing terms, at least if we look for their Christian expression in the teachings of official dogmatic theology. We are familiar with such oppositions as sin and justifying grace, or faith and knowledge—believing and knowing.

We are equally familiar with another opposition said to follow from them, commonly and crudely framed as “mysticism” versus “sensuality”: as though love of God excluded love for a created being, as though beauty were a demonic trap, as though traditional asceticism had no response to doubts about these claims except to denounce a revival of “paganism.” Our secular sociologies have simply recorded these oppositions; one could hardly expect them to do more. In a society we might briefly call “post-Christian,” people may no longer speak of sin, but they speak of a “guilt complex.”

Is the symptom not the same? Does it not betray the same sickness of the “unhappy consciousness”? As for the supposedly “broad-minded” concessions, the servile accommodations to what is called the “modern spirit,” we need only look at some examples of what, in a bitter reversal of meaning, is still called “sacred art.” It becomes clear that their inspiration is far removed from the Renaissance longing for a beauty banished from the world by the consciousness of sin.

Alongside these conflicts inherited from our moral tradition are others of a more specifically intellectual kind: the opposition between historical fact and inner truth, between what historical faith takes as its object and a spiritual reality not dependent on an event in historical time; the opposition between the literal form of what revelation gives us and its spiritual meaning, between dogmatic consciousness and a consciousness that perceives all outward things as symbols.

These oppositions run so deep that they persist even where we might expect secularization to have made them disappear. They may depend, above all, on what we call historical consciousness: on the assumption that the material historicity of irreversible events is the measure of value and the guarantee of truth. The burden of historical consciousness, which has weighed tragically on so many Christian souls since Origen, has never been heavier than in the sociological philosophies of the “post-Christian” world.

Yet the Quranic words “O soul at peace, return, content and pleasing...” speak to the Sufi from within a spiritual universe foreign to these assumptions and oppositions. There is something astonishing, even tragic, in the fact that contemporary philosophical exchanges between East and West so rarely reach the heart of the matter. A Sufism conscious of its own meaning, and of what it undoubtedly shares with a very ancient Christianity, would have its own refusals and affirmations to set against a conformism so adept at disguising itself that it manages to pass for a force of liberation.

The Sufi does not think of himself as a sinner; he feels no need to be “justified.” He is an exile. And his distress, his longing—a longing he shares with the spiritual seekers of every age—makes him yearn, from the depths of his being, for a messenger, a teacher of truth, a spiritual Guide who can show him the road home.

No other future is desirable or even imaginable to him than to find again the place from which he came, to be at home once more. The post-Christian person may no longer be a “sinner,” but is even less willing to be an “exile”: he wants to make his home in this world.

Yet he may be driven out of it at any hour of day or night, without ever having suspected the path onto which he will then be cast. The idea of the Guide is inseparable from that of the prophet (see the discussion of prophecy above, Book I). A prophet's function is not exhausted by the giving of laws.

Rather, the purpose of the shari'a, the revealed law, is to open the Path (tariqa) toward rediscovered spiritual Truth (haqiqa). So, although a contrast has elsewhere been drawn between prophetic religion and mystical religion4, for the Sufi mystical religion is the truth—the true meaning of prophetic revelation—just as the prophet's task is to open to the seeker of spiritual knowledge the path of Return (ma'ad).

We can already begin to see that a certain opposition, increasingly prominent in Christianity, presents itself quite differently to the Sufi. On one side stands what is called the natural meaning of scriptural Revelation, identified with historical truth; on the other, its spiritual or esoteric meaning. Matters have been made worse because this spiritual meaning has so often been confused with allegory, or tolerated by the Church's teaching authority only when confined to a typology that remains entirely within the bounds of empirical history.

For the Sufi, this is neither a choice between two meanings nor the addition of some higher structure to the literal one. It is a passage to be made, a passage on which spiritual birth depends. Every genuine interpretation of scripture—that is, every spiritual interpretation—is an exodus of the soul.

Because the Sufi is not captive to the assumptions of our historical consciousness, the opposition we have established between contingent factual truth and eternal truth becomes, for him, an inward pilgrimage: from the shari'a to the haqiqa. Literal revelation (tanzil) is transfigured through the interpretation that brings out its hidden meaning (ta'wil). That meaning refers to real events, but events taking place on a plane other than the one we call History.

Islamic society has not developed anything comparable to what we call the Church. A Sufi would find it utterly incomprehensible to be told that he must receive his faith, and therefore eternal life, from “the Church.” Even if theology, having become atheistic, gives way to sociology, the Sufi remains a witness standing in accusation. He has his own resources for resisting the demands that collective consciousness imposes.

In their place he sets the personal bond between disciple and initiator, the bond with the Guide, the shaykh or pir; or, in Shiism, the bond with the Imam, above all the Hidden Imam. In Sufism this corresponds to the bond with a personal heavenly Guide, whom Najm al-Din Kubra calls the invisible master (shaykh al-ghayb), the Witness in Heaven (shahid fi'l-sama')5. It would be hard to find a more radical basis for safeguarding spiritual individuality, once and for all. This individuality, of course, is not the everyday ego represented by the nafs ammara, the commanding soul with its disorderly appetites.

It is what our authors call the “Holy Spirit” within a human being: the higher self, existing before earthly life, which must be freed or won back. That is precisely the aim of the whole spiritual struggle of Sufism: to subdue the nafs ammara and transform it into the nafs motma'yanna, the “soul at peace.” This understanding of transformation gives the spiritual struggle, particularly in Iranian Sufism, an altogether different character from that of traditional Christian asceticism.

A comparison with Mahayana Buddhism would be more apt: what is at stake is much less destruction than a raising and transformation of the soul. Through the method and purpose of this spiritual struggle, we may begin to see how the Sufi resolves in experience his deepest confrontation with the ordinary, outward formulation of Islam's fundamental doctrine: tawhid, divine unity. The outcome is a passage from outward to inward tawhid: a metamorphosis of abstract monotheism.

In its naive or dogmatic form, monotheism sets a Supreme Being, the Ens supremum, above the sum of all beings, rather like adding one more term to the total—x + 1. Instead of a view that merely places absolute Being alongside other beings, there emerges an inward relationship that, at its furthest reach, can be expressed only through paradox, startling excess, or “pious blasphemies” (shath)6.

The abstract monotheism of outward tawhid finds its resolution in the idea—or, more accurately, the experience—of divine self-revelation, the theophany (tajalli).

This brings us to the whole question of the relationship between the divine Essence, the divine Attributes, and the divine Acts. In fact, it is a relationship of identity: the divine Acts (af'al) are manifestations through which the Attributes appear, and the Attributes themselves are identical with the Essence. Until the seeker reaches this awareness of divine manifestation, he remains caught in duality, in a world of oppositions. That is why the devout monotheist, no less than the dogmatic theologian engaged in argument and debate, is at bottom an unwitting polytheist.

Yet one does not reach this awareness by turning away from the visible and the tangible. One must first recognize them as a veil, then transform that veil into a mirror. The “ordeal of the veil” is overcome when the veil becomes a “mirror of divine revelation” (mir'at-e tajalli).

A new relationship is then established between uncreated Beauty, the archetype, and the beauty that can be seen and felt. Instead of the negative relationship we are accustomed to seeing between Christian asceticism and the Greek sense of beauty, we must speak here of a recognition that gives beauty a prophetic role.

Sufis such as Ruzbihan and Ibn Arabi find a special bond between each prophet and Beauty as a divine Attribute and the supreme form of divine manifestation. Among the most fascinating discoveries is the figure of the Prophet of Islam as Sufism understands him: the prophet of a religion of beauty, whose sayings abound in echoes of Plato.

But theophanies have no limit. The soul finds peace in discovering the secret of divine self-revelation, yet the inexhaustible variety of these revelations keeps it moving, restless with longing. The invitation “Return, O soul at peace” should not be understood primarily as a return that takes place after the soul has become peaceful. The return is the soul's progressive coming to peace. So the certainty of these restless souls grows within their serenity, just as restlessness persists within their peace. They know nothing of the dizzying sense of nothingness or absurdity, or of the panics that drive individuals and crowds into ready-made shelters of dogma, religious or secular.

As Ibn Arabi interprets it, this is not a return to God in general, to a God conceived collectively, but to your own Lord. It marks a radical release of the divine relationship from collective forms, and the emergence of an individual bond between Lord and devoted servant (rabb and marbub), bound up with the sense that spiritual individuality has roots before earthly existence, in eternity itself.

The divine Being manifests itself to the believer in a theophany suited to the particular being that believer has possessed within God from before eternity; in revealing that being, God also reveals Himself to Himself. This is the mystery of spiritual individuation (tafrid): at once the passing away (fana') of the nafs ammara, the domineering soul with its possessive instincts, and enduring, intensified existence (baqa') within God's act of revealing Himself to Himself.

Here lies the key to everything we shall hear about theophany as the resolution, through inward tawhid, of the impasse of abstract monotheism. There is identity within difference between the One who reveals Himself and the one to whom He is revealed.

Among all human experiences there is one, and only one, through which this identity can be lived and truly known: human love for a beautiful person. The form of love in question is not, of course, directed toward a social end, such as founding a family. Through its own discipline, it has freed itself from the possessive bodily impulses of the nafs ammara, whose unchecked force we see at work in outward social life. It is essentially the soul shaken and carried beyond itself by a theophany—by the revelation of divine Beauty in a beautiful human being.

Ibn Arabi taught this devotion to beauty; in Iran it was practiced above all by Ruzbihan and those of his school. Ruzbihan distinguishes the pious worshippers and mystical ascetics (zohhad) for whom human love did not mark the beginning of the spiritual Path7 from those for whom human love was the first step toward divine love: the khawass al-mahabba, whom I have proposed to call the “Faithful of Love,” to bring out their affinity with the Fedeli d'amore of Dante's age.

There is a further point. Inward tawhid affirms an identity: the divine Being is at once love, the lover, and the beloved. Only the experience of human love for a beautiful person can lead us to understand this identity, to make it real within ourselves, because only there, at the furthest perfection of such love, can that identity be lived. This is the point reached by Majnun, the legendary lover, when he knows himself to be Layla. He is so completely absorbed in her image, so entirely inwardly present to her, that when someone asks his name, he answers: “Layla.”

Human Eros and divine love, then, are not opposed. Divine love can be discovered and experienced only through human love. And this is because Layla's beauty is none other than divine Beauty, of which it is a visible manifestation. Her beauty is a sacred sign (ayat), a sacramentum. To reach this summit, of course, everything ordinarily and casually called love must be utterly transfigured. This transfiguration demands a spiritual struggle, a secret personal effort of which pious devotees cannot even conceive: they see nothing in it but “aestheticism.”

Yet it was precisely this transfiguration that all the minstrels of Iran's religion of love affirmed—Ahmad Ghazali, Awhad al-Din Kermani, Fakhr al-Din Iraqi, and so many others. One great figure among them, however, had until now remained almost unknown, together with a body of work long left unpublished: Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz. It is this work, the very image of a life if ever a work deserved that name, whose stages I wish to trace here. Through it, we may understand the distinctively Iranian phenomenon of a mystical religion of human beauty, in which human love initiates the soul into divine love and gives that love the form of an inward, esoteric Islam.

Ruzbihan's own interpretation of our Quranic verse tells us what is at stake. He understands it as a call back to one's origin, addressed to the Holy Spirit that constitutes the spiritual individuality of the human being. It is addressed to the one who, from beginning to end, has turned toward no vision but the vision of God: to the soul content with Him through Him, and therefore pleasing in His sight by virtue of a choice made before eternity8. What makes this Path distinctive, however, is that the vision of God does not require turning away from a created being.

Instead, in the very sight of that being's beauty, one sees divine Beauty directly—not by deduction, but immediately, without intermediary or pause. As a disciple of Ibn Arabi declares in commenting on the same verse, upon one who reaches this state “the Sakina, the Peace, has descended; he has been illuminated by the light of certainty, and in God he has found rest from restlessness9.” Ruzbihan is an outstanding representative of this spiritual path. Perhaps he was the first to express it with such clarity and to gather such testimony to it.

Among Ruzbihan's surviving works is a document of extraordinary visionary richness: a Spiritual Diary, a record of his inner life, his dreams, and his visions10. Almost the only comparable account is one left by the great Central Asian Sufi Najm al-Din Kubra11, or, in the West, Swedenborg's Diarium spirituale. Ruzbihan's doctrinal writings continually return to events recounted in his Spiritual Diary. One might say that this shaykh never advances a teaching that is not grounded in his own experience.

And however strange those experiences may seem, we must beware of speaking of schizophrenia. In mystics of his kind, it is striking how clearly consciousness distinguishes between real events undergone in visionary states and real events undergone while awake. The recurring desire throughout his spiritual life is the longing for vision: the vision denied to Moses but granted to the Prophet of Islam. This is why the Prophet appears to Sufis as the Sayyed-e Ashiqan, the “Prince of the Faithful of Love.”

The gift of such vision is a theophany; but theophany is given only in and through a created being, without the divine becoming incarnate in that being. It enters “as an image enters a mirror.” Ruzbihan will be constantly concerned to dispel the misunderstanding sustained by the hostility, or the inability to understand, of the guardians of legalistic orthodoxy.

A theophany (tajalli) is not an incarnation (holul). The two notions could be brought together only if incarnation were understood as taking the form of the human body, in the full perfection of that form's beauty, rather than assuming its material substance, its “flesh.” This is no doubt what gives so many Sufi statements their “Docetic” quality: they speak of an appearing in human form without a material incarnation.

Yet this view is nothing less than a realism of the spiritual.

Ruzbihan does not hesitate to describe himself as a malamati: one of those Sufis who do not fear the disapproval of official religious conformity, and may even seek it out, wearing blame like a disguise that conceals the purity of their inner face. In this sense Ruzbihan may be regarded as a forerunner of another famous son of Shiraz, one of Iran's greatest mystical poets: Hafez. He even helps us clear up the misunderstandings of Hafez that have arisen in the West. In Iran, Sufis read Hafez's Divan as a mystical Bible.

Yet in the West people have asked whether its words should be taken literally or mystically. Ruzbihan would answer that the question is wrongly framed, because it assumes a choice between denying and accepting a material incarnation. There is another possibility, which he calls by the technical term amphiboly (iltibas): the presence of two meanings at once, which can be mistaken for one another. No theophany takes place without a moment of this ambiguity.

Whoever understands it has found peace. Such a person no longer fears some divine deception, and no longer seeks refuge either in literal faith or in the material certainty of sensory facts. Only one certainty remains: the certainty given by seeing the invisible and hearing the inaudible. Once the secret of their hidden agreement is deciphered, the ambiguity that colors everything in this world proves to be nothing other than the correspondence of all things with one another.

Indeed, our two terms, amphiboly and symbolism, come from the same Greek root.

Chapter II Ruzbihan of Shiraz

Ruzbihan was born in 522/1128 at Fasa (or Pasa), a town some 140 kilometers from Shiraz, in Fars—the region known as Persis, Persia in the strict sense of the name. He died in Shiraz in 606/1209. The sixth century of the Islamic calendar, the twelfth century of the Common Era, nearly coincides with the span of his long life, and is of decisive importance in Iran's spiritual history. Unfortunately, the great events of that history are rarely considered alongside contemporary events in the West.

Our understanding of human cultures still has far to go before we can imagine a comprehensive account of human consciousness that neglects no period and no region. It was in this twelfth century that Suhrawardi revived the philosophy of ancient Iran, its doctrine of Light. It was in 1164, in northwestern Iran, that the proclamation of the Great Resurrection at Alamut established reformed Ismailism as a spiritual Islam, a religion of personal salvation.

Having thus rediscovered the path and meaning of its origins, Ismailism would survive the Mongol upheaval by assuming, without any usurpation, the cloak of Sufism. In Transoxiana, another great spiritual master, Najm al-Din Kubra, gave Sufism a new direction, turning it toward attentive contemplation of the colored lights perceived by the mystic during spiritual states. His school would produce illustrious disciples: Najm al-Din Razi, Aziz al-Din Nasafi, Ala al-Dawla Simnani, and others. In that same century, at Nishapur in Khurasan, Farid al-Din Attar composed his magnificent mystical epics in Persian.

These are the events that help us place Ruzbihan of Shiraz within the spiritual world of his time. He left this world a few years after Ibn Arabi departed his native Andalusia to become, for the rest of his life, a pilgrim in the East, where he spread a mystical philosophy of incomparable power. Ibn Arabi's teaching on love has much in common with Ruzbihan's. We are still far from being able to reconstruct the origins and development of this Sufi spirituality. In any case, that is not our task here.

We are concerned with Ruzbihan's own life, both personal and exemplary. He expresses his experience sometimes in Arabic, sometimes in Persian of remarkable individuality, beauty, and difficulty. His writings disclose the secret of a soul that found peace after confronting the severity of tawhid, the assertion of divine unity, and its double danger. This is the dilemma that haunts Islamic scholastic thought: in trying to avoid assimilating the divine to created beings (tashbih), one may end by reducing God to an abstraction (ta'til).

Only access to inward tawhid can escape that trap. Ruzbihan found such access through a mystical experience pushed to its furthest limit, one that goes beyond the Platonic echoes recognizable in his writings. It goes beyond them because, at its heart, it is a mystical verification of prophetic religion itself. And that verification presupposes a perception of the prophetic meaning of beauty, expressed in one of the favorite sayings of the Sufism of the Faithful of Love: “God is beautiful, and He loves beauty.”

Beauty is not simply one divine Attribute among others. It is the essential Attribute. God Himself is therefore both the source and the reality of Eros, and two ways of desecrating it must be ruled out: the libertinism that profanes love, and the asceticism that denies it, whether through calculation or an ingrained cult of misery.

To follow Ruzbihan's spiritual life, let us recount a few episodes from his extraordinary Diary. It reveals that from childhood he possessed both exceptional emotional sensitivity and an exceptional gift for visions, as though the solid wall separating ordinary humanity from the invisible world had never existed for him. His certainty came from this experience, not from the construction of theories. He knew through experience the presence of gentle and noble beings, beautiful figures, angels, prophets, and saints, in whose company the shaykh of Shiraz lived.

At the center—or summit—of all this stood the repeated vision of the One who is by nature forever invisible: the One who refused Himself to Moses, yet of whom the Prophet of Islam could testify, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms12.” This paradox is affirmed and lived throughout Ruzbihan's experience, for love in its fullest sense can be directed only toward a being with a distinct personhood and face.

God, loved in this way, must take on the form of the eternal Companion, the “Witness in Heaven.” (Here, as so often, Sufism recreates a teaching about the Imam without naming it.) To discover inward tawhid is precisely to resolve a contradiction that philosophy or theology, when it thinks only in terms of objects, cannot overcome: the contradiction between God's transcendence beyond all personhood and these personal manifestations, each suited to the soul that loves. The solution is the very secret of theophanies, and initiation into that secret is nothing other than initiation into the divine mystery of love. For that mystery is the identity of love, lover, and beloved.

Ruzbihan wrote his Spiritual Diary at a friend's request. He was then fifty-five years old13; the mysterious experiences, he tells us, had begun when he was fifteen. The interval is long, but he tries to recover his memories as closely as possible. He writes: “I was born among ignorant people, people lost in drunkenness and error, coarse and vulgar, like startled donkeys fleeing from a lion (Quran 74:51).

“I had reached the age of three when this question arose in my heart: Where is your God, and the God of all creatures? There was a mosque beside the entrance to our house. One day I saw some young boys and asked them: Do you know your God? They answered: People say He has neither feet nor hands. They had heard their parents say that God Most High has no limbs or bodily organs.

“After asking this question, I was overwhelmed with emotion and began to run. Something happened to me like the sudden flashes that come from remembering, or the unexpected glimpses that open up in meditation; in truth, I did not understand what was happening.” Perhaps we can begin to understand it.

On one side stood abstract monotheism and the philosophy of rational theism, united in affirming a divinity beyond all forms, descriptions, and personal attributes. On the other stood a young mystic who already sensed that the eternal Beloved could not be without a face—a face whose secret, once revealed and once it had shaken him to the depths, he would have to conceal with reverence.

“From the age of seven,” Ruzbihan continues, “my heart fell in love with the practice of dhikr”—the remembrance of God—“and with devotion. I began to seek my secret (sirr)14 and to learn its ways. Then passionate love (ishq) blossomed in my heart, and I felt my heart melt in that love. Throughout this time I lived in deep longing, for even then my heart had plunged into the ocean of remembrance of my eternal pre-existence and into the fragrance of the heavenly world.

“Later, sudden intuitions of fleeting ecstasies began to flower within me. There was no physical trembling, though a certain sweetness filled my heart, while tears streamed from my eyes... I saw every being as a beautiful face; and as they appeared to me in this way, I felt drawn toward particular kinds of retreat, toward intimate prayers (monajat), acts of devotion, and pious visits to the tombs of the most eminent Sufi shaykhs.”

Then came the event of adolescence that would determine the course of his whole life. Ruzbihan was fifteen. Seeing all beings as beautiful faces already shows us the quality that will dominate his mature inner life.

But another feature reveals the Sufi's deepest aspiration: a vocation to the prophetic state, the state of the nabi, or prophet. The adolescent hears an inward voice assuring him of this calling. He resists: it seems to him that the physical weaknesses of ordinary humanity cannot be reconciled with the state of a prophet. Besides, has he not been taught that there will be no prophet after Muhammad? Certainly.

But is Muhammad's heavenly ascent not the model for the experience the mystic seeks to repeat? And is the spiritual interpretation of the Quran not a continual renewal of prophetic interpretation? This problem, which arose and was resolved within Islam through Shiism itself, also lies at the heart of Sufism. That is why, in practice, a study of religious experience should never treat these two spiritual traditions in isolation15.

One evening after supper, the young Ruzbihan, who until then had kept a small shop in Shiraz, rises from his place of business and makes his way toward a familiar spot in the nearby desert. Suddenly he hears a gentle voice calling him. He climbs a hill and finds himself before a person of extraordinary beauty, with the appearance of a Sufi shaykh, who says a few words to him about tawhid.

Ruzbihan cannot speak. He barely understands, and is carried beyond his senses. When he comes to himself, part of the night has passed. He returns home, where he remains until morning overcome by emotion and unrest, sighing and weeping. “I was astonished and shaken,” he writes. “Without my willing it, my tongue kept saying: Your forgiveness! Your forgiveness! Then it subsided. It seemed to me that it had lasted for hours and hours. I waited another hour.

“Finally my emotion grew so violent that I threw aside my cashbox and gathered everything in the shop into a bundle. I tore my clothes and went out into the desert. I remained in that state for a year and a half, longing, astonished, weeping, swept away by emotion. Every day brought magnificent visions of ecstasy and sudden visitations from the invisible worlds. During these visions, the heavens and the earth, mountains, deserts, plants—everything appeared to me as pure light. Afterward, I came to know a certain peace.”

We should notice the defining feature of these first events, lived at the threshold of consciousness beyond the ordinary. Just as the universe begins to appear to the adolescent transfigured into beautiful faces, his first personal encounter with a beautiful messenger from the invisible world comes as a shock centered on tawhid, the declaration of monotheistic faith. At first Ruzbihan does not understand what he is told; his later life and teachings will explain it to us.

What is at stake is the very secret of theophanies: how the unity affirmed by tawhid multiplies itself in each of its manifestations while remaining one (1 × 1), and how uncreated Beauty can be seen only in the beautiful faces through which it appears. Through this secret, the “soul at peace” makes “its return to its Lord.” The visions that follow in the Spiritual Diary mark the first stages of his initiation into that return.

At the same time they reveal the archetypal figures that shape the consciousness of an Iranian Sufi. “I remember this, too,” Ruzbihan writes. “I was on the roof terrace of my house when I saw God in the attribute of might and majesty. The whole universe appeared to me as a vast, teeming, brilliant light. Then, from the center of that light, He called to me seven times in Persian: O Ruzbihan!

“I have chosen you for the station of My Friend (walayat); I have chosen you for love. You are My friend, one who loves Me. Give way neither to fear nor to sorrow, for I am your God, and I watch over you in everything you undertake.”

Another event then appears, like a genuine ordeal of initiation lived in a visionary state. “This time it seemed in my vision that I was on the Mountain of the East, and I saw a whole company of angels there. From East to West stretched an immense sea; I could see nothing else. The angels said to me: Enter this sea and swim toward the West. I entered the sea and began to swim.

“When I reached the place where the sun sets, at the hour of its decline... I saw a company of angels on the Mountain of the West, lit by the setting sun. They cried to me: You, over there! Swim on, and do not be afraid. When at last I reached the mountain, they said: No one has crossed this sea except Ali ibn Abi Talib, and you after him.”

Two things stand out in these visionary events of initiation.

First there is the double reference: to walayat, originally a Shiite idea, and to the First Imam of Shiism, who appears here as the exemplary hero of the young initiate. Then there is the setting of the vision itself. The perilous journey toward the setting sun, into the region of Darkness, belongs to the great theme of the Quest for the Source of Life. Two archetypal figures dominate the legend: Alexander and Khizr (Khezr, or Khadir), who is sometimes paired with the prophet Elijah and sometimes identified with him.

Khizr reaches the Source of Life; whoever, like him, succeeds in finding light in the region of Darkness is a disciple of Khizr. Suhrawardi's mystical tales have already introduced us to this figure and his role (see above, Book II, Chapter V). We should add that Khizr's role, and his superiority to the lawgiving prophets—he is Moses' initiator—remain incomprehensible apart from Shiite teachings about prophecy and walayat. Some Shiites have even identified him with the “Hidden Imam.”

Hence his extraordinary role in Sufism. He is the master of all those who receive their initiation directly from him, without contact with any human master and independently of any historical chain of initiation passing through successive generations of a tariqa. He is the master of those who have no outward master: those known in Shiism as the Uwaysis. To be a disciple of Khizr, as so many Sufis have been—and as Suhrawardi teaches in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel—is to become what Khizr became and to do what he did.

Through him, a Sufi receives a direct connection to the heavenly world and its invisible hierarchies, an initiation whose authority and meaning transcend history because they do not depend on the succession of human generations in earthly time16. In the deepest sense of the Quest, this is the return of the soul at peace: the attainment of one's own true being, of the divine counterpart of oneself, of which Khizr is one of the great symbols.

Two further visions lead Ruzbihan first to Khizr himself and then to two shaykhs who are the very “image” of the mystical pilgrim and reveal to him the inward rank he has now attained. Having reached the region of Darkness near the “pole,” Ruzbihan, like Khizr, discovers light there—the vision of angels blazing in the light of the setting sun—and finds the Source of Life in the form of luminous water.

Here the initiation received directly from Khizr does not take the form of bestowing the khirqa, the Sufi cloak, as it does in the stories of other Sufis. Instead, it takes the form of eating a fruit. “At that time I knew nothing of the higher sciences of divine wisdom, and then I saw Khizr. He gave me an apple, and I ate part of it.

“Eat it all, he said to me; that is how much I ate. Then it seemed to me that from the Throne to the Pleiades there stretched an immense sea, and I could see nothing else. It was like the radiance of the sun. My mouth opened against my will, and all the contents of that sea of light poured into it. Not a single drop remained that I had not swallowed.”

The next vision completes this stage of initiation. Its symbolic figures express with extraordinary eloquence the fullness of spiritual life Ruzbihan has reached. The whole of creation appears to him enclosed within a house.

Many lamps shed brilliant light inside it, but a wall prevents him from reaching them. He climbs onto the roof terrace of his own house, where he finds two figures of great beauty in whom he recognizes his own image. (We could hardly wish for a clearer illustration of the theme of the image, the heavenly alter ego, developed earlier in connection with the “history” of the seeker of spiritual knowledge: Book II, Chapter VI, sections 1 and 4.) The two figures look like Sufis and smile at him with affection.

The visionary notices a hanging cooking pot. Beneath it burns a subtle, pure, smokeless fire, fed by fragrant herbs. One of the figures then unfolds a cloth, bringing to light a graceful bowl and several loaves of pure wheat bread. He breaks one of the loaves into the bowl and pours over it the contents of the pot: an oil so subtle that it seems to be made of spiritual substance.

The three then share what is almost a meal of communion. “One of them said to me: Do you know what was in the pot? No, I said, I do not. It was oil from the Great Bear, which we had gathered for you. When I came out of my vision, I pondered this, but only after some time did I understand that it referred to the seven poles in the heavenly realm (malakut).

“God had granted me the pure substance of their mystical rank: the rank of the Seven, who are invisibly distributed over the face of the earth. Then I turned my attention toward the Great Bear, and I saw that it formed seven openings through which, all together, God showed Himself (tajalli) to me. My God, I cried, what is this? He answered: These are the seven openings of the Throne.”

Ruzbihan, a disciple of Khizr, now knows that he has taken his place among the seven Abdal, at the summit of the mysterious, invisible hierarchy surrounding the “Pole,” the “Hidden Imam” of the age, without whom earthly life could not continue. The idea of such hierarchies, apparently linked in its origins to an esoteric astrology, pervades the spiritual philosophy of Sufism. It seems so closely bound up with Shiite spiritual knowledge itself that it has again assumed a fundamental role in more recent times, within Shaykhism.

For Ruzbihan, too, this experience of initiation is so decisive that, as he goes on to recount, “every night thereafter I continued watching those openings in the heavens, driven by my love and ardent longing. Then one night I saw that they were open, and I saw God manifesting Himself to me through them. He said: I manifest Myself to you through these openings; they form seven thousand thresholds leading to the threshold of the angelic realm (malakut). And see: I show Myself to you through them all at once.”

“Through them all at once.” In other passages of Ruzbihan's Diary we shall see that here lies the secret of the meeting of unity and multiplicity. Whoever is allowed to penetrate the secret of theophanies understands what the masters mean by the “ordeal of the Veil.” To overcome that ordeal is to hold one's gaze steady, as the Prophet did at his vision by the “lotus tree of the utmost boundary” (53:17): when faced with each theophany, the gaze neither turns aside nor oversteps its limit. These few autobiographical glimpses are enough to suggest the spiritual character of the great mystic of Shiraz.
