As we have described the outward circumstances of his life more fully elsewhere, we shall only mention them here: the shaykhs from whom he later received his theological education; his journeys through Iran and Iraq and to Mecca; the crowds of disciples who came from all directions to be initiated by him into the Sufism of the Faithful of Love; and the part played by the khanqah, the Sufi lodge he founded in Shiraz, in the spiritual and social life of southwestern Iran—not only in the shaykh's lifetime, but through his descendants for several generations17.

We should nevertheless recount two further episodes that reveal something essential about Ruzbihan himself. It is said that on the day he first took up his duties as a preacher at the mosque in Shiraz, he was passing through the crowd on his way to the pulpit when he heard a mother advise her daughter: “My daughter, keep your veil on. Show your beauty to no one, lest it afterward be despised.” Shaykh Ruzbihan stopped and said: “O woman!

“Beauty cannot bear to be shut away in solitude. Its whole desire is to be joined with love, for from before eternity Beauty and Love exchanged a promise never to part.” (Their separation, as we may recall, supplied the dramatic impulse of Suhrawardi's Vade Mecum of the Faithful of Love; see above, Book II, Chapter VII, section 3.) The later pages of Ruzbihan's Spiritual Diary show him living in familiar intimacy with faces of heavenly beauty. The words he uses to describe them will reappear when he tells us how the faces of earthly beauty look to him.

Another episode reveals the private anguish that every vision of beauty awakens in Ruzbihan's heart: the meeting of attainment with the unattainable; the vision withheld within the vision granted; absence tasted in presence; the longing for something still beyond, even within the peace sometimes tasted here below. Moment after moment, through this coexistence of opposites, the soul makes its Return, and there is no respite.

Ruzbihan himself speaks of this during his final illness. He had been struck by a form of paralysis affecting one side of his body. Far from wanting to cure it, he seemed almost to wish the illness would grow worse. Without telling him, one of his disciples traveled to Cairo and obtained from the royal treasury a quantity of balm intended to heal the shaykh. When the disciple returned to Shiraz and presented himself before Ruzbihan, he heard these words: “My child, may God reward your good intentions!

“But now, go to the gate of the khanqah. A poor mangy dog lies there. Rub this balm on him; perhaps it will do him some good.

“But know that Ruzbihan's suffering is not the kind that can be eased with a balm from this world. It is one of the chains of love that God has fastened around his foot, and there it will remain until he reaches the happiness of meeting Him.”

It was only natural that someone so deeply moved by feeling should also be a musician, and should embrace the practice of the spiritual concert, or sama', which many other Sufis regarded with suspicion. Ruzbihan was an ardent practitioner until the last years of his life.

But then he no longer needed the mediation of audible sounds: what cannot be heard began to make itself heard within him as pure inner music. He gave this explanation to a friend who asked why he had stopped attending the gatherings: “From now on,” he said, “it is God Himself, in person, who is the oratorio I listen to. I refrain from listening to any other music but Him.”

It was as though Ruzbihan could even, beyond the grave, share with one of his dearest friends and disciples the gathering of voices beyond the senses that he heard within the oratorio of his soul. That disciple, Shaykh Abu Bakr ibn Taher Hafez, was especially inconsolable after Ruzbihan's departure. He himself tells this story: “Every morning at dawn, Shaykh Ruzbihan and I would take turns reciting the Quran aloud. He would chant about ten verses, and I would chant the next ten. When he had gone, I felt trapped in an anguish of grief.

“Toward the end of the night I would rise and perform the Prayer. Then I would go and sit beside his grave, and there I would begin chanting the Quran, my tears flowing as I suffered the pain of being left alone, separated from him. One morning, suddenly, I heard the shaykh's voice. It seemed to rise from the grave; and there it was, chanting the verses of the Book with me, ten at a time, as we had always done. This continued until the Companions gathered, and then the voice stopped.

“But the same thing happened on the following days, and so it went on for some time. Then one day I told a friend about it. From that day onward, I never heard the shaykh's voice again...”

PreviousI. Sufism and the Peace of the SoulNextIII. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Chapter III The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

We can begin to understand the suffering Rûzbehân spoke of when he told his over-devoted disciple that it was not among the pains “that can be soothed with a balm from this world.”

The key lies in a short treatise that sets out the ideas we need in order to understand another of his works, devoted entirely to the transformation of human love into divine love. This transformation takes place not so much in the beloved as in the lover. It is a change in the way one sees, and it opens the way to tawhîd in its esoteric sense: the inward realization of divine unity.

Rûzbehân called the short treatise “An Explanation of the Veils and Screens in the Spiritual Dwelling Places of the Mystics,” or simply the “Book of the Clouding.”18 Its inspiration came one night when he awoke and heard, within his heart, a summons from the divine Friend. He was to write about the hidden meaning of the Veils that come between the Friend and those devoted to Him: the stages of their mystical journey, the spiritual states through which they pass, and the divine Attributes that appear to them as manifestations of light. His purpose was to warn them of the snares and dangers along the way, and to help them perceive and recognize the miracle quietly taking place within themselves.

Rûzbehân takes as his guiding theme a saying attributed to the Prophet: “A cloud passes over my heart; indeed, I ask God's forgiveness for it seventy times a day.” A second saying explains the first: “For prophets and the friends of God (Awliyâ), there is a clouding of the innermost consciousness (sirr, the ‘secret’) and a veiling of the lights. This is the ordeal through which God makes them pass”—the ordeal of the Veil.

In some forty pages of extraordinary intensity, Rûzbehân's meditation produces something like a theosophy of Spirit, a wisdom concerned with divine reality. In our own vocabulary we might call it a phenomenology of Spirit, provided we do not import our modern “sense of history” into it. What matters here is its understanding of Spirit, centered entirely on its understanding of prophecy.

As in much Sufi theosophy, Rûzbehân begins his account of creation with a famous tradition in which the Divine Being declares that He was a Hidden Treasure longing to be known, and that He brought creation into existence in order to be known and to know Himself in His creatures.19

The first reality in Rûzbehân's account is neither the First Intellect of the philosophers who followed Avicenna, nor Nafas al-Rahmân, the Breath of the Compassionate, as in Ibn ‘Arabî. It is Spirit. Through the primordial bringing-into-being of Spirit, all the “Holy Spirits” subsist: the spiritual individualities that have existed from before time, the beings who make up the “offspring of the most sacred Light.”

To these Holy Spirits the primordial divine Light made itself known in a mysterious scene beyond the beginning of time. Through them, the Light put a question to itself: “Am I not your Lord?” And they answered with one voice. It was for these Holy Spirits that the Veils were created, to become their ordeal. Their descent into earthly life, the mission for which they are sent here, has no other purpose than to lead them through that ordeal to victory.

But if the ordeal of the Veil contains the very meaning of creation, it also betrays a hidden anguish within God Himself.

The first veil is simply the condition of these Holy Spirits as beings.

We must not imagine a sequence of events measured by ordinary time, yet we have to say that “at first” they did not exist, and “then” they were called into being. Rûzbehân shares here a premise of the Avicennian philosophers: beings do not possess within themselves what is needed to exist. Only the One possesses, in Himself, all that is needed to be what He is.

“I am not saying,” Rûzbehân writes, “that nonbeing is something. I am saying that the eternal priority of their nonbeing”—a priority that is therefore eternally present—“is, for that subtle reality (latîfa) which is Spirit, the first of the Veils.” From this Veil, we might say, all the others arise. It is the source of every misunderstanding about who truly acts whenever anything comes into being. Here, then, is the very origin of the ordeal of the Veil.

Rûzbehân now offers an extraordinary insight. Every distinct particle of being within the subtle reality of primordial Spirit comes into existence through a divine self-disclosure, a theophany that reveals one of God's Attributes—as though God, in an ecstasy of love, were revealing Himself to Himself.

Thus every particle of being is an eye (‘ayn) opened by His light, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it came.

But now God experiences jealousy toward Himself. By making Himself visible to Himself, by revealing Himself, He is no longer simply His own witness. There is a Witness (shâhid) “outside” Him, someone “other” than Himself. In this jealousy, as though seeking to reclaim Himself from Himself, God turns the eye of Spirit—His first subtle creation—away from contemplating Him, and directs the creature instead toward contemplating itself. “Then it contemplated itself and became absent [or was hidden, ghaybat] from the contemplation of the original Being. And this vision of itself by itself became its second Veil.”

The second Veil thus grows out of the first: the very fact of being a creature. Here the crucial idea of the “witness of contemplation” (shâhid; see Chapter V below) begins to take shape.

We can already see that being sent back to self-knowledge is the ordeal above all others. One emerges victorious only when the famous saying has become a truth verified in one's own experience: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” Victory will put an end to the divine jealousy of love, which meanwhile sets the worlds in motion. God wants to be known by a Witness, but that Witness can be none other than Himself. To recognize this identity, the Witness must undergo the same ordeal again and again.

Divine jealousy tries to lead him astray, to make him turn his gaze away from God and toward himself as though toward something separate, forgetting that, if he witnesses the divine acts of contemplation, it is because he is the very “eye” through which God contemplates Himself. That is why the Divine Being reveals Himself through His supreme Attribute, Beauty.

He brings forth the invisible worlds, the worlds of mystery, and appears within them in Adamic form, as the heavenly Human Being. He brings forth the worlds of becoming, then the microcosm of earthly humanity, with its subtle spiritual physiology centered on the heart, and finally the bodily and psychic organs, with their inner and outer senses. Each stage, each field of perception opening before its corresponding faculty, becomes a Veil for Spirit as it descends from one level to the next.

Each offers a fresh temptation to “look away” from the true object of contemplation and desire. And when Spirit, during its earthly journey, begins to ascend and return to its origin, each new station or spiritual dwelling place (maqâmât) raises another veil between it and its true goal. Here Rûzbehân shows the psychological insight of the greatest spiritual masters. In the end he identifies seventy Veils, thereby suggesting an explanation for the Prophet's words: “A cloud passes over my heart; I ask God's forgiveness for it seventy times a day.”

In Rûzbehân's language, divine jealousy as the cause of the heart's clouding means this: God can be reached only through His revelations, His theophanies.

Yet when those theophanies are perceived by a gaze other than His own—a gaze conscious of itself as separate—they become something other than Him. And this, with consequences of immeasurable importance, is precisely what outward tawhîd does: the monotheism of official religion, of Islam understood only in its literal sense.

For the Sufi, monotheism amounts to the worst kind of metaphysical idolatry so long as the believer has not attained the mystic's awareness: the knowledge that one's own gaze is the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, and one's own testimony the testimony through which He bears witness to Himself.

Unfortunately, official theologians call this monism or pantheism. Whatever their misunderstanding, the theophany remains both a veil and an ordeal. God appears as though to turn our attention away from Him; we then seek Him beyond the Veil, until we experience what Rûzbehân calls the “madness of the unattainable.”

But we triumph over the ordeal when the veil has become a mirror. Then we must look into that mirror, and nowhere else, because what it reveals is visible nowhere else. The contradiction is overcome. The theophany, the beautiful face, does not draw us away from uncreated Beauty, for it reveals that Beauty. The mystic follows the Prophet's example: “His gaze neither swerved nor overstepped” (53:17). He neither swerves by looking at the mirror without seeing what appears within it, nor oversteps by seeking elsewhere what wishes to reveal itself here.

The secret of this transformation lies in a transfer of the Witness's act of witnessing, a reversal of roles. When the creature withdraws—or rather, becomes transparent—it is no longer simply a creature looking at God. In and through the creature's gaze, God Himself looks at Himself. Once we grasp this, we already have some idea of what Rûzbehân's religion of love will mean: a love that answers God's self-disclosure through Beauty.

But this is very far from the ordinary state of human consciousness. Most people do not even suspect that there is an ordeal of the Veil. The Veil itself, a blind unawareness, is their accepted “normal” condition. In this way they complete God's estrangement from Himself. To enter into the secret, we must turn to the heart of creation, where we see how completely this understanding of Spirit is centered on prophecy.

Here we encounter the idea of a mystical hierarchy: initiates invisibly dispersed throughout the earth and other worlds. The sources of this idea, and its place in Sufism, still call for much further research. We already know, from the vision that led Rûzbehân to reflect on the hidden meaning of the seven stars of the Great Bear, that he considered himself one of the seven Abdâl of his age.

The highest members of this mysterious hierarchy are those who have triumphed over the ordeal of the Veil. This helps us understand what esoteric theosophy means when it says that the earthly world continues to exist through them, and that without them it could not endure for even an instant.

The acts of creation are divine gazes, divine contemplations (nazarât). This is why we have just read that every particle of being emerging as an individual within the divine Light is an eye (‘ayn) through which that Light contemplates itself. These acts of contemplation bring forth every order of creation, from the angels who bear the Throne to Adam, who is “the eye in which all is gathered” (‘ayn al-jam‘), because all the divine Gazes converge in the Adamic form. Creation, understood as divine contemplation, is not an object separate from the act of contemplating.

Rather, it is the very organ through which contemplation takes place. Every created being is thus a divine eye: nothing can become visible without an organ of sight. In this sense every creature, as a divine eye, is a theophany (tajallî), a manifestation of God. From Adam, the first prophet and a complete theophany, the divine gaze is divided and reflected anew, from Messenger (Rasûl) to Messenger, from prophet (Nabî) to prophet, from friend of God (Walî) to friend of God.

At every period in the cycle of prophecy, there are always 360 persons on earth upon whom the divine Gaze rests (mawâqi‘ al-nazar). They are at the same time the eyes through which God contemplates His creatures and contemplates Himself within them. This also means that they are the eyes through which God makes Himself visible to His creatures.

Notice, in passing, that we have arrived at an essential Shiite idea: the Imam as the Face through which God looks upon humanity and, at the same time, the Face through which humanity looks upon God.20

We can see how, in Sunni Sufism, the person of the Imam disappears, yet the place he occupied remains unmistakably marked. Speaking of the “Earth's lament,” Rûzbehân writes: “After our Prophet's death, the Earth complained to God: ‘My God! The prophets and Messengers have passed away. Will no nabî ever again walk upon my soil? Yet I cannot remain without them.’ And God said to her: ‘By My might and My glory!

“For every nabî and every Messenger (rasûl), I shall create for you a protecting Friend (Walî), until the Day of Resurrection.’”21 Is this not precisely the Shiite idea that every prophet is succeeded by his Imam? After the mission of the last Prophet brought the “cycle of prophecy” to its close, the “cycle of walâyat”—the spiritual guardianship of God's friends—began. Each of the friends of God in this latter cycle occupies a rank corresponding to that of a prophet in the earlier cycle.

Where could the idea of this protecting Friend, who succeeds the Prophet until the Resurrection, have come from, if not from the Shiite understanding of the Imam? The Imam is the keystone of the mystical hierarchy Rûzbehân now describes: the beings who, generation after generation, are the eyes through which God looks upon the world and through which the world looks upon God.

In these mysterious figures, the innermost heart of each being corresponds to the heart of the theophany of the divine Names, Attributes, and Essence. They are at once the eyes through which God appears to His creatures and those through which He contemplates them. They are like a mirror struck by sunlight, reflecting that light outward upon this world and other worlds.

“God possesses on Earth three hundred eyes, or persons (‘ayn), whose hearts correspond to Adam's heart; forty whose hearts correspond to Moses' heart; seven whose hearts correspond to Abraham's heart; five whose hearts correspond to Gabriel's heart; three whose hearts correspond to Michael's heart; and one whose heart corresponds to Seraphiel's heart.”22

That solitary one, whose heart corresponds to Seraphiel's, is the mystical pole of the world. Once again, how can we fail to recognize here the spiritual rank that Shiism assigns to the Imam—now the “Hidden Imam,” the “Seal of Muhammadan walâyat”? Are we not confronted, inevitably, with an “Imamology that dares not speak its name”?

On the other hand, transferring the Imam's prerogative to someone else dislocates not only the whole structure of the doctrine of the Imam, but the structure of the doctrine of prophecy as well. This is one reason why Shiism, as the esoteric dimension of Islam, has reservations about certain forms of Sufism.

Yet it is true that one of Rûzbehân's visions, discussed earlier, explicitly names the First Imam as the source of walâyat.

We have already spoken several times of the mystical hierarchy itself, and shall return to it again (see Book I above). The details of its ranks vary considerably; this is not the place to attempt a comprehensive account. We need only note that the hadîth just quoted by Rûzbehân—which itself exists in different versions—lists a total of 356 persons. Four further figures are ordinarily added: Christ, Khezr, Elijah, and Idris (Enoch, identified with Hermes).

This brings the number to 360. Each of these 360 persons represents, or corresponds to, one of the 360 divine Names. Every Name is rooted in an Attribute of the divine Essence; it is also the proper name of a divine activity, the act of self-disclosure that reveals that Attribute as a created being, an eye through which God contemplates Himself or contemplates that Attribute.

The number 360 is also connected with the image of the celestial sphere divided into 360 degrees, by which the full cycle of day and night is measured. Likewise, according to a saying attributed to the Prophet, “Every day and every night God casts 360 gazes. With each gaze He creates and provides, gives life and gives death, takes away the means of being and grants the means to sustain existence.

“Every gaze, at every hour of day and night, is directed toward an eye among His eyes”—God looks upon His own eyes—“and not toward the profane world (donyâ, the world whose eyes are turned only upon itself). For that world God has never looked upon since Creation, holding it in abhorrence.” In other words, that world has never looked toward Him, and so could not become the divine gaze that would look upon it. At most, the world declares that God “does not look at it”—meaning that God is no concern of its own.23

Thus God looks upon the world through beings unknown to the unseeing mass of humanity. As His creatures, they are the eyes through which God contemplates Himself; equally, they are the eyes through which His creation contemplates Him. They are the eyes of their age. Adam, for example, was the eye of his age (‘ayn zamânihi), the theophany of his time.

At the heart of this teaching we find the remarkable persistence of a single fundamental insight, appearing again and again among mystics as different as Rûzbehân and Meister Eckhart. Eckhart expresses it in his celebrated formula: the eye with which I know God is the very eye with which God knows me.

This is what it means for a creature to be God's eye. It is the secret of the theophanies that fill Rûzbehân's life, and the secret by which the mystic triumphs over the ordeal of the Veil: he resolves the ambiguity inherent in everything that becomes manifest. Recognizing his own existence as the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, he becomes the organ through which God looks upon the world at every hour of day and night. This is why we have spoken here of a phenomenology of Spirit.

For if that gaze were to close, if those beings who are the divine Gaze through which God knows the world ceased to exist, the world itself would collapse. This is what all the Sufi theosophers mean when they say that without the complete company of these beings—unknown to the multitude, sustained by their “pole,” whom Shiites identify with the Hidden Imam—earthly life could not continue for a single instant.

Something far greater is at stake than any “social role” our age might still be willing to acknowledge in people of the spirit. This is a function of cosmic salvation. Each mystic, over the course of a spiritual life, becomes connected with one or another of these mysterious figures, as do the disciples of Khezr. Through that figure, and by becoming like him, the mystic becomes the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, His witness of contemplation.

Yet Rûzbehân gives us no grounds for thinking that victory over the ordeal of the Veil confers lasting security. The divine Essence must remain forever inaccessible: it can be approached only through the theophanies at the different levels of existence, and through the beings who are their eyes. There is a Veil for the Angel to overcome, a Veil for the prophets, a Veil for the Awliyâ, a Veil for each rank of the mystical hierarchy, for every degree of spiritual attainment, for every step along the Way. Here too Rûzbehân's analysis is remarkably penetrating.

In short, the Veil in every case is the act of looking away from what the theophany reveals, and attending instead to the one who sees it, considered in isolation, and to that person's own experiences. It is the temptation to settle into a state of repose whose effect would be the opposite of the command, “O soul at peace, return to your Lord.”

As Abû Yazîd Bastâmî says, even the sweetness of love, the purity of devotion, and spiritual gifts themselves can become a Veil. The creature becomes opaque when it stops at its own nonbeing—the nothingness of its pretensions and ignorance. The world loses its transparency and sets itself up as an Other facing God, an Other upon which not even God can look. Rûzbehân returns to the point with striking insistence.

God has never looked at this world devoid of transparency since its creation, for He can look only upon His own eyes, which look toward Him. How then could He see this world, when it has no eyes and does not see Him? But no spiritual rank is exempt from the ordeal of the Veil. Every prophet has encountered it, endured it, and overcome it in his own way. Each Veil, each ordeal, corresponds to a particular spiritual station or dwelling place.

What is a veil for the advanced mystic may be the furthest point a beginner (morîd) can possibly reach.

An incident involving a disciple of Abû Torâb Najashî makes this clear. The disciple was a young man with an exceptional capacity for ecstasy and a high spiritual state. He laid claim to numerous spiritual stations (maqâmât) and states of mystical experience (ahwâl). Again and again his master would say to him, “My friend, if only you could see Abû Yazîd Bastâmî!” One day the disciple lost his temper.

“I see the God of Abû Yazîd,” he declared. “I have no need of Abû Yazîd.” His master replied, “Poor boy! You see God with your own eye. If you saw Abû Yazîd, you would see God with Abû Yazîd's eye.” The disciple was astonished. “You are right!” he said. “Get up, and let us go to him.” The master rose, and they set out to find Abû Yazîd.

When they reached him, Abû Yazîd was just emerging from a grove, wearing a fur coat turned inside out. The young man looked at him, cried out, and fell lifeless to the ground. Abû Yazîd gently shook him and said in Persian, “Poor child! You could not bear to see God!” Abû Torâb asked him, “My lord, does everyone who sees you die?” “Certainly not,” Abû Yazîd answered.

“But there was a secret within your disciple, and that secret had not revealed itself to him as he wished. When he saw me, it was disclosed to him; he could not bear it, and he died, because he was weak.”

The story, whose mysterious psychology is somewhat illuminated by what we have just discussed, teaches us how dangerous mystical experience can be when the many different degrees and paths are ignored. Because the mystic's contemplation is itself the act by which God contemplates him, it would be perilous—or rather, impossible—for one person to force another into the same form or the same level of contemplation.

Curiously, we can again see in this story a transformation of the Shiite idea of the Imam, who, as Imam, is the shâhid, the Witness through whom God looks and through whom the mystic looks upon his God, within God's own gaze upon him. Here, in the absence of the Imam, Abû Yazîd took his place.

But the young disciple died of it.

Finally, a visionary account handed down by the celebrated Sufi of Baghdad, Jonayd (originally from Nehâvand in Iran, tenth century), shows us in the language of actual spiritual experience how creation as the “eye of God” is bound up with the ordeal of the Veil, and what it means, in a theophany, for the gaze “not to swerve.” The central figure is Jonayd's own master, the equally renowned Sufi Sarî al-Saqatî. One day Jonayd was with him in the company of several friends when the master suddenly passed into ecstasy.24

When he came to himself, he was surrounded by a light so intense that it dazzled everyone around him. Then he began to tell them what had happened. He had been snatched away from the circle of his friends and carried upward from heaven to heaven. He had passed through Veils of dazzling light: first the Veil of Beauty, then the Veil of Majesty, then the Veil of Condensation (motakâthifa, whose nature he could not describe), and finally the Veil of Power.

There, overcome with awe and filled with both fear and longing, he understood that he stood before the Divine Being. From behind that Veil came a call: “O Sarî!” At the sound of the voice he felt as though his limbs were breaking and his joints coming apart.

But God “gathered him together” and addressed him a second time: “O Sarî! Do you know how My creation exists together with Me (kayfa khalqî ma‘î)?” The divine Voice then recalled the mysterious scene of the covenant made before time, which we encountered earlier: “Am I not your Lord?” To the Spirits who had acclaimed Him, God showed the grace and beauty of the earthly world.

Nine-tenths went toward it; one-tenth remained. To those who remained, God showed paradise with all its delights and joys. Nine-tenths chose it; one-tenth remained. To these God then showed hell with all its torments and humiliations. Nine-tenths fled; one-tenth remained. The successive tests continued. Each time, of those who had persevered, nine-tenths fell away.

God subjected them to the ordeal of Experience, under which nine-tenths were broken; to the ordeal of love, before which nine-tenths took fright; to the Veil of Nearness, in whose light nine-tenths were consumed; and to the Veil of overwhelming Majesty (hayba, the tremendum), beneath which nine-tenths were submerged. After these seven ordeals, each leaving only a tenth of those who had survived the last, God revealed the Veil of Power to the final remnant. They stood before it, amazed and stunned.

At this point the divine account, which Sarî heard spoken in the first person during his ecstasy, takes on a dramatic force in which the whole experience of these Sufis reaches its height: “I called to them, congratulated them, and clothed them in the lights of Power. ‘O My faithful ones!’ I said. They answered: ‘Here we are, our Lord, our Prince!’

“I said: ‘I showed you the earthly world. Some went toward it, but you remained. I showed you paradise. Some chose it, but you remained. I showed you hell. Some fled, but you remained. I tested you with the Ordeal. Some were broken, but you were not. I revealed to you the ordeal of love. Some were afraid, but you did not turn away.

“I lifted for you the Veil of Nearness. Some grew proud, but I kept you tranquil. I lifted for you the Veil of overwhelming Majesty. Some went beyond it, but you came to a halt. I lifted for you the Veil of Power, and you remained before it, astonished and dazzled, for I had made you steadfast. What, then, do you want? What are you seeking?’

“‘We want only You. We seek nothing but You. You are our goal.’ ‘O My faithful ones! You are exposing yourselves to the ordeal that has destroyed countless others before you, world after world, more than anyone but I can number, before the time of your father Adam, from age upon age and into eternity upon eternity. Torment was foretold for them.

“Only those who know have knowledge of it. Between Me and you there lies one of My torments, which no one can endure, a torment that grows ever more intense. The hardest rock could not bear it, nor can human beings withstand it.’ ‘Our Prince, our Lord! Is it You Yourself who will lay this torment upon us?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘That is enough for us.’

“Then I said to them: ‘Now I know that you are the sincere ones, true in the very truth of your seeking. Now I set you free: I make you the vessels of My Knowledge, the dwelling places of My secret.25 It is through Me that you speak; you are those who call others toward Me.26

“I am yours and you are Mine. I share My secrets with you and you share your secrets with Me. You are the initiates into the mysteries, the intimate companions, those who belong within the kingdom; you are the pure-hearted intimates.’ ‘Then make known what you have received from Me, O Sarî, My creature. Truly, I am the Subtle, the All-Knowing.

“Understand through Me, make known what you have heard from Me, and be forgiving and merciful toward My faithful ones.’” Having passed on the account he received from his master after the latter emerged from ecstasy, Jonayd adds: “I never spoke of this account until after the shaykh had departed this world. If I have added anything to it or left anything out, may God forgive me.”

After recounting this vision in full, Rûzbehân adds: “I have cited this sublime vision so that the contemplative may meditate upon it ... so that he may understand what the Veils and Unveilings are on the path to the highest mystical knowledge, and grasp what we mean when we speak of the clouding (ighâna) that occurs even at the spiritual station of love and attainment.

“For through this God has made known to us that in the hearts of those who belong to the hidden world (ahl al-ghayba) there is both veiling and theophany. Even the hearts of the gnostics (‘arifîn), those who know God, cannot escape these until they reach their goal: the unveiling of the vision of vision (kashf ‘iyân al-‘iyân) in the contemplation of the Merciful. This is the ordeal reserved for the spiritual family of those who truly know the ordeal of the Veil.

“Do you not see how He tested them in the account the Shaykh (Sarî) gave of his mi‘râj, his ascent through the heavens? God subjected them to the torments of the Veil as an ordeal reserved especially for them, that they might burn with the fire of longing in the station of separation. Sarî al-Saqatî himself had sought refuge in God, his innermost consciousness (sirr) taking flight toward Him, when he said: ‘Whatever punishment You wish to inflict on me, do not cast me into the misery of the Veil.’

“One of them said: ‘The impossibility of reaching Him is worse than death.’”27 To triumph over this ordeal, we may say, is also to escape the “madness of the unattainable,” the despair of never reaching one's goal. Why is this? What brought about the wonderful reversal in Sarî al-Saqatî's “dialogue in heaven”—“I am yours and you are Mine.

“I share My secrets with you and you share your secrets with Me”—was that, each time the ordeal returned with greater force, those who held firm never let their gaze swerve. Others allowed themselves to be distracted by what was offered to them; they contemplated “something other than You.”

But those who held firm, amid beauty and torment, fulfillment and abandonment, saw only You—even while, in the very act of attaining You, they suffered the anguish of Your inaccessibility. Here lies the whole secret of the faithful lover: one must neither turn away from human beauty nor turn toward it as an end in itself. One must keep one's gaze straight, “neither swerving nor overstepping”: not swerving from what human beauty reveals, and not overstepping the dignity of that beauty as a creature, whose task is to reveal God.

The clouding occurs when one sees only the outward appearance; it awakens the divine jealousy that refuses to be seen. To see what is inward and invisible is to see the gaze of God that the creature itself is, to become the very eye of that gaze. This is the “vision of vision” (‘iyân al-‘iyân), the highest attainment.28 It frees God from His jealousy: “I am yours and you are Mine.” To become the eye through which God sees Himself is to realize esoteric tawhîd.

By contrast, the outward believer's attitude—an abstract monotheism that posits a transcendent God and imagines it glorifies Him by worshipping from the outside—ultimately comes close to that of the unbeliever who is captivated by visible appearances. Both confuse holûl with tajallî: incarnation with theophany.

“Oh, what a little child,” cries Rûzbehân, “whoever sees the Moon above a mountain peak and imagines that by climbing to the summit he will be able to seize it! How could he lay hold of it, when the Moon lies beyond the Veil of Mount Qâf, the cosmic mountain? ... I contemplated the new Moon of Unity, but a jealousy older than time raised a cloud and kept me from reaching it.

“So I remained between the two, between separation and reunion, with nowhere to flee and no refuge where I could weep. ... I wrote this book at the dictation of a wounded consciousness and a wounded heart, and sealed it with the inspirations born of my ordeal—in the presence of the Merciful.”

From childhood, when he first received the “touches of God,” until his death, Rûzbehân lived through this continual movement: from joy before a vision of the Beloved recognized in His image, to the torment of an unattainable presence felt even in the moment of attainment.

Let us return to some pages of the “Journal” of his visions. What predominates there is an enchanted joy before faces of heavenly beauty—a beauty that can disclose itself only to someone whose gaze is so pure that it becomes the very organ of divine vision, the “vision of vision.” At other moments, however, he becomes conscious of a fear that he may be betraying the sharî‘at, Islamic religious law, and the constraint imposed by outward tawhîd: no tashbîh, no symbolic likeness between God and created things!

Yet if one observes tanzîh, refusing to attribute any qualities of created beings to the divine, how can one ever bear witness: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms”? This contradiction will be overcome in the mystical experience of human love—or rather, in the very essence of divine love as it is tasted in the form of human love, as understood by the Sufism of the Faithful of Love.

To understand how the two dwell within one another, how divine peace likewise dwells within human restlessness, we must become acquainted with the horizons that open before Rûzbehân's consciousness—or, more precisely, his consciousness beyond ordinary consciousness—the figures that inhabit it, and the beings of heavenly beauty whose companionship he shares.

PreviousII. Ruzbihan of ShirazNextIV. Diarium spirituale

Chapter IV Diarium spirituale

After recording the first events of his spiritual autobiography in his “Journal”—whose title, The Unveiling of Secrets (Kashf al-asrâr), is by no means a mere figure of speech—Ruzbihan describes the visions of his childhood and adolescence. He then declares:

“Afterwards, the doors were opened to me of the sciences inspired by God (‘olûm ladonîya): knowledge of hidden and subtle realities, and of mysteries before which even learned men stand bewildered. Then I found that certain prayers of mine had been answered, and that I had been granted certain miraculous gifts. My secret consciousness (sirr, or ‘transconsciousness,’ the innermost mystery of the soul) became established in the realities beyond the senses (haqâ’iq), and I began to ascend the degrees of the mystical ladder. I experienced the spiritual stations (maqâmât), the passing states of the soul (ahwâl), revelations (moshâkafât), and the higher knowledge of divine unity (tawhîd).

“In short, through countless discoveries of the invisible worlds, I journeyed into the enchanted regions of the heart.29”

The visions and revelations recorded throughout this Diarium are no longer arranged chronologically once the episodes of his early youth have been recounted. Instead, certain themes emerge with extraordinary force. Particular visions, figures, confidences, and prayers recur so insistently that, as we read, we begin almost unconsciously to group them according to their subjects. What this exceptional document discloses to us, in some measure, are the archetypal figures that dominate the consciousness of an Iranian Sufi—and, through him, the consciousness of his entire spiritual family.

We can mention only a very small number of these visions here, but they may at least suggest their importance for a general understanding of visionary consciousness among mystics. Our attention will be directed especially to the scenes of encounter in which the subtle reality of the “world of Mystery” takes on the vivid, tangible forms of gentle beings inhabiting an enchanted heavenly Earth: visions of the prophets, the angels, and the paradises. Above all, we shall consider those repeated encounters in which a contradiction that reason cannot resolve seems to dissolve: the transcendent, inaccessible God appears as the eternal Companion of the soul in love. For a Shiite mystic, that Companion would be his Imam.

But without a theology of the Imam, the loving soul cannot simply forget what official theology has taught it. Even in moments of peace, it remains troubled. Yet this very unease gives rise to a visionary initiation through which the conflict itself disappears.

“And I saw, in the world of Mystery, a universe illuminated by a radiant Light. I saw God (al-Haqq, the Real) clothed in Majesty, Grace, and Beauty.30 He gave me to drink from the sea of divine affection (wadâd), raised me to the station of intimacy, and showed me the holy world (‘âlam al-Qods).

“After I had travelled through the expanse of pre-eternity, I came to rest at the Threshold of Power. There I saw all the prophets assembled. I saw Moses holding the Torah, Jesus holding the Gospel, David holding the Book of Psalms, and Muhammad holding the Quran. Then Moses let me taste the Torah; Jesus let me taste the Gospel; David let me taste the Psalter; and Muhammad let me taste the Quran.

“But Adam gave me to drink of the ‘Most Beautiful Names of God,’ together with the Supreme Name. Then I understood as much as I was permitted to understand of the higher knowledge of divine wisdom—the knowledge with which God has set his seal upon his prophets and his Friends (Awliyâ’) (§ 32).”

Another vision of the prophets gives Ruzbihan an opportunity to clarify one of his characteristic technical expressions. It also begins to show us the place that Abraham will occupy among the prophets of the religion of love.

“I saw Abraham among certain mountains, where the light was rising from the star of the divine acts of manifestation (af‘âl),31 which are the Mirror in which the Essence and Attributes become visible (mir’ât tajallî). Abraham was searching for God and saying: ‘This is my Lord’ (Quran 6:76–78). Then I saw an imposing shaykh descending from a mountain. His eyes blazed with an awe-inspiring majesty. His hair was whiter than snow. I understood that it was Moses coming down from Sinai (§ 67).”

This vision is followed by a vision of angels that displays the characteristic features of Ruzbihan’s angelology. In his state of ecstasy, he recalls the world of the malakût, the heavenly realm of the angels:

“And behold, that world revealed itself openly to me. I saw the Angels of the Spirit (Rûhânîyûn), the Angels of Divine Lordship (Rabbânîyûn), the Angels of Holiness (Qodsîyûn), the Angels of Majesty (Jalâlîyûn), and the Angels of Beauty (Jamâlîyûn), all seated together. Their robes were like those of brides, more beautiful than anything I had ever seen. Before me I saw the two angels called the ‘Noble Scribes’ (Quran 82:11),32 and they seemed to be in love with me.

“In the foremost rank of their assembly I saw Gabriel, like a bride, like the moon among the stars. His hair resembled that of women, arranged in very long braids. He wore a red robe embroidered in green. He wept because of me, out of longing for me. And all the angels likewise passed their time in the sweetness of looking upon me, as though they longed for me and rejoiced in my spiritual state (§ 68).”

This loving emotion, these feminine features, recur throughout Ruzbihan’s visions of angels. They belong to an absolute Feminine, since—as the Hurufis would later insist33—they are shared by the young woman and the adolescent boy.

“Another time, I saw God bearing the attributes of Majesty and Beauty.34 With him were angels resembling extraordinarily beautiful women, whose braided hair fell all the way to the ground. I said: ‘O my God! How will you take possession of my spirit at the moment of my death?’ He answered: ‘I shall come to you from the depths of pre-eternity. I shall take your spirit in my hand, like this, and carry it to the dwelling of intimacy.

“I shall give you the wine of Nearness to drink, and I shall show you my Beauty and Majesty as you desire, without any veil.’ Then I saw Gabriel, Michael, Seraphiel, and Azrael, all dressed in robes of light so beautiful that I cannot describe them. Then I saw Munkar and Nakir, appearing as two handsome, graceful youths. They were playing the rebec beside my tomb and saying to me: ‘We are in love with you. This is how we shall come to meet you in your grave.’ And then every fear vanished from me (§ 37).”

The mystic who thus received a vision in advance of that perilous passage had already, in effect, answered the summons: “O soul at peace, return…” One striking feature of these visionary landscapes is their colour. Red predominates, but it is a red inseparable from the colour of flowers.

“Many times I saw God among cradles of roses, beneath veils of roses, in a universe of red roses and white roses. Often he showered me with roses, pearls, and hyacinths. Often I was allowed to drink with him the wine of the houris, in the Holy Dwelling (§ 39).”

This red is also spontaneously associated with the mystical perception of blood being shed. Ruzbihan senses its meaning in advance, but ambiguously: it inspires both fear and hope. It seems linked, moreover, to the idea of a “martyrdom” undergone in vision, at the very point where Ruzbihan knows, somewhere in his unconscious mind, that he is transgressing the Law—the doctrine of divine unity upheld by literalist theologians. This is suggested first by the prophetic motif of seeing God “in the most beautiful of forms,” and then by the frenzy of love in which the rules governing tashbîh and ta‘tîl are forgotten. These name the two dangers that theology seeks to avoid: making God resemble created beings by attributing their qualities to him, or, at the opposite extreme, reducing him to an abstraction.

“And behold, I saw him in my dwelling, bearing the attributes of Majesty and Beauty, in the most beautiful of forms…35 I felt a longing, a love, a desire, each intensifying the others. During my ecstasy, the whole question of tashbîh and ta‘tîl was banished from my heart, because in His presence all the standards of intellect and knowledge collapse. Some time passed. Then I saw Him again, rising from the world of Mystery with the attribute of Majesty.

“For several hours I remained immersed in ecstasy. Then I saw Him at dawn. He appeared in Majesty and Beauty in the solitudes of Mystery, at the very threshold of the Place of Mystery, painting the streaks of the eternal dawn with the blood of the Abdâl—the hidden saints. I said to myself: ‘What am I beside them? Could I possibly be one of their number?’

“At that moment I saw a hue still more subtle than theirs, above their own, and He indicated to me that it was my blood. Then I was seized by an ecstasy of joy. Again and again I cried out. My secret consciousness (sirr), my heart, my intelligence, and my spirit were on the verge of taking flight into the expanse of the divine Selfhood (howîya) and being annihilated in the lights of Mystery.

“Yet I was afraid that what I saw might have to be understood as a trial. For in an earlier vision He had shown Himself slaughtering me and pouring out my blood into the streams36 of Mystery, and afterwards I had passed through a terrible ordeal. Then I cried: ‘I take refuge in you against You’ (L. 155a).37”

The earlier vision to which Ruzbihan alludes is described by him in these words:

“One night I was contemplating the Place of Mystery.38 There were what looked like empty streams. Suddenly God seized me and cut my throat. A great quantity of blood flowed from my neck, and soon all the streams were filled with it.

“But behold, my blood took on the appearance of the rays of the sun at dawn, when the sun seems greater than the whole expanse of heaven and earth. And multitudes of angels took my blood and painted their faces with it (§ 28).39”

Among these angelic companies, the four figures known in Islamic esotericism as the “Bearers of the Throne” acquire a particularly vivid presence in Ruzbihan’s visions, as we have already observed. Three of them have an even more personal relationship with him, as the following two accounts show.

“The hosts of angels came forth from the depths of Mystery. Their leaders—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—appeared as young pages,40 their hair braided like that of women. Then God showered me with roses and pearls. The prophets (Nabî) and the angels did the same. Our Prophet spoke to me and kissed me on the face. After him, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and all the prophets kissed me in the same way. Then God pronounced blessings upon Muhammad and his prophets and praised them.

“Afterwards He said: ‘I have chosen my servant Ruzbihan for eternal happiness, for the station of one of my Friends (walâyat), and for the investiture of my miraculous gifts. I have made him the vessel of my knowledge and my secrets… He is my representative (khalifa) in this world and in the worlds. Whoever loves him, I love; whoever is his enemy is my enemy’ (§ 49).41”

The other account runs as follows:

“It appeared to me that I was in the Sacred Mosque at Mecca (al-masjid al-harâm). I saw the Prophet, who seemed to be in a state of ecstasy. He was walking around the Kaaba and was near the Black Stone, on its left side. Gabriel stood beneath the portico, near the gate of Safa. Michael stood beside him, and Seraphiel beside them both, while a group of angels stood in the courtyard of the sanctuary.

“I approached the Prophet, overwhelmed with wonder. He turned towards me and called me by my name. Then each of the three angels—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—approached me in turn and addressed me by name: ‘O Ruzbihan!’ All three were in ecstasy. Then they drew near to the Prophet, and it seemed to me that the Kaaba itself began to move and came closer to them. Then I danced with them. God made Himself visible to them, and I was there among them, sharing their ecstasy of love and tasting a profound peace (§ 52).”

Among these three archangels, Gabriel acquires a particularly striking significance. This is connected with his role in Islamic teachings about prophecy, upon which the mystical experience is modelled. The mystic experiences the Angel of Revelation as his own personal Holy Spirit, as the figure of the divine Other Self.42 One night, Ruzbihan receives a revelation of the Night of Destiny (laylat al-Qadr):

“On that night the angels and the Spirit descend, by permission of their Lord, to carry out every command. And peace reigns until the breaking of dawn” (Quran 97:4–5).43

“God showed me all the angels, each of them appearing in human form, smiling messengers of glad tidings. Among them was Gabriel, the most beautiful of the angels. Their braided hair was like that of women. Their faces were like the red rose. Some wore veils of light upon their heads; others wore crowns set with precious stones; still others were clothed in mantles of pearls. I saw them on several occasions, when they also had the appearance of beautiful youths.44

“I saw the angel Rezwân (Ridwân) and Paradise, and I entered it. I saw the houris and the young attendants, whose appearance was as God describes it (see Quran 37:47; 56:17–22, etc.). I entered the heavenly palaces. I drank from the flowing waters and ate the fruits of the Garden. Many times I also saw the Throne (‘arsh) and the Korsî. And I saw God clothed in a form that gave him the appearance of a shaykh. He wore a Persian mantle. Then I felt myself melting away before his majesty and his bearing (§ 24).”

On another night, Ruzbihan contemplates God:

“Above the Throne, in the bridal chambers of intimacy, revealing Himself with the attributes of Beauty and Majesty. No one stood before Him except Gabriel, who was weeping and suddenly tore his garments in the violence of his frenzy of love before the divine Beauty. Some time passed… I saw rocks over which flowed a great river, like a river of pearls. I saw Khidr and Elijah, together with all the Abdâl, washing their clothes in the river. Never had I seen a sight more enchanting than the vision of them at that moment (L. 157b).”

Ruzbihan repeatedly confides to us his visionary journeys into Paradise. After the great vision in which he had been joined by the three archangels and the Prophet around the Kaaba, he passes through a long period of relaxation until morning approaches. Then ecstasy seizes him once more:

“I was shown a man in the middle of the sanctuary. He seemed to be carrying sand from that place to somewhere else, until a door appeared beneath the sand. That door was opened for me. I passed through it and entered beyond. I saw another man standing beneath the doorway. The first was Ishmael; the second was Rezwân.

“Then, having crossed the threshold, I saw Paradise, with its trees, its flowers, and its countless lights. I saw Muhammad and all the prophets, the Friends of God (Awliyâ’), the martyrs, and the angels. I saw a multitude of believers there. I saw nothing that resembled this world. There was only light upon light, radiance upon radiance, beauty upon beauty (§ 53).”

Another vision adds:

“Never have I seen anything more beautiful. There I saw the angels, the prophets, the houris, and the heavenly palaces. All were filled with divine Lights. Among the trees of Paradise I saw a tree of turquoise, resembling a palm tree. If that tree, in all its grace and beauty, were shown to the people of this world (ahl al-donyâ), they would all die of longing for it (§ 81).”

The visionary also contemplates his own family there:

“I saw my family in one of the paradises, before God, appearing as beautiful young people, for I saw everyone who kept company around God in the form of youthful beauty.45 Then I saw my family in one of the upper chambers of Paradise, before God. This upper chamber was made of red hyacinth. My family were seated near God, along a row of cushions. They seemed to be waiting for me. Then I heard His word resounding from the world of Mystery: ‘…those of their fathers and their spouses who have been righteous.’

“I reflected upon these words addressed to me inwardly, and returned to the beginning of the Quranic verse: ‘The gardens of Eden: they shall enter them, together with those of their fathers, their spouses, and their children who have been righteous; and the angels shall come to visit them, entering through every gate’ (13:23). I understood that this was good news for me. At dawn I sat watching for the rising of the eternal morning (§ 82).”

It is a commonplace of a certain kind of Christian argument against Islam to disparage the joys of the Quranic Paradise on the grounds that they appeal to the senses. It is therefore important to see how those joys are anticipated and inwardly experienced by spiritual seekers within Islam itself. Among them, the dilemma that torments the Christian ascetic’s conscience has never been felt in any comparable way.

The description of the joys of Paradise belongs to the wider problem of tanzîh and tashbîh: on the one hand, declaring God utterly beyond every attribute (tanzîh); on the other, affirming the correspondences that link the invisible and visible worlds (tashbîh). The point is neither to sacrifice one to the other nor to surrender to either.

The mystical soul finds peace by passing between them, remaining equally distant from—and equally close to—both. Such a reconciliation is probably possible only because Sufism is animated by a sense of theophany: the experience of the divine making itself present and perceptible. The problem lies at the very heart of Ruzbihan’s teaching about divine manifestations, just as it does in the thought of Ibn Arabi. On its resolution depends the possibility of tasting the sweetness and peace of divine love within human love.

But here we have more than a theoretical explanation. We have the experience itself, lived in a visionary state. In any case, these are not perceptions made through the physical senses in the ordinary world. They are perceptions of the imagination in the intermediate, imaginal world—the mundus imaginalis, a world of forms experienced inwardly as real, rather than merely imagined.

“I saw the Divine Presence (Hazrat) filled with angels of the highest rank, seated beneath the pavilions of Glory. I saw God. All the prophets and all the Messengers were seated, waiting beside the pulpit (minbar). When I had taken my seat at the pulpit and had spoken the words concerning the mutual recognition of spirits, the angels wept, and so did the prophets. And God was listening. A Light shone through His person, as though showing that He was in agreement with them. Then He said: ‘So it shall be on the Day of Resurrection.’

“Ah, shame upon anyone who thinks these revelations are mere fantasies to be suspected of tashbîh—of making God too human! Such a person is only a beginner. He has experienced nothing. He has never breathed the fragrance of the flowers of Paradise. These are experiences of the holy world, spiritual stations attained by those whose insight is deepest even as they remain most discerning. Such people know very well that these are forms in which divine Lordship (robobîya) appears: manifestations of the eternal Lights, forms taken by the divine Attributes through theophanies (§ 84).”

We know that Ruzbihan served for many years as a preacher in Shiraz. The passage just quoted shows him fulfilling the same role “in Heaven.”

Yet the subject of his preaching remains unchanged. We may recall the anecdote already mentioned at the end of Chapter II: when he first made his way through the ranks of his listeners to mount the pulpit in Shiraz, he stopped to admonish a mother whom he had just heard instructing her daughter to conceal her beauty beneath a veil. His preaching cannot help returning, on every occasion, to the mystery of the divine appearing through beauty.

The reverence and ethical demands that arise from this “manifestation of the divine” must never lose sight of what Ruzbihan calls iltibâs: the double meaning of the human Image, which at once is and is not what it appears to be. Everything accessible to the senses—everything visible or audible—has this double meaning.

What we can see reveals what cannot be seen; what we can hear reveals what cannot be heard. This is precisely the function of created beauty as a manifestation of the divine. Naturally, preaching such a doctrine may scandalize the devout defenders of orthodoxy: people who can sense no second meaning in the text of beauty, any more than in the revealed scripture. Ruzbihan himself can sometimes begin to doubt what he preaches.

But his visions restore his certainty. On the very night when he has contemplated the treasures of Paradise, he begins to meditate upon the immediate, direct vision permitted by the spiritual station of iltibâs, the twofold appearance of the divine. He is troubled by scruples. It is as though the demands of collective orthodoxy—the religion of legal rules and social conformity, which would impose a socially determined form upon faith—have risen again in his consciousness against his personal faith.

“I was troubling myself about what is eternal, trying to turn away from everything created. Then God appeared to me in the Holy Assembly (Majlis al-Qods), in a form so beautiful that every lover was captivated by it. He approached me and said: ‘Come now! There is no reason for you to distress yourself over this.’ I had the impression that He disliked my anxious effort to keep His transcendence apart from the forms perceived by the imagination.

“My heart was enchanted by this divine manifestation in a form suited to the secret of my love. And so I remained in ecstasy, sighing and weeping, until morning. Then, hour after hour, He revealed Himself to me under a new attribute, drawn from the hosts of pre-eternal Lights. When He had once more become invisible, I remembered what I had preached from the pulpit.

“But He said to me: ‘What you preached was indeed worthy of my secret. You preached it to guide created beings and to make known to them the beauty of the divine favours prepared for them’ (§ 83).”

When Ruzbihan speaks of God appearing “in a form suited to the secret of my love,” he gives us the secret of theophanies themselves. Each divine manifestation corresponds to the spiritual capacity of the person who receives it.

Yet precisely here the conflict reappears. These manifestations must necessarily be many and varied; each is like a distinct appearance of the divine. What becomes of this multiplicity when confronted with the absolute demand of tawhîd, the oneness of God? The conflict is indeed insoluble so long as we remain within an outward, literal understanding of monotheism, which places God before us as a transcendent object. The secret of esoteric tawhîd is that God is never an Object.

Rather, He is the active Subject of those acts through which created beings relate to Him. Such a truth can express itself only through paradox. These are the shath—the startling utterances of mystical ecstasy—from which Ruzbihan derives his title of shaykh shattâh, the master of ecstatic paradoxes.

The mystic himself becomes a paradox. It is not merely that he sometimes speaks in the first person, his human ego having withdrawn, and utters statements whose true subject can only be the Divine Being. His situation also compels him to challenge religion understood as a system of legal rules. He must accept, courageously and without concern for the judgment of others, that his wholly inward and personal religious life may appear outwardly impious or sacrilegious in the eyes of the Law and of organized religion. Such are the Sufis known as the Malâmatî, those willing to incur the blame of others.

The great mystical poet Hafez of Shiraz was one of them. As though to confirm the affinity that has already led us to see Ruzbihan as a precursor of Hafez, Ruzbihan tells us here that, in his youth, he had a Malâmatî shaykh. It is significant that this master should become the form of a divine manifestation in a vision that affirms the paradox of the many manifestations of the One and the identity of the Many.

“In my youth I had a shaykh. He was a master of great mystical knowledge, perpetually in a state of spiritual intoxication. He was a Malâmatî shaykh, whose true nature was unknown to ordinary people. One night I was contemplating a vast plain among the plains of Mystery. And behold, I saw God appearing in the likeness of this shaykh, at the entrance to the plain. I approached Him.

“Then He made a sign to me, pointing towards another plain. I went forward into that plain, and there again I saw a shaykh just like the first—and this shaykh was God. Once more He made a sign, pointing towards another plain. And so it continued until He had unveiled seventy thousand plains to me. Each time, at the entrance to each plain, I saw a figure resembling the one I had seen in the first.

“I said to myself: ‘And yet God Most High is unique, one, indivisible, beyond every number, great or small, beyond equals, opposites, and likenesses.’ Then it was said to me: ‘Such is the manifestation of the eternal Attributes, for they are without limit.’ At that moment I felt myself seized by the esoteric realities of tawhîd, rising from the sea of Magnificence (§ 34).”

Another account alludes to the same mystery:

“I saw a Light whiter than the brightness of pearls and snow… He revealed to me the beauties of the Attributes… No distance remained between Him and me. Then I saw in the divine Face such majesty and beauty that the inhabitants of Heaven and Earth might have died of delight. I saw that every region of Heaven and Earth was filled with them… He brought me into the station of the nearness of nearness. He showed me seventy thousand majesties, beauties, and perfections, and spoke words to me which, if the mountain of Qaf—the cosmic mountain—could hear them, would make it melt with pleasure…

“Then He seated me before Him and treated me with every kind of gracious attention. From His own hand He gave me a drink that I cannot describe. And I was allowed to hear things that I have no power to put into words (§ 47).”

The symbol of this drink returns in another vision, at the very moment when Ruzbihan, paradoxically, seems to wish to remind the Divine Being of His own transcendence.

“God lifted the veil from the angelic realm (malakût), assuming the form of Majesty and Beauty and revealing the whole series of Attributes corresponding to the human form. Then He showed me His Sublimity and Majesty in another spiritual station, and so it continued until I had contemplated Him in seventy stations,46 each time under an Attribute I had never seen before. Then He seated me at the Table of tender care, while I contemplated in Him colours of majesty that had never before entered my consciousness. He offered me food from that Table. I said: ‘My God!

“Yet surely You transcend the acts of eating and drinking! If the tears of repentance are the drink of angels, what, then, are the tears of longing and intimacy when one beholds You?’ Then He said to me: ‘That is my drink.’ Such is the tenderness with which He treats His prophets and His Friends, even while remaining transcendent above every attribute of created beings (L. 153b).”

The entire Diarium could be read as a series of variations on this theme of double meaning and direct vision: God clothes Himself in attributes corresponding to those of created beings (tashbîh), without contradicting the absolute transcendence of His pure Essence (tanzîh). For rational dialectic, there is no way out of this contradiction. Only pure love resolves it in actual experience. This is what Ruzbihan will learn through his visions and confirm through the experience of his life.

In the account in which he describes the veils of red roses and white roses beneath which he so often contemplated God, he admits that, had anyone been able to witness those intimate exchanges between himself and God, that witness would have recognized him as a zindîq—a heretic. This was a designation by which Islamic orthodoxy associated with the old Zoroastrian religion of Iran anything that seemed to violate the letter of the Law.47 How could the strict defender of orthodoxy understand that, beneath a divine form “suited to the secret of the mystic’s love,” the mystic perceives transcendent Majesty itself—precisely because that Majesty cannot in fact be perceived in any other way or anywhere else?

“What I describe, and what I allude to, are the embroideries woven by the symbols of the higher sciences of love. God reveals Himself within them under the attributes of Majesty and Beauty. He has invested them with this love and this mystical knowledge, because in the true Reality of tawhîd there is a sea of negation before which the prophets and the Messengers, the angels and the Friends of God, all flee. And in the mystical station of tawhîd burn the fires of Magnificence, which consume thought, understanding, and every form of perception (§ 39).”

Impenetrable is the mystery of the One who is utterly one. He can reveal Himself only by assuming a veil of clouds proportionate to the heart that receives Him, whether the heart of an angel or of a spiritual seeker. That veiling must at once be accepted and pierced.

“He appeared to me in the aspect of the Uncreated, from among the Orients of pre-eternity, and He said to me: ‘I have travelled towards you from the Mystery of Mysteries. Between you and me lies a distance of seven hundred thousand years…’ He treated me with tender consideration and said: ‘I have chosen you, in your time, for this rank above the worlds.’ He unveiled to me holy beauties and the particular qualities of the eternal Attributes. I contemplated a beauty within a majesty, and a majesty within a beauty, which I shall never be able to describe… In my youth I was accustomed to keeping vigil until deep into the night.

“Thus, one night, while I was praying, the Divine Being passed close to me, appearing in the most beautiful of forms. He smiled at me and threw little sachets of musk towards me. I said: ‘Give me a great many of them.’ He answered: ‘Each one is an angel, and you are an angel of Persia’ (§§ 21–22).”

Again and again, the mystic tries to force his way beyond this double meaning of appearances, to overcome it and attain absolute knowledge. Only later will he learn that it can be transcended only by being transfigured. Otherwise, he exposes himself to the same danger that Moses encountered upon the mountain.

“And behold, I was contemplating the strange wonders of this double meaning. I said: ‘My God! My Lord! How long will You continue to show me the vision that is proper to me, under the form of these appearances? Show me the pure Uncreated, existence beyond all existence in its pure state.’ He said to me: ‘Moses and Jesus desired this spiritual dwelling, but did not attain it.’

“Then He revealed to me a single atom of light from His eternal Essence, and my spirit was almost dissolved. I feared that I was about to die. I saw our Prophet, the other prophets, all the Companions, and all the shaykhs asking God to grant me the ultimate station of Magnificence (§ 45).”

The same appeal, and the same failure, recur in another vision:

“The wonders of tawhîd appeared to me, but I was still seeing only the traces of the world of divine manifestations. I said: ‘My God! Bring me to Yourself in the state of tajrîd al-tawhîd’—that is, in the pure stripping away of everything that might qualify Your unity. Then the world of becoming appeared to me like the full moon emerging above the summit of a mountain, or like the radiance of a glowing fire burning without smoke. God caused me to enter this other world.

“I was stripped of the weaknesses imposed by ordinary ways of understanding, but I could not endure there to the end. For this dwelling was the realm of holiness, of the stripping away of all attributes (tanzîh), and of annihilation (fanâ’). Then the essential realities of the Essence (haqâ’iq al-haqîqat) became evident to me. My secret consciousness was brought to incandescence. And it was said to me: ‘This is the world of absolute Oneness (wahdâniyat), the one I proclaimed in my Book, the Quran, when I said: Nothing is like Him’ (42:9) (§ 66).”

Thus, whenever the mystic attempts to grasp transcendence itself, he is sent back to the symbol, to the divine manifestation, to the double meaning of the Veil—a veil that his innermost consciousness (sirr) will make as transparent as a mirror. Once again, flowers appear as symbols announcing the Mystery.

“Once, in the second half of the night, after seating myself upon my prayer carpet to await the appearance of the invisible Brides (‘arâ’is al-ghayb), my secret consciousness took flight into the regions of the malakût. Many times I contemplated the divine Majesty in the station of double meaning, under the awe-inspiring aspect (hayba) of His Beauty.

“But my heart was not satisfied. It longed for the unveiling of the eternal Majesty that sets ablaze the deepest secrets of consciousness and thought. And behold, I contemplated a Face more vast than all the Heavens, the Earth, the Throne, and the Korsî together. As it radiated the lights of Beauty, it transcended every idea of likeness or resemblance.

“Yet I perceived its beauty as having the appearance of a red rose—but like a world within a world, as though red roses were continually flowing forth from it, and I could see no limit to them. Then my heart remembered these words of our Prophet: ‘The red rose is a part of the divine Beauty’ (§ 71).”

Here we begin to glimpse an initiation into the secret of the double meaning inherent in created existence—an initiation that Ruzbihan will develop more fully in his doctrinal writings.

“During one of my visions… I was rising gradually through the forms of the divine manifestations. My intention was to reach the Uncreated, when I would at last be able to pass beyond the limits of these manifestations. Then I saw God in the most beautiful of forms, rising before me at the entrance to the great plain of the world of Mystery. I lost all control of myself. I wept and cried out, for this form overwhelmed me with wonder… as though white roses were being showered upon me from His Face.

“Then He became invisible, and afterwards reappeared in a form even more beautiful than the first. I went to join Him, and He spoke to me through my secret consciousness: ‘Where are we going?’ I said: ‘Towards pre-eternity.’ ‘What are you seeking?’ ‘I am seeking my annihilation (fanâ’) in the overwhelming force of what is pre-eternal, for I cannot be satisfied with the vision of appearances that bear a double meaning.’ ‘It is a long journey,’ He said. ‘I shall come with you. I shall be your travelling companion.’

“So we advanced towards what lies beyond the Throne. We made the journey through Mystery. Then He became invisible to me. An hour later He reappeared, bearing the attribute of the Jabarût, the realm of divine power, and there I was annihilated. Then He showed me a tender graciousness and said: ‘Seek me in the mystical station of love, for neither the world nor anything within the world can withstand the assaults of my Majesty.’ And I remained within the sweetness of my vision (§ 58).”

Hence the mystery of the heart: the supreme organ of the subtle spiritual body, and the centre of mystical perception. Once more, in the second half of the night, Ruzbihan meditates while contemplating the mysteries of the world of Lights.

“And behold, I saw Him upon the paths of Mystery. He held something in His hand. I said: ‘My God! What is that?’ He answered: ‘It is your heart.’ ‘So my heart has a dwelling place in Your hand?’ I asked. Then He folded my heart, so that it became like something rolled up. Afterwards He unfolded it, and now my heart stretched from the Throne to the Pleiades. I said: ‘Is this my heart?’ ‘This is your heart, and it is greater than the universe.’48

“Then He carried it, just as it was, in His hand towards the regions of the malakût. I entered with Him, until I came upon the dîwân, the heavenly court of the Mystery of Mysteries. At that moment I said: ‘How far are You taking it?’ ‘To the pre-eternal world, so that I may contemplate Myself within it… and reveal Myself to it for all the eternities to come, in the form of Divinity (olûhîya).’

“I said: ‘I want to see You as You are in pre-eternity.’ ‘There is no path by which you can reach that.’ Then I pleaded with Him: ‘I want it,’ I said. And behold, the Lights of sublimity appeared. I was annihilated, utterly brought to nothing. After that, created existence could no longer offer itself to the overwhelming flood of Magnificence.

“Then my secret consciousness was addressed, and it was said to me: ‘Do you now understand the hidden meaning of these words of the Prophet: The hearts are between two of the fingers of the Merciful One, and He shapes them as He wills?’ What I saw between His fingers was the outer form of the hearts of His lovers. He shapes them—turns them—from this world towards the enclosures of His Majesty. When He withdrew into concealment… that vision left an immense joy in my deepest consciousness (sirr), until the moment when I returned to awareness (§§ 61–62).”

Little by little, the visionary is thus initiated into the secret of esoteric tawhîd. This is the secret of who truly acts in the experiences of the mystic: the eternal Companion, the divine Other Self. Until the mystic has understood this, he may suffer the pain of absence, because he does not yet know who it is that has really become absent. On the day after a spiritual concert, Ruzbihan experiences a certain relaxation. Then evening returns, and at the hour of the prayer offered during the first third of the night, he asks himself:

“Why did the wonders of Mystery not reveal themselves during yesterday’s spiritual concert (samâ‘)? Suddenly, behold, I saw God through the openings of the malakût, appearing to me with the attributes of Beauty and Majesty. I said to Him: ‘Where were You? Why did You remain invisible during the spiritual concert?’ He answered: ‘I was with you, in the very form in which you see me now.’

“Then I cried out. My secret consciousness, my intelligence, and my heart were filled with joy. ‘My God!’ I said. ‘Why, then, did I not see You?’ He answered: ‘I was behind you and above you, watching you; I was at your right and at your left, in this very form.’ Then it was as though I saw Him just as He was describing and revealing Himself. Half the night passed.

“I sought Him in the aspect of Divinity (olûhîya), without the double meaning of the Attributes and the divine Acts that reveal them. I began to plead. And behold, the lights of the Essence and the Attributes appeared to me in the pre-eternal world. There were layers of vapour rising one above another. I saw radiance upon radiance, majesty upon majesty, beauty upon beauty. I saw the holy sea (bahr al-Qods)… It seemed to me that all these Lights were smiling upon my face (§ 65).”

For there to be, at one and the same time, the unification of the One (tawhîd) and the joy of being two, we must overturn the ordinary way of seeing things, founded upon the outward understanding of religion. What the Book of the Clouding of the Divine Presence has taught us, the Diarium confirms through lived experience.

The Witness (shâhid) is no longer a separate eye looking upon God. The Witness is the eye through which God looks and reveals Himself to Himself, in the infinite variations of “the most beautiful of forms.” It is in this sense that you are His eyewitness, and that an outward understanding of tawhîd is nothing but a trick and a deception.

“And behold,” Ruzbihan relates, “I saw my soul in a state of fanâ’, of annihilation, and I was saying to myself: ‘I am the least of Your creatures. I am Your servant and the son of Your servant.’ Then the overwhelming force of divine unity and Sublimity struck against my heart. He said to me: ‘Who are you, to be a servant in relation to Me?’ I was overcome with shame before this God whom my words had no power to describe. I said: ‘What attribute could I possibly name, when I myself am merely one thing among all the things that belong to You?’

“But He said to me: ‘You are not one who truly affirms divine unity until you have forgotten both yourself and everything other than Me, from the Throne to the Pleiades.’ I remained dazzled, as though enveloped in an immense veil. I was still unable to speak when He caused me to remember something of His dhikr, the remembrance of His Name. He made me understand my annihilation in Him and my longing for Him. The great plains of Mystery grew bright, and behold, pointing to Himself, He said to me: ‘It is I who belong to you (Anâ laka).’

“Then I was seized by an emotion of ecstasy, and my heart was filled with joy. Afterwards He approached me in the form of a beautiful youth.49 My soul and my heart were annihilated in His grace and beauty.
