Coming near to me, He said: ‘Here your heart is not distressed by the declaration of divine unity. For here, tawhîd is a trick and a deception, since you are my eyewitness, and I am present in the form of grace and beauty’ (§ 77).”

The state of someone who “truly affirms divine unity” is precisely that which was attained by the last group of the Faithful in the account of the Mi‘râj, the heavenly ascent of Sari al-Saqati, which concludes the Book of the Clouding of the Divine Presence. Having remained faithful to the oneness of their Desire, this last group survived in a higher state of existence after the original company had been decimated seven times by a sevenfold ordeal.

All those who bear witness to God “objectively,” without forgetting themselves, and who believe that they themselves are the ones bearing witness, are in reality no better than polytheists. The monotheism of religion understood as a legal and social institution remains at this level. It merely places a Supreme Being (Ens supremum) above the sum of created existence. Only esoteric tawhîd, by contrast, escapes the trap of this metaphysical idolatry. The multiplicity of divine manifestations is the multiplicity of forms through which the one divine Subject appears to Himself and recognizes Himself through His creatures.

But this requires that those creatures keep their eyes open—and open upon Him alone. For then their eyes are His eyes: the eyes through which He looks, and through which He beholds Himself within them. There is therefore no longer any conflict between the One and the many. There is the multiplicity of the One, but each manifestation of that multiplicity is always, in itself, One.50 This is the unity of the One—or, more precisely, the mystery of unus-ambo, the two who are one.

Of both the One and the other it is equally true to say that each is the One who sees and the One who is seen. There is therefore nothing to prevent certain scenes of ecstasy that would be openly scandalous to every kind of outward religious conformity. Let us quote one more vision:

“One day I fell into the sea of Desire. The crashing waves of the Ocean of Magnificence carried me away, until I reached the mystical station in which existence beyond existence is contemplated. And behold, I saw God. Through His Beauty and Majesty, the dazzling flashes of His Face were revealed to me. I remained contemplating that beauty. I was at the height of spiritual intoxication. My spirit was almost stripped from my body, my intelligence abolished, my heart carried away, my secret consciousness annihilated…

“When dawn broke, I saw that the world seemed filled with the Divine Being. I was at once absent and present. It seemed both that I saw Him and that I was not the one who saw Him. Then, behold, He came towards me. He drew me into a dance, and I danced with Him. But as I emerged from ecstasy, I returned to consciousness at once (L. 148a).”

To close this all-too-brief examination of Ruzbihan’s Diarium spirituale, let us quote its final page. It opens with something like a threefold cry of longing and exultation:

“Then I saw Him! Then I saw Him! Then I saw Him! So many times that I could never tell their number… He caused me to travel through the highest malakût, unveiling to me the depths of pre-eternity in their state of absolute transcendence (tanzîh). He unveiled to me Beauty and Majesty. Then He revealed Himself to me under one of the forms that bear a double meaning (iltibâs).

“All the Cherubim stood before the pavilions of Magnificence. Their wonderful forms were themselves the forms of grace and beauty. Their hair was braided like that of women. The houris, dressed in robes such as the inhabitants of Paradise wear, separated and came together again. And I saw Gabriel, possessing a grace and beauty that I cannot describe. He passed very close to me, in all that grace and beauty. And I saw the Prophets and the Friends of God (Awliyâ’), immersed in the Lights flashing forth from His Majesty.

“I myself was suspended between concealment (istitar) and divine manifestation (tajallî). I was beside myself, crying out and groaning, filled with longing and driven almost mad by burning desire, like those overcome with intoxication. Then He took away all my worries and sorrows. My heart was filled with joy through His intimacy and His beauty. After that, I prayed to God for the community of Muhammad. This was at a time when a terrible epidemic had struck Shiraz. There were crowds of the dead and the sick.

“Finally, I prayed that God would deliver me: that I should no longer have to enter the palace of the Emirs. When morning came, a divine command was issued, and from that moment onward I was delivered from the sight of them and from their company (L. 51a).”

PreviousIII. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the VeilNextV. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Chapter V The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

The passages we have just drawn from Ruzbihan's Spiritual Diary give us a glimpse of the hidden forces at work in his innermost consciousness—the sirr, or consciousness beyond ordinary awareness—as they emerge through a succession of visionary states. He experienced these sometimes in dreams, but more often at night or around dawn, in the state between waking and sleep. Certain recurring features show us how a Sufi actually experiences and overcomes an inner conflict, not merely as a matter of theory but through the trials of spiritual life.

On one side stands the longing shared by all Sufis: the longing to see God personally. On the other stands the demand of tawhid as understood by outward, established religion: an abstract monotheism that treats divine oneness as though it were the unity of an object. Overcoming this demand, imposed by a collective and socially established religious norm, requires a long, arduous, and daring personal spiritual experience. That experience finds expression in the paradoxes, the “pious blasphemies,” which horrify and scandalize those devoted to the outward forms of religion.

Two situations embody this conflict and its resolution: the denial of the vision of God to Moses (Quran 7:139), and the prophetic testimony, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” We have already had occasion to examine one aspect of this theme in the speculative mysticism and experience of Ibn Arabi.51

But it remains to be explored throughout the different forms of Sufism. In Ruzbihan's work, both the terms of the conflict and its resolution—a conflict that shapes the different paths taken in Islam by the religious believer and the mystic52—find expression in two works of exceptional importance. One is his Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis, a comprehensive account of the Sufism of his time.

The other is a jewel of Persian literature, which Ruzbihan called The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love.53 The Jasmine is no less difficult than the Commentary. It is both a work of doctrine and an autobiography. Its highly personal language, beautiful as it is, makes it hard to read and harder still to translate. Almost the entire work thinks in images. These are not rhetorical ornaments: they are concepts expressed in another form, and the book's inner dialectic works upon them just as it would upon concepts. The reader must keep a hand on both keyboards at once.

We can approach the book's central theme in this way. Through an inward pilgrimage along the stages of love, it resolves that conflict by leading from a legalistic, socially organized Islam to the personal, spiritual Islam of Sufism. In other words, it leads from outward tawhid—the monotheistic faith of a consciousness that takes God naively as an object—to inward tawhid, which perceives and speaks of the mystery of the Subject of divine unity. This esoteric understanding effects a genuine alchemical transformation of tawhid.

Official Islam no longer recognizes itself in it and refuses to acknowledge it as its own. (The existence of something called “orthodox Sufism” does nothing to diminish the meaning of the rejection made here in the name of religious legalism.) Because this transformation overturns our whole perspective,54 the Book of the Clouding has already announced it in certain striking formulations: the mystic must himself become the eye through which God beholds Himself. This requires a return to a state preceding the division between subject and object, a state in which the Divine Being can neither be turned into an object nor made into a social institution. In that state, the Divine is experienced as the absolute Subject for and through each individual existence.

That state—the very meaning of inward tawhid—is what the Sufis found expressed in a Neoplatonic formula, known to them through the work called the Theology of Aristotle: the Divine Being is at once love, the lover, and the beloved.

Consider the distance between the one God affirmed by the literal faith of official Islam and the Sufi understanding of divine unity as absolute subjectivity: absolute because it stands in no relation to anything other than itself. The distance between the two reveals the scale of the spiritual transformation that Sufism brings about in relation to the outward religion of the Law.

Now, if the divine mystery offered to inward religion is expressed as the unity of love, lover, and beloved, then there can be only one path by which the initiate approaches and experiences that mystery. The formula itself tells us what the path is.

Inward tawhid can be understood, experienced, and realized only in and through love. Human love—eros—opens the way to it, because human love is the one actual experience which, at its furthest limit, can give an intimation of, and sometimes bring about, the unity of love, lover, and beloved. This is the command Ruzbihan heard in one of his visions: “Seek Me in the mystical station of love.”

Here, too, lies the profound difference between the spirituality of Ruzbihan and those like him, and that of the Christian ascetic in general. The difference also sets them apart from the Sufis whom Ruzbihan calls the “pious ascetics” (sohhad), as opposed to the faithful in love.55 These are, broadly speaking, devotees for whom human beauty—and beauty perceived through the senses generally—is a snare, perhaps even a temptation from the devil, and for whom human love is not a way toward divine love but an obstacle to it.

The distinctive character of Iranian Sufism lies here. It entails a challenge, and an individual ethic that is heroic and secret, embodied in the javanmard, the knight of the soul. For Ruzbihan, as for Ahmad Ghazali, Fakhr Eraqi, and Hafez, there is only one love.

As Ruzbihan writes: “There is only one and the same love, and it is in the book of human love (ishq insani) that we must learn to read the rule of divine love (ishq rabbani).”56 It is, then, one and the same text, but we must learn to read it. Here, above all, interpreting the text turns out to mean interpreting the soul itself.57

We must be initiated into a spiritual way of interpretation, a ta'wil of love, because human love is a prophetic text. That means it has a double meaning, an ambiguity or overlap of meanings—the iltibas that Ruzbihan made a technical term of his teaching.

And since Beauty is the source of the text, discovering that source is itself a prophetic act: the mystical lover is a partner of the Prophet (Nabi). Conversely, the message borne by beauty is prophetic. It invites us to pass from figurative love (majazi)—the literal text, love as experienced through the senses—to love in its true sense (haqiqi), the inner meaning of love. These terms are all familiar from the classical Sufi teaching on love, whose defining movement is precisely this passage from figurative meaning to true meaning.

Here again, Ruzbihan's life gives us a concrete example. Ibn Arabi relates a remarkable story from one of Ruzbihan's stays in Mecca.58 If we set it beside the autobiographical prologue to the Jasmine, the two accounts shed light on one another. Ibn Arabi had heard the story in the Sufi circles of Mecca, where it must have been well known,59 and included it in a chapter of his vast work, The Meccan Spiritual Conquests.60

During what was probably an extended stay in the holy city, Ruzbihan fell in love with a beautiful young singer. In a man like Ruzbihan, such love could take only one form: adoring love carried to the point of ecstasy. A characteristic feature of his devotions and ecstatic states, as the Diary also shows, was that he sighed and cried out aloud, sometimes to the point of disturbing those worshipping near him. This was exactly what happened in Mecca, where his exclamations disturbed others walking around the Kaaba in the ritual circumambulation.

Ibn Arabi also attests that Ruzbihan was a man of complete inner sincerity. We have already recognized in him the traits that connect him with the Malamati: those fearless people who, precisely to remain completely faithful to their own inner truth, do not shrink from public blame. Whatever image nourished his ecstasy, its outward manifestations remained the same.

Because no one knew of his love, Ruzbihan sensed that people might misunderstand him. They might suppose that his ecstasies still arose from God alone, as they had before. Or, rather, he must have realized that the people around him could not even imagine the experience he would later describe in the Jasmine: for the pious ascetics, divine love and human love were irreconcilable opposites.

So, with the fearless simplicity of a pure heart, Ruzbihan went before the assembly of Sufis. There he took off his khirqa, his Sufi cloak, threw it down before his companions, told them what had happened, and concluded: “I do not want to lie to anyone about my state.” From that moment he devoted himself entirely to this young beauty of Mecca.

But we must look closely at what he did. Ruzbihan was behaving as a true member of the faithful in love. This was no ordinary “affair,” as we might say today. Ruzbihan kept his secret; in silence, his ecstasy was nourished by the vision of her beauty. Others told the young woman that she was the unknowing object of ecstatic adoration by someone already regarded as one of the great spiritual figures (min akabir ahl Allah).

What happened then was this. The news deeply moved her. Overwhelmed, she renounced the way of life she had followed until then and turned toward God. Ibn Arabi says that her conversion was the blessed fruit of Ruzbihan's sincerity. She became his disciple in turn, just as Ruzbihan had been hers: contemplating her beauty had led him to the point where the mystic ceases to be attached to outward form.

The outcome perfectly reflects the ethic of the faithful in love. The beautiful person who receives this adoration is ultimately transformed by it. The lover invests her with a theophanic role—the role of revealing the divine—and this leads her to the inner truth of her beauty, a truth henceforth beyond the changes of time.61 The story ends with a gesture just as simple as the first. Ruzbihan returns to the Sufi assembly and takes up his khirqa again.

Comparing this moving and revealing story with the opening chapter of the book Ruzbihan called The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love, we cannot help noticing certain parallels. From the autobiographical details in that prologue, we learn that when Ruzbihan set out to write the book, he had already reached a high degree of spiritual advancement.

But he still had to undergo the trial of love. That meant being initiated into his own distinctive form of spirituality: one that experiences human love not as a temptation to conquer, as ordinary ascetics do, but as a summons to spiritual transformation. Upon this transformation depends access to inward tawhid: the discovery that one and the same being is love, lover, and beloved.

All of this agrees with the situation described in the prologue to the Jasmine, and with the teaching it promises to unfold: “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I sought to understand the secret of the human form.”62

The prologue is itself a spiritual autobiography. Through images and allusions, it describes the point Ruzbihan had reached on the spiritual path when his progress was to be tested through love. I have translated the prologue elsewhere, so I will quote only a few passages here: “Having returned from the heavenly world, what I experienced in this world was the very condition of being put to the test: the desolation of finding and yet not finding (the feeling that what one has attained remains inaccessible even in the moment of attainment). It was then that I made my home in the world of Beauty [...].

“Consumed by this loving melancholy for divine Beauty, I migrated into the passing world of created beings. My destiny carried me toward the company of beautiful people [...]. And suddenly, at the edge of the Square of Bounties, in the mirror of the Signs of beauty, I perceived the divine Attributes.”63

Then, just as in Mecca—to such a degree that we are tempted to wonder whether one event has been transposed into the other—a beautiful being suddenly appears before a man already far advanced on the inward Way. Ruzbihan leaves her identity vague, referring to her simply as a “charming fairy” (jinni lo'bati) or a “heavenly maiden,”64 although he draws on every resource of the Persian language to describe her extraordinary beauty.

The moment of her appearance is precisely located on the horizon of his soul's inner time. He has just recalled meditating upon two Quranic verses that are among the sacred “texts” of the mystical devotion to human beauty: “We created the human being in the most beautiful of forms” (95:4); “Oh, how beautiful is your form!” (40:66; 64:3). This is the moment when the revelation of human beauty floods Ruzbihan's consciousness in the way that a Sufi experiences it: at once an enchantment of joy and a kind of sacred dread before the very secret of the divine within the human. To encounter beauty face to face is therefore to suffer the torment of finding and not finding.

Our modern civilizations have so thoroughly “desacralized” human beauty—through metaphysical secularization following upon religious asceticism, through unconscious profanations committed in the name of advertising or sporting conventions, and through supposedly enlightened “demythologizations”—that the numinous, or awe-inspiring sacred, character beauty possesses for the faithful in love may be among the strangest, most alien things imaginable to a person today.

Yet this is as fundamental a phenomenon (Urphänomen) as perceiving a sound or a color. A sound or a color cannot be “proved.” Either one is able to perceive beauty as at once fascinating and terrifying, awakening joy and desperate longing, bearing witness to a presence that is nevertheless not there and to an absence that nevertheless gives a sign of itself here—as Ruzbihan will describe it—or one is unable to perceive it. In the latter case, it is better not to speak of the religion of the faithful in love at all.

Ruzbihan suddenly sees this beauty before him, leaving us uncertain whether he is describing a vision or a physical encounter. Or rather, he is describing what normally happens in his experience: every event in the visible world opens out into a visionary perception of the invisible. A dialogue then begins, held together by a delicate thread, its alternating exchanges artfully arranged.

We must follow its stages, because they disclose the whole purpose of the book. The opening situation is this. In Mecca, the beautiful young woman initially knew nothing of the mystical adoration directed toward her. Here, the woman who will become the book's dedicatee is no doubt fully aware of her own beauty, but she knows nothing of what that beauty can mean to a Sufi.

To put it technically, she does not understand the theophanic role—the power to reveal the divine—with which her beauty has been endowed. The irony of the dialogue is that she herself takes it upon herself to remind the Sufi Ruzbihan of the orthodox teaching of the “pious ascetics”: to make her beauty an object of contemplation is to go astray.

Ruzbihan greets her with enthusiasm: “You belong to the company of the mystics faithful in love, O beautiful icon! You are supremely worthy of them, even though you do not join us in drinking the wine of love at the gathering of ecstasy.” She answers: “To turn away from the divine world would be a culpable neglect. To make me the object of your contemplation would be the place of your ruin—unless, indeed, you are already lost.”65

The first episode reveals that this apparent dialogue is really a monologue. Ruzbihan replies: “Many have lost their way in love. Rational intellect has no power, through the treasure of your love, to enter into that other love”—divine love. And he dares to ask: “As you are known to the gaze of God”—that is, as God beholds Himself in you—“who, then, are you? Tell me. And as you are in the secret of the theophanies, what are you?”

The answer rises from Ruzbihan's own consciousness. It is the young woman who is supposed to speak, certainly, but she speaks as she exists in his vision: “She said to me: The secret of divinity (lahut) is within humanity (nasut), without the divinity being disturbed by incarnation. The beauty of the human creature is the direct reflection of divine Beauty. Creation begins with me; it comes to its fulfillment in God.”

There follows a short poem that might have flowered on the lips of Sophia, divine Wisdom, in the Book of Wisdom: “You are the appearing of beauty to me, O Beloved! Will you not tell me where your being comes from?—I am the work of the hands of divinity (lahut). I am the leader and guide of humanity (nasut). I was the first creature to exist in the world (...). It is me whom God contemplates through every creature; yet my own nature remains separate from every creature.”66

Ruzbihan sinks deeper into his inward dialogue: “I perceived the mystery of Beauty in the human image offered me by this bride, in the majesty that made the grace of her essential nature so imposing.... Through prolonged contemplation, the qualities of her soul's purity took on for me an immaterial form (bi-makan, independent of the place where they appeared).”67 What constituted the essence beneath her outward human form became independent, for him, of its visible symbol.

So independent, indeed, that his charming interlocutor finds the conversation is going on too long and tries to break it off. Still no closer to understanding what she has to do with any of this, she repeats her first thoroughly orthodox warning: “To my mind, Sufism is incompatible with license. Making me the object of contemplation is no business of people who profess the spiritual life (ahl-e walayat).”

In short, the “charming fairy” speaks with an orthodoxy that neither Qushayri nor Ibn Taymiyya would disown. The contemplative should contemplate the Creator's power in His work. There is no place for emotion in that.68

Now the questions alternate, becoming more urgent and more decisive. “After all this, she spoke again to test me: ‘O Sufi! What place does human love have in divine love?’—I said to her: ‘The love I feel for you is precisely the beginning of that divine love.

“The condition of iltibas—the double meaning in which one reality appears through another—is absolutely unavoidable if one is to experience the ecstatic intoxication of divine love, whether one is a beginner or the most accomplished of mystics.’—She: ‘On the path you follow, to feel love for me can only be an error.’—I: ‘The Book revealed to our Prophet itself bears witness to chaste love.’”

Ruzbihan invokes in support the magnificent twelfth surah of the Quran, the story of Joseph. He adds traditions handed down from the Prophet, among them one especially dear to the faithful in love: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies without betraying his secret, dies as a true witness (shahid, ‘martyr’).” Or this one: “Whoever is possessed by love and an overwhelming preoccupation with God, for God and in God, loves beautiful faces.” And there are all the sayings of the Sufi masters, such as this one from Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri: “Whoever has become intimate with God is intimate with every beautiful thing and every graceful face.”69

These are impressive authorities, and Ruzbihan could multiply them. (He might have referred to Suhrawardi's Vade Mecum of the Faithful in Love, had he known it.) Beneath their densely allusive language lies the decisive question for the faithful in love: what does it mean to love God? Whom does the mystic love when he speaks of his love for God? Can one love a being of whom one has no image or conception at all?

But if an image is needed, where can it arise, and from what? In the absence of such an image, is it even legitimate to use the word love in speaking of God? Ruzbihan's beautiful interlocutor, whose stern orthodoxy seems to be wavering, now asks: “Tell me, is it permissible to use the word love (ishq, eros) of God? May anyone claim to love Him with passionate love? Is the word love, as mystics use it, merely a homonym—a word that has different meanings in different contexts? Are we permitted to speak of love in relation to God: love of God, in God, through God?”

This question is so important that it not only defines where Sufism stands in relation to the monotheism of outward Islam; it has also divided the Sufi masters themselves. Ruzbihan replies at length, invoking those who allow such language.70

After all, was David not said to have been called “the passionate lover of God” (ashiq Allah)? And did certain members of the Quraysh not declare, “Truly, Muhammad has fallen in love with his God”? For Ruzbihan, the fact that such love is attested in the person of the Prophet carries more weight than all the arguments proving that one may legitimately love God.71 For the Prophet Muhammad, the model of prophetic Sufism, had seen his God “in the most beautiful of forms.”

Ruzbihan then recalls the celebrated pairs of lovers in Arabic and Persian courtly poetry. He goes back as far as the Prophet's own circle, to Bishr and Hind, and recalls the Prophet's moving words about them: “Glory be to God, who has raised up within my community rivals to Joseph and Zulaykha!”72

“Moreover,” he continues, “it was of human love as the royal road to divine love that these words were spoken: Be chaste before God, and keep hidden in your soul what He causes to blossom there (33:37).... Read again the books that preserve the memories of the prophets, and understand that we are not concerned here with theoretical reflections on love.

“As for divine love, we cannot cross the rushing river—the Jayhun—of tawhid without first crossing the bridge of your love. The prophets and the spiritual friends of God (Awliya) are protected from suspicions of carnal desire. This is the subtle point in love that those versed in iltibas, in its double meaning, know so well.”73

At the end of this prologue, which so clearly announces the book's purpose, we encounter once again this characteristic term from Ruzbihan's vocabulary.

We can now begin to grasp what it means for a teaching that will present the experience of human love as initiation into inward tawhid.

We can also appreciate the concise definition Ruzbihan gives elsewhere: “The beginnings of divine love require human reality (bandagi); the sublimity of tawhid requires divine reality (khoda'i). It is this situation that I have named iltibas, the overlap of meanings.”74

Now Ruzbihan's interlocutor is shaken. Is he not revealing her to herself by revealing the meaning of the beauty she bears, the beauty that makes him her disciple, one of her faithful in love? The roles become reciprocal, just as they did in Mecca when the beautiful singer became Ruzbihan's disciple in turn.

“By God!” she asks, “could you explain to me in Persian how human love is involved in divine love? Could you write a little book that would serve as a spiritual guide—an Imam—for us, and for all lovers and beloveds, a subject of meditation for pilgrims devoted to the religion of love?”

Ruzbihan hastens to fulfill his beloved's wish, to obey her command: “And so I began to compose a book to make human and divine love clear, that it might bring lovers and the faithful in love the joy of intimacy, the flowers of the most holy Paradise. I have called it The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love.”75

The book's governing intention, and the occasion that gave rise to it, have now been set out. Ruzbihan will write in the inward presence of the woman to whom it is dedicated. That presence is recalled at the end of each chapter in a kind of lyrical psalm evoking the power of her beauty to reveal the divine.

Together, the book's thirty-two chapters trace the route of an inward pilgrimage. Here we can mention only its major stages. We already possess some of its essential ideas and terms. We have just dwelt on iltibas, the overlap or ambiguity of meanings, a term we have met several times because it is inseparable from the idea governing all Ruzbihan's Sufism: theophany (tajalli, zohur), the manifestation of the divine.

From that idea follows his understanding of how the divine and the human are related, and how such a relationship is possible. From it follows, in turn, the idea that human love can initiate us into inward tawhid. This stands in the sharpest possible contrast to habits of thought inherited elsewhere from a negative asceticism, so alien to the vision of the faithful in love that their teaching appears to it as a paradox.

The idea of theophany itself calls for another key term, already found in the Book of the Clouding and frequently used in the Jasmine. It is one of the essential words in the vocabulary of all those spiritual teachers who have professed the religion of mystical love for the supreme divine Attribute, Beauty—the manifestation of the divine in beauty. That word is shahid.76 It is difficult to translate with a single English term. Its Arabic root, from which it forms the word for the person performing an action, conveys the ideas of being personally present at an event, witnessing it with one's own eyes, and testifying to what one has seen.

Thus shahid can mean “one who is present,” “one who contemplates,” or “witness.” The Sufis also use it for a psychological phenomenon: the inward image of something absent, which the image makes present, or even any content of consciousness that predominates at a given moment. In a more specialized sense, finally, they mean by it any beautiful person one loves, either because that person's beauty makes present and bears witness to distant, absent, invisible divine Beauty—re-presents it—or because one carries that person's image within one's heart.77

The shahid, then, is the beautiful face the mystic takes as a “witness of contemplation,” whether in inward imagination, during the sama or spiritual concert, or in a personal encounter.78 Insofar as the beautiful person bears witness to invisible Beauty, making it present and visible, this person is a witness who testifies.

But at the very same time, the beauty of the witness is the object of the mystic's contemplation. The shahid—the one who performs the witnessing—is also the mashhud: the one contemplated, the one attested to, the one made present. The word thus has two meanings and performs two functions. We believe both are best conveyed by “witness of contemplation”79: active and passive, subject and object. The witness is a subject who calls forth contemplation by bearing witness and by being present; and precisely in doing so, the witness also becomes the object of that contemplation.

This double meaning becomes fully intelligible at the level of inward tawhid, the consciousness the initiate must ultimately attain. We need only turn to the mystical commentaries on the Quranic verse (85:3, the surah of the Zodiac), where the two words appear together in a mysterious oath. They are interpreted through the idea that God is at once love, lover, and beloved.

Ruzbihan declares, for example: “The shahid is He, and the mashhud is He. He sees Himself through Himself, for in truth no one sees Him.... The shahid is He, and the mashhud is the hearts of the mystics to whom He is present”—that is, He is their shahid precisely by being their mashhud: it is He who contemplates them when they contemplate Him—“and the shahid is also the hearts of the mystical lovers, while their mashhud is having Him face to face. He is their shahid and He is their mashhud. He is the gnostic's shahid, and, in return, the gnostic is His shahid.”80

This is why Ruzbihan's understanding of shahid, with the reciprocity and reversibility belonging to the “witness of contemplation”—the one who both contemplates and is contemplated—is inseparable from the image of a mirror. Our spiritual writers constantly turn to the mirror to explain what inward knowledge involves. The mirror, in turn, holds the secret of theophany (tajalli), the appearing of the divine.

We are dealing with a whole network of images and ideas, each closely bound to the others. Understood as something like a reflection in a mirror, theophany distinguishes Sufism both from the monotheism of Islamic orthodoxy and from the Christian orthodox doctrine of incarnation. Precisely because it works like a mirror, theophany allows us to conceive the mystery within the divine itself—the identity of love, lover, and beloved—and enables the mystic to glimpse and experience it.

The idea of theophany reveals Sufism's enduring kinship with Shiism, just as it marks Sufism off from every abstract monotheism. It involves the idea of divine anthropomorphosis: the divine taking the appearance of human form. The Human Form, the heavenly Anthropos, the spiritual Adam, is the manifestation of God. This human form is at once the shahid that contemplates God and shows God His own Image, and, in showing that Image to Him, also becomes His mashhud—the Image He contemplates.81 It is through this form that God becomes visible.

It makes possible the prophetic affirmation: “I contemplated my God in the most beautiful of forms.” This vision stands midway between tashbih, making God resemble created things, and ta'til, stripping divinity of its qualities until nothing remains but an abstraction. These are the two dangers that threaten abstract monotheism, into one or the other of which it falls when it lacks the help of theophany. (The whole Shiite understanding of the Imams rests upon this insight.)

Yet this is also what distinguishes Sufi theosophy from the dogma of the Incarnation defined by the Christian councils.

What is at issue is a taking of human form on the heavenly plane, in the Malakut, the angelic fullness of being—not an irreversible historical event on earth in which divinity enters human clay, human “flesh.” It is not with their bodily eyes that witnesses behold this theophany in “history.” They behold it “in Heaven,” through the faculty of heavenly sight (chashm-e malakuti), as caro spiritualis, spiritual flesh.

And because it is an “event in Heaven,” not a material occurrence irrevocably fixed in history, the theophany can be repeated as often as a shahid is present—as often as a beautiful face is invested with its prophetic meaning. It is neither enôikêsis (holûl, indwelling or immanence) nor ensarkosis (tajassod, incarnation). Nor is it kenosis, an emptying, exhaustion, or withdrawal of the divine. It is the triumphant manifestation, radiant with majesty, of the divine Attribute above all others: Beauty.

Every renewal of this heavenly event gives rise to the ecstatic devotion to Beauty. To reject beauty, as do the various forms of asceticism—in religion, art, or social life—is a sacrilegious betrayal on humanity's part. In so doing, humanity takes it upon itself to drive God out of Paradise. For beauty is the very way of being of Paradise: to see it, and truly understand what it announces, is to enter that way of being. Adam—that is, human beauty—is the shahid, and Paradise is the mashhad, the place of this witnessing, this Presence.

The mystery of this mashhad is what every comparison with a mirror tries to make clear. God does not become incarnate: divine Beauty “enters into” beautiful forms as an image “enters” a mirror. The earthly human condition cannot be redeemed by dragging the divine down to its own level, but only by the transfiguration the divine brings about within it.

The Image is not incarnated in the mirror. Rather, by appearing there—in that mashhad—it sees and shows to himself the person looking into the mirror, the person whose image it is. The one looking sees himself by means of this image. Without it, he could not see himself. That is why the eye of the Image is the eye through which he sees himself. Ruzbihan has already taught us this.

To look at the image is vision. To see that the gaze of the Image—the gaze of the shahid—is my own gaze looking back at me through that Image: that is the vision of vision. Ultimately, there is a gaze directed upon myself without my own act of looking. It is Majnun's gaze, which is Layla: the secret of the Lover who is the Beloved. These reflections lend support to some of the most striking passages we previously encountered in the Book of the Clouding. It is out of longing for a shahid, a witness, that God creates the world.

Yet the gaze of that witness can only be God's own gaze beholding Himself: the vision of vision. Otherwise God “cannot see it.” And that is why, since its creation, God has not looked upon this eyeless world—a world blind through refusal or unconsciousness.82

We can now begin to see why the divine identity of love, lover, and beloved requires the idea of theophany. As with a mirror, theophany consists in God's being both shahid and mashhud: the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. And because the theophany is a manifestation of Beauty, and Beauty's theophany takes human form, it follows that shahid and mashhud have been human beauty—the heavenly Anthropos—since before all beginnings, in the pre-eternity of pre-eternities.

When Ruzbihan's young interlocutor says83 that the mystic should contemplate the Creator's power in the creature and form an idea of that power from the creature, she is innocently speaking the rational language of cause and effect used by theologians and pious ascetics.

The feeling for theophany among the faithful in love is altogether different. They do not need to start from one thing in order to reach another. They must look directly, face to face. We see an image only in the mirror, not elsewhere, and not by reasoning our way toward it from the mirror. This is the whole basis of human love in the idea of theophany.

Creation is theophany; and as theophany it is anthropomorphosis, the manifestation of God in the heavenly human form (see further below). It follows that from the pre-eternity of Creation there has been a unio mystica, a mystical union, between divinity and the human form. It is this same relation of theophany—the speculative or mirror-like (speculum means “mirror”) foundation of the identity of love, lover, and beloved—that grounds the revelation of divine love in human love.

For at the furthest limit of its mystical experience, human love is precisely this form of divine love. We are reading the one text at last in its true sense, provided that we do not look at the mirror without seeing the image. To do that would still be merely figurative love (ishq majazi).

We must look instead at the Image appearing in the mirror (ishq haqiqi, love in its true sense), an Image that is your very gaze.

Human love leads us toward inward tawhid because we must pass through the trial of the Veil—the “clouding”—and love alone can make that Veil transparent as a mirror. Majnun is Layla. He knows that it is Layla loving herself through Majnun's love for her.

Majnun has then understood inward tawhid: it is God loving Himself through Majnun's love for Layla's beauty, which reveals God to him. That is why, at its ultimate limit, as we shall see, inward tawhid speaks in the very language of the highest consciousness of human love. It requires a transformation of self-awareness of the kind Ruzbihan describes in his Risala-ye Qodsiya: “The inward meanings of tawhid are not for just anyone who sets out on the Way to discover.

“For the secret of tawhid that must be discovered is the garment covering the divine condition, through which the soul of the soul (the Beloved in the true sense) appears under a double meaning. Until the mystical pilgrim becomes 1 × 1 (wahid dar wahid, not 1 + 1), he cannot attain the vision of vision (iyan-e iyan), which is tawhid.”84

We can now group the themes marking the stages of the inward pilgrimage that the author of the Jasmine invites us to undertake beside him.

They are, in broad outline: (1) the idea of theophany as the divine taking human form in the beauty of the human figure; (2) the understanding of Adam that follows from this, which entails a prophetic meaning of beauty, since Beauty is the supreme sacred, religious, and mystical revelation: Muhammad is the prophet of this revelation and of the religion of love it sustains; (3) the discovery of beauty's prophetic meaning by whoever penetrates the secret of iltibas, the double meaning expressed in the mirror; (4) the pre-existent foundation of this recognition in the pre-eternity of the Holy Spirits (arwah-e qodsi), the spiritual identities of human beings existing before their earthly lives; (5) the realization of this prophetic meaning through an interpretation of the soul that passes from contemplating the mirror as an object to contemplating the Image revealed within it as shahid-mashhud, the one contemplating and contemplated—a schooling in love that leads from figurative love (majazi) to love in its true sense (haqiqi); and (6) the discovery, and lived experience, at the furthest perfection of human love, of the secret of inward tawhid: that in the perfection of love, God Himself is love, lover, and beloved. It is here that the “story” of the faithful in love comes to an end.

PreviousIV. Diarium spiritualeNextVI. The Inner Pilgrimage

Chapter VI The Inner Pilgrimage

The more one reads and rereads The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love, the harder it becomes to place the work within any established literary genre. To follow the movement of its inspiration, one would need to approach it as a piece of music, tracing its themes, counterthemes, responses, transpositions, episodes, and so on. Any attempt to impose a system on it introduces a rational order that conceals its richness.

Almost every chapter returns to the six themes outlined above. They sound through one another, sometimes as hints, sometimes in overlapping voices, carried by a language of incomparable beauty, though so archaic and difficult that even an Iranian reader today finds it challenging. And it is through these recurring notes, now subdued, now resounding, that the inner pilgrimage unfolds, leading ever deeper into the mystery of beauty and the love that initiates us into it.

1. The Theophany in Beauty

The first theme is the divine assumption of human form: the primordial theophany, or manifestation, of the Divine Being, who is at once love, lover, and beloved. When the creative command fulfilled the desire of the Divine Being to reveal itself in creation, and forms and figures appeared, “it was in the human form that the quintessence of all existence was concentrated, because this form was the most subtle of the essences of the heavenly realm (malakût).”

Rûzbehân expresses the point in a brief formula, also taken up by his anonymous commentator85: “Adam [the heavenly Human Being] is God himself, clothed in the garment of existence (libâs-e hastî) and assuming the human condition [that is, taking on human form]86.” This theophany was itself the act of an eternal love whose “object” was its own beauty. It necessarily unfolded through the attributes of grace and beauty and passed through successive veils, already described in the Book of the Clouding: Intelligence, Spirit, Heart, and physical nature. These are at once stages of the cosmos and levels of consciousness within the human microcosm87.

Qur’anic verses and sayings of the Prophet (hadith) proclaiming the divine beauty of the human form are frequently invoked. Earthly humanity is the veil of physical nature covering the radiant beauty of the One who contemplates and is contemplated (shâhid-mashhûd). For—and this must be stressed again—the divine assumption of human form takes place on a heavenly plane. Adam belongs to the malakût: he is still the angelic Adam.

That is why Rûzbehân repeatedly insists: “Know that the mystery of the theophanic Manifestation is in no way an incarnation. Otherwise, when the divine Essence revealed itself in its theophanies, the majesty of that Essence would be abolished; and these many qiblas [the beautiful faces toward which love turns] would lose their proper function, which is to make direct vision possible within the vision of the theophanies themselves88.”

We must say it plainly: the belief that the divine literally takes material flesh is what leads love astray. It places the first obstacle in the path of the faithful lover, an obstacle that must be crossed and overcome before one can know love as theophany. That knowledge means seeing the Image that appears in the mirror without imagining that it has become part of the mirror’s material substance.

The divine assumption of human form concerns form, not the materiality of “flesh.” When these are confused—by Christians who affirm incarnation and by the jurists (foqahâ’) who condemn it—human Eros is likewise confused with bodily sexuality. Without a genuine sense of theophany, one can never experience human love as Rûzbehân does: as an initiation into the divine love that is itself the source of the divine assumption of human form. Rûzbehân admits that he once faced this obstacle himself.

At first he, too, could not distinguish the immaterial appearance of the Beloved: “He did not yet understand that this event takes place outside human clay, without any material penetration of the divine Attributes within the boundaries of created being, and without anything resembling an emanation of those Attributes beyond those boundaries. Had he understood, he would have sought beyond the realm of created being what cannot be contained or held within it; and with the dew of tears shed in love’s sorrow, he would have wiped the dust of transience from the face of the Eternal Bride89.”

To “wipe away this dust” is to perceive the theophany where it appears—in its place of manifestation, its mazhar—while recognizing that the eternal Image remains, as it were, suspended there, not physically incorporated into or confined to that place.

The Eternal Bride thus initiates Rûzbehân, her faithful lover, into a freedom from both incarnationism and idolatry, “filtering for him the pure draught of love, leaving in it not the slightest trace of an impure material mingling of divinity with humanity, yet softening the features of her sublimity so that a human being can bear her beauty, through that sweetly scented tinting to which the verse alludes: We created the human being in the most beautiful stature.” Rûzbehân says all this in incomparable language, not through abstractions, but through images that symbolically evoke his spiritual experience90.

The anonymous commentator is a remarkable ally to Rûzbehân’s insight, making explicit what lies behind his words. “Outwardly,” he says, “the case of the Faithful in Love resembles that of those among the Jews who associate (moshrikûn) another divinity with the One; it also resembles that of the Christian associators who have made Jesus and Maryam partners in divinity; and finally that of the Incarnationists in general (holâliyân), who professed that God dwells (enoikesis, immanence, holûl) within created beings.

“Just as these three groups, after affirming divine oneness (tawhîd), were drawn toward dividing the divine nature or believing in incarnation, so the Faithful in Love, after attaining tawhîd in its purity, were troubled by the beauty of the human form and recognized signs of theophany (tajallî) in that form of manifestation (mazhar).

“But there is a difference. The former did not know what they were doing; unaware, they uttered absurdities. The Faithful in Love, however, became aware and saw: they explained and interpreted what their vision implied. The three expressions joined together by the venerable shaykh [Rûzbehân]—a draught filtered from this cup … despite the suspicion of incarnation … without the disturbance of any mingling of divinity and humanity—are three allusions meant to make clear the difference between the religion of love, on the one hand, and associationism and incarnationism on the other. Understand91!”

This entire spirituality, then, rests upon the idea of theophany92. Within Christian spirituality, one can speak of incarnatio continuata, a continuing incarnation, only figuratively, if the dogma of the Incarnation is maintained as a unique historical event. Theophanies, by contrast, are without limit, because the divine Attributes are without limit. With everything the idea entails—the mirror, the shâhid or witness of contemplation, the endless renewal of manifestation—theophany becomes the supreme pattern and governing principle of mystical experience.

Rûzbehân explains: “When God, through love and inclination, makes his faithful servant both the Desiring and the Desired, both the Lover and the Beloved, that servant of love assumes toward God the role of witness of contemplation (shâhid). It is God who, in an eternal act of contemplation, contemplates himself within him and clothes him in his own Attributes. No incarnation takes place, for God remains apart from all created being. Or rather, here is something beyond the reach of understanding and intelligence.

“Until you have understood what theophany is—God! God!—recite this precept: Shape your being according to the pattern of the divine qualities. When the divine lights have given his being a twofold significance [belonging to two orders at once], God invests him with the privilege of divine lordship (robûbîya). He becomes God’s beloved, for the divine intention toward this mystical lover is this: until in love you become identical with the Beloved, you cannot become one with the Beloved in the retreat where union is attained93.”

In other words, divine love is the secret of theophany, and theophany is the very form that divine love takes. Until human love is shaped by that pattern, it has not attained perfection—which is to say, the divine reality of love—for that reality is theophany.

But once this perfection has been reached, the one who contemplates is the one contemplated, and the lover is the beloved. This announcement of a transformation anticipates our final theme (see theme 6 below).

2. The Prophet of Beauty

This mystical understanding of Adam—the manifestation of God in the heavenly human form, itself the manifestation of God’s essential attribute of beauty—gives rise to a corresponding understanding of prophecy. Prophecy, too, is understood through the revelation of the divine in human beauty. The importance of this theme cannot be overstated.

By presenting Muhammad as the prophet of the religion of mystical love, it shows how Sufism understands itself: as a mystical religion that discloses the inner meaning of prophetic religion94. The Prophet as he lives in the consciousness of Sufism—a young Arab “in love with his God”—is quite different from the figure usually presented by the historical study of religions.

But we are not concerned here with historical criticism. We are describing the structure of a spiritual experience. For the Sufis, Muhammad is the prophet of the divine assumption of human form, the revelation of divine beauty in the beauty of the human form. This was his distinctive prophetic gift, setting him apart from all the prophets before him. He testified to it both in inspired sayings that echo the verses of the Book revealed through the Angel and in his own visionary experience, which, together with his prophetic calling, makes him the model of mystical experience for the Sufi.

Among the sayings that have given Sufis inexhaustible material for meditation is one that bears witness to the Imago Dei, the divine image.

We must give it its full force. It speaks of an image whose visible shape corresponds to the invisible divine reality: the Form of God (sûrat al-Haqq) to which the Prophet himself testified when he told of seeing his God “in the most beautiful of forms.” This resemblance, this meeting of the two, is not a result of the divine Act; it is that Act, the act of divine self-manifestation.

“The whole substance of Adam’s being was poured into the mould of the theophany.” Similarly, the other hadith in which God declares that, when his faithful servant draws close to him, God himself becomes that servant’s sight, hearing, hand, and so on, already applies to Adam. We have encountered this archetype of mystical union (unio mystica) arising in the very first theophany.

When the Prophet, bringing together the threefold initiative of religious Law (sharî’at), the spiritual Path (tarîqat), and mystical Truth (haqîqat), “saw with the eyes of the soul the imprint of the Beloved in the mirror formed by Adam’s very substance, he proclaimed to the holy Spirits (arwâh-e qodsî, the spiritual individualities of human beings), in a voice of triumph: God created Adam in the image of his own form95.”

Muhammad thus takes on the role of the archangel Michael, calling the angels to adore the human form96—that is, divine humanity, the purest substance of their own heavenly realm. The heavenly Adam was their shâhid, their witness of contemplation. They knew that this did not contradict the declaration that “nothing resembles Him,” and that, conversely, to deny every resemblance in order to avoid tashbîh (likening God to created things) is to fall into the emptiness of abstraction (ta’til, stripping God of meaningful attributes).

“The Light of divinity rose first upon that Niche of Lights (meshkat) which is the form of Adam; from there its Sun rose over all the witnesses of contemplation who make its beauty present … All things and beings that have received some of this light are, in this world and for the Faithful in Love, flowers in the garden of the one Beauty and Majesty97.”

“The nearer one is to the source of beauty, the nearer one is to the covenant of love.” That is why the Prophet, with a “gesture of feminine tenderness,” would hasten to kiss and lift to his eyes anything in this world that had freshly blossomed forth from the Beloved. Whenever he saw a rose, he would raise it to his eyes and say: “The red rose belongs to the beauty of God!98” Such, for him, was the privilege of every beautiful being.

“Whoever has been granted beauty has been chosen by the divine light, singled out for the sweetness of intimacy; such a one is called a second Adam99.” And so the other famous saying follows naturally: “God is beautiful and loves beauty100.” The beauty he loves is his own beauty, which he shows to himself in the form of Adam.

This is why the Prophet’s saying points both to the beauty of Adam as shâhid, the witness of contemplation, and to the beauty of Paradise as mashhad, the place where this witness makes the beauty of the primordial divine contemplation present. For this is what Paradise is: “Every being whose beauty we admire bears the trace of this twofold beauty—that of the shâhid and that of the mashhad, of Adam and of Paradise101.”

Paradise, then, is wherever beauty bears witness to, and makes present, the identity of love, lover, and beloved. In turn, that identity is reflected in another: love, Paradise, and beauty are one.

Thus the Prophet affirmed that “the supreme Good toward which beings aspire in this world and the next appears to every human being in the features of lover and beloved. For the love between lover and beloved is the direct influence (ta’thîr) of the love inherent in the divine realities (ilâhîyât)102.” The force that moves the lover is therefore a love that existed before all time. Beauty is the “phenomenon of the divine,” the divine appearing that sets this love alight. Beauty bears the divine lights in its twofold nature, and leads whoever loves it back to the very Source of those lights103.

In a third saying, the prophet of divine Beauty gives the Faithful in Love their rule: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies keeping the secret of that love, dies as a true witness104.”

Another saying alludes to the eternal foundation of this rule: “Concerning the pre-eminence of the Faithful in Love, there is a subtle allusion which can serve beginners as a sign guiding them along the path of love, while for those who have attained perfection it is a symbolic account of love’s origins105.”

This “subtle allusion,” this “symbolic account,” will be developed below (theme 4). It concerns the existence of the holy Spirits—the spiritual individualities of human beings—before their earthly lives, a theme in which Platonic memories grow into a prophetic philosophy of love.

As for “dying of love,” we must understand it, first, in the literal sense of physical death, brought about by a passion so overwhelming that it engulfs the whole person. This presupposes a human constitution in which psychic energies exert all the greater force because unconscious life has not yet been restrained by the rational organization of existence or by the demands and prohibitions of a complex society. The physical organism is then less protected; the soul’s upheavals are felt, and their effects resound, with their full intensity.

A deep belief in the eternity of Spirits is itself a sign of a cultural world in which the relations between psyche and body are experienced quite differently from societies dominated by agnosticism and rationalism. That death from love must also be taken “literally” is suggested by the stories of certain famous heroes of ‘Udhrî love, as well as by those gatherings of mystical preaching in which merely speaking of the Eternal Bride could cause a number of listeners to fall unconscious106.

But “dying of love” must also be understood as a mystical death. Here it means the complete burning away of the desires of the carnal soul, the very thing the Prophet calls the chastity of love107. When the soul has been entirely consumed and the fire dies down, the soul has kept its secret. It is now ready for the transformation in which the contemplator becomes the contemplated, and the lover the beloved, for the gaze with which the soul looks is the very gaze of the face it beholds; and that face, in turn, beholds the soul that looks upon it.

At the end of this chapter (theme 6), we shall see that this was the case with Majnûn, and that it distinguishes him from the heroes of ‘Udhrî love generally. When Majnûn’s original ego has been so completely consumed that he can speak as Layla in the first person, he becomes the pure image of esoteric tawhîd, the innermost truth of divine oneness.

To reach it, one must undergo the “mystical death of love.” The witness of contemplation is no longer merely a shâhid, but a shahîd: a true witness, a “martyr”108. This is the degree of love the Prophet meant in his saying.

The lover who attains such faithfulness becomes a companion of the prophets, because Beauty itself has a prophetic function above all others: it is Beauty to which the “witnesses” testify, Beauty which they make present and bring into contemplation. The Hurufis would later stress this idea: the Qur’an is a silent book, while the beauty of the human face is a speaking Qur’an. Both therefore call for a prophetic interpretation109.

But every ta’wîl, every uncovering of an inner meaning, is also an interpretation of the soul—an exodus in which the soul returns to the true meaning.

To pass through the “true meaning” of beauty is to undergo this mystical death, which raises the faithful lover to the rank of true witness, shahîd, and prophet, Nabî: “When love has raised the lover to the rank of true Witness (shahîd), he becomes the companion of the prophets in the world of Jabarût [divine power] and the fields of Malakût [the angelic realm], riding with them upon love’s mount, for the royal road of love is the place (mashâhid) where martyrs are slain and prophets bear witness110.”

It was upon this Path, where prophets and faithful lovers share the same witness and the same prophetic contemplation, that Muhammad encountered the mystery of theophany in a form suited to him. The account is among the most famous and cherished of all hadith for the Sufis.

Rûzbehân writes: “The light that rises upon the visible form of a beloved being is the light of archetypal divine beauty. The beloved, invested with these qualities, derives them from God, for it is the Sun of Majesty that rises upon that face from the height of the mountain before all time. If you have the eyes to see, contemplate how this Sun rises over a beloved face.

“In the mirror formed by the delicate substance of its visible shape, contemplate the light of the star that is its soul. See how that star rises in the East formed by the visible expression of its qualities, and lights up the entire universe of that person111.” Whoever understands this can begin to penetrate the secret of beauty’s twofold significance.

Archetypal beauty appeared to the Prophet in a face that served as his shâhid, his witness of contemplation; yet he realized that he himself was also the shâhid: the one who sees and is seen. Whether we say that an outward form was perceived in the visionary state as a theophany, or that a form inwardly perceived in vision appeared with all the objective, mind-independent reality of a visible form, is a difference of interpretation. What remains is the Prophet’s testimony in the extraordinary hadith of the vision: “I saw my Lord in the most beautiful of forms112.”

This testimony is invoked again and again in Rûzbehân’s Jasmine. It can indeed be regarded as the central pillar of the theophanic religion of the Faithful in Love. It stands equally far from tashbîh, the crude likening of God to created things, and ta’til, the emptying of God of every attribute. It resolves the difficulties of tanzîh, the insistence that God is beyond all resemblance, through a perception arising at a level unknown to abstract monotheism.

During this theophany, the Prophet “asked for the love without whose sweetness he could imagine no sweetness in the world. He said: I ask You for Your love, the love of everyone who loves You, and the love of a deed that brings me nearer to Your love. Through the beautiful witness of contemplation [the Youth seen in the vision], eternal Beauty had broken into his soul; and now, beneath the overwhelming power of that vision’s beauty, pure love blossomed in him113.”

Muhammad was thus the prophet of divine Eros. By announcing that “He created the human being in the image of his own form,” he showed himself capable of enduring the shock of the divine appearance: the theophany in the radiance of human beauty. He testified that he had truly seen this vision “in the most beautiful of forms.”

The hadith of the vision sounds like a paradoxical answer to the refusal given to Moses: “You shall not see Me (lan tarânî)114.” The mountain from whose summit Moses asked God, “Show Yourself to me,” was, according to Rûzbehân, the mountain of Moses’ own being. “Look at the mountain,” he was told.

But when God manifested himself to it, the mountain was shattered, and Moses fell unconscious115. Muhammad was the first to bear the shock of this theophany. This also distinguishes him, as the prophet of visionary love for divine Beauty, from Abraham, the hero of faith. Scattered through several pages of the Jasmine are subtle teachings on the matter, all affirming the pre-eminence of human beauty over every other kind of beauty.

Abraham entered the path of the malakût through the “openings” of the divine Act—that is, the manifestations of divinity visible to the eye of astrology, the heavenly bodies. In the event that led to his prophetic calling, he directed his vision toward the Signs (âyât) themselves.

Thus, in the urgency of his search and the force of his longing, he exclaimed, “This is my Lord” (Qur’an 6:76–78). It follows that if the Eternal Bride had shown herself to him, as she did to Muhammad, in the form of human beauty, what befell Moses would have befallen Abraham at this stage of his search116. For in the mirror of the cosmos God appears through the attributes of Sublimity and Power, whose onslaught breaks the harmony of contemplative knowledge.

Abraham awoke to consciousness of the invisible malakût and freed himself from the wandering stars of the heavens. The “three that set” (Sun, Moon, and Venus) are manifestations of the Signs (majâlî-e âyât); they are the place of faith. They are not, as human beauty is, the manifestation of the Essence (majâlî-e dhât)—the divine assumption of human form, the “place” of direct vision117.

But Abraham’s “turn” (nawbat) had not yet come to behold human beauty. The turn of such direct vision was reserved for the one who would be the Seal of the Prophets118. Therefore, realizing that direct vision of eternal archetypal Beauty was not to be found among the Signs (the marvels in the heavens), Abraham withdrew toward his Lord (37:97). Becoming a stranger to all else and rediscovering himself in the beauty of his own soul, he chose the mirror of the heart over the visible Signs, for in that mirror he saw God with the eyes of his innermost consciousness119.

Abraham was content to see what is hidden—the invisible reality of God (ma’nâ-ye Haqq)—with the eye of that innermost consciousness. The time had not yet come to “contemplate the eternal Face of God in the mirror offered by the eyes of human lovers120.” After the prophet who was the hero of faith, the prophet announcing love still had to come. Through him the prophetic meaning of human Beauty would blossom, raising its witness to the rank of a prophet.

Rûzbehân has much to say about this point, so decisive for the Faithful in Love and their understanding of prophecy: “As for the difference between human beauty and beauty other than the human kind—the beauty of colours and things in this world—it is that human beauty is privileged to bear the lights of the theophany of the Essence (anewâr-e tajallî-e dhât), whereas other things owe their beauty to the freshness of a newly blossoming divine manifestation (tarâwat-e f’l).

“Contemplation of the cosmos is the qibla [direction of devotion] of the pious; contemplation of human beauty is the qibla of the Faithful in Love. The powerless defenders of religious conformity criticize us. The Signs of creation in the heavens are more sublime, they say. Why do you not contemplate them? Certainly there are Signs (âyât) in the heavens, and they show the way to inconsolable hearts.

“But upon the human face rises the sun of the theophany of the divine Essence and Attributes. For it was through human beauty that love entered this world, while faith entered it through the body of the cosmos. Whoever has entered the state of love (‘âshiq) no longer looks at the outer world; the only event he sees in the world is what appears upon Joseph’s beautiful face. Love and beauty spring from the same mine: the divine Attributes … To love beauty is to see eternal existence with the very eye of God121.”

3. The Prophetic Meaning of Beauty

Whether human love experiences beauty as a theophany—or, in other words, experiences itself as the consciousness through which beauty is revealed as a theophany—depends on awakening to this hidden meaning within the twofold nature of what the senses perceive. Here Rûzbehân continues his “phenomenology” of spiritual experience, examining the lived state in which the phenomenon of beauty becomes manifest.

The spiritual state that allows beauty to appear, that serves as the organ through which it is perceived, and on which its character as a theophany depends—the “divine eye” contemplating itself—is essentially love. A phenomenology of beauty is a phenomenology of love. Beauty reveals its prophetic meaning to the perfected lover, who has become a companion of the prophets.

Rûzbehân identifies four elements or “pillars” (arkân) of love’s first appearance. (a) The lover’s inmost nature must have become wholly spiritual. The lover must have learned to distinguish the soul’s nature from physical nature and have acquired the capacity to join with purely spiritual beings. (b) The veil hiding the soul is then lifted.

Through its inward powers of seeing and perceiving, the soul joins with the light of the pure beings of the malakût; and their light is the very source and archetype of beauty. (c) Through the meeting of these two lights, the soul has become a pure mirror, a mazhar, a place where the divine appears. It has become akin to love itself and taken on love’s colour (ham-rang, yak-rang: of one colour, perfectly one in hue).

Until now, its capacity was still wholly undetermined. Now, corresponding to that capacity, there is a particular form through which Beauty can appear to the soul, be recognized by it, and be invested with the character of the beloved (ma’shûq). (d) The form of beauty corresponding to the form of love for which this heart has the capacity had so far existed only as a possibility, not yet as an event. “When the light of uncreated Beauty rises out of the fine mist and shines upon the beauty of a lovely creature, archetypal Beauty at last presents itself face to face before the lover’s eyes122.”

These two lights—the light of archetypal Beauty shining through the beloved’s beauty and the light present in the lover’s gaze—appear outwardly to be two separate realities. In their true being, however, they form a single whole expressed in two inseparable and mutually dependent conditions: that of the lover (‘âshiq), whose presence makes possible the perception of beauty and the recognition of the beloved as beloved; and that of the beloved (ma’shûq), whose presence makes possible the lover’s condition as lover. This is why their respective qualities—the capacity of the one and the beauty of the other—are intimately attuned.

Here, too, there is a twofold meaning, an ambiguity that belongs to the experience itself: the one who contemplates becomes the one contemplated, and the lover sees his own face in the beloved, because the light of his gaze and the light of that beauty are, in reality, two aspects of one light. The beloved’s qualities—that is, the invisible spiritual attributes hidden within the beloved’s capacity to be loved (ma’shûqîya), through which the beloved holds sway over the lover—are made manifest through beauty by means of the lover’s active imagination. Inner and outer realities are perfectly synchronized123.

What occurs here corresponds to the indivisible relationship between rabb and marbûb: the personal Lord and the person devoted to that Lord. This is a radical freeing of the relationship from its social and collective framework, unlike the relation generally envisaged by outward-looking theologies between God as universal ruler and humanity as a whole124.

Here lies the prophetic meaning of beauty. As the beloved, without even knowing it, comes to exercise the lordly power conferred by beauty, the God who is love reveals himself both to himself and to the world. This revelation takes the form of a power so foreign to every attempt to turn the divine into a collective institution that it brings such attempts to an end. The beloved’s power thus reveals the true nature of the “victorious,” royal authority belonging to the divine condition of lordship.

In relation to the servant of love, the beloved is God and Lord (rabb); yet this rabb, this personal Lord, could not continue to exist for even an instant without the faithful lover125. In other words, the secret of robûbîya, the divine lordship of the personal Lord loved by the mystic, and the secret of ma’shûqîya, the beloved’s condition of being invested with lordly power, are one and the same secret: an eternal companionship.

And in that companionship, as Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator quietly suggests, even if power and authority belong to the beloved, perhaps the benefit and advantage belong to the lover in servitude, since the beloved’s very reign depends upon the lover’s service of love126.

Now the four “pillars” (arkân), the four elements that constitute love, have been brought together. Love takes shape in the two persons of lover and beloved.

Yet all this, even taken together, still amounts only to love in an imperfect, figurative sense (majâzî), not love in its full reality. An inner pilgrimage must now begin. Its success will determine whether the lover reaches real love, love in its true sense (haqîqî): the awareness that the beauty he loves is a theophany, and that it is not despite its twofold character but because of it that beauty can lead him toward the reality it reveals. In other words, it falls to the lover to bring the prophetic meaning of beauty into flower. That is why, as love awakens, anguish and restlessness awaken in the lover’s heart as well.

The intellect remains captivated by the ambiguity inherent in love awakened by a beautiful human face. The spirit (rûh) turns away from the direct vision of the true Beloved, whom the beauty of the shâhid, its witness of contemplation, makes present to it.

To recover that vision, it must keep watch through the openings of the five senses, attaining through each organ of sense perception the particular theophany proper to it. This is love’s twofold nature, and why the lover must pass through every experience of human love127 as through stages of an ascent, until their fullness is attained: “direct vision (shohûd) of the divine Face in a beautiful form offered to contemplation, in the person of a human creature with a beautiful face128.”

But the pilgrimage is difficult and dangerous (its stages are described below, in theme 5). It holds severe suffering in store and demands a personal discipline sterner than any collective rules of morality or religious Law.

When the veil of human love (‘ishq insânî) that concealed divine love (‘ishq rabbânî) is lifted, the lover’s love becomes an initiate’s love, “not in the sense that his eyes close to the beloved’s outward, visible form or turn away from it, but in the sense that the lover now reaches an inward unveiling of love (kashf-e ‘ishq, an intuition that reveals love’s transcendent meaning, its haqîqat). It becomes clear to him that the Divine Being reveals itself to him in the beloved’s beauty [that is, he contemplates a theophany, tajallî, in that beauty]. He becomes aware of mysterious divine actions working upon him through the beloved’s form, even though the beloved’s visible form [the person who exists outwardly, independently of the lover] remains unaware of them129.”

The beloved is invested with this theophanic function before even becoming aware of the capacity to fulfil it. For this to happen, the beloved must awaken to self-knowledge, must know herself as the lover knows her, as she exists in her Image—the very Image she herself presents to him as her shâhid, her witness of contemplation130.

The prophetic meaning of beauty is then fulfilled within the very person entrusted with it, and there is “light upon light.” Something occurs, for example, like the conclusion of Rûzbehân’s experience in Mecca, which Ibn ‘Arabî recalls when he speaks of the beautiful singer’s “conversion.” This is also the conclusion toward which the Jasmine reaches as it offers itself to the woman to whom it is dedicated, inviting her to know herself as God contemplates himself within her.

Yet the rule is unyielding: “If the initiate has been purified of every sensual weakness in human love, he will stand firm in divine love [that is, the love through which human beauty is perceived as a theophany].

“But if any stain of carnal appetite remains upon the soul’s robe, then, in the world of divine love, the initiate will be thrown from the mount that carries love’s mystical reality (haqîqat)131.”

Whatever the dangers, the answer is not a harsh and negating monastic asceticism. If bodily love is the path leading toward spiritual love, it is because it arises from an alchemy older than time. “Although, from the standpoint of what is essential, bodily love is a lower stage, love is nevertheless the influence of the Red Sulphur of divine Magnificence, cast into the light of the soul’s eyes.

“Thus, from before all eternity, the alchemical work has hidden a soul within the soul of the soul132.” This is why, in the two persons of lover and beloved, love is in truth one and the same tinctura, one colouring brought about by their unitive fusion (yak-rang: perfect oneness of colour). The mystical reality within love sounds a certain note, if you know how to listen.

Until you have tasted this drink133—God! God!—you will understand nothing of our condition. Look into the garden of our love, and hear the singing birds give voice to “Glory be to me!” (the cry of Bastâmî) and “I am God!” (the cry of Hallâj). Listen to those melodies; hear how the minstrel plays the song of love134.

There is a poignant urgency in this appeal from Rûzbehân to the beautiful being to whom his book is dedicated. He wants her to understand the light in which she stands, the theophanic vision he sees in and through her.

But the responsibility for revealing the prophetic meaning of her beauty to her rests upon the mystical lover himself. Should he falter, everything would be jeopardized. And the way is difficult. We have already heard Rûzbehân confess as much135. “Since, by divine command, he had been able to contemplate only the veil of the Eternal Bride, he was veiled from the beloved [or rather, the beloved was veiled from him] by reason of the beloved herself.” He had first to undergo love’s ordeals and its madness, still without any clear understanding of himself.

He returns to this theme in an entire chapter. Speaking of himself in the third person, in the veiled language of personal confession, Rûzbehân takes up once again the four elements of love that he analysed earlier, now as a description of his own story. The passage is especially characteristic of his style: “This nightingale, this singer of a thousand songs, who suddenly fell into the net of the hunters of Trial, lured by the bait of vision, remained caught among the thorns of the rose garden: a certain moon-faced image.

“And there he is, the constant companion of the sufferings she inflicts upon him … Leaving the paradise of tranquillity, he came to the place where love humbles him to dust, though he brought with him love’s thousand prides … Among the pure-hearted Sufis in love’s retreats, he sings again the song of your gestures and washes with his tears the robe that his passion for you has dyed with the blood of love … Ask those who know the harsh law of anguish, those who read and reread the text of melancholy.
