“Then you will learn the courage of this spiritual knight (javânmard, Rûzbehân) upon the Path of love, and discover who this sorrowing heart is among the kings of Knowledge … Oh, the wonder of this Phoenix, who turned from the heaven of everlastingness toward the world of annihilation, and from the world of annihilation turns again toward the world of everlastingness! See what kind of bird you have caught in your snare: the nest of the Sîmorgh of the Throne cannot hold the grain on which he feeds. The bride of Paradise asks God for nothing but his face.

“But look closely: in the heart of love lie all the caskets holding the mystery of the Face of Majesty, for the contemplation of a single hieroglyph in that heaven is enough to exchange angelic modesty for the exuberance of the lover’s condition.

“Then this faithful lover tears apart his heaven-coloured cloak [his Sufi cloak] and tastes the crumbs of the heavenly ones’ feast. Among the ranks of the Sufis, he proclaims the secret of Ego sum Deus (Anâ al-Haqq, ‘I am God’) … Who knows the cipher of this story except the Faithful in Love? Who can decipher the hieroglyphs of this way of being except the people of longing136?”

For the pilgrimage of the faithful lover is governed by two concerns. The lover must meditate upon, uncover, and bring to life the prophetic meaning of beauty; and must remain alert to the danger of giving way to sensual desire. It is significant that among all the Iranian Faithful in Love, from Sanâ’î to Hâfez and beyond, every evocation of beauty’s prophetic meaning awakens memories of Zoroastrianism and finds expression in their distinctive “veiled language,” whose vocabulary is borrowed from the Mazdean tradition.

Whether in Sohrawardî or among the Sufis themselves, the religion of love brought forth the prophetic meaning of ancient Persia’s religion by transforming its technical terms into symbols (see Book II, chapter VI, section 3 above).

Thus Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran, came to be recognized as a prophet of that religion of love which Muhammad announced and to which he bore witness (see theme 2 above). Here Rûzbehân calls zand and pâzand—a choice his commentator particularly emphasizes—the spiritual interpretation of Beauty through which the soul also interprets itself and makes its own exodus from the regions ruled by the carnal soul. “At times, bowing down in love, he chants the zand and pâzand of love’s inspirations, reading them upon the tablet presented to him by the earthly image of the Eternal Bride’s beauty.

“At other times he must drive the pillagers, the ruffians of carnal nature, away from the place where his highest aspirations are gathered137.” He must keep himself far from the shores of the transient, “and yet, within the darkness of nature in its elemental state, at the very source of the passions of the carnal soul, the gnostic, following in Khezr’s footsteps, drinks the Water of Life138.” This is what the faithful lover finds hardest of all to make others understand: the very paradox of theophany, the presence within the world of the senses of a Presence that is not itself contained in that world.

“Although this pearl (the pearl of contemplation associated with the shâhid, the beautiful figure through whom the divine is contemplated) has the purity of a jewel, the hypocrites of legalistic religion and the small-minded devotees see in it a kind of incarnation. Great God! If those who have eyes fail to see, what will become of those who have none?

“Yet this is what was declared (by the Prophet) in an inspired saying: My friends are beneath my canopies; no one knows them but I. And the secret of the prophetic message has revealed that the Eternal Brides are kept in the bridal chambers of trial, hidden behind the veil of jealousy that has existed from before time. It is said: They look at you, yet they do not see you (7:197).

“Thus the beauty of this majesty, which throws the world of the soul into turmoil, is protected from the fury of those whose envy drives them to violence139.”

The Qur’anic verse invoked here appears elsewhere in support of a kind of “docetism,” understood as a theological critique of appearances. It accords with the very rule governing our perception of divine manifestations, or theophanies: Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui—I saw him as I was capable of seeing him. Ruzbihan’s commentator explains this in turn through two famous verses.

The first is by Hafez: “Our idol appears before everyone's eyes; and yet the enchantment I behold is seen by no one but me.” Sa'di had already offered what might be called its answering verse: “Not every eye is fit to behold such beauty—only yours, for you draw around yourself the protecting circle of the divine Name140.”

4. The Pre-eternal Source of Love

The development of the preceding theme led us to an allusion to an alchemical transformation accomplished before time began, the source of the mutual correspondence between lover and beloved. The idea that souls—the “holy Spirits”—recognize one another on earth because of a bond established in pre-eternity, before their earthly existence, is a favorite theme of this Sufism. It certainly recalls Plato. It also accords with the Zoroastrian belief in the preexistence of the fravartis before their descent to earth; and within Islam itself, Shiism explicitly professes the preexistence of souls. This is the “symbolic history” mentioned earlier141, expressing the preeminence of those faithful to love.

We have already noted a distinctive feature of the religion of love professed by our Sufis: Muhammad is its prophet, but its language is one of Platonic symbols. In the Jasmine, this “prologue in heaven” to the earthly history of love takes two forms.

The first is simply Platonic. It is natural to encounter it here, just as we encounter it in Leone Ebreo’s Dialogues of Love. Ruzbihan, however, does not speak of the androgynous being. That idea does find a counterpart in his final conception of lover and beloved as two ways of being united in a single being. The other form of the story comes from the Qur’an. Seen from the outside, the connection between it and the event symbolized in the Platonic account may not be immediately obvious.

But the connection becomes clear as soon as we understand the relationship between human and divine love established in Ruzbihan's mystical teaching. We need not ask, as though faced with a contradiction: Since the holy Spirits knew one another before earthly existence, is it their companion they long to find again (the Platonic version)? Or is the one they long to find the Lord whom they acclaimed before time began (the Qur’anic version)? There is no dilemma.

Human love initiates us into the secret of divine love, which brings it to perfection; in finding their companion again, the Spirits find their Lord. More precisely, the passage from one kind of love to the other does not mean transferring love from one object to another. This is what esoteric tawhîd, the inner meaning of divine oneness, will reveal.

Ruzbihan presents the first version of the story in these words, following the Prophet's saying that alludes to it: “The religion of love grounds human love in this sacred symbol. It knows that in their homeland, in the high city of God, the holy Spirits gazed upon one another when they dwelt within the canopies (sarâdiq) of the divine Presence. As they contemplated one another, they saw the traces of God that permeated their being. Moved by this beauty, they joined together, each drawn to others according to the degree of their affinity.

“When they came into this world, they looked at one another again with those same eyes, according to their prevailing capacity, the purity of their being, the understanding possessed by each intelligence, and the nearness of soul to soul. In one another's faces they recognized each other and came to love one another. As our Prophet said: The Spirits are like troops gathered together; those who recognize each other form bonds of mutual affection, while those who do not recognize each other remain at odds142.”

Here, then, is the second version of this symbolic history. It appears in the chapter devoted specifically to mystical love, understood in terms of three modes or degrees of vision among contemplatives capable of visionary perception (ahl-e moshâhadat). The central figure in this scene “in heaven” is the Eternal Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e qidam).

Here the relationship between the Eternal Witness and the shâhid in the ordinary sense—the human beauty that manifests the divine and makes it present in the mystic's heart—comes into sharper focus. It cannot be resolved by treating them as two objects standing in relation to one another. It can be understood only through a transformation in the seer's own vision, precisely the subject of this chapter.

In such a transformed vision, the shâhid appears to human love in such a way that it is God himself who looks upon this shâhid, and who looks upon himself through it. To understand what a witness of contemplation is, we may think of a wedding custom still observed in Iran today.

The bridegroom stands a little to one side of a mirror, so that he sees the bride enter the ceremonial room in its reflection. Likewise, the mystic never sees the divine Being directly. In the shâhid, the beautiful person to whom he gives his love, what he sees is the Image in which the divine Being contemplates himself; the shâhid is the mirror of that contemplation. Such a vision presupposes the transformation Ruzbihan describes.

At this summit, human love marks the end of divine jealousy and of the blindness of the world “without eyes”—jealousy and blindness being two sides of the same condition (see chapter III above). Ruzbihan's words are as beautiful as they are exact. They are not words one can summarize.

“There are three kinds of vision among contemplatives capable of seeing:

  1. The first precedes earthly existence. It was the vision enjoyed by the Spirits before they entered material bodies, when they stood in the Presence of Glory. Gathering them together with the leaders of the Spirits (Ro’âsâ-e arvâh), that Presence asked them: Am I not your Lord (A-lasto bi-rabbikom, 7:171)? And with one voice they answered: Yes! The delight of those words entered their very being. They asked God for beauty, so that mystical knowledge might reach its highest perfection. Then God lifted the veil of the Jabarût, the realm of divine power, and the majestic beauty of the divine Essence appeared to them. The Spirits of the prophets and of the Friends of God (Awliyâ’) were overwhelmed by the intoxication of sacred listening and majestic beauty. They fell in love with the Eternal Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e qidam), free from the limitations of created existence. Thus walâyat, their spiritual intimacy with God, grows in them little by little through God's schooling in love. For when the holy Spirits entered earthly bodies, their passion, which had existed before this new condition of being, made them all cry out: Show yourself to me! And each in turn found the place of exaltation, the mystical Sinai. That is why everything they saw in this world they saw as Him, so much so that one of those especially faithful to love (khowass-e mahabbat) declared: ‘There is nothing upon which I set my eyes without seeing God in it.’
  2. Of all those who, carried away by spiritual emotion, spoke in startling paradoxes and extravagant utterances (shattâhân), not one failed to long for the sight of God or to claim to have seen him. At their gatherings, all repeated in the same language of love: I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms. As they passed through the mystical stages, all experienced the second form of love through the second kind of vision. For after passing through the initiatory trial of the veil of human existence, a person whose spiritual substance is no longer hidden by the accidents of that condition, and whose spirit overcomes the violence of physical nature, rediscovers here on earth the Original Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e awwal). Created existence no longer disturbs him, for love has been added to love.
  3. The third kind of vision is the highest. It takes place in the palace of mystical abiding beyond self-annihilation (baqâ’). When body and spirit have become harmonious with one another, love reaches its summit. Love grows with vision, and in the mystic it never ceases to grow, because there is no limit to the vision of the beloved. Yet among those faithful to love, the relation works the other way round: vision grows according to the degree of love. The vision of ordinary people is one thing ... The vision of those faithful to love is another ... From this you will understand that the capacity to find is proportionate to the heart. Not just anyone who tastes love's leftovers is a knight of love143. For those personally initiated into love (khâssân), love is a gift bestowed upon them individually. Only then comes the vision of beauty. This station of vision has its stages, and love corresponds to the height of each stage. Love begins with the vision of grace and beauty. In the vision of supreme sublimity it ceases. When, in the state of union, a created being is invested with a lordly condition (robbânî), every divine Attribute that stirs love brings it another love to experience. If you reach this point, you will understand the teaching. Love is the shaking of one's whole being, the impetuous surging of the Spirit, the melting of the heart's innermost depths. As for the sweetness of finding, the roles of lover and beloved answer one another. It is for the beloved to awaken burning desire; for Majnun to be the man possessed by longing. Majnun's state (jonûn: enthousiasis, mania—rapture, frenzy, possession): that is love. And Majnun comes at last to be himself the mirror of God (A’yûna-e Haqq), for God makes anyone who looks into that mirror fall in love. Read this verse: He will bring forth love for them (19:96). And understand the interpretation of this one: I have cast upon you a love that comes from me (20:39)144.”

The Book of the Clouding Over had told us about those who are the “eyes of God,” without whom God would neither see the world nor be seen by it. Majnun's love makes him such a “divine eye.” The man who once gazed into the mirror has himself become the mirror in which God is contemplated, for his vision of Beauty was a vision of God contemplating himself. Ruzbihan could hardly have expressed more forcefully his understanding of human love as divine love. These are among the most astonishingly concentrated passages in the Jasmine.

Consider their claims carefully: among those faithful to love, vision is proportionate to the degree of love; the power to find depends on the heart. It is love that makes us see. The object we see is not what causes our love—one could scarcely express this more clearly in terms of the experience of perception itself. Love is the organ through which beauty is perceived. Where love is absent, beauty will never reveal itself.

But whoever possesses love—whoever is a Majnun—rediscovers the Eternal Witness of Contemplation here on earth. Speaking of himself, and wishing to dismiss the pitiful imitators of a way of life whose secret they do not understand, Ruzbihan will say elsewhere that it was by virtue of the Spirit's preexistent nature that “this audacious champion of tawhîd,” “this truly free man (âzâdeh),” rediscovered the secret of the uncreated within the created world itself145.

But reaching that point requires the whole schooling of love, every stage of the inner pilgrimage.

The end of the chapter considered here announces that destination, anticipating the pilgrimage's end. When the mystic has become the eye through which God sees himself, the human shâhid, the beautiful human face, is seen by this divine eye.

But what God sees is his own face: that is precisely what his shâhid is. It is God who loves himself in Majnun's love for Layla. The human shâhid becomes the mashhûd, the Contemplated One, of the Eternal Witness. “When He makes him both the one who desires and the one desired, both lover and beloved, his servant in love assumes before Him the role of Witness of Contemplation (he is the shâhid-e Haqq). God contemplates himself in him with an eternal contemplation and clothes him in his own Attributes.

“Yet there is no incarnation, for the divine Essence remains apart from everything temporal146.” That is why Ibn Arabi, interpreting the same theme of the “Am I not?” (A-lasto?) developed here by Ruzbihan, will say that in posing the question the divine Being was questioning himself. And that is also why the passage from human to divine love—the transformation of love that is not yet love in its true sense (majâzî) into true love (haqîqî)—is in no way the transfer of love from one object to another.

God is not distinguished as one object that would be love, lover, and beloved, alongside another object that would not. Rather, the unity of love, lover, and beloved is the mystery of divine love; that three-in-one is God himself147. To say this is already to anticipate our final theme, the destination of the inner pilgrimage. Every chapter, every moment of the Jasmine, announces it, foreshadows it, and points the way toward it.

5. The Stages of Initiation

This is the most difficult theme in the Jasmine to analyze. Its elements are scattered throughout the book, as the preceding pages have shown. Nearly every statement of doctrine is accompanied by an autobiographical allusion, like a second melody sounding alongside the first. Then both melodies rise into a higher register and become an invocation to the beloved, always present in the mind, asking her not to fail in her role as shâhid. There are advances and returns, assertions and recollections, and aphorisms woven together. Anyone attempting an analysis can only mark out a few of the most important points along the way.

a) The Necessary Course of Love and Its Consequences (chapter XII)

“It happens in the course of time that love for the pre-eternal Beloved emerges into human love through a revelation of divine majesty (tajallî-e jalâl) shining through from the spiritual world. Ah! Do you not know what a book of wonders this story is? Once the divine eye (that is, the visible form of the Eternal Beloved)148 has been unveiled in the manifestation through which the divine appears, God shows himself to the mystics under the forms of created beings, in kindness and loving care.

“Thus, by way of created existence, the mystic is led into the very heart of the uncreated. For on the level of created things, it is from the dwelling place of created things that the journey must begin149.” As Ruzbihan's anonymous commentator observes (Gloss 211): “The whole cycle of mystical experience (da’ira-ye ’irfân) is contained in this teaching.

“Through the self-revelation of the uncreated, the mystic contemplates the uncreated with the Spirit's inner sight; and at the very same time and in the very same place, he contemplates it in created forms of divine manifestation (majâlî-e hadath), with the eye that sees their outward, visible appearance.” And so, “although the Uncreated (through these manifestations in created things) leads them back to the Uncreated, the pilgrims on the path of love delight with childlike exuberance among the flowers of human beauty. For those flowers are the steps of the heaven of pre-eternity.

“Do not treat me cruelly, tender beauty, for in this incense burner the fragrant aloe of a particular divine manifestation burns before you, and the cup that is your pure soul holds the drink of intimacy with the Witness of Contemplation of the Uncreated. At this stage, this modest Sufi (Ruzbihan) is separated from pure tawhîd and suffers in the trial of your love ... You have become the qibla, the direction of prayer, of my soul ... Do not turn my soul into a world from which the Beloved is veiled, for the soul cannot remain deprived of the Beloved150.

“Ever since the world of the soul (that is, the world before earthly existence), my soul has endured the pain of loving you. The soul that brought your soul into being is hidden within you, who are the soul of my soul. Tell me, what wonder is this that passes between these two ways of speaking?

At times the soul is the symbol of you,
And at times you are the symbol of the soul.
The soul is the earth on which you walk,
And the earth on which you walk is the soul of my soul151.”

b) Love as a School of Initiation (tarbiyat-e ’ishq, chapter XIII)

“The divine Being, in his eternal loving care, is neither inside nor outside the totality of created beings (neither immanent nor transcendent), yet he truly shows himself to their souls, or rather to the very eyes of their bodies. It is precisely by passing through the bounds of human existence that the Merciful One pours his grace upon the soul, so that the mode of being of the uncreated is perceived in a creature which, by comparison, is almost nonbeing.

“The dwelling place of imperishable love now becomes visible to them, because for a created being there is no road to the uncreated that begins in the uncreated. Some say, it is true, that such a road can be taken; but in reality a creature reaches divine love only through the teaching and initiation given by human love. There is one exception: a spiritual degree called the pure vision of the uncreated.

“But that dwelling place lies beyond the conditions of created existence. It was the rank of an elite among the prophets, the divine Messengers, and certain spiritual people152 ... Very few remain established in that spiritual state ... For most, their spiritual states come from the particular forms of divine manifestation suited to them, beginning, for example, with a manifestation in the form of human beauty153.”

“The masters of mystical knowledge know that a created being has not the strength to endure the uncreated in its pure state. God's purpose is to begin by educating the disciple so that the laws of divine love may be revealed to him through human love. Then comes the succession of stages they describe, through which the soul must pass. Once kindled, the soul must experience fear of the beloved, then hope; then tears, groans, the tearing of clothes, exultation, crushing grief, passion, bewilderment, consolation, self-annihilation, speech, silence.

“All these states of lovers appear in those faithful to love. As they struggle with their own souls, they sound every one of these notes with the bow of tawhîd, when they attain that degree of mystical singleness which brings them face to face, alone, with their God. Everything that befell them at the beginning returns at this highest stage. They are great masters, and their knowledge carries authority.

“O my friend! How can I tell you that in the flowing waves of a lock of hair there trail the long streamers of inner revelations radiant as dawn? ... O wisest of all those who understand love! Wine from the Grail of pure Unity, poured into the cup where meanings mingle and overlap!

“The image of the two temples (ka’batayn) framed by curls, within the sacred precinct where one confronts the Face of Majesty ... Rise; lift up your right hand and display the majesty of love. For the muezzin's call announces that the hour of Prayer has come ... Enter the arena of my soul; and, like the rider's polo mallet striking the ball, let your love send my faith leaping from the ford of passing things to that high bank: We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit (Qur’an 2:83 and 254)154.”

c) The Descent of Love to Take Up Its Abode

One chapter (chapter XIV) returns, in the form of an autobiographical confidence addressed to the woman he loves, to the entire genesis of love: from the soul's preexistence to the moment when the four constituent elements analyzed earlier come together (chapter VI; see theme 3 above). “Then, with irresistible suddenness, this Sufi (Ruzbihan), cast out of the heavenly convent of pre-eternity, bursts into the streets of Shiraz. In mining the depths of unknown mystical knowledge, he has become, in the very school of the religion of the Law (sharî’at), a disciple of the religion of inner truth (haqîqat)155.”

What follows is a characteristic sequence in which images are not ornamental figures of speech but take the place of concepts, performing their work on a level beyond conceptual thought. The beautiful beings do not appear to the Sufi somewhere outside himself. They emerge from his most intimate secret—the very form of his destiny before time began. His bodily eyes merely serve the soul. Then comes the mystical birth of one faithful to love. His mother is none other than divine Beauty, which gives birth to him by revealing its mystery.

But Beauty must be assisted by a concrete form of beauty, the one corresponding to the lover's capacity established in pre-eternity. The place of this birth is the theophanic form issuing from the divine Act, the “mystical tavern” (compare Hafez), where one drinks from “the cup filled with the wine of double meaning.”

Hence these words: “(This Sufi) did not yet know that from the chamber of the most intimate secret of his own human reality there would emerge, draped in the veils of ambiguity, those beings of beauty in whom the divine Attributes take on personal form. He had to venture his head beyond the cloak of meditation; the eyes of his soul had to enlist his eyes of flesh in their service. Among visible forms, he watched for the distinguishing sign that would announce the Beloved.

“Suddenly, from the little street where the divine Act opens its mystical tavern, this maiden of the convent of Omnipotence emerged, covered by the great veil of her guarded chastity. Then she unveiled herself to the soul's gaze, which saw her without seeing her, for it saw her through the faculty of active imagination ... Is she not the midwife who helped bring him into the world, the mother of this earthly being, this Sufi who, following the traces of divine manifestations, burst into the street where Omnipotence unveils itself? ... And suddenly, repeating the Prophet Muhammad's words, he too declared: I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms156.”

“Sometimes the lover's soul is among flowers, sometimes among laughter; sometimes burning with fire, sometimes trembling with music; sometimes the very substance of human clay is consumed by love's fire, and sometimes the lute of pre-eternity accompanies the sacred chant. Sometimes lost in inward intoxication, sometimes clear-minded, sometimes extinguished to itself. Sometimes in anguish, sometimes exulting; sometimes in fear, sometimes in hope; sometimes in separation, sometimes in reunion. In separation there is no station at which to rest; even in reunion there is no place to settle.

“All this is required of one faithful to love whom God leads through the stages of human love in this world toward the ascent of divine love, because it is one and the same love, and because it is in the book of human love that we must learn to read the law of divine love. This is the path of the Trial that initiates the faithful into pre-eternal love: they must follow the sweetness of human love along a path as narrow as a single hair, without falling into the depths of the hell of carnal nature157.” Not to fall into that hell is to follow the example of the Prophet.

Through a ta’wîl, an interpretation that uncovers the inner sense of scripture, Ruzbihan finds this teaching in the Qur’anic account of the Prophet's great visions, in a way that beautifully illustrates the prophetic meaning he perceives in beauty. The Angel of Revelation descends upon the horizon: “He drew near, then hung suspended” (53:8). Addressing the beloved, Ruzbihan declares: “The scene in which this vision takes place is your very face, whose beauty overwhelms us with wonder158.”

Yet the Qur’an also says of the Prophet: “His gaze neither swerved nor went beyond” (53:17). We already know the lesson Ruzbihan draws from this: one's gaze must neither “swerve” away from the vision of what the senses reveal, nor “go beyond” the image it presents, forgetting the image and seeing only the mirror—for that is how one falls into the hell of carnal obsession. He will return to this theme in another chapter which echoes his Book of the Clouding Over.

“When you have experienced love's ascent from (the stage expressed in this saying): Truly, I ask God's forgiveness seventy times each day159—the fault of fixing your contemplation on the world of ambiguity while neglecting the Eternal Bride is forgiven through the power of this Sign: We have granted you a resounding victory so that God may forgive your former faults (48:2). Then you understand the hidden meaning of this verse: His gaze did not swerve, nor did it pass beyond the limit (53:17)160.”

Ruzbihan concludes, still addressing his beloved: “Perhaps you do not know how deep the heart's distress can be, or where the beloved dwells in relation to the soul.

“Open a page of my suffering and decipher there the letters of a mystical knowledge still unknown, so that you may understand how, in the presence of the visible form of the invisible, my love remains free from the troubling suggestions of carnal nature. What can I say? This story is the secret of the masters of mystical knowledge. They alone know its cipher, and in the anguish of what cannot be attained, they are the ones who can decipher its signs. There is a secret hidden from the concerns of ordinary people; and those who have revealed it have had their tongues cut out161.”

d) Love's Journey Through the Heart of One Faithful to Love (chapter XV)

“Since the lights of Beauty have entered the mirror of the human face from the eye of God (the visible form of the Beloved), it is this human mirror that the human soul contemplates. In it, the soul discerns the particular divine Attributes in the manifestation meant for it (that is, in the form of beauty corresponding to its own capacity).

“Once the soul has discovered the secret of that capacity, it cannot help becoming intoxicated with love as it contemplates this Witness of Contemplation (shâhid) with the purity of sight appropriate to it. This story is the soul of the souls of the prophets; it feeds the souls of the spiritual Friends (Awliyâ’) and nourishes the soul of the Angel. At last it rules even the soul's innermost secret (sirr-e jân).

“The soul's essential reality (haqîqat) becomes one with love for the beloved. Through the triumphant power of the divine manifestation, the very soul of love becomes one with the soul of the beloved in the innermost depth of all (that is, the beloved becomes one with the love with which the lover himself becomes one). The soul of love floods the world of the soul with light, cleansing it of everything other than love. In a human being it replaces human conduct with the conduct of an Angel. From man's natural dispositions, love for the beloved removes all that is merely natural162.”

“All this happens when, from the first beginnings of human love, the pilgrim is seeking divine love, and in the very human love that carries him away he travels in longing for the vision of God. Moment by moment, the soul of the soul, invited to the feast of this love by the invisible Eternal Bride, removes from love's secret the covering made necessary by the divine manifestation. Love itself then becomes the soul's protection.

“But if the soul clings to love's literal appearance, that attachment to the letter makes it a traitor to love; it will never reach love in its true sense (haqîqat, its divine reality). For whoever stakes everything on himself, remaining his own hostage, falls into a condition that leaves him unable to understand the human image of love and the beloved ... In the night when my heart was dispossessed, which wrapped me in a great veil, I offered an evening prayer in the little street of wandering.

“I spoke with the Angels of the soul of the feeling of absence experienced within the feeling of presence itself. Then, suddenly, amid the mourners of my secret anguish, I saw her who is the Venus of the heaven of mysteries become the harp of those who mourn163. Come, let us see how the army of love's temptations behaves in the sanctuary of this beauty from Qipchaq; how, in the arena of a struggle that is both separation and attainment, those temptations are shattered in the vanguard of imagination by the army of her beauty164.”

e) The Ascending Stages from Human Love to Divine Love (chapter XVI)

They are many; it would be an illusion to try to count them. The first, at any rate, is to acquire the necessary capacity. Next comes the awakening of the divine Attribute manifested in the theophany corresponding to that capacity. Then comes the inspiration that gives the first intimation of the deception or ambiguity of appearances (iltibâs). After that comes the light that makes it possible to see the archetype in the vision of a material form.

Then follow watching, waiting, undivided attention, fleeting glances, contemplation, vision ... Then the image is brought to life by active imagination (takhayyol-e khayâl); then the spiritual image (khayâl-e râhânî) is integrated into consciousness; then come consummation and the fire of love. Next, the feeling of having been robbed of everything; within that loss, searching; within that search, overwhelming passion. Temptations entering thought; astonishment that paralyzes the heart's subtle faculty of perception. Intimidation before the world of legalistic religion, a world with no insight into love.

Then comes the pursuit of passing inner states: terror at the prospect of perishing, desperate searching; the approach of the soul, the approach of the intellect, desolation of the heart; Abraham's laments, Moses' cries; fear without hope, hope without fear. There is the first great anguish; then the discovery of all-encompassing vision; complete intimacy, complete exultation; conversations in the night, private psalms, retreat, solitude. In the violence of what is undergone, one feels one's own annihilation; in the exquisite sweetness of what is tasted, one feels one's own abiding beyond annihilation165.

“In the realm of human love's many qualities, each one, in thousands of possible forms, affects the lover's way of being, according to the figures produced by divine manifestations throughout the celestial cycle of the heavens that measure out the time of love. Once the lover has received the gift of a capacity for love, it is through the very perfection of human love that he reaches the beginnings of divine love166. Then love, like an initiator, strips him of that first condition and lifts him, riding upon the divine manifestations, into the world of uncreated Majesty.

“From all eternity and for ever, he participates in the eternally enacted divine ceremony in the world of the Jabarût, in the company of those who dwell continually in the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom. That eternal contemplation is now his dwelling and his home ... So speaks this exile whose heart is in love (Ruzbihan). He states it plainly: love experienced for a human being is the ladder of love for the divine Being. This love is given to whom it is given; it is known by whoever knows it.

“And so, when I was walking beside the wall of the house of ambiguity, I saw this young beauty from Turkestan; her long eyelashes, like a volley of arrows, cut me off from everything that was not love. This inconsolable Sufi (Ruzbihan) speaks in such strange allusions that he misleads even the convent (khanqâh) of those intent on scrutinizing the mystery of Beauty. Do not imagine that this suffering has brought me any gain, or that this state of being confers any dignity upon me. This state resembles the chameleon of divine manifestations, each suited to its own occasion.

“Here, in the mirror of self-annihilation, the beauty that is abiding beyond annihilation must appear. Beware! Beware! For in this furnace Gabriel's wing, which is the soul, is consumed167, and in the palace of servitude to love the garment of suffering is sewn. This young beauty thinks that this man (Ruzbihan) is the veil. She does not know that she herself is our veil168. So be it: I call my suffering to witness.

“Or rather, no—it is neither this nor that. In truth, love has existed from all eternity. It needed only to enter the house of the desolate one night, for a single hour, and it made us one faithful to love. From then on, the soul had to advance step by step in the tracks of the mystery, beyond the heavens of becoming and passing away169.”

Ruzbihan allows us to follow this ascent step by step. In a few magnificent lines he lets us witness the dawning of the lights of divine manifestation: “From the depths of the invisible, from the mystery of the divine manifestation170, a Light among the Lights, one particular divine Attribute, begins to grow in the inner world of heart and soul.

“All the hidden figures shine through the veil of the manifestation, taking their places in the wide field where divine manifestations appear in their purity, in the meadow where lightning reveals the unseen reality of the divine Attribute. Each appears bearing the twofold mark of its origin: human and spiritual at once, material and yet alive. Each rightfully claims its proper place.

“Although in themselves these figures are mirages without independent reality, they take their stand in the shadow of the divine Attribute. Then the lights of divine self-revelation (anwâr-e tajallî) flood them, free of ambiguity, and give every one of them the savor of reality in its true sense (haqîqat). Those who have not yet attained the vision of divine manifestations are led by these figures to the very source of the light of manifestation (nûr-e tajallî).

“There, within true reality, they are led out of the stage of ever-changing diversity into the world of lasting establishment ... In sovereign power, the divine manifestation frees the soul of the soul, in its search for the beloved, from everything other than the beloved, everything belonging to the stage of ambiguity. It leads the Spirit breathed into man at the beginning out of its vessel of clay into knowledge of the divine Attributes that belong to it in its own right171.”

Little by little, the image of the Eternal Bride (’arûs-e qidam) emerges and becomes more distinct. “The sovereign divine manifestation leads the bride who is the soul out of the recesses of human existence into the bridal chamber of divine intimacy. It clothes her in a robe woven from the lights of true Beauty.

“When the light of the divine Attribute makes itself felt by the consecrated soul, she sees nothing but the divine Being in the mirror of a being destined to pass away. For having passed through the first beginnings of human love, she has now reached the first beginnings of divine love172.” This transition passes through three stages, corresponding to the three stages of tawhîd (see theme 6 below).

The first is simply the inclination of love experienced in the particular form proper to each being. At this stage, ambiguity has not yet appeared. It enters halfway along, at the second stage, when, for fear that the Spirits may yield to “longing for Paradise” (malah-e behesht)173, “Beauty reveals itself to them in the forms of divine manifestation, so that they may taste the peace of love in its divine Source.

“The third stage, the dwelling place of higher knowledge and tawhîd, is where the Spirit recovers its clear awareness (sahw) and loses itself (mahw)174.” Within that very self-effacement the Spirit once again discovers the secret of the uncreated hidden in the secret of what passes away.

But the old self has been burned away and annihilated, and perception is now entirely new: the lover knows that he himself is the beloved, and yet it is not himself that he loves175. “He sees with the eyes of the innermost consciousness (sirr); beings that have received the gift of existence and must pass away taste peace at the murmuring of the doves of Uncreated Love.

“Otherwise how could he say: I contemplated my God in the most beautiful of forms?” “Up to this point,” Ruzbihan explains, “we have been speaking of the dwellings of the wandering stars in the heavens of the uncreated, as they travel among the constellations (abrâj) of the created world176.”

“From now on, in the garden of tawhîd, the nightingales of mystical singleness (tafrîd) settle only on the branches of the rosebushes of freedom from material things (tajrîd). From the divine Being they receive the wine of the divine Attribute, tasted within that Attribute itself.

“Those acquainted with the highest teachings, pilgrims of the lights that reveal, know that these stages concern only pilgrims seeking the divine Being. They can say: the stages of divine love are explained by human love; for the grace of the young beauties of Turkestan is itself the tablet upon which the characters of an unknown writing must be deciphered. And it is from the battlements of the highest tower in the heaven of love that the wondrous Bride is glimpsed177.”

Addressing the woman to whom his book is dedicated, Ruzbihan goes on: “Alas! If you understood what this means, you would draw aside the veil that conceals the human image of the one Eternal Bride. For the beauty of that image is the East in which rises the sun of Unity, a Unity bound to no particular form. Then this Sufi might secretly decipher, in the dwelling place of tawhîd, the writing of the divine Attribute between the intricate lines of the divine manifestation.

“Yet even now he reads, in the tresses of your amber-scented hair, radiant with the light of your beauty, this verse of the Book: You cause night to enter day, and you cause day to enter night (3:25).

“I know that the Spirit's reflection shines upon the face of this human icon. It is nothing less than the shadow of the divine Attribute, for the sovereign is God's shadow upon the earth. It is the hell of trial, rising in successive terraces; the wood that feeds the soul's fire; the ladder to eternal Paradise; the imprint of the seal: He shaped you—ah, how beautiful is the form he gave you! (40:66). There too the circle of the soul's horizon is arched.

“To it also refers the promise: We shall show them Our Signs (41:53). It is the influence of the stars of the uncreated East, for it bears the mark that prompts the cry: This is my God (6:76–78)178.”

In saying these things, Ruzbihan knows perfectly well the dangers and misunderstandings he is inviting. We have already heard him boldly profess malâmat, the willingness to bear other people's reproach179. Here another opportunity for defiance presents itself: “I found acceptance among the mystics adorned with love.

“But to the pious devotees (zohhâd) my story is scandalous impiety. For those who steal into the palace of the Beloved, the color of reproach (rang-e malâmat) cast upon them covers the true face of their integrity. They keep the soul hidden in the soul's deepest recess. Outwardly they bear the mark of blame; but on the Preserved Tablet the letters of their names appear to the heavenly beings (malakûtiyân) in the reverse order from that in which earthly people read them.

“Within the inviolable boundary of their souls they possess the light of eternal blessedness, for the path along which their secrets (asrâr) advance is lit, in the deepest night of nonbeing, by the Uncreated Light. This is the fulfillment of the promise: God protects you against men (Qur’an 5:72)180.”

To have “reached the first beginnings of divine love” means that the passionate, commanding soul (nafs ammâra), brought under the Spirit's victorious authority, has become the soul at peace (nafs motma’yanna), the very soul addressed by the Qur’anic summons recalled at the beginning of this book181. “Among the witnesses of contemplation (shawâhid) she has rediscovered the traces of that same Witness (shâhid). The purity of the divine Attributes has shone for her in the mirror of divine manifestation (âyînah-e fi’l).

“But she does not yet know which way lies the uncreated East, for she still dwells in the house of love's sorrows. The Joseph of true Reality has not yet risen for her out of the well of trial.

“When at last she leaves the prison of trial, she no longer finds quite the same sweetness in human love. She has tasted the traces of divine Beauty, whose subtle graces have freed her from the need for intermediaries. She has now reached the stage where, her education complete, she waits for the appearances of light ... From this point onward, love begins anew. From this stage the journey will lead to the furthest limit of love. Between these first beginnings and that final limit—I mean in divine love—there are twelve mystical stations182.”

These are the twelve mystical stations described, one after another, in the final chapters of the Jasmine of the Faithful in Love (XXI–XXXII). Increasingly, the lived experience of love is expressed in the language of the problems raised by tawhîd. The journey is approaching its final destination: the secret of esoteric tawhîd, which cannot be discovered without experiencing love. It is precisely that experience which allows one to feel and to describe the relationship between divinity (lâhût) and humanity (nâsût) in terms of divine manifestation, without confusing it with incarnation.

For a theophany concerns the form of the body, not its material substance, its flesh. Ruzbihan's understanding of love, and of the implications of human and divine love for one another, is possible only where thought moves within a horizon of divine manifestations, transfiguring all flesh into caro spiritualis, spiritual flesh. It does not belong to a horizon defined by a historical incarnation, by an Incarnation of the divine in the human within History. We noted earlier how this distinction helps explain the affinity between Manichaeism and a mystical religion of love sustained by manifestations of the divine in beauty.

Finally, the characteristic point is that every question concerning the two aspects of one and the same Eros can be expressed in theological terms—more precisely, in the language of the esoteric wisdom of tawhîd—and the reverse is equally true.

We shall see a striking illustration of this before we finish.

At this point we can do little more than mark a few landmarks along the Way. Ruzbihan interprets the Qur’anic verse “God loves those who turn back to him” (2:222) as applying to those who “turn” to the religion of love. He wishes to invite those capable of seeing with more than the body's eyes to understand what that religion really is.

Yet this secret can be understood nowhere but among those faithful to love: “It is in the garden of love that the flowers of the Merciful One bloom.” For everywhere else, “whoever seeks divinity in humanity can only be, in view of the requirement to preserve God's transcendence (tanzîh), a scandalous unbeliever (kâfir).”

The light of tawhîd has remained ambiguous to them, and hundreds of thousands of souls still in bondage have failed to cross its threshold. When the Eternal Bride reveals herself, hell becomes paradise and the ascetic's cell becomes the Fire Temple. This guest from the heaven of pre-eternity (Ruzbihan himself) has contemplated pre-eternal Beauty through the veil—or mirror—of what passes away. Before divine Beauty, the veil hiding divinity was lifted.

Yet there are hundreds of thousands of cases in which the earthly beloved remains without a partner, while the whole universe of divine manifestations remains unknown, concealed within the majesty of the pure Essence183.”

“Without a partner”: that is, without someone faithful to love, someone capable of recognizing a manifestation of divine Beauty in her beauty. At the same time, the entire universe of divine manifestations remains unknown. The majesty of the Essence remains in its transcendence. The threshold of tawhîd has not been crossed. In other words, the inner meaning of tawhîd has not even been suspected.

We shall see in the end what this correspondence means.

By contrast, “ecstatic experience (wajd) is dispossession, rapture, the Beloved’s secret cipher, the shock of sublimity, the onslaught of the pre-eternal world, the discovery of the wondrous realities of the Mystery. It is the irruption of the guards of the theophany, descending upon the Sinai of the Show Yourself to me (7:143) uttered by this new Moses, the soul.

“It is the crashing together of the waves of the Ocean of the uncreated; it is humanity’s innate capacity, the root of the universe; it is the vision of the forms shaped by the divine self-manifestations. It announces itself through an inwardly heard, personal summons; it breaks forth with the unveiling of the light of beauty. At that inward summons, in that transfiguration of being, the whole transient world offers the pure drink of ecstasy in countless cups. Ecstatic feeling has no limit, for existence itself has no limit184.”

And then there is this invocation, spoken at the stage of certainty: “O image of beauty! Come to the aid of those who are beginners in love. For if mystics, troubled by the wound of the spear of ardent longing, look upon the witness of contemplation (shâhid) whom they behold in their gathering185 as though they were beholding the divinity itself, they are unbelievers, violating tawhîd, the oneness of God.

“But if I contemplate you while feeling the distance that separates me from the Inaccessible, then I am one of the faithful of love. Since this is so, I beg you, turn your gaze toward us, you who are the joy of the mystics, so that your gaze may lift us to the summit of pre-eternity.

“Love is the first fruit to ripen in its garden. I stand amazed; how could I not? For although the divine Attributes are present in these visible Signs (ayât), I know that tawhîd cannot admit incarnation (holûl). Is what I know of you, then, no more than presumption? If it is you whom I know, my knowledge amounts only to tashbîh—assimilating God to a creature.

“But if I know nothing of you, I reduce God to nothingness and abstraction (ta’til)186.”

Here the problem of love’s theophanic function—its power to reveal God—is stated with extraordinary precision. Tashbîh and ta’til are the two reefs on which abstract monotheism is forever in danger of running aground: making God too much like a creature, or stripping God of every living quality.

The theology of love demanded by the doctrine of theophany finds a passage between them. It cannot be confronted with a dilemma that arises only for the tawhîd of ordinary faith, because love is precisely what opens the way to esoteric tawhîd, an inward understanding of divine oneness. And only that understanding, in turn, can do justice to love’s paradox.

6. Esoteric tawhîd

Islamic thought has steered between these two reefs with difficulty and varying success. Shiism in general, Ismailism, and the mystical philosophy of Sufism, however, have found a way through in the idea of theophany: the divine taking human form on the plane of the Malakût, the heavenly Pleroma or fullness of spiritual being. Rûzbehân has taught us enough about this heavenly manifestation in human form to show what it means. It is the mystery of the divinity revealing itself to itself; and, from the mystic’s side, this self-revelation is experienced and understood as the very mystery of love.

Here lies the origin of the relation between divine and human love, for there is only one and the same Eros. Human love must therefore be the indispensable initiation into divine love. To experience human love is to be initiated into the divine mystery, into the esoteric tawhîd professed by the “elect of the elect” among the mystics. This mystery is expressed as a seemingly paradoxical identity.

Our spiritual thinkers knew its Neoplatonic formulation well from the work known as the Theology of Aristotle. Rûzbehân gives it his own expression: “Before worlds existed, before there was any becoming of worlds, the Divine Being was itself love, lover, and beloved187.” Or again: “Know that the Divine Being’s love is like its knowledge. It never ceases to be the lover of itself, just as it never ceases to know itself and contemplate itself through itself188.”

This statement is paradoxical only to a religious or theological way of thinking that ends by turning the Divine into an object, pure and simple.

Indeed, a naïvely dogmatic consciousness accepts the statement only to begin reasoning boldly about God as though God were one object among others, distinguished from them by being a transcendent object—an object with that single exceptional property.

But once God is conceived in this way, the relationship Rûzbehân and the faithful of love experience between human and divine love becomes unthinkable. Divine love must be understood in the same way as divine knowledge. If God is the object of God’s own knowledge, and has revealed himself to himself in the divine Image—the primordial Human Form, the Anthropos, or heavenly Adam—in order to know himself within that Image by being known through it, then the Image’s knowledge of God must be precisely God’s knowledge of the Image.

In the same way, the love felt by this creature, which is God’s theophany and image, cannot be an event alien or external to the loving longing and ecstasy that the divinity experiences within itself for itself.

This is exactly the moving predicament into which the Book of the Clouding has brought us. It is altogether different from a theology calmly debating which attributes may or may not be assigned to its transcendent object. Here we experience the drama of divine love itself being played out in human love, because God’s revelation to himself through love takes place precisely through the trials and raptures of human love. Rûzbehân has described this contradiction within the divine with remarkable force.

From before eternity, God longs to be known; God yearns for a witness of contemplation (shâhid), yet immediately finds it intolerable that an Other should know and contemplate God. God therefore turns this Other away from knowing God, impelling the Other to know only itself rather than direct its gaze toward God. This is the great Trial of the Veil. Since, by essence, God can know only himself, the Witness’s knowledge of God must be none other than God’s own knowledge. The attainment of this transparency is experienced as victory over the Trial of the Veil.

The Witness then becomes God’s very act of contemplation—or rather the very eye through which God beholds himself. And it is through all these Witnesses, who in contemplating God are themselves those whom God contemplates—since God contemplates himself within them—that God looks upon the world. They are the eyes through which God contemplates himself. Such are the prophets, the abdâl (the spiritual “substitutes”), and the faithful of love: that small company who, in Sarî al-Saqatî’s account, withstand the sevenfold divine trial tempting them to “look away.”

To look away is to become conscious of oneself by losing oneself in an object—even paradise or hell—instead of recognizing oneself as the gaze through which God contemplates himself while contemplating them. Without these eyes, God would not see the world; for the world is that which has no eyes, and without this gaze it could not continue to exist. This drama of the shâhid, the Contemplator who is also the Contemplated, is the specifically Sufi orchestration of the Neoplatonic theme of the identity of love, lover, and beloved.

Since divine love is like divine knowledge, the same point must be made again. The Contemplated is the Contemplator; the act of contemplation is not other than what is contemplated. So it is with love, both in its act and in its object: the lover reveals himself to himself in the beloved, and, in return, the beloved reveals the lover to himself. This statement brings together all the stages through which the Book of Jasmine has led us. It makes that book the resolution of the problem, the answer to the Book of the Clouding, written “at the dictation of a wounded consciousness.”

The small band of mystical heroes who, in Sarî al-Saqatî’s story, survive the sevenfold trial because they have not “looked away” foreshadows the whole history of the faithful of love. They are “those to whom God communicates his secrets and who communicate their secrets to him.”

But God’s secrets and theirs are one and the same secret: the threefold identity of act, subject, and object.

It is human experience of love that gives us an intimation of this drama within the divine. At first a veil is cast, delaying self-revelation. The lover does not know that his love is what he himself is; he does not know that he is contemplating his own Image.

But to recognize it, he must pass beyond the limits both of a consciousness that turns everything into an object and of the carnal nature—the possessive instincts of the lower self. He must undergo a metamorphosis that changes the very subject within him, for the identity of love, lover, and beloved is precisely what divine love is. By undergoing this metamorphosis, human love fulfills the divinity’s own desire to have a shâhid, a witness of contemplation whose contemplation of the divine Essence is the divinity’s own.

In this way, human love truly becomes the path that makes divine love possible. Triumph over the “Trial of the Veil” is the joining of human love to divine love; it is divine love unveiled to itself as the human lover discovers the real divine Beloved. This is what it means to recognize a manifestation of divine beauty in human beauty. Human beauty thus initiates the mystical lover into the threefold identity of love, lover, and beloved; human love teaches him the solution to the equation.

The whole Sufi contemplative practice involving beautiful witnesses of contemplation rests on this assumption and pursues this end. And this is Rûzbehân’s great insight: it allows esoteric tawhîd to be expressed in the very language of love’s supreme experience, and makes that supreme experience the fulfillment of tawhîd.

To understand this, we need some knowledge of the three forms or degrees of tawhîd. The last, that of the “elect of the elect,” ends the divine anguish over the Other, because the deepest expression of the divine mystery can be glimpsed and experienced only through a tawhîd of love: the triumph of a higher, enduring existence that is itself a mystical death through love. Rûzbehân discusses these degrees at some length189.

The first is what Sufism calls the tawhîd of ordinary people (tawhîd-e ’âmm): the abstract monotheism of ordinary, naïve, dogmatic faith, which is satisfied only when the Divine has been completely objectified. It sets the Ens supremum, a single transcendent Supreme Being, above the totality of created beings. It constructs proofs and arguments for God’s existence, seeking shelter in them against the shocks of doubt and the risk of denial. Its overriding concern is which Attributes may be assigned to a divine Essence set apart from creatures and becoming. It proceeds by stripping away (tanzîh), haunted by the twin dangers of anthropomorphism (tashbîh) and excessive abstraction (ta’til). Having removed the divine object from every category of created existence, it believes it has safeguarded God’s transcendence.

Yet these rational purifications have made God into precisely the kind of object that serves a “sociomorphic” religion—a religion that conceives the divine relationship on the model of social relations. Once the Divine is turned into an object, it is also socialized. Every free spiritual movement, such as Sufism, that discovers contact between human and divine in the depths of personal consciousness becomes suspect.

The totality of beings, gathered on a level plane and held at an equal distance from the transcendent object by its all-encompassing claim, could be represented by a formula such as n + 1. For Sufism, as for Ismailism, this ordinary tawhîd never ceases committing the very metaphysical idolatry it so deeply fears.

There is next the tawhîd already called that of the elect, a special tawhîd (tawhîd-e khâss). The affirmation of the One moves from the assertion of one unique transcendent object to the affirmation of the unity of being. All beings are experienced as vanishing before the sublimity of the one Being, as mere negations in relation to its divine lordship (robbîya). Before eternity, God was and nothing else was; even now, nothing has changed.

All existence is immersed in the divine reality (res divina, amr ilâhî) through an intuitive vision that replaces rational knowledge, “for rational knowledge belongs to ordinary people, whereas intuitive vision is the prerogative of the initiated (khawâss).” The tawhîd of ordinary people keeps company with the intellect’s proofs and the objects it constructs. For the initiated, all these proofs disappear, and they themselves disappear from those proofs and objectifications. They experience their own passing away, their fanâ’, within the divine abiding existence, whose attributes alone remain. If the idea of fanâ’ is made commonplace, we arrive at that all-too-easy, tiresomely familiar picture of mystical experience as the dissolution of individual personality.

So caricatured, it is no less naïve than the tawhîd of ordinary believers: it simply replaces n + 1 with something like the sterile equation 1 = 1. Unable to recognize appearances as apparitions—as things through which the divine appears—the metaphysical identity it constructs is no less illusory than the metaphysical illusions it denounces. In fact, for our Sufis this second degree of tawhîd, corresponding to the experience of fanâ’, is only the passage toward a third form, which brings about the annihilation of annihilation itself.

As Rûzbehân emphasizes, the first tawhîd proceeds from the visible world toward God (az ’âlam-e molk be-Haqq). The second proceeds from the personal self toward God (az khwôd be-Haqq).

But there is a third, which proceeds from God to God (az Haqq be-Haqq). It never leaves God: it takes place within the divinity itself. And because it takes place within the divinity, the secret of human love belongs within the very mystery of divine love and brings that mystery to fulfillment. This is the tawhîd of the elect of the elect (tawhîd-e khâss-e khâss). It involves a double negation: the annihilation of the annihilation achieved by the second degree. All the forms submerged by that second degree in the undifferentiated identity of God now rise again, resurrected and restored.

But the perspective is reversed: “Below becomes above, and above becomes below.” Rûzbehân says further: “It means casting oneself into the sea of nonbeing, but in order to be annihilated to nothingness—or to annihilate nothingness within oneself. It means emerging from the sea of abiding existence (baqâ’).

“Henceforth the mystic sees, without himself—that is, having been carried outside himself—God through God (bi-khwôd Haqq-râ be-Haqq binad).” He sees, certainly, yet it is not he who sees190. It is God who sees through him. He is the eye through which God contemplates himself. This is what “above has become below” means, and vice versa: “He knows that this is one step from nonbeing into being.

“The second step carries him from the servile human condition (bandagî) on the wing of divine lordship (robbîyat), into the free expanse of divine Selfhood (howîyat).”

This second step transforms his condition from that of an object subject to a power (maqdarî) into that of a subject possessing power (qâdir). It is a transmutation of his very subjectivity. In understanding that he is “the eye through which God sees himself,” he knows himself to be divine knowledge, divine hearing, and so forth. All the forms, all the theophanies, have risen again from the abyss of undifferentiation.

Yet the mystic’s “Holy Spirit” sees that every Attribute he contemplates is the very eye through which God contemplates him. “You must travel, journey through the being of being, with and as the divine Gaze, until being disappears into being for you. Then, without you—that is, with you outside yourself, absent from yourself—the vision of vision (’ayn-e ’iyân) blossoms within you.

“When you reach that point, after the two stages of effacement and recovered consciousness, your very existence proclaims through each of its atoms: ‘I am God.’ To be annihilated in the sea of abiding existence is to annihilate annihilation within yourself, to be annihilated to nothingness—or to have nothingness annihilated. Then, yes, God grants you the being of a divine eye (dîdeh-hastî, so that you see each being as a divine eye).

“God clothes you in the robe of abiding existence: to abide through God’s life, to live from that life, to live within that life. It is through God and in God that you contemplate—that is, your gaze is God’s own gaze contemplating itself. This is the secret of lordship (sirr-e robbîyat), the very secret of tawhîd.”

To see that your own gaze is the eye through which the Divine Being contemplates himself: this is what Rûzbehân calls the vision of vision. The Image has itself become a mirror. It reveals its secret to the person who sees it, for in seeing it that person sees himself; and as the Image sees him, he sees himself seeing himself outside himself. This resolves the conflict Rûzbehân has repeatedly felt in his visions between the oneness of the pure divine Essence and the multiplicity of theophanies—a conflict that surfaced in his consciousness as an anxious question. It cannot be resolved if its terms are treated as objects that can be added together or reduced to an undifferentiated unity.

We can represent ordinary tawhîd as n + 1, and the second degree as 1 = 1.

But Rûzbehân has already suggested the formula corresponding to the third degree: “Until he becomes the product of unity multiplied by unity (wâhid dar wâhid, 1 × 1), the mystical pilgrim does not attain the vision of the vision of tawhîd191.” (In musical terms, think of the relationship of the octave within the upper harmonic series.) This expresses precisely the relationship between unity and the multiplicity of theophanies. It is realized each time—kath’héna—as unity multiplies itself by itself, the same gaze multiplying itself by itself: unity of unity, vision of vision. For each time, the one contemplated is the contemplator’s own gaze.

Esoteric tawhîd thus expresses exactly the unity that brings love, lover, and beloved together, at the moment when human love, in supreme clarity, becomes the revealer of divine love. This is the passage from love still understood metaphorically (’ishq majâzî, because it sees only the outward or “literal” form) to love in its true sense (haqîqî, because it sees what is invisible within that form).

The identity affirmed by the Neoplatonic formula is not, then, an identity belonging uniquely to a transcendent object set above other objects. It expresses the very essence of love, whose underlying principle is the same in its divine and its human forms. Human love is an intimation of divine love and the path toward it. It is its initiation and therefore its first realization, for through human love the veil falls from the mystery of the Contemplator-Contemplated.

Addressing the beautiful woman for whom he wrote the Book of Jasmine—who is herself his shâhid—Rûzbehân writes: “Such is the story of the faithful of love, O flame that draws the souls of men of longing as a flame draws moths! … If we ourselves are not love, lover, and beloved, then who is? Everything outside this indivisible instant belongs only to the world of duality, the world of objects.

“Ponder this strange thing: it is I myself who, without myself—that is, with myself absent, outside myself—am the lover of myself (man bar man bi-mân ’âshiq-am). I never cease to contemplate myself, without myself, in the mirror that is the beloved’s existence. Then who am I?” Here, in this tawhîd of love, we find the very terms and paradoxical turn of phrase that express the secret of esoteric tawhîd.

The gaze the lover contemplates in the mirror is his own gaze. At the same time it is not his, because it is the gaze of the other; and yet this Other is himself. The vision of vision: this is what the Sufis would meditate upon endlessly in the exemplary story of Majnûn and Layla—the “Tristan and Isolde” of their mystical epic. Rûzbehân seals his statement of the tawhîd of love with these four verses:

In search of Jamshîd’s Grail, I traveled the world.
Not for a day did I rest, not for a night did I sleep.
But when I heard the Master describe the Grail of Jamshîd,
That Grail which reveals the universe—behold, it was myself192.

And Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator, to whom we owe so much illumination of difficult chapters of the Jasmine, quietly draws out what matters most: “When the mystic reaches perfection in love,” he says, “he brings together within himself two modes of being: that of the lover (’âshiq) and that of the beloved (ma’shûq). Then he cries: I am the one I love, and the one I love is me; we are two spirits dwelling within a single body193. This is the authentic interpretation of this mystical station: the lover’s person is the dwelling place of two spirits.

“The language of the religion of love has a special beauty and elegance for those who understand it, in calling the mode of being of the lover, of the beloved, and of love itself a spirit (rûh). When this spiritual state reaches the utmost limit of perfection, God himself, through his own eternal gaze, contemplates his own eternal face. Then the existence of my own human reality no longer enters into it. And that is exactly what the venerable shaykh means when he says: it is I myself who, without myself—or outside myself—am the lover of myself194.”

The subject of vision is the same in esoteric tawhîd and in the supreme tawhîd of love. In esoteric tawhîd, Rûzbehân told us, the mystic henceforth sees God through God, “outside” himself (bi-khwôd); he is the very gaze with which God sees himself. In the tawhîd of love, his commentator has just told us that God himself contemplates his eternal face with his own gaze.

The identity of these statements conveys Rûzbehân’s entire teaching in a few words: the relationship he establishes between human and divine love, in which the latter brings the former to its utmost perfection. This teaching distinguishes the faithful of love from the “pious devotees,” whose spiritual path knows nothing of initiation through human love. Speaking again of the faithful lover who reaches the utmost perfection, Rûzbehân says: “He is the Desiring and the Desired, the Lover and the Beloved.

“In relation to God he assumes the role of witness of contemplation—the shâhid in whom God contemplates himself. It is God who contemplates himself in that person with an eternal gaze195.” This is the meaning of the vision of vision, of 1 × 1; and it is the meaning of the Qur’anic verse: “Light upon light” (24:35)196.

In the mystical lover’s supreme state, the Divine Being’s longing to have a witness of contemplation who is no other than himself is fulfilled. Divine jealousy vanishes before the transparency of this pure Witness, whose gaze is God’s own. This is what the story of Majnûn exemplifies. It is therefore true to say that the supreme ecstasy of Majnûn’s human love is the mystery of divine love made transparent. It answers and fulfills that mystery, since from before eternity it was in human form that God revealed divine beauty to himself.

The drama of God’s jealous longing, shown to us in the Book of the Clouding, thus finds its resolution in the extreme ecstasy of Majnûn’s love. Human and divine love are therefore not opposed to each other. The passage from one to the other is an initiation into love’s true meaning and perfection, and this initiation is indispensable. It is not a passage from one object to another, from an object that is not God to an object that is God.

When Majnûn’s love reaches its supreme ecstasy, he becomes a witness of contemplation for God himself. He becomes, in Rûzbehân’s words, the “mirror of God” (mir’ât-e Haqq), the mirror in which God contemplates himself and is revealed to himself. Majnûn has overcome the Trial of the Veil. This is why divine love can contemplate itself only in someone like Majnûn, and why Rûzbehân built his mystical teaching upon this experience of human love.

7. The “history” of the faithful of love

The last elements of our final theme now fall into place. Because this is the relationship of human love to divine longing, which aspires to reveal itself to itself; because it is in the mystical lover that the Divine Being finds a pure mirror, an eye directed toward God that is God’s own gaze—the Trial of the Veil is necessary.

God must bring before the earthly lover a beautiful face which, by becoming the lover’s witness of contemplation, will initiate him into a transformation of vision. He will learn to discover in the beauty of that face a theophany of eternal Beauty. By overcoming the Trial of the Veil, the mystical lover discovers that his contemplation is the Divine Being’s contemplation of himself through the gaze that belongs to him.

Thus some have been able to say that it is God who loves himself in Majnûn’s love for Layla.

Someone uninitiated into this experience might hear the Neoplatonic formula as an expression of solipsism, abolishing the energetic tension between subject and object on which love depends. The truth is exactly the opposite. The Neoplatonic statement describes a real polarity, the polarity of a two-in-one unity. If its object remained external, love’s spiritual energy would eventually be exhausted.

But when that energy is drawn into the mutual inwardness of lover and beloved, it grows more intense and multiplies itself. Love is driven by ardent longing, and longing only increases with love, because love is what makes us see, and the power of vision increases with love. “Ardent longing is further strengthened by the Spirit’s flight,” Rûzbehân writes.

“The higher it flies, the greater the longing becomes, because in the mirage of dazzling light, thirst itself is the longing to feel thirst. In the religion of the faithful of love, there is never a final attainment of union, though there is never separation either, because the laws of time do not apply to what is eternal. The soul, while longing, is granted a vision of Majesty.

“But the very act of seeing only melts the heart into still greater ardor, because longing never ceases to yearn for vision197.”

But if the lover is identical with the beloved, Rûzbehân continues, what can he still long for? What can his love be the love of, other than himself? (To ask the question in this way is to confuse what the formulas 1 = 1 and 1 × 1 represent. Needless to say, the confusion is common.) No, Rûzbehân replies: this is the moment to reflect on the Qur’anic verse, “They have not measured God with the measure due to him” (6:91).

For this is what love means: to be two. What we must understand, however, is the kind of two-ness implied by the essential unity of love, lover, and beloved. It is a two-ness for which we shall once again translate the Persian du’î as dualitude, not duality: a One and a One which, in multiplying one another, are One.

For esoteric tawhîd and the tawhîd of love are the unity of Contemplator and Contemplated, of lover and beloved. That is why “Love, the rider mounted on Longing, travels as far as the sea of tawhîd, but no farther. Beyond that point, neither love nor longing would remain.” To go farther would be to pass beyond the mystery of the divine revealing itself to itself within this unity.

“But love advances by longing; only in this vessel does it reach the shores of vision”—on the sea of tawhîd. And because the lover must reach those shores if God is to find a witness of contemplation in him, God causes the vision to rise before the sanctuary of his soul. Then “this man of longing becomes the partner of a bride like you. For those who seek intimacy with God, you are the place of intimacy; for those who truly understand what moves their longing, you are the flower blooming in the garden of mystical knowledge198.”

Rûzbehân has already taught us what it means to be a “partner.” The existence of the theophanic universe depends on him, in the sense that it rests with him to recognize human beauty as a manifestation of divine beauty. In turn, by bringing her partner to this recognition, the beauty that reveals God initiates him into recognizing the face Rûzbehân calls the Eternal Bride (’arûs-e qidam), until he sees that face alone in the mirror of the transient world199.

This is the whole love story of Majnûn and Layla, to which we have already alluded so often and which our Sufis never tired of pondering. The transformation Majnûn undergoes through his love for Layla is precisely what finally makes him a witness of contemplation, the “Mirror of God.” His passion is understood as the mystical death through love that makes possible the advent of the vision of vision, the tawhîd of the “elect of the elect.”

In South Arabia, in Yemen, there once existed—or at least poetic tradition imagines there existed—an ideal tribe renowned for its practice of a chaste, Platonic love known as ’odhrîte love. Poets celebrated its famous pairs of lovers; Rûzbehân names several at the beginning of his Jasmine. Majnûn and Layla would be the North Arabian counterparts of these ideal lovers celebrated by the poets of South Arabia. They have counterparts, too—perhaps even predecessors—in the Persian mystical epic, where the theme has survived into modern times.

We need not enter here into the extremely complex question of its historical origins. What matters for our present purpose is to bring out certain differences. Despite the similarities, Majnûn’s case is distinct from those of his counterparts, the heroes of ’odhrîte love.

Moreover, although it was indeed through Sufi reflection that Majnûn came to be regarded as an exemplary hero of pure love, there is a difference between the way certain Sufi masters before Rûzbehân used his story in their preaching and the significance Rûzbehân gives it. That significance follows directly from Rûzbehân’s understanding of human love as an initiation into divine love, and as the lived experience, at its highest perfection, of what esoteric tawhîd implies. This interpretation bears the deep imprint of Iranian Sufism. It defines those whom, following Rûzbehân, we call the faithful of love, distinguishing them from pious devotees and ascetic devotees (zohhâd).

Two features characterize Majnûn’s love as the Sufis understood it, and together they are enough to distinguish it from ’odhrîte love in the ordinary sense200.

First, Majnûn’s consciousness is so completely absorbed by the thought and image of Layla that every other feeling is banished. Ask him about Layla, and he answers, “I am Layla.” Ask his name or how he is, and he gives the same answer. More than that, he perceives the entire outer world through this image. Whether he sees a wild animal, a mountain, a flower, or a human being, the same word rises to his lips to identify it: Layla.

Second—and this is surely the underlying condition of such a state of consciousness—Majnûn has completely internalized the beloved’s person.
