It goes so far that he no longer desires Layla’s physical presence, for fear she would distract him from his love for the Layla within him, more real than the real Layla201. These two characteristics describe an experience of love not necessarily implied by the definition of ’odhrîte love.

In any event, this total absorption in the beloved’s inward presence is why Sufi masters such as Shiblî (861–945 CE) present Majnûn in their sermons as the model of the true mystic, whose consciousness is so utterly absorbed in God that he knows himself and perceives the outer world only through God. For how could a mystic claim to love God while remaining able to distinguish and take as his own the trivial certainties of ordinary consciousness? On this point the Sufis certainly recognized in Majnûn something different from simple ’odhrîte love.

Yet they still treated him as a model, an example. It is as though the mystic were merely being invited to love God as Majnûn loves Layla. One could then perfectly well remain within an understanding of God as an object, and imagine “conversion” to divine love as the transfer of love from one object, Layla, to another, God.

But what Rûzbehân has taught us about human love initiating us into divine love is something quite different, and it reveals what is essential to the originality of his Sufism. First, Majnûn’s love for Layla must be understood as the path of access to divine love.

Second, the dawning of divine love must not be imagined as the transfer of affection from one object to another; it is a metamorphosis in which Majnûn becomes a mirror where the Divine Being contemplates himself and finds a shâhid. As to the first point, we have heard Rûzbehân say to the beloved: “It is impossible to cross the rushing river—the Jayhân—of tawhîd without the bridge of your love.”

But crossing that bridge is not simply moving from a human object to a divine one. It means passing through a metamorphosis that overturns the very idea of an object. “Above becomes below; below becomes above.” The transformation is so complete that it speaks in paradoxes and ecstatic outcries (shathîyât) that scandalize the conventionally devout.

For Rûzbehân, Majnûn is far more than a model whose example needs only to be transposed into the practice of divine love. Majnûn’s condition has made him the “Mirror of God.” And what is that, if not divine love itself? It means that his very being has become the eye (dîdeh-hastî!) through which God looks upon himself. He could not say “I am Layla” in the way he does unless he had become that mirror.

If Majnûn experiences himself as Layla, it is because he has himself become the “mirror of God,” or the “eye of God” revealing himself to himself in Layla’s beauty. His extravagant outcry of ecstatic love thus answers the question Rûzbehân asked his interlocutor in the prologue to the Jasmine: “As God contemplates himself in you, contemplates the eternal Face in the beauty of your face, who then are you?” Majnûn’s outcry presupposes that he has crossed the torrent of tawhîd by the bridge of love for Layla. That is the crossing itself, the blossoming of human love into divine love.

Rûzbehân and his commentator have told us that when the mystical lover’s human love reaches this supreme ecstasy, it is God who, in the lover’s gaze, contemplates God’s own eternal face through God’s own gaze. And it is precisely upon reaching the vision of vision that Hallâj’s famous ecstatic declaration is uttered: “I am God202.”

Rûzbehân instructs the mystic: “When you have attained the vision of vision, every atom of your being proclaims: I am God.” For then “every atom of creation is an eye of God.” Recall everything he has taught us about the way the beauty of the shâhid reveals God—Layla being Majnûn’s shâhid—and we can understand why Rûzbehân and his commentator describe in the same terms the mystical state expressed both in Majnûn’s outcry and in that of Hallâj.

Each is a vision of vision. In it the mystical lover, outside himself, carried beyond himself (bi-khwôd), sees his own gaze as the gaze with which God contemplates himself. The theophanic Image is the organ of this vision of vision. The Image’s complete inward presence is, as it were, balanced by the mystic’s being placed “outside himself,” his departure from himself, his ek-stasis.

Because the vision of vision requires this ek-stasis of ecstatic love, producing the perfect transparency that makes Majnûn the eye and mirror through which God contemplates himself, it presupposes the “annihilation of annihilation” that constitutes the third degree of tawhîd. The movement of the subject “outside himself” demanded by esoteric tawhîd therefore appears spontaneously as the “mystical death through love,” of which Majnûn is again the perfect embodiment. Now the prophetic saying we encountered earlier takes on its full meaning: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies having kept his secret dies as a true witness203.” For Majnûn’s ecstatic love is, in the fullest sense, an initiatory death.

Here we see all the technical terms in the language of the faithful of love meet and cross. The witness of contemplation (shâhid) becomes the true witness (shahîd, “martyr”). The place of his witness-bearing—the place of his “martyrdom,” mashhad—is the place where divine Beauty appears (mazhar): the beautiful being who is its theophany. The same word, mashhad, has also been explained to us earlier as a name for paradise. Rûzbehân’s whole teaching about the divine appearing in beauty aims at this transubstantiation of the contemplative lover into a pure mirror, so that he endures as witness to the Absolute, as the very eye with which the Absolute contemplates itself.

The final pages of the Jasmine now sound like a finale, allusively bringing together every theme of the book. Rûzbehân quotes Sanâ’î, that other great Persian mystical poet (d. ca. 535/1141), several times. Following him, he repeats:

Let the sword of love wound you
So that you may find eternal Life,
For at the stroke of Azrael’s blade,
No one shows any sign of rising again204.

This means that physical death, the exitus, is neither the prelude to resurrection nor its announcement. Only initiatory death opens the way to it. That is how our Sufis understand mystical death through love, for “love does not accept a soul that it would leave alive205”—alive, that is, in its former life.

Yet “for someone whose only guide is love, unbelief and orthodoxy are alike a veil blocking the threshold. Everything partial or total among beings forms the arch of a bridge on the path of love206.” “Alone with God, I taste the moment reserved for those who transcend ordinary humanity207.” Rûzbehân presses Sanâ’î’s fearless words still further: “For the faithful of love there is no false religion and no heresy; neither immorality nor naïve innocence exists for them. … Paradise is the dwelling place of pious devotees. The Fire Temple is the mystical tavern of the faithful of love.

“Love does not tolerate immaturity. The path of love does not tolerate weakness208.” This mystical death, he says again, is the lover’s complete assimilation to love, that is, “to the substance of love, which is coeternal with the soul209.” To translate his terms (yakrangî, ham-rangî) fully, we would need to coin words such as symmorphosis and synchromatism: a transformation that makes the lover conform to love, accomplished in four phases parallel to those leading to esoteric tawhîd.

“All that we have just said,” Rûzbehân writes, “does no more than describe the state of being of love and of the faithful lover. The outermost limit of love is the beginning of mystical knowledge (ma’rifat). In mystical knowledge, love reaches its highest perfection. If the Lover becomes of one color (ham-rang) with the Beloved, he has attained the mystical station of tawhîd. If he is struck with wonder in mystical knowledge, he has attained the station of that knowledge. These two stations mark the furthest reach of love.

“When he has become a perfect knower of the divine, the divine Attributes appear to him through the attributes of his own mystical knowledge. To remember the Essence and meditate upon the Attributes is still to advance with modest restraint in the footsteps of eternal Wisdom.

“But the coming together of the Lover’s gaze—or person, jam’-e ’ayn—with the gaze—or person—of the Beloved is contained within the unifying gaze (’ayn-e jam’) that is love’s very essence.

“Thus, when love blossoms in a being, it draws that being toward this union of gazes. Through four phases—the annihilation of his own actions and qualities; the annihilation of that annihilation; the abiding existence of both; and the abiding of that abiding existence—the Lover becomes the Beloved.

“In the kingdom of divine lordship he possesses the divine mode of being and experiences supreme felicity. Then, if his love, a royal falcon, carries him to the vision of tawhîd, the mystical lover knows the joy of the One who reaches the goal: he contemplates the eye that contemplates him (shohûd-e ’ayn), as though he himself were that eye210.”

Now we can also understand fully the words of Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator, whom we must quote one last time. They seem to sum up the entire doctrine of theophany by describing three mirrors of contemplation. There is, he tells us, “1) The mirror in which to contemplate what is invisible, hidden, esoteric in the Divine Being: the three organs of subtle perception—the heart, the innermost secret (sirr), and the spirit. 2) The mirror in which to contemplate what is outward, manifest, the visible form of God, the divine as it appears (sûrat-e Haqq): the external senses, the faculties of sensory perception illuminated by the three subtle organs. 3) The mirror in which to contemplate God’s eternal Face: human eyes illuminated by love211.”

This is why, if so many of Rûzbehân’s statements have reminded us of a central teaching of Meister Eckhart—“the gaze by which I know Him is the very gaze by which He knows me”—we must add that Rûzbehân of Shîrâz would be a Meister Eckhart who had also written the romance of Tristan and Isolde.

We would thereby identify the twofold character of the Iranian mystical genius as it speaks both in its vast mystical epics and in Sufism, from Sanâ’î in the eleventh century to Nûr ’Alî-Shâh in the nineteenth. Our philosophies have recast the relationship between God and the world in social terms, whether to affirm or deny that relationship.

But the sense of the divine that we learn from this Sufism is not of a God who governs the world. It is of a divinity revealed to the intuition of the heart through the love awakened there by divine manifestations in beauty. This is perhaps the supreme paradox bequeathed by that Sufism to a world which may seem to us, even more than it did to Rûzbehân, a world “without eyes”—and therefore a world that God does not look upon, that God is not “concerned” with.

We have heard Rûzbehân’s anxious question during one of his visions: Where were You yesterday during the spiritual concert (samâ’), that I did not see You? This question, “Where are you?”, is one we hear these seekers after God asking, one after another, down through the centuries; for the matter so deeply “concerns” them. We hear it, among other places, in a very simple and moving poem by Fakhroddîn ’Erâqî (d. ca. 686/1287), one of the most celebrated poets of Iranian Sufism and a disciple of Sadroddîn Qonyawî. It was under Qonyawî’s influence that he became passionately devoted to Ibn ’Arabî’s mystical theosophy.

Love for you has driven me out of my senses. Where are you?
With all my soul I seek you, O soul of mine. Where are you?
I travel the world in search of you.
Everywhere I seek you. Where are you?
Since the world cannot contain your beauty,
How could I know what you are like, or where you are?
Since no one can pass into the place where you are,
Whom shall I ask? Who could know where you are?
You are manifest, yet hidden from everyone.
And if you are not hidden, where do you appear? …
To my startled and bewildered heart,
Give a sign along the Way. Where are you?
Since poor ’Erâqî is beside himself because of you,
Will you not at last say to him: O madman of love, where are you?212

What a revealing poem. The question “Where are you?” turns back upon itself. The person who asks it longs to hear it addressed to himself. For if he does hear it, he will at last have heard the answer to his own question. In other words, the poem announces that mysterious reversal of vision in which the Contemplator discovers that, in the very act of contemplation, he is himself the Contemplated: the Cogito (“I think”) becomes a Cogitor (“I am thought”).

The Book of Jasmine closes upon this mystery. Rûzbehân takes leave of the woman at whose request he wrote the book, recalling one last time the divine manifestations that can be read in the beauty of her face—provided one reads with the eyes of the soul. For him this beauty is what the vision of the Angel descending toward the horizon and “remaining suspended” there (Qur’an 53:8) was for the Prophet. As the manifestation of the divine Attribute above all others, it is itself the very eye through which the person who witnesses it contemplates it.

“All that we have just said is the history of the faithful of love, those who love with a spiritual and divine love. O you whose eyes are like jasmine; you who bear upon your face the secret of the divine self-manifestations (sirr-e af’âl); you whose blinking eyelids threaten the unique faithful of love with the sorcery of Hârût and Mârût; you whose love is the center of the imperishable heaven, though it holds a thousand complaints and laments over the transient world in store for the faithful of love; you whose brow reveals hundreds of theophanies to those who look with the eyes of the soul, while the gracious feints of your gaze give the understanding hundreds of occasions to remain suspended (53:8) beneath the very eye of the theophany! Only one who shares the inconsolable heart’s condition can know its inmost state.

“Let us say it plainly: the lamp of the divine Attributes is set in the Niche of the visible Signs. In this chapter the faithful of love will find many allusions to that mystery. In the following couplet by the wondrous mystical lover, that royal creature of ardent longing, Hosayn ibn Mansûr al-Hallâj, we find a similar ecstatic outcry, rich with hidden indications. He uttered it in the intoxication of tawhîd, under the influence of a gaze that discerned Unity, while his blood was flowing and he recited:

Glory to Him who revealed His humanity
As the glorious mystery of His radiant divinity,
And then appeared openly within His creature
In the form of one who eats and drinks213.

The moment when the Contemplator becomes the Contemplated, when the one asking “Where are you?” hears that very question addressed to himself, is the moment when he penetrates the secret of the famous saying: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” And then he also understands the mystical meaning of the Qur’anic summons: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him.”

PreviousV. The Jasmine of the Faithful in LoveNextI. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism

Book IV

Shiism and Sufism

Chapter I Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism

1. Discovering a Body of Work

The name of Haydar Amoli will already be familiar to readers of this book. We have referred to his writings more than once when discussing essential aspects of Twelver Shiism.

In particular (Book I, Chapter III, §2), we drew attention to his interpretation of the Quranic verse (33:72) concerning the divine trust entrusted to humanity. That interpretation carries a further idea: the trust can be passed on only to someone who shows himself to be its rightful heir by being capable of receiving it. This is one of the Quranic verses on which the inner, esoteric understanding of Islam—and therefore Shiite Islam—is founded.

Haydar Amoli's work brings us to the heart of a question that has arisen repeatedly in these pages, and that anyone seeking to recover Islamic esotericism at its source—the inner life of spiritual Islam—must confront.

How does the spiritual knowledge (ʿirfān) of Sufism, now relatively familiar in the West, relate to Shiite spiritual knowledge or theosophy (ʿirfān-e shīʿī), which remains far less well known? The conviction of the Iranian ʿārif, the person who possesses this spiritual knowledge, is that Sufi gnosis could never have existed without Shiite gnosis before it. Its original source, they believe, lies in the teachings of the holy Imams, who explained to their disciples the hidden meaning of the Quranic verses.

Taken as a whole, Haydar Amoli's writings are an outstanding expression of that position. They offer one of the clearest opportunities to study a form of Shiism fully conscious that, in its essence, it is Islam's inner or esoteric teaching. The great treatise we have recently published bears the title Jāmiʿ al-asrār, a Compendium of Esoteric Teachings.

Haydar Amoli was neither an isolated figure nor the first in a succession of such thinkers. We have already observed that the secrecy to which Twelver Shiism was forced for several centuries means that we must allow for a great many people who were Shiites in secret; it also helps explain why relatively few works of this kind have survived.

Even so, in the thirteenth century Sa'doddin Hamuyeh and his disciples were already prominent representatives of Shiite Sufism, or Sufi Shiism. In the following century—the eighth century of the Islamic calendar, the fourteenth of the Christian era—Haydar Amoli, although he belonged to no particular ṭarīqa or Sufi order, deserved, alongside a few others such as Rajeb Borsi, the description given to him in the title of this chapter.

The pages devoted to him here are intended only as a brief introduction to his writings, pending the translations and studies they deserve. His work is one of the keys to the hidden spiritual dwelling of Twelver Shiism.

We shall begin by outlining its meaning and its place among the full body of Shiite writings.

We shall then recount how we were led to discover the work of Sayyed Haydar Amoli, and how a series of fortunate manuscript discoveries enabled us to reconstruct both his life and the list of his writings.

As Haydar Amoli tells us in the opening pages of his great compendium of Shiite theosophy, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, his central concern is to recall the original relationship between Sufism and Shiism, and consequently to set out a doctrine of Shiism that is not of his own invention but goes back to its very beginnings: to what the Imams taught their disciples and closest companions.

Traditions (hadith) from the Imams are quoted abundantly throughout his work. Their teaching is the foundation of his thought and the authority to which he constantly returns. If he embraces Sufism, he does so out of fidelity to the Imams themselves. In this he differs both from Shiites concerned only with the outward meaning of religion and from Sufis who are not Shiites.

Haydar Amoli's understanding of Shiism as the inner teaching of Islam has not merely endured from century to century. It is thoroughly alive today, and is shared by all the ʿurafāʾ, those devoted to spiritual knowledge. I have heard it expressed repeatedly, not only by venerable shaykhs but also by young mullahs.

One had only to ask, for example, why Shiism has no missionary spirit, why it does not try to win converts. The answer invariably expressed the same conviction: if the Imam does not guide a person inwardly, then whatever words you address to that person, however sublime, will reach their ear as no more than a passing breath of wind.

As for someone guided by the inward Imam, let that Imam guide them. For this reason I was repeatedly reminded that Shiism, in its essence, is an inward initiation: an initiation into the inner meaning of Islam's highest teachings, handed down and enriched through a long tradition from one century to the next. Although Shiism addresses everyone, a young mullah told me, its meaning and vocation are to bring forth, little by little and across the centuries, a spiritual elite.

Did the Imams not say again and again, “Our cause is difficult and heavy to bear; only an angel brought near to God, a prophet sent on a mission, or a believer whose heart has been tested can bear it”? To become a religion of the masses, then, would put Shiism in danger of being reduced to the ẓāhir, its outward aspect, until it was nothing more than a particular rite alongside the other legal traditions of Islam. One may of course object that since the Safavid period such a transformation into a mass religion has already taken place.

But that is precisely the question to which these inexhaustible conversations continually return. In exchanges of this kind, I have heard young mullahs display a profound awareness of their spiritual task, however difficult its immediate future may be. They may be few, and even less widely recognized.

But was their situation not already foreseen in the First Imam's conversations with Komayl ibn Ziyad? At the very least, these young men bore witness that the silsilat al-ʿirfān, the lineage of spiritual knowledge, would not be broken.

Haydar Amoli's work shows, perhaps better than any other, that a tradition remains alive only through continual spiritual rebirth. The spirit of tradition remains truly a spirit only while it is creative; without that creative spirit, tradition would be little more than a funeral procession. Here, “creative” describes the activity that follows from unceasing inspiration (ilhām). Without such inspiration, the living interpretation of the sacred Book could not disclose what had remained hidden. This idea belongs with the notion of continuous creation (tajdīd al-khalq). Spiritual interpretation is a source of perpetual renewal.

But renewal is not the same as innovation: innovation implies, in one way or another, a break with what came before, or an act of force. What makes these renewals “original” is precisely that each returns to the origins. For a long time, Western studies of Sufism were conducted in such a way that Haydar Amoli's views on Shiism and Sufism might strike a Western scholar, at first, as an unprecedented innovation.

Yet his purpose is essentially to restore the tradition of Islam in its fullness: an Islam embracing both the ẓāhir, the outward meaning, and the bāṭin, the inward meaning. For him, this fullness is the very meaning of Shiism. Unfortunately, we have already had reason to regret how badly Shiite thought and theology have long been treated in the West.

A certain scholarly conformism accepted as an unquestioned premise that everything in Shiism was “tendentious,” when it did not go so far as to use frankly insulting descriptions, such as those that somehow found their way into the writings of Nöldeke. Others claimed to explain everything through “political intrigues” and “social facts,” even turning Shiism into a political creation of the Safavid age.

Yet politics scarcely figures in the Imams' teachings. More than a century before the Safavids, Haydar Amoli's writings show Shiite thought capable of constructing its own great systematic works—so much so that the major writings of the Safavid era can no longer be studied without reference to our Sayyed.

We must return to the essential point. The Imams' teaching requires us to attend to the religious meaning of Shiism: in its essence, it is a phenomenon of spiritual life. This religious meaning sustains both a spiritual experience and a metaphysics that give shape to vast inner worlds.

We will not discover it through troublemakers or agitators. No one has ever succeeded in preventing such people from making careers for themselves, not even in the circle surrounding the Imams. We need only avoid confusing them with what is truly at issue. Once we learn to see what is at issue, the statements made by Haydar Amoli and thinkers like him about Sufism will no longer surprise us.

But if we insist on reducing everything to secular terms, we close off a sanctuary of Islamic consciousness and radically distort any possible study of religious experience as it is lived and understood. Perhaps the consequences of that distortion have already spread to the East, among a generation educated in Western schools. If so, Haydar Amoli's work may appear more relevant than ever.

The significance of his work becomes clear when we consider the purpose that guided him from early youth, as he himself confides to his readers. Drawing on the texts, he wanted to remind them that the holy Imams' teaching certainly explains many obscure details of the sharīʿa, the religious law, but that in its essence this teaching is directed toward the inward meaning (bāṭin), from which it cannot be separated.

When the Imams' explanations are systematically gathered around each Quranic verse to form a continuous commentary, their teaching becomes a guide to the “seven hidden depths of Quranic Revelation.”214 Unfortunately, some people who called themselves Shiites failed to recognize this teaching. Some wanted to retain only what concerned law and ritual.

Why, then, did so much of what the Imams taught about the inner dimension—the hidden, spiritual meaning, the asrār or mysteries, the bāṭin—bear fruit instead in non-Shiite Sufism? It was this paradox that led Haydar Amoli, at the very beginning of his great book, to formulate a corresponding paradox of his own: “The Sufis are those who truly deserve the name of Shiites (al-shīʿa al-ḥaqīqīya) and of believers whose hearts have been tested (muʾmin mumtaḥan).”

A Shiite Sufi, of course, will have no difficulty accepting this claim. It has borne fruit throughout the centuries; much of Ma'sum Ali-Shah's great encyclopedia of Sufism amounts, in effect, to an extended commentary upon it.215

But a Shiite who rejects esoteric knowledge (ʿirfān) and confines religion to its outward meaning will find the claim much harder to accept. As Haydar Amoli himself puts it, it is a “hard blow.” There are doubtless also Shiite spiritual teachers of the kind we have already mentioned—mystics in the fullest and most genuine sense of the word—who would wish to qualify the statement. They maintain a certain reserve toward Sufism, preferring to speak of ʿirfān, spiritual knowledge, rather than taṣawwuf, Sufism.

Even Molla Sadra Shirazi, whose work is steeped in the spirit of Sufism—or perhaps precisely because it is—wrote a vigorous attack on a certain kind of Sufism: the Kasr aṣnām al-jāhiliyya, or Shattering the Idols of Ignorance.

Haydar Amoli himself shows the same clear judgment. He distinguishes one kind of Sufism from another, and does so without mincing his words. In him, clear sight and independence of mind go together. His attitude toward Ibn Arabi offers another example. He admires Ibn Arabi fervently, follows his teaching, and writes commentaries on his works.

Indeed, he was among the Shiites who did most to bring Ibn Arabi's thought into the Shiite tradition. For these thinkers recognized something of their own intellectual and spiritual inheritance in Ibn Arabi's theosophy. Many of his chapters—those on Salman Pak or the Twelve Imams, for example—might have been written by a Shiite.

Yet on one question Haydar Amoli firmly refuses to follow him. His criticism is respectful but persistent and uncompromising, because the issue bears directly on the Shiite understanding of prophecy and of the Imams. Who is the “Seal” (Khātim) of the walāya, the spiritual authority and guardianship transmitted through the Imams? Haydar Amoli devotes considerable attention to criticizing Ibn Arabi's position on this question—a position perhaps made more daring still by Ibn Arabi's commentator Dawud Qaysari.

The criticism is important both in his great theosophical compendium, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, and in the introduction to his extensive commentary on the Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam, the treatise read and reread, generation after generation, by spiritually minded Muslims.

In short, the idea governing our Sayyed's thought is this. On the one hand, the Shiism of the Twelve Imams is Islam in its esoteric fullness: spiritual religion, the true meaning of Revelation, the spiritual knowledge at the heart of Islam. Insofar as Sufism also upholds this inward teaching, while certain Shiites reject it for one reason or another, we may say that Sufism is true Shiism—its representative, as it were, incognito within Sunni Islam.

On the other hand, Sufism has unfortunately sometimes lost sight of its origins and fallen into serious errors, particularly over the identity of the “Seal of the walāya.” The process is easy to understand. Sufism received the very idea of walāya from Shiism. To separate itself from Shiism and claim independence, it therefore had to alter that idea at its roots. Many Sufis are unaware of this. They denounce Shiism, forgetting that it is the source of their own ʿirfān.

Some maintain that the inward meaning (bāṭin) can eventually dispense with the outward meaning (ẓāhir), and that mystical truth (ḥaqīqa) releases a person from the obligation to observe the religious law (sharīʿa). These are two related errors, whose excess mirrors an opposite excess: that of Shiites who think they can dispense with spiritual knowledge altogether. They imagine that the outward sense, by itself and without any inward sense, is the true meaning of religion. Such people, in the end, are Shiites only figuratively (majāzī), not in the fullest sense of the word.

Haydar Amoli thus conducts his struggle on two fronts. He challenges those who recognize nothing beyond a literal reading of religion as law, whether they are Sunni or Shiite. And he challenges Sufis who have forgotten the origins and implications of their own spiritual knowledge, and of the consecration symbolized by the Sufi cloak (khirqa) that they wear. This was his life's work. It also helps us place him within the four periods we have proposed, here and elsewhere, for understanding the dramatic history of Shiism.216

Any adequate division into periods ought, above all, to take account of Shiite thought and spirituality as they unfold into a world of their own, with a history of its own. That history is a hierohistory—a sacred history whose meaning is shaped by the divine. Because it is always oriented toward the ultimate fulfilment of things, it must break through history in the ordinary sense whenever the two meet.

Any scheme based simply on the outward succession of dates and events can therefore describe only the external aspects of this spiritual world; it remains outside sacred history itself. For the reader's convenience, I shall briefly recall the broad outline of the four periods we distinguish in the outward history of Twelver Shiite thought.

First: the initial period, that of the holy Imams and their immediate disciples, ending with the “Greater Occultation” (Ghaybat al-Kubrā) of the Twelfth Imam.

Second: the period from Kolayni (d. 329/940), who compiled the great collection of traditions from the Imams, to the philosopher, theologian, and astronomer Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 672/1274).

Third: the Mongol period, extending from Nasir Tusi to Mir Damad and the School of Isfahan in the eleventh Islamic/seventeenth Christian century. Fourth: the period from Mir Damad to our own day, when another period may perhaps be beginning.

Sayyed Haydar Amoli, living in the eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century, is thus a leading figure of the third period. Now that some of his major works are known to us, we can say that they tower over the philosophical, theological, and theosophical writing of his century.

What, then, is the decisive feature of Shiite thought during this third period, both in its content and in the form it takes? It seems we may answer, briefly, that the defining development was precisely the one mentioned a few lines ago: the integration of Ibn Arabi's thought into Shiite thought.

Ibn Arabi died in 1240. We have already indicated the exact question on which Haydar Amoli, despite his extraordinary reverence for Ibn Arabi, puts forward a decisive criticism: the identity of the person who is the “Seal of the walāya”—in other words, the identity of the Imam. We have had occasion to mention this criticism before.

Nonetheless, in Haydar Amoli's work, as in that of Ibn Abi Jomhur in the following century, the entire metaphysics of being, the understanding of tawḥīd (divine unity) in its two aspects, outward and inward, the doctrine of the divine Names and the forms in which they become manifest (maẓāhir), and hence the whole elaboration of the teaching concerning the Imams—all these extend and deepen Ibn Arabi's doctrines.

The fact remains, too, that Ibn Arabi's immense body of work has educated spiritually minded Muslims generation after generation. His short compendium, the Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam (The Bezels of the Wisdoms of the Prophets), has been the subject of some 150 commentaries. Around 130 of their authors, writing in Arabic or Persian, were Iranian.217 Some commentators were Sunnis, others Shiites. Haydar Amoli's extensive and highly individual commentary stands among the foremost works of the latter group.

We said earlier that Haydar Amoli's work, together with that of Ibn Abi Jomhur, did more than almost any other to integrate Ibn Arabi's thought into Shiite thought, as though Shiism were recovering something that already belonged to it from Ibn Arabi's immense intellectual legacy.

This raises the whole question of the origins and sources of the thought of the Shaykh al-Akbar, the “Greatest Master.” Future research will have to pursue the question through both Ibn Arabi's own writings and the surviving works of Shiite philosophy.218 It concerns Ibn Arabi's early influences and education during his youth in Andalusia, and the spread of both Ismaili and Twelver Shiism among the spiritual teachers of Andalusia—above all Ibn Masarra and the School of Almeria, whose teachings Asín Palacios was able to reconstruct from quotations in Ibn Arabi himself.

One begins to discern an extraordinary cycle: Shiite thought travelling as far as the westernmost lands of Islam, then returning to the East through Ibn Arabi, who could no longer live and think as a theosopher under the conditions prevailing in Andalusia. Ibn Arabi might even have reached Iran himself had the upheaval of the Mongol invasions not kept him away.

But just a century after his death in Damascus, a young Iranian Sayyed left his native land—the city of Amol and the shores of the Caspian Sea—and settled at the holy places of Shiism in Iraq. There he would become perhaps the most outstanding Shiite commentator on Ibn Arabi, the thinker who, above all others, would lead the theosophy of the Shaykh al-Akbar back to what he believed to be its source.

This brings us to the stages of our own discovery of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's writings. We have described them elsewhere, on the occasion of the first publication of two of his major treatises, and shall recall only the essentials here.219

Our path was guided by two interests that came together: Ibn Arabi's work and Shiite thought. Frequent quotations in the authors we were studying suggested to us that Haydar Amoli's writings ought to be among the first approached by anyone wishing to understand that Shiite thought which permeates the philosophy and spirituality of Iranian Islam, where philosophical reflection retained a vitality and momentum unknown elsewhere in the Islamic world.

After locating two of his treatises in Iran and obtaining photocopies, we therefore devoted several years of research and teaching to his work.220 Eventually we found ourselves in the anxious predicament familiar to so many scholars: vita brevis—life is short. We were convinced that we must publish those of our Sayyed's writings which were accessible to us and which we had already translated to a considerable extent.

Yet other equally urgent tasks made us hesitate to undertake so monumental a project alone. It was then that Osman Yahia, a leading specialist in Ibn Arabi who shared our assessment of Haydar Amoli's importance, kindly offered to collaborate.

His help put an end to our hesitation, and work on the edition began.

Moreover, Osman Yahia's own research led to discoveries of inestimable value. In Istanbul, he found Haydar Amoli's great commentary on Ibn Arabi's Fuṣūṣ. In Najaf, Iraq, among the treasures preserved at the Imam's shrine, he discovered the autograph manuscript of Haydar Amoli's great tafsīr: his extensive Shiite mystical commentary on the Quran, in seven substantial volumes. It is a monumental work of taʾwīl, the spiritual interpretation of scripture whose importance to philosophical thought in Shiite Islam we have stressed throughout this book.

Six volumes of the author's own manuscript are at Najaf; the first is at Qom, where a copy of the opening of the commentary is also kept in the library of Sayyed Shihaboddin Mar'ashi Najafi, who generously placed it at our disposal.221 At Najaf, the collection is completed by the autograph of the last treatise composed by Sayyed Haydar, the Treatise on the Higher Sciences (Risālat al-ʿulūm al-ʿāliya), whose importance is not hard to imagine.

Furthermore, the introductory writings to his commentary on Ibn Arabi and the opening of his Quranic commentary contain two autobiographical accounts that complement one another. Together they reveal the spiritual drama our Sayyed lived through and the radical decision by which he resolved it. They also provide detailed titles of his writings and allow us to arrange them chronologically over the course of his life. There are thirty-four works, written in Arabic and Persian. Some are short treatises; others are vast works filling several volumes.

We would be completely satisfied as researchers if we had already found manuscripts of every one of our author's works. Unfortunately, we have not yet reached that point.

But there is another possibility, all too rare, in which an author's own account of his life brings his writings closer to us. We then long to find the surroundings in which he lived, meditated, and worked, and sometimes that wish can be fulfilled.

In Isfahan, for instance, we can revisit the Sadr madrasa, the college where Mir Damad taught and where Sadra Shirazi and so many others spent their student years. In Shiraz we can revisit the Khan madrasa, where that same Molla Sadra taught, including the room in which he gave his lessons and the place he occupied there.222 With Sayyed Haydar Amoli, things are more difficult, at least as far as the Iranian period of his life is concerned.

We shall see that before the great rupture dividing his life into two periods, he spent most of his youth in Amol, in his native Tabarestan. The upheavals of history, and the storms unleashed by the Mongols, have left few ancient monuments standing there.

Nevertheless, those of us preparing the edition of Haydar Amoli's works were eager to make a pilgrimage together to Amol and the shores of the Caspian Sea. A new road, opened only a few years earlier, cuts directly through the Alborz mountains and brings one from Tehran to Amol, immediately to the north, in a journey of some two hundred kilometres.

We went in search of buildings that Sayyed Haydar might have known or visited in his lifetime. Only one seems likely: the imamzadeh, a shrine known in local tradition by several names, including Seh Sayyed (“the Three Sayyeds”) and Mir Haydar. The mausoleum stands in a garden beside a stream and is generally dated to the seventh Islamic/thirteenth Christian century or the eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century. Our Sayyed probably knew it. The same cannot be said of any other surviving monument.223

Today the banks of the Haraz River (Harāz Rūd), which runs through Amol, have been pleasantly landscaped. What did they look like when Amol was the capital of the princes of Tabarestan? One thing certainly remains: the landscape. There is the forest clothing the mountain slopes, from which the road emerges onto the broad plain of Mazandaran; the exuberant greenery, so different from the austerity of Iran's high plateau; the shifting moods of the sky, changing with those of the sea, held captive here within the continent.

Sayyed Haydar could have seen all this much as we see it, allowing for a few differences. Perhaps we need to see it with him if we are to hear the full resonance of the moving confession translated below: that of a young man who possessed everything and who, at thirty, chose to abandon it all and become nothing more than a “pilgrim toward God.”

His decision coincided with a dramatic moment in the history of Mazandaran, which includes Tabarestan—a name formerly applied especially to its mountainous region. Biographical reference works often call our Sayyed “Amoli Mazandarani.” Through his family's standing and the duties he performed in his youth at the court of his ruler, his life became linked to one of Mazandaran's most celebrated dynasties, the Bawandids, descendants of Bawand.

When he recalls the prince he served, he proudly emphasizes the dynasty's noble descent from the Sasanians of pre-Islamic Persia. Throughout the centuries, names of purely Iranian origin, borrowed from the heroes of the national epic, stood alongside Islamic names among the rulers of this house.

A few essential facts will help place the autobiographical account we shall examine below. The Bawandids ruled Tabarestan for seven centuries, from 45/665 to 750/1349. Their descent was traced back to the Sasanians, through Parwiz, Andeshrawan, and Yazdgard. The dynasty comprised three successive branches.

The third, the Kinkhwariyan, ruled from 635/1237–38 to 750/1349 and began with Hosamoddawleh Ardashir ibn Kinkhwar. His eighth successor and the dynasty's last sovereign was Fakhroddawleh Hasan ibn Shah Kay-Khosraw ibn Yazdgard, who ruled for sixteen years, from 734 to 750 of the Islamic calendar. It was this prince who welcomed Sayyed Haydar into his intimate circle and then appointed him minister.

We shall see our Sayyed recall both the prince and his father with deep feeling. Fakhroddawleh had succeeded his own brother, Sharaf al-Moluk ibn Shah Kay-Khosraw, whose short but fortunate reign lasted six years and who died in 734/1333–34. At that time Sayyed Haydar was a boy of fourteen or fifteen; it is therefore unsurprising that his memory of this prince was equally vivid.

Fakhroddawleh had married the sister of Kiya Afrasiyab of Cholab. Afrasiyab brought a false accusation against him before the religious scholars (ʿulamāʾ), using it as a pretext for the prince's murder. Fakhroddawleh was treacherously assassinated by his brother-in-law, or by the latter's two sons, on 27 Muharram 750/17 April 1349. It is almost as if the name Afrasiyab had destined its bearer, ever since the heroic age, to the sinister role of traitor.

Fakhroddawleh left four sons and a daughter. The eldest, Malek Ka'us, was only ten when his father died. Those loyal to the dynasty failed to recapture Amol, but Afrasiyab would enjoy the fruits of his crime for only about ten years.224

These details belong to the path by which we are coming to know Sayyed Haydar Amoli and his writings. In the very year, 750/1349, when his prince was murdered and the Bawandid dynasty came to an end, Haydar decided to abandon his brilliant worldly career and “turn toward God.”

Yet although he describes in detail the spiritual circumstances that brought his conversion to its decisive conclusion, he says not a word about the tragedy that ended the dynasty in that same year. If we weigh the wording of his autobiographical account, it seems likely that he made his decision a little before the tragedy took place, while he was still a minister at the court of Amol.

Much later, when he wrote two accounts of his life, he could speak of his ruler in the past tense, offering only a fervent blessing and saying nothing of his violent end. All this was already far behind him. Did he ever see his native Mazandaran again, where Tamerlane's Mongol horsemen were preparing to sweep through? We know nothing of his death. He takes his leave of us quietly with his final book, the Treatise on the Higher Sciences (787/1385–86).

2. An Autobiographical and Bibliographical Outline

We have just mentioned two autobiographical accounts through which the course of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's life comes clearly into view.

We shall call them Autobiography A and Autobiography B.

The earlier of the two, Autobiography A, appears at the beginning of the great Tafsīr ʿirfānī, the mystical commentary on the Quran entitled al-Muḥīṭ al-aʿẓam (The Supreme Ocean), which Haydar Amoli completed in 777/1375–76. It gives enough detail for us to glimpse his years of learning and his youth, as well as the reasons for the momentous decision that sent him out as a solitary pilgrim along the roads of Iran toward the Shiite holy places in Iraq.

Unfortunately, the narrative breaks off abruptly at the bottom of its last surviving leaf, just as the author is describing in detail his extended stay in Isfahan on the way to Mecca. Was the writing interrupted and never resumed? Were pages torn out? Or were they simply misplaced when the manuscript was bound? Only a prolonged examination of the photocopies will allow us to decide. Whatever the explanation, this break currently deprives us of the fuller information that our Sayyed undoubtedly intended to give us there about the second period of his life.

The second account, Autobiography B, is found in the introductory sections of the Naṣṣ al-nuṣūṣ, Haydar Amoli's commentary on Ibn Arabi's Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam, which he completed at Najaf in 782/1380–81. Here he reviews his youth and the spiritual crisis that led him to set out as a pilgrim toward the Holy Places, but in briefer terms than in Autobiography A. This time, however, the account does not break off.

Instead, the author goes on to survey his activity as a writer, providing a catalogue of his works that is of inestimable value to us. By bringing the two narratives together, we can obtain an overall outline of his life. We have distinguished an Iranian period ending with his conversion (750/1349–50) and an Iraqi period beginning with his arrival at the Holy Places (751/1350–51). The Iraqi period, in turn, can be divided in two on the basis of the dates supplied by his writings.

We shall therefore consider three periods in Sayyed Haydar Amoli's life, which we shall designate A, B, and C.

Autobiography B allows us to establish the year of Sayyed Haydar's birth at Amol to within a year: 720/1320 (possibly 719 of the Islamic calendar, but more probably 720). We learn from it that he reached the holy places of Iraq in 751/1350–51. Allowing a year between his departure from Amol and his arrival there, he must have left the Caspian shores in 750/1349–50. He tells us that he was then thirty years old. Those first thirty years constitute the Iranian period of his life.

Sayyed Haydar ibn Ali ibn Haydar Obaydi Hosayni Amoli belonged to a distinguished family of Sayyeds in Amol, a city whose population had been almost entirely Shiite from the earliest times. During this Iranian period he received his education and gained his first experience of life.

In his great theosophical compendium, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, he confides that from his youth—even from childhood—he had devoted himself passionately to the study of Twelver Shiite spiritual knowledge and theosophy (ʿirfān-e shīʿī-e davāzdah Imām). For this whole period, Autobiography A gives us the clearest portrait of his character, tracing the distinctive features of his spiritual and moral personality. Here we shall simply summarize it.225

The reverence Haydar Âmolî felt for his status as a Sayyed—a descendant of the holy Imams—led him to begin by tracing his family line. Generation by generation, it reached back to the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-’Âbidîn, son of the Third Imam, Hosayn, the martyr of Karbala.

As he also tells us in his Jâmi’ al-asrâr, from childhood until the age of thirty he devoted himself to studying “the teachings of my forefathers, the immaculate Imams,” though at first he confined himself to the outward, religious-law aspect of the sharî’at. He then completed the full course of traditional learning, both transmitted and rational (manqûl and ma’qûl): theology based on received authority and speculative philosophy. He began his studies in Âmol, then travelled to Khorasan and studied at Astarâbâd; from there he went to Isfahan, where he remained for a considerable time. All these studies, begun in early childhood and pursued in Âmol and elsewhere, had occupied some twenty years.

Sayyed Haydar therefore returned to his native Âmol when he was about twenty-five. Tabarestan was then ruled by Fakhroddawleh Hasan, son of Shâh Kay-Khosraw ibn Yazdgard, whose place in the Bâwandiyân dynasty we have already discussed. Sayyed Haydar himself explicitly recalls the origins of this dynasty. The pride with which this Shiite Sayyed emphasizes that his princes could trace their ancestry, generation after generation, back to the Sasanian rulers of pre-Islamic Persia is especially revealing of Iranian Shiite consciousness: a feeling of loyalty to both lines of descent, that of the Imams and that of the princes of ancient Persia.

King Fakhroddawleh showered Sayyed Haydar with favors. He admitted him to his intimate circle, made him his confidant, and eventually appointed him minister. Our Sayyed seems then to have enjoyed every pleasure the world could offer: family life, honors, wealth, power, social connections, fine houses, agreeable companions and friends. His many allusions suggest that nothing was denied him.

Yet, as so often happens in accounts of spiritual conversion, it was in the very midst of this life of abundance, with everything promising what we would now call “a brilliant career,” that Haydar Âmolî discovered its emptiness, its taste of ashes. “So it continued,” he writes, “until, in the innermost secrecy of my being, the calls of Truth finally prevailed, and God revealed to me the vanity of the heedlessness, ignorance, and unawareness in which I was living.

“I then saw how far I had strayed from the path of Truth: I was heading straight down the road to ruin and unbelief. So I spoke privately with my God, asking Him to deliver me from it all. And there arose within me, taking possession of my whole being, a longing to renounce everything and to be alone; a desire to turn toward God by entering the path of tawhîd, the realization of divine unity.

“But I knew that this would be impossible as long as I remained among kings, in my familiar native land, in the company of my brothers and friends. I understood that it would be better to renounce them, to leave them behind, and to go somewhere that would give me every possible help in living a life worthy of the name. So I abandoned family and fortune, king and honors, father and mother, brothers, close friends, and companions.”

Stripping himself of everything, our pilgrim kept only an old, discarded khirqa, a Sufi cloak, and set out to visit the Shiite holy places, then Jerusalem, and finally the sanctuary at Mecca. His route took him through Qazwîn and Ray and back to Isfahan, where, not long before, he had spent so much time enjoying the pleasures of a privileged youth.

Now he associated only with Sufis, entering into a pact of spiritual brotherhood (fotowwat) with them. He placed himself especially under the guidance of a shaykh named Nûroddin Tehrânî. “This shaykh was a great mystic, an ascetic acknowledged by the entire spiritual elite...” Alas, it is in the middle of this unfinished sentence that autobiography A abruptly breaks off, leaving us little hope of finding its continuation elsewhere.

For the moment, we can learn nothing more about our Sayyed’s spiritual experiences in Isfahan, apart from two dreams to which we shall return. It is autobiography B, which takes up the story after his decisive choice of voluntary exile, that tells us about Haydar’s work and literary output during the second period of his life.

This marks the beginning of his Iraqi period, or more precisely its first phase (period B). Sayyed Haydar travelled to Mecca and Medina, where he would have liked to settle. He dates this pilgrimage to 751 AH (1350–51 CE). Ill health, however, forced him to return to Iraq and its Shiite holy places. Since the Treatise on the Knowledge of Being is dated at Najaf in 768 AH (1366–67 CE), we shall use that work as our point of reference for distinguishing the second phase of his Iraqi period (period C), at least as far as his writings are concerned.

As for the first phase, the biographical accounts tell us that in Baghdad Sayyed Haydar studied under two eminent shaykhs: Mawlânâ Nasîroddin Kashânî Hillî (d. 755/1354) and the shaykh commonly known as Fakhr al-Mohaqqiqîn (682/1283–771/1370), son of the celebrated ’Allâmeh Hillî (648/1250–726/1326). The latter had himself studied under Nasîroddin Tûsî and Kâtibî Qazwînî and was one of the leading figures in Shiite theology at the time.226

In 761 AH (1359–60 CE), Fakhr al-Mohaqqiqîn granted Sayyed Haydar an ijâzat, an authorization to teach the books he had studied with him. It was at this teacher’s request that Haydar wrote the Risâlat raf’ât al-khilâf, a treatise defending the First Shiite Imam’s conduct toward the first three caliphs recognized by Sunnism; the two men also exchanged a number of questions and answers.227 Beyond this, the only reliable information presently available comes from our Sayyed himself, in autobiography B and in the account of his own writings.

Let us recall that the latest date we can establish is that of his Treatise on the Higher Sciences, written in 787 AH (1385–86 CE). Sayyed Haydar was then sixty-five years old, or sixty-seven by the lunar calendar. After that, all trace of him disappears. We know neither when nor under what circumstances he died.

As already noted, autobiography B appears in the introduction to Haydar’s great commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs al-hikam, completed in 782 AH (1380–81 CE). He was then sixty-two lunar years old and had been away from his native Iran for thirty-two years. Here is what he writes:228

“When God Most High commanded me to renounce everything other than Him and to turn toward Him in true conversion, He inspired me to seek a place, a dwelling where I could settle and devote myself to serving and worshipping Him, as His command and guidance required—a place beyond which there would be none higher or more illustrious in this world.

“And so I set out for Mecca—may God Most High exalt it—after renouncing my office as minister, power, wealth, honors, my father and mother, my brothers and companions. I put on an old, worthless khirqa that had been thrown away and left my native country, Âmol and Tabarestan, toward Khorasan.

“There I had been the minister (vazîr) of the ruler of the country, one of the most illustrious sovereigns of Persia, for he was among the august descendants of Kesrâ [Khosrow]. His name was al-Malik al-Sa’îd Fakhroddawleh, son of the late king Shâh Katkhodâ229—may God grant them both a dwelling in Paradise. I was thirty years old at that time.

“In this way, until the moment I reached Mecca, I had to face trials of every kind and struggles of every sort. It would take several volumes to tell the whole story.

“Yet in most of the circumstances I passed through, I found myself repeating these words of God: ‘Whoever leaves his home to migrate toward God and His Messenger and is overtaken by death—his reward is surely with God; and God is forgiving and merciful’ (4:151). Or, in the words of a gnostic whose ardent longing resembled my own: ‘For Your pleasure I have renounced all creatures; / I have made orphans of my own people so that I might behold You. / Even if You cut me limb from limb, / My heart would yearn for no one but You.’

“In short, this was my condition until I reached Mecca. There I performed the obligatory pilgrimage and carried out the prescribed rites, together with the voluntary acts of devotion and the other observances. This was in the year 751 of the Hijra (1350–51 CE). I had intended to settle there, but then an ardent desire arose within me to make my home in Medina, for I had not yet paid my visit—my pilgrimage of devotion—to the Messenger of God, his descendants, and his companions.

“So I made my way to Medina. I visited the Messenger of God and resolved to remain there.

“But obstacles once again intervened, first of all physical illness, until I had no choice but to return to Iraq, to that familiar place, the magnificent and most sacred shrine at Najaf—may God’s peace be upon the one who gives it its glory [Imam ’Alî].

“I returned there in health and settled permanently, devoting myself entirely to spiritual exercises and retreat, to worship and the service of God, with a breadth, fervor, and seriousness beyond which it would scarcely have been possible to go. Then, during this period, from God and His suprasensible Presences, there flowed into my heart the spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) of the Quran and the commentary on the Fosûs that I have already mentioned: a whole world of ideas and higher knowledge, truths and subtle perceptions, which it is impossible to set out in detail in any way, because these are the Words of God (Kalimât Allâh), which can neither be counted nor brought to an end nor interrupted.”

This long passage does more than acquaint us with the outward setting and chronology of a spiritual adventure. It lets us glimpse the man’s secret: the personal, inward rule of his life, unbending and reducible to no other. A restrained emotion runs through it, revealing the gifts that made Haydar Âmolî the man he was.

Among the qualities that most clearly mark his personality, we must also single out the vitality of his active imagination: his ability to perceive the suprasensible world on the plane of the imaginal world (’âlam al-mithâl). This faculty reaches the level of visionary perception, sometimes in dreams, sometimes in an intermediate state between waking and sleeping. Haydar Âmolî has left us accounts of several dreams and visions, including two dreams he had in Isfahan while passing through the city on the great journey that took him from his native Tabarestan toward the Shiite holy places.

“Know that I was travelling, and my route took me through Isfahan. I was bound for Baghdad, to visit the holy places of the Imams and to make the pilgrimage to the most sacred sanctuary at Mecca, both to fulfill a religious obligation and with the intention of settling there. Then, one night, I had the following dream-vision: I found myself in the cloth merchants’ market in Isfahan.

“I was looking at my own body lying full-length on the ground. It was dead, wrapped in a white shroud, while I stood gazing at it with curiosity, amazed by my predicament: how could I be standing there, and at the same time be a dead man lying on the ground? I remained in this condition until I awoke.

“On another occasion, also in a dream in Isfahan, I was leaning against the shop of a certain companion... On my shoulders was a gilded pewter vessel, like those carried by some of the water sellers who move among the people offering them a drink... And I was giving water to those present, all the while observing myself with curiosity.230”

Both dreams give a characteristic picture of our Sayyed’s inner condition after he had decisively broken with the youth still so close behind him and given himself entirely to divine service. In his dreams he thus gives visible form to an experience well known in the psychology of mysticism: the spiritual birth of a new person.

We possess other accounts of his visions, notably one of the night sky above Baghdad, in which he saw—whether dreaming or in an intermediate state he does not say—a blazing diagram embodying all his Shiite devotion: the names of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones written in letters of fire within circles of lapis lazuli, arranged as an immense quadrilateral across the starry sky (see § 5 below).

To the extent that it is true to say each person is what they love, and that we can therefore understand someone only through their love—through everything that gave their life its purpose and meaning—Haydar Âmolî’s dreams, like those of his fellow mystics (a Rûzbehân, a Shams Lâhîjî, a Mîr Dâmâd, and others), must be interpreted together with his work, to which he entrusted his deepest purpose. And Haydar Âmolî’s purpose, the one to which he gave all the strength of his love because it was the very expression of that love, is perfectly clear. We have sketched it above.

Let us now draw out its implications, by way of introduction to the pages in which he will explain it himself.

Sayyed Haydar is an Imami Shiite for whom Shiism represents Islam in its fullness and also Islam’s inner, esoteric dimension. It represents Islam in its fullness because it rests on three things at once: the sharî’at (the outward religion and its law), the tarîqat (the spiritual path), and the haqîqat (the realization of spiritual truth). It is Islam’s esoteric dimension because the haqîqat is the inner truth of the sharî’at, just as the sharî’at is its outward form, and because the holy Imams are both the keepers of this hidden truth and the truth they keep—both its bestowers and its substance.

Yet the situation Haydar faces is this: Shiites condemn Sufis, and Sufis condemn Shiites. In doing so, the Shiites confine themselves to the sharî’at alone, the outward religion, while the Sufis forget where their khirqa—the cloak symbolizing their spiritual initiation—came from, and thus leave the haqîqat, the inward religion, hanging in midair.

Both sides make the same mistake when they act as if the teaching of the holy Imams had nothing to do with the higher spiritual sciences, when it was the Imams who first taught them. The tested believer (mu’min momtahan) is the one who embraces the Imams’ cause and teaching in their entirety, holding together sharî’at, tarîqat, and haqîqat. This is why, beside a Shiite who stops at the sharî’at, it is the Sufi who is the true Shiite.

But beside a Sufi who rejects religious law or forgets the origins of his khirqa, it is the Shiite who embraces the whole teaching who is the true Sufi.

Thus the whole effort of Haydar Âmolî’s great Jâmi’ al-asrâr is directed toward persuading the two groups, Shiites and Sufis, that neither can do without the other. Its central proposition is this: the true Shiites are the Sufis—a claim whose meaning emerges fully only when it is reversed: the true Sufis are the true Shiites. We should read the book’s opening and conclusion together (see § 3 below), for these passages reveal our Sayyed’s character better than any other account. In opening up the spiritual world to which he bears witness, they also show us the importance and the courage of his undertaking.

Elsewhere in the book, too, there are moments when the secret of his inner life suddenly shines through. Here is one:

“You should know that our purpose in conducting this discussion with you and with others is neither fanatical zeal nor controversy—God preserve us from such things! No, our aim is to bring harmony between the two sides and to lead each of you toward the truth that is yours... Otherwise, through God’s care and the excellence of His help, I myself put such things behind me long ago. For twenty years I have witnessed the situation as it really is, as I mentioned in the introduction to this book.

“I have been delivered from that darkness and have emerged from those depths: the darkness of contention and controversy, the depths of fanaticism and argument. And for this I give glory to God... In this state of mine, I recite a poem written by someone before me, because it expresses my own experience perfectly; these are the lines I so often find myself repeating: ‘I love You with two loves: a love of passion, / And a love of which You alone are worthy...’231”

Passages like these make one long to see all of Sayyed Haydar Âmolî’s writings brought to light. The discovery of his autobiography has enabled us to identify almost all their titles: thirty-four, as we have said, to which we may cautiously add three or four more mentioned by bibliographers. Unfortunately, of this vast body of work we have so far been able to discover manuscripts of only six.

Admittedly, the author’s own statements make it clear that these six are his most important works, and publishing them alone would require some twenty volumes in the usual octavo format. A systematic, chronological inventory of our Sayyed’s bibliography has already appeared elsewhere, in the introductions to the first published volume of his writings.232 There is no need to repeat it in detail here.

We shall concentrate on just four works of major importance.

  1. The Jâmi’ al-asrâr wa manba’ al-anwâr, literally The Sum of Esoteric Teachings and the Source of Lights. Asrâr means “secrets”: hidden, inward, esoteric realities disclosed through the act of knowing called kashf—inner unveiling, mystical intuition, visionary perception. Taken together, these realities constitute theosophy, or wisdom grounded in spiritual insight, whereas rational understanding (’aql) is the instrument of philosophy, and transmitted tradition (naql) provides the material of theology. This is the great treatise already mentioned, from whose opening and conclusion we shall read several passages below. It was written early in Haydar’s Iraqi period (period B), around 752 AH (1351–52 CE). We have already described its central purpose; let us add that it contains many autobiographical allusions. It consists of three books, each called an asl (source or principle), and each book is divided into four major chapters, or qâ’ida (foundational teaching). The structure of the work is thus organized around the number twelve.

Book I sets out the essence and truth of tawhîd, the affirmation and realization of divine unity. It establishes the distinction between theological tawhîd (olâhî, outward or exoteric monotheism) and ontological or esoteric tawhîd (tawhîd wojûdî), which affirms the transcendent unity of being (wahdat al-wojûd)—not some supposed “existential monism.” The author shows that theological tawhîd can conceal a shirk, a hidden dualism or unconscious idolatry. Ontological tawhîd is then presented in terms of Ibn ’Arabî’s metaphysics.

Finally, Haydar links the argument to a spiritual interpretation of Quran 33:72, from which it emerges that the burden accepted by the human being in an act of sublime madness is nothing less than the secret of the Imams. They themselves repeatedly said that their cause is so difficult and so heavy that only an angel, a prophet, or a believer whose heart has been tested can bear it. This provides the basis for affirming that Sufis, insofar as they claim the gnosis handed down from the Imams, are the “Shiites in the true sense”; conversely, those Shiites who accept the entirety of the holy Imams’ teaching are “believers whose hearts have been tested,” and therefore Sufis in the true sense.

Book II carries this argument forward by assembling the evidence in sequence: Quranic verses, sayings of the Prophet, sayings of the holy Imams, and teachings of the great spiritual masters (the Mashâyekh).

Book III is perfectly symmetrical. Each of its four chapters deals with three fundamental concepts in Shiite theosophy, arranging the terms so that their corresponding places within each triad become clear.

The four triads are: 1) the outward, literal religion (sharî’at), the mystical path (tarîqat), and the truth of gnosis and spiritual realization (haqîqat); 2) the prophetic message (risâlat), the prophetic vocation (nobowwat), and the Imam’s walâyat—his standing as Walî Allâh, Friend of God and guide of spiritual initiation; 3) revelation or divine communication through the Angel (wahy), inspiration (ilhâm), and inward unveiling (kashf, mystical intuition or sacred knowledge received through vision); 4) islâm (the act of surrendering oneself to God), îmân (faith understood as fidelity in the Shiite sense, requiring the heart’s assent to a threefold testimony: divine unity, the Prophet’s mission, and the walâyat of the Imams), and îqân (certainty that is at once pistis, faith, and gnôsis, knowledge).

The chapter on prophecy and walâyat is especially extensive. Here Haydar Âmolî argues against Ibn ’Arabî that it is impossible, both historically and in the structure of the doctrine, to regard Jesus son of Mary as the “Seal” of absolute walâyat, or to accept, as certain of Ibn ’Arabî’s disciples did, that Ibn ’Arabî himself was the Seal of particular, or Muhammadan, walâyat. The Seal of absolute walâyat can only be the First Imam; the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat can only be the figure whom Twelver Shiism recognizes as the Twelfth Imam: the presently Hidden Imam, the awaited Mahdi, son of Imam Hasan ’Askarî.

Haydar will develop this argument at even greater length some thirty years later, in the introduction to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs. By following through all the implications of the doctrine that walâyat is the inward truth of prophecy, Haydar Âmolî’s work marks a major moment in the development of “prophetic philosophy” within Shiite Islam.

  1. The Treatise on the Knowledge of Being (Risâlat fî ma’rifat al-wojûd), completed in Najaf on 15 Jumada II 768 AH, corresponding to 17 February 1367. This date allows us to distinguish the two phases of our Sayyed’s Iraqi period (periods B and C). He wrote the treatise at the request of a friend whom he does not name, but for whom he felt deep affection. It is a summary—quite a substantial one, despite the author’s description—of a much larger work on metaphysics, of which no manuscript has yet been found. Sayyed Haydar tells us that he had just completed a major treatise examining every aspect of being, explaining the disagreement between the Motakallimûn, the scholastic theologians, and the philosophers who profess the transcendent unity of being, and bringing forward testimony from the Word of God and the words of the prophets and the Awliyâ, God’s Friends. At that point, he writes, “one of my brothers, dearer to me than the pupils of my eyes, earnestly asked me to make a concise and useful summary of it: a book small in size but rich in instruction.”

Like the larger work it condenses, the treatise has an introduction and three “pillars” (rokn), or chapters. They deal, respectively, with: 1) the problem of being (status quaestionis): being understood as absolute being (itlāq al-wojûd) and being as something immediately given. Here Haydar stresses the impossibility of deducing being, of deriving it rationally through a principle of sufficient reason.

This leads to the question of tarjîh: why does being prevail over nonbeing? Why is there something rather than nothing? 2) The necessity of being and its unity. 3) The manifestation of being (zohûr al-wojûd) and its multiplicity. From the outset (§ 5), the author explains that he approaches the metaphysics of being from three perspectives: that of the philosophers, through intellect (’aql); that of the theologians, through tradition (naql); and that of the mystical theosophers, through intuitive perception (kashf). This is wholly consistent with his characteristic position and with the method employed in his great Jâmi’ al-asrâr.

Thus, when announcing his book’s title, Sayyed Haydar dedicates it to those who possess the necessary readiness, the full capacity, the subtlety and penetration the subject requires. He excludes those who deny and dispute, all who stand far from God and the Friends of God.

We hardly need emphasize the importance of works like these for the history of Islamic philosophy, which historians long supposed had come to an end with Averroes in Andalusia. Haydar Âmolî approaches the metaphysics of being neither as Avicenna did nor as Averroes did.

Yet he confronts precisely the same problem inherited from Greek philosophy. What differs is his manner of confronting it, and the resources he brings to bear: his profound knowledge of Ibn ’Arabî’s writings, his ceaseless meditation on the Book of God, and his study of the traditions of the Shiite Imams. It would be inconceivable to him, as to the Shiite philosophers we are studying, that anyone should try to develop a metaphysics of being while accepting the division, so common in the West, that isolates philosophy from theology.

To insist on keeping the two apart is to mutilate the questions—and the intellectual aims—of both. It blocks the passage through which each, by way of the other, can reach the higher plane of theosophical metaphysics. The result is the absurd position in which some people deny that our philosophers are dealing with philosophical questions at all, when it would be simpler and more “objective” to acknowledge that their understanding of philosophy extends beyond the limits imposed on the word by “modern” philosophy.

Haydar Âmolî and thinkers like him have much in common with the Neoplatonic theosophers of the European Renaissance. It is as a Neoplatonist that Sayyed Haydar meditates on the threefold structure of the bismillâh: Allâh signifies the absolute One, oneness in its most absolute sense (ahadîya); al-Rahmân, the Merciful, signifies the One as multiple, the Nous or divine Intellect, the Imam or metaphysical Adam; and al-Rahîm, the Most Compassionate, signifies the World Soul, the metaphysical Eve.

The Shiite philosophy that Haydar Âmolî sought to present in its fullness would be developed still further by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, and several others. It is of exceptional interest, as we see it, for the study of religious consciousness as it is experienced.233

  1. The two works just discussed have recently been published. We must now mention two further works of central importance, both immense in scope, about which we have already said something. The first is the Tafsîr ’irfânî, Haydar’s monumental spiritual and mystical commentary on the Quran, completed in 777 AH (1375–76 CE). It fills seven large volumes, preserved in the author’s own manuscript, whose recent discovery at Najaf and Qomm we have described above. This tafsîr, or Quranic commentary, bears an elaborate, symbolically charged title. Haydar Âmolî explains it as follows when he refers to his earlier writings in the introduction to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs.

“Our own books fall into two categories: those that have been poured down upon us from above, and those that have proceeded from ourselves. Those poured down upon us from above are the ta’wîlât, the spiritual interpretations of the holy Quran. They contain the most precious and exalted divine teachings and Quranic sciences; they gather together the symbols and forms belonging to the Prophet, the subtle teachings and Muhammadan realities faithfully expressed by what God says of the chosen among His servants: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what has never entered the heart of any human being.’

“Accordingly, this book has received the title The Supreme Ocean and the Loftiest Mountain: A Book on the Spiritual Interpretation of the Precious and Unshakeable Book of God (al-Mohît al-a’zam wa’l-tawd al-ashamm fî ta’wîl Kitâb Allâh al-’azîz al-mohkam). Its plan is divided into seven volumes, placing it under the auspices of the seven great prophets, the seven spiritual poles, and the seven abdâl [a rank of hidden spiritual figures].

“Thus the introductory sections, together with the Fâtiha [the Quran’s opening sura], form one volume, and each successive sixth of the Quran forms another. This tafsîr stands in relation to us as the Fosûs al-hikam stands in relation to Shaykh Mohyiddin Ibn ’Arabî, and as the Quran stands in relation to the Prophet. The structure of our tafsîr is as follows: we begin by establishing nineteen premises and circles, consisting of seven premises and twelve circles, corresponding to the outward world and the spiritual world, to the ‘Book of the Horizons’ and the ‘Book of Souls,’ each of these worlds being bounded by the number nineteen.”

Two observations arise here. First, Sayyed Haydar is referring to the way Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs can be regarded as an “inspired book”: according to the account, the Prophet gave it to Ibn ’Arabî in a dream, having himself received it in the Malakût, the spiritual realm. By comparing his own Tafsîr to Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs, our Sayyed illustrates and confirms what he has just said: that the Tafsîr is not a book originating in himself, but one that he knows was “poured down upon him from above.” It came by way of the inspiration that Shiite thought about knowledge holds to remain open even after the cycle of prophecy has closed.

Second, the structure of the Tafsîr’s introductory sections, as Haydar Âmolî describes them, corresponds to the structure of the esoteric hierarchy: seven prophets and twelve Imams, nineteen figures in all. His talk of circles also calls to mind the elaborate diagrams he constructed with such artistry. We have already discussed the meaning of what we propose to call the “diagrammatic art” that illustrates Haydar Âmolî’s writings.

Elsewhere in the same introduction, Sayyed Haydar describes his magnum opus as “divided into seven large volumes, corresponding to the ta’wîl of the eminent shaykh Najmoddin Râzî, known as Dâyéh. For he too divided his work into seven large volumes, having given it the title Ocean of Spiritual Truths and Mystical Realities (Bahr al-haqâ’iq wa’l-daqâ’iq).

“Our intention was to produce a book comparable to his in every respect, and satisfying the hadîth that also underlies his work: ‘The Quran has an outward [exoteric] meaning and an inward [esoteric] meaning; this inward meaning itself has a further inward meaning, and so on down to seven inward depths’ [...]. This tafsîr [that of Najm Dâyéh] is famous in every clime and every country.

“The theosophical truth of its structure is recognized by the most eminent philosophers and mystical theosophers. They acknowledge that it has no equal or parallel, especially in the Quranic sciences, and that it was attained neither by acquiring knowledge from outside nor by prolonged dialectical inquiry, but through a secret gift from the All-Merciful, by means of mystical perception (kashf).”

Sayyed Haydar thus allows us to glimpse at least the plan of his mystical tafsîr and something of the secret of its contents. Until we can study it in detail and prepare an edition, we already know the perspective in which its author places it. By referring to Najm Dâyéh Râzî’s work, Haydar Âmolî is also evoking the whole body of mystical Quran commentaries. This literature is vast. It still awaits systematic classification and study, work that can be undertaken only by scholars trained in philosophy and religious studies.

For their essential interest lies in how the Quran was read by Islam’s spiritual masters and metaphysicians. There is no point in objecting that those thinkers’ methods of interpretation do not conform to the aims or procedures of our own “positive,” historical-critical scholarship.
