Instead, he sees five privileged names from among that company: those known as the “People of the Cloak.” The name refers to the famous episode of the mubâhala, the proposed ordeal of mutual imprecation between the Prophet and the Christians of Najran, including their bishop, from which the Christians withdrew at the last moment.

The Prophet had come with his own family, “with his souls,” sheltering them beneath his cloak, which was stretched between two poles against the backdrop of the desert.262 It is these five names that Haydar Amoli sees written in letters of white light upon emerald tablets. We are reminded here of the emerald tablet possessed by Fatima, upon which the names of the Twelve Imams were inscribed. Muhammad al-Baqir, the Fifth Imam, once showed it to his close disciple Jabir al-Ansari.263 As in the preceding accounts, Sayyed Haydar is absorbed in contemplation of the starry sky, like someone trying to decipher the lines of writing traced by the constellations.

“I was standing in the courtyard [of the sanctuary], contemplating the sky and its stars. Someone unseen said to me: ‘Read—or recite—the lines you see written there.’ Then I saw lines written in white light upon emerald tablets. They were the supreme Name of God together with the names of the Five Blessed Ones among His Friends and intimates: Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn.

“Then the unseen voice said to me: ‘These are the very essence of existence and the purpose of God. They are the Words through which God turned toward Adam and accepted his repentance.264 And it is through them that God accepts your own return to Him, for you are one of their number [like Salman]. You belong among those who are objects of God's love, those of whom He said: “God will bring forth people who love Him and whom He loves” (2:59).’”

This Qur'anic verse contains the whole idea of walâyat (Persian dûstî) as friendship with God and love for God. The Imam is its pole and its Seal, because he is the form in which the inward reality of the Muhammadan Reality becomes manifest—the form around which this love is centered.

“Then,” Sayyed Haydar continues, “I returned to myself, filled with intense joy and gladness. I thanked God for all of this, and for the many things that had repeatedly happened to me, but which this is not the place to recount.”

It was important to make these three visions known here. Without them, our understanding of a Shiite spiritual thinker as representative as Haydar Amoli would remain incomplete. For him, as for the Shaykh al-Ishrâq—Suhrawardi, the master of the philosophy of Illumination—philosophical knowledge is directed toward personal spiritual realization. In Suhrawardi’s case, this realization culminates in visions of pure beings of light, the Perfect Nature, and other such presences.

In Haydar Amoli’s case, it is the vision of the heavenly fullness of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones: “persons of light” who together constitute one and the same light, the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî). This is not a merely figurative vision. It is symbolic in the fullest sense: their names blaze in the depths of the starry heavens. For both Suhrawardi and Haydar Amoli, such personal experience of sacred knowledge is irrefutable testimony, evidence more compelling than any philosophical or theological demonstration based on dialectical reasoning or the authority of transmitted traditions.

Yet Sayyed Haydar does not lose sight of the question at issue in this chapter—the question that prompted him to recount his visions in the first place. It concerns the Seal of walâyat in the person of the Twelfth Imam.

“That is why,” he says, “I have recounted these visions here, principally as testimony to counterbalance the dream of Ibn Arabi.” He means the dream Ibn Arabi had interpreted as referring simply to himself, rather than to the Seal of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.

Haydar Amoli considers that he has fully accomplished his task on this point. He believes he has given “prophetic philosophy” the threefold philosophical, theological, and theosophical foundation he had set out to establish. Much was at stake. The reference to the “Words that interceded for Adam” brings into full view the relationship between the understanding of Adam and the understanding of the Imams, and therefore between Adam's transgression and the saving role of the Imams. The Imam is called the “Adam of the awliyâ’,” the Friends of God.

Ibn Arabi had disrupted this relationship by transferring to Jesus a designation which, once the cycle of prophecy had closed, could belong only to the Imamate of the Twelve. Here is a point of fundamental importance for any future comparative theology, one that has so far gone entirely unnoticed. The issue is how Shiite theologians understand Adam's transgression, something we have already touched upon.

Let us therefore conclude by quoting a few more lines from Haydar Amoli, a hadith recorded on the last page of the same chapter of his introduction to his commentary on the Fosûs:

“When God wished to turn again toward Adam [toward humanity], He said to him: ‘Contemplate the heavens.’ Adam looked, and the veil was lifted before him as far as the supports of the Throne. He saw written upon the Throne, in letters of light, the names of the Five Persons:265 Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn. He cried out: ‘My God! What are these names? Have You created other beings before me?’ ‘No,’ came the reply. ‘These are your descendants and your children.

“But if I created you, if I created the universe, it was for their sake and because of them. Recite their Names, so that through their blessed influence I may turn toward you again.’ Then Adam recited their Names, and God turned toward him. These are the Words mentioned in the Qur'an (2:35), which God taught Adam in order to accept his repentance.”

The “Five People of the Cloak” present at the mubâhala were also the Five whom the angel Gabriel considered it an honor to join as a “sixth.” This occurred when Gabriel appeared on the day the verse was revealed that consecrates the earthly persons of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones:

“God wishes only to remove all impurity from you, O People of My House (ahl al-bayt), and to make you utterly pure” (33:33).

On this verse, as on the verse concerning the Words that interceded for Adam, Haydar Amoli can appeal to the agreement of all Shiite commentators. The Imam, the Perfect Human Being, is the ultimate purpose of creation, the secret of cosmology and salvation, the redeemer of Adam. We know that Sayyed Haydar had reflected particularly deeply on the meaning of Adam's transgression: the paradox of a sublime error, an act of daring that was bound to turn against Adam and his descendants, because his powers were not equal to the burden he had agreed to bear. That was paradise lost. With the cycle of walâyat, following the cycle of prophecy, the return to paradise regained begins.

And the form of this return corresponds to the distinctive character of Shiite mysticism, at once theosophical and ecstatic. This is not an ecstasy that seeks to extinguish the world and the self by immersion in the divine current. Theosophical wisdom opens the way to vision. And visionary experience is, above all, the joy of being-with: being with the one and the beings who, for the mystic, give form to love.

Chapter II An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an

1. Interpretation and the Types of Spiritual Seekers

The chapters that follow will, in effect, develop more fully the themes introduced at the beginning of this work (Book I, Chapters IV and V), and taken up again in our discussion of Haydar Amoli, whose writings have shown us the importance of interpreting the Qur'an's inner meanings.

We shall first examine an anonymous Persian treatise from the eighth/fourteenth century. It offers an excellent Sufi interpretation of the celebrated hadith affirming that the Qur'an possesses seven inner meanings.

We shall then turn to a ninth/fifteenth-century treatise by Sa'inoddin Torkeh Isfahani, a Shiite author of exceptional intellectual depth. His work is, in a sense, a practical exercise in interpreting the inner meaning of a Qur'anic verse. It shows how this method of interpretation gives rise to a classification of different spiritual types.

Finally, returning to the preceding century, we shall give particular attention to the major work of Alaoddawleh Semnani (d. 736/1336). In Semnani we shall find the same conviction as in Sa'inoddin Torkeh: every way of understanding expresses a corresponding way of being, from which that understanding arises and upon which it depends. For both thinkers, interpretation therefore develops in relation to a spiritual typology—or, more precisely, through the discovery of the kinds of spiritual seekers to whom the successive levels of interpretation correspond. By connecting the organs of subtle spiritual physiology with the stages of interpreting hidden meaning, Semnani carried the inward appropriation of Revelation and the doctrine of prophecy to their furthest possible point.

Step by step, he leads the mystic to reproduce inwardly the experience of the Prophet. The meaning of the supreme shari'a revealed to the mystic on his own “Sinai”—that is, at the summit of his soul—is the religion of the “supreme prophet of his own being.” It is a genuinely personal religion that supersedes all others, because the Sufi measures their lateness not against the history of the world, but against the history of his own being.

Before examining the methods required for this ever-deepening interpretation of inner meaning, let us consider how, as recently as the preceding century, the distinguished Iranian Shiite theosopher Ja'far Kashfi summarized the function and task of spiritual interpretation.266 His explanations would be enough, if any reminder were needed, to show how radically this approach differs from allegorical interpretation.

But they also reveal the same concern that we have encountered in the authors just mentioned: the desire to establish a relationship between levels of interpretation and types of spiritual seekers. In this respect, these Iranian thinkers anticipated questions that are now associated with what we call “philosophical anthropology.” Ja'far Kashfi relates the different levels of interpretation to different kinds of philosopher and different forms of philosophy. Interpretation in general, he says, has three levels: tafsîr, ta’wîl, and tafhîm.

Tafsîr, the interpretation of the literal text, is a discipline centered on the established Islamic religious sciences. It also requires a sound knowledge of the relevant literature. Its concern is exclusively with what the text explicitly says. It represents the lowest level of knowledge and learning. Ta’wîl literally means “to lead back” or “to return” something to its origin, principle, or archetype. The term is commonly used for any symbolic interpretation, as distinct from tafsîr. This form of knowledge depends on spiritual guidance and divine assistance. When intention, capacity, effective help, and attainment of the goal all come together, happiness is complete. It represents the middle level of knowledge and of those who possess it.

Finally, tafhîm literally means “to make someone understand.” Here it designates interpretation in the deeper, technical sense that concerns us. It is a form of knowledge centered on an act of Understanding (fahm) through God, and on an inspiration (ilhâm) of which God is at once the subject, the object, and the goal—or, equivalently, the source, the means, and the end. This is the highest level of knowledge and of those who possess it. The knowledge proper to ta’wîl is an intuitive unveiling, a penetration of meaning through inner vision (kashf). The knowledge proper to tafhîm is divine inspiration.

If we wish to relate these three levels of interpretation to three levels of philosophical wisdom, our author explains, we must first say that tafsîr involves no philosophy (hikmat) at all. If we nevertheless insist on drawing a parallel, it would correspond to the philosophy of the Peripatetics. The knowledge of ta’wîl corresponds to the philosophy of the Stoics (hikmat al-Rawâq), because it is a wisdom concerned with what lies behind the Veil (hijâb; rawâq = stoa, a portico).267 The knowledge of tafhîm—interpretation in its truest sense, or transcendent interpretation—is “Oriental” or Illuminationist wisdom (hikmat al-Ishrâq) as Suhrawardi understood it (see Book II).268

We shall encounter the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of Illumination, again in this very discussion (Chapter III), where they are assigned this elevated place. That alone would be enough to demonstrate the influence exerted over the centuries by this “Oriental” theosophy. Since Suhrawardi, it has maintained a continuous tradition linking ancient Persia with Islamic Iran.

We can immediately see how Ja'far Kashfi's Shiite conception of interpretation gives expression to concerns that arise wherever a sacred Book is experienced not simply as material for philological research—the province of tafsîr—but as a source of spiritual life. Understood in this way, the “phenomenon of the Book” extends beyond the limits traditionally associated with the Ahl al-Kitâb, the People of the Book. It appears wherever a book can be read in the way that one reads the Bible or the Qur'an.

The Mathnawî of Jalaloddin Rumi, that immense poetic composition devoted to the symbols of the soul, is studied and lived as the “Persian Qur'an” (Qorân-e fârsî). Hafiz's Dîwân is still used daily by Sufis in Iran as one might use the Bible. We know the remarkable interpretation of the Odyssey developed by the Pythagoreans. Likewise, the later Neoplatonists, such as Proclus, practiced a fully developed ta’wîl upon the traditions handed down from the ancient Greek “theologians.” For them, too, the successive levels of interpretation corresponded to a hierarchy of spiritual types.

2. The Eternal Event of the Book

Let us now examine the first of the short treatises announced above. As we have already mentioned, the manuscript preserving this little work in Persian—so far the only known copy—does not give its author's name.269 The copy is dated 731/1331, exactly five years before the death of Semnani (736/1336), whose spiritual interpretation we shall examine below. It also dates from the period of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's youth.

Both its vocabulary and its contents suggest that the copy was made not very long after the unknown author lived. The treatise is a commentary on a fundamental hadith to which we have already had occasion to refer. The author shows how the seven inner meanings of the Qur'an correspond to a hierarchy of seven levels of spiritual understanding. The same idea will appear in the classification of spiritual seekers developed by Sa'inoddin Torkeh (Chapter III below).

“There is,” our anonymous author writes, “a saying attributed by tradition to the Prophet (hadîth nabawî) upon which I have meditated deeply and conducted a careful investigation. I plunged into the ocean of the Qur'an's secrets and brought forth the pearls of its subtleties.

“I lifted the veils of sounds and letters from before its true Realities (haqâ’iq), the hidden meanings kept beyond human sight. This hadith declares that the Qur'an possesses an outward meaning and an inward meaning. In other words, it has a zâhir—a back or outward surface, the literal meaning—and a bâtin—an inward depth, like a womb, the hidden or spiritual meaning. And this inward meaning itself has an inward meaning: one depth contains another, as the celestial spheres are nested within one another. So it continues, down to seven inward meanings, seven depths within depths.”270

This hadith, then, proposes a progressive deepening of Qur'anic understanding through seven levels. Before showing that these seven levels correspond precisely to the seven levels of spiritual seekers—because each degree of understanding corresponds to a distinct way of being, an inner state—the author considers it necessary to take a position on two questions that govern the entire study of the Qur'an.

As we have emphasized at length, these questions arise directly from the phenomenon of the sacred Book itself (see Book I, Chapter IV). They therefore confront every religious community whose life is centered on a revealed Book, a text proclaimed by a Nâtiq, a prophetic speaker. The first question is this: what is the relationship between a revealed text, expressed in a particular language at a particular moment, and the eternal truth that it communicates?

The second concerns the very process of revelation. How are we to understand it? In other words, do we possess a psychology of prophecy capable of explaining the passage from the divine Word to its human expression? The first question leads us back to the fundamental controversy that, because it was wrongly framed, threw the early Islamic community into turmoil: Is the Qur'an created or uncreated? The question was wrongly framed because the two alternatives do not refer to the same thing.

Unfortunately, recognizing this requires a minimum of philosophical understanding—something the political authorities scarcely possessed as they successively imposed one position and then the other.271 It is equally clear that the problem goes far beyond the assumptions and resources of critical philology. For the philologist, the Qur'anic text as we read it appears to be historically conditioned. Its natural meaning must therefore, in the philologist's view, be reconstructed from the historical circumstances of a particular religious environment.

But for our author, as for all those who share his approach, the true meaning of the Qur'an cannot be confined to the external circumstances surrounding the letter of the text.272 Their demands are precisely what have led us to formulate the problem of interpretation in its full rigor.

Moreover, the variety of possible meanings depends on the spiritual development of the reader, whoever that reader may be—including the Western philologist who encounters the Qur'an at some particular moment in historical time. If the philologist decides that the true meaning is the natural, philological meaning of the words, that very decision places him, by virtue of his spiritual state, among the exoteric interpreters: those who remain at the level of outward appearances. No one escapes the strict law of this situation of interpretation.

The same law applies when we turn to the second question, that of prophetic psychology. The Western interpreter seeks to understand a prophet by studying his environment, education, or particular genius. The Sufi interpreter seeks to understand him by meditating upon the nature of his relationship with the eternal Source from which his message proceeds—the Revelation whose text he proclaims. The psychology of the prophet is therefore an essential part of the doctrine of prophecy.

Every philosopher and every theosopher within Sufism is concerned with it. And the fact that each individual takes responsibility for this question is itself a sign of a community founded upon the authority of the Book alone, and upon every believer's personal relationship with that Book and the meaning it possesses for that believer's own existence. Such a community is not founded upon the authority of a teaching institution that determines what meaning the sacred text must have according to a doctrine whose development it controls.

Our author deals with both questions in a short prologue. Through his mystical theosophy, he escapes not only the dilemma posed by the theologians of Kalâm, but also the dilemma that a modern philosopher might put to him: How can truth be historical, and how can history be truth?

“Know,” he writes, “and may God come to your aid and ours through a Spirit proceeding from Him,273 that the eternal essence (haqîqat) of the Qur'an is the divine Logos or Word (Kalâm-e Haqq). It abides with and through the divine Selfhood, inseparable from it, without beginning or end in eternity. This is what the verse indicates: ‘It is We who have sent down the Reminder (dhikr), and it is We who preserve it’ (15:9). The Divine Being speaks a single Word that never changes, although languages, technical terms, and forms of expression differ.”

This Word is not even conditioned by whether the world exists or does not exist. For the world is not a reality existing outside God. Creation is a manifestation of God; it is not the coming into existence of something separate from, and alongside, the Divine Being. Here our author agrees with all the Sufis of Ibn Arabi's school. The saying “God was, and there was nothing with Him” must therefore immediately be qualified by another: “And it is still now as it has always been.” One objection can easily be anticipated.

If the divine Word is eternal, and if the events it reveals are consequently eternal as well, what becomes of the very notion of an event? How, for example, can we imagine that, in pre-eternity, when the Prophet had not yet appeared and the unbelievers still lay hidden behind the veil of nonbeing or nonmanifestation, God could have said to him: “O Prophet, struggle against the unbelievers” (9:74)? And how can we conceive, without absurdity, that Moses, before he had even entered into existence, could have said to God, “Show Yourself to me, so that I may behold You,” and received the reply, “You shall not see Me” (7:139)? The Sufi master's answer rests on one consideration alone: this entire objection is illusory, because it depends on a completely mistaken way of imagining the matter.

The illusion arises from a confusion between different kinds of time. It is precisely this confusion that Semnani avoids by distinguishing, in technical terms, between zamân âfâqî, the time of the objective world—the quantitative, continuous time of history—and zamân anfusî, the inward time of the soul, which is purely qualitative. Before and after presuppose a uniform, continuous, irreversible time, measurable by the revolutions of the heavenly bodies.

But an event that takes place within the soul, in the soul's own time, cannot, in what essentially constitutes it, be situated before or after some particular calendar date. Such a date does not determine it. The event does not belong to the history of the world, “beneath the horizons of the world.” As we have said before, neither theophanies—manifestations of God—nor their visionary events can be turned into ordinary objective history or historical time. Visionary events possess their own time, whose relation to measurable calendar time is expressed in the verse:

“One day with your Lord is like a thousand of the years that you count” (22:46).

To say that a day is equivalent to a millennium is to say that there is no rational common measure between the qualitative time of the soul and the quantitative time of worldly history. It would be equally mistaken to imagine the moments “with your Lord” as mathematical points without duration. Even that description would smuggle in a quantitative idea, if only by denying it. There is indeed an eternal duration. There are “days with your Lord.”

But none of our methods of reckoning time can measure them. These are the days of eternal events. It is therefore absurd to ask how Moses could have said this or that “before he existed.” It is precisely because such a question is absurd that the revealed text possesses both an outward, apparent meaning and an inward, hidden meaning. The inward meaning is spiritual, but it is not an allegory. It is a higher order of reality, grounded in the relationship through which the invisible becomes manifest. If we fail to understand this, we can find reality only on the plane of history.

But then the phenomena of history cease to be phenomena in the full sense, because they no longer disclose any spiritual meaning. To search for that meaning is to give events a dimension they cannot possess within a conception of history that regards its own continuous unfolding as sufficient to provide it with meaning. Our anonymous Sufi declares:

“Whoever has once risen above the world of material objects, freeing himself from the narrow passage of nights and days, and turns resolutely toward the world of the soul, drawing time and place inward, will become aware that the divine world knows no before or after or now, no alteration and no passing from one form to another.

“At this level of being, this divine ‘Presence’ (hazrat), one must not imagine any extension measurable by our standards, not even the extension of an atom or a point. This is what is meant when we say that, by the reckoning of the gnostics, a thousand years are equal to the blink of an eye, or to a flash of lightning that bursts forth in the Orient of divinity. Then one becomes aware that, for the Divine Being, the Qur'an is the Word uttered through His own breath, His divine Exhalation. It embraces pre-eternity and post-eternity. It is not a new event that comes into being when the person to whom it is addressed finally appears.”

Thus the phenomenon of the Book—its visible, outward appearance (zâhir)—is led back to its eternal archetype. The Book in its outward form is not merely paper and ink. It consists of readable words, audible sounds, and apparent meanings accessible to human understanding.

Yet behind this form lies the “Mother of the Book” (Omm al-Kitâb), the eternal divine Word concealed beneath its outward covering. This is what establishes the legitimacy of ta’wîl: the spiritual practice of leading the literal form of every Revelation back to its inward meaning. Our author freely acknowledges the difficulty.

“Know,” he says, “that this is one of the most obscure questions in the whole of theosophical wisdom. One cannot understand it by accumulating rational arguments and proofs. But if there is a receptive soul, possessing at least some measure of inward purity and endowed with a mystical sensitivity to spiritual realities, then it is possible for that soul to understand.”

However difficult it may be to understand the sacred Book in relation to its archetype, the eternal divine Word, this very relationship supplies the answer to the second preliminary question. How can that divine Word “pass through” the language of the successive prophets entrusted with proclaiming it? This question belongs simultaneously to the study of prophecy, the study of angels, and psychology. It has concerned philosophers and theologians alike. We have already encountered it at the very origins of Shiism.

For what a psychology of prophecy must explain, if it is to account for the sacred Book, is the passage from inward to outward meaning brought about by revelation through the prophet (tanzîl), and the return from outward to inward meaning accomplished through spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl). Our author confines himself to a brief outline of the essentials. He presupposes the notion of the “holy intellect” (’aql qodsî, intellectus sanctus), already established in Avicenna's philosophy, and the notion of the “angelic soul,” the faculty that receives prophecy in the psychology of the Brethren of Purity (Ikhwân al-Safâ’). These concepts are of fundamental importance.

Here, as elsewhere, they form the foundation of “prophetic philosophy.” Thanks to them, mystical philosophers and speculative mystics can recognize a correspondence between two kinds of union: the union of the mystical sage with the Agent or Active Intelligence (’Aql fa’âl), understood as the Holy Spirit, and the union of the prophet's soul with the angelic Spirit, the Holy Spirit through whom Revelation actively takes place. In this way, the vocation of wisdom and mysticism can be brought into correspondence with the prophetic vocation.

The same spiritual faculty can therefore be identified in the philosopher—or, more accurately, the theosopher—and in the prophet. This is the holy intellect, also called the holy spirit (rûh qodsîya) or holy faculty (qowwat qodsîya). These terms refer to the highest capacity of the human intellect: its ability to enter into frequent, habitual union with the Angel who is the “Active Intelligence,” and to receive directly from this angelic Spirit both intelligible truths and knowledge of spiritual realities generally, without requiring instruction from another human being.

What distinguishes the prophet is the binding command to proclaim a message (risâla) before other people, in the case of the Nabî morsal, the prophet who is sent as a messenger; or initiation into the secret meaning of Revelation, in the case of the Nabî in the more general sense.

Yet the highest stage of philosophical knowledge, where philosophy culminates in mystical experience—as it does among the Ishrâqîyûn—leads the spiritual seeker through the same heavenly ascent (mi’râj) as the Nabî. Mystically, the seeker too becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” The Angel of Knowledge is therefore none other than the Angel of Revelation. For this theosophy of the Holy Spirit, mystical religion and prophetic religion are not opposed. On the contrary, they find their shared fulfillment in a “prophetic philosophy,” because such a philosophy culminates in mystical experience. This experience is also individuation in its highest form. It takes place in the direct, one-to-one encounter between the philosopher and the Angel who is the Holy Spirit, without any human intermediary—not even a Church.

(Perhaps this was one of the reasons why Avicennism eventually disappeared from the medieval West.) This prophetic philosophy is also “speculative” in the original sense of the word, which is connected with the idea of a mirror. As our anonymous Sufi explains, whenever the prophet needs knowledge, he turns the mirror of his soul (âyîna-ye jân, speculum animae) toward the “holy world” to receive from it the true Reality (haqîqat).

Just as a figure becomes present in a mirror through reflection, taking on the particular coloring of that mirror, so these true Realities become actual within the prophet. They are the truths of spiritual knowledge projected into him from the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh mahfûz)—that is, from the heavenly fullness of sacred essences that have not yet appeared in the visible world. The image of the mirror constantly recurs in the writings of these spiritual thinkers. The interpenetration of spirit and body leads them to conceive of a spiritual embodiment and a bodily spirituality (compare the Geistleiblichkeit found in Oetinger, Schelling, and others).

But for them this interpenetration cannot mean what Christian dogma calls the Incarnation, because the Incarnation involves a self-emptying (kenosis) of the divine into flesh. Here, by contrast, the interpenetration of spirit and body can produce only a transfiguration, an elevation of the bodily into a higher mode of being. The result is an intermediate world with an existence of its own, situated between the spiritual and bodily worlds: the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world (’âlam al-mithâl), “where spirits take on bodies and bodies become spiritual.”

As we know, visionary mystics can enter this world in dreams or ecstasy, or even while awake—though in the waking state it requires a distinctive mystical way of perceiving reality.274 Such perception transforms reality, giving it the radiance and depth of a mirror through which something else shines. The mystic perceives the world as the “form of manifestation” (mazhar) of an invisible spiritual reality.

Yet that invisible reality is not incorporated into the substance of the sensible world. It is not present there as an accidental quality inhering in a substance. Rather, it is present precisely as an image is present in a mirror—and that is why it becomes visible. The word “Docetism” is generally invoked to ridicule the gnostics who professed it, as though they had been content with mere phantoms. In reality, when the sensible world becomes the bearer of a divine manifestation, when it is raised to the condition of a mirror, it may indeed lose the privileged solidity that ordinary outward perception attributes to it. Such perception may judge that, once made transparent, the world has become nothing but appearance.

But in truth it has become not merely an appearance, but nothing less than the place where a spiritual reality appears (mazhar). Only in this way can we understand the role of the letter and its literal meaning in the transcendent interpretation practiced by Sufism and Ismailism. When our author, following his predecessors, says that the prophet's soul functions as a mirror, we must keep these considerations in mind.

The invisible appears within this mirror according to the mirror's capacity to make it manifest, and it takes on the mirror's coloring—just as water takes on the color of the glass containing it. The prophet's soul is here the subjectum incarnationis, the subject or bearer of incarnation, if it is not too paradoxical to speak of a “spiritual incarnation.”

But the event is not complete until the complementary process takes place. Once the spiritual has taken bodily form through the prophet's soul, the bodily must itself be spiritualized through the work of the interpreter—who, in Shiite terms, is the Imam. According to our treatise, what is given to the prophet's “holy intellect” in an immaterial and universal form is reflected and multiplied within it. It assumes a “real appearance” by clothing itself in sounds and letters, so that the prophet's message becomes understandable to the community to which he has been sent. It is because of this process—the “embodiment of the spiritual” in the mirror of the prophet's soul—that the outward meaning of the Qur'an (zâhir) is the meaning (ma’nâ) we gather from its letters and sounds, from the words composed of them.

The inward meaning (bâtin), the hidden depth of the Qur'an, is the true Reality itself: the divine Word that subsists eternally with and through the divine Selfhood, and manifests itself in the body of letters and literal meaning just as an image appears in a mirror. To reach this true Reality of the Qur'an, to gain spiritual knowledge of the divine Word, the interpreter must therefore accomplish the complementary operation, reversing the first: the spiritualization of the bodily.

Otherwise the event of divine manifestation would remain unfinished, and its purity would be endangered. It would fall into one of two traps: holûl, the idea of incarnation or indwelling, or enslavement to the literal text. These are two aspects of the same materialization, the same complete darkening of the mirror. Interpreting the inward meaning must bring about a kind of “dematerialization”: the restoration of matter and the letter to their essential, spiritual state.

Only this operation makes it possible to “perceive the fragrance of the other world.” And if the operation proceeds through seven depths, seven inward meanings, that is because there are correspondingly seven levels of spiritual seekers. Their hierarchy reflects the seven stages of ascent (’orûj), through which the matter of the Book's letters and sounds is raised to its essential reality. This ascent is the great work of ta’wîl: interpreting the Book by leading it back to its spiritual meaning, its original inward reality.

The work of ta’wîl is conceived as an ascent that is, at the same time, a descent into the depths. That is why the Prophet's ecstatic ascent on the night of the Mi’râj becomes the model of the highest mystical experience: an ascent into the ultimate depth. Our author can now deal briefly with ordinary outward exegesis, the kind that restricts itself to literal meaning.

“This is a form of knowledge,” he says, “through which one must pass. It is the starting point, the entrance, the threshold. But one must cross that threshold and enter the interior.”

This knowledge is drawn from the traditional Qur'anic sciences as a whole: lexicography, grammar, syntax, the rules of recitation, the study of verses that abrogate other verses and those that have been abrogated, the study of narratives, and so forth.

“But all these sciences, when compared with the true Realities and the spiritual knowledge contained in the Qur'an, are merely empty husks, skins, and discarded coverings.

“However distinguished the commentators on the literal meaning may be—the outward interpreters (mofassirân-e zâhir) and the authorities of religious law—and however elevated their pronouncements may sound, all of it, everything they teach, is still no more than a husk, an empty shell. Perhaps only one person in a thousand possesses knowledge of the hidden spiritual meaning. Even among a great multitude, the number who possess it is very small. Most people know and understand nothing of the Qur'an beyond the letters written on paper.”

Our author then quotes a Persian couplet:

“No wonder that their share of the Qur'an is nothing more than the letter. The eye of a blind man, facing the sun, feels only its warmth—not its light.”

3. The Seven Inner Depths and the Hierarchy of Spiritual Seekers

“As for the seven depths or inward meanings of the Qur'an,” our author continues, “they designate a succession of hidden meanings understood respectively by seven groups of people. Each group understands according to its own capacity, its degree of preparation, and the subtlety of its contemplation.”

We know that every initiatory experience can be described either as a descent or as an ascent. It is simultaneously a movement toward the center of the Sphere and toward the celestial pole. This is why a descent into the depths of inward meaning corresponds to the Prophet's ascent from Heaven to Heaven. Equally, as our author is careful to point out, each new level of depth can be described as a higher level of elevation.

A simple diagram of the system of concentric celestial spheres would be enough to make this language visually intelligible. To characterize each of the Qur'an's seven depths, the author takes a particular description of the Book from the Qur'anic text itself. Each description becomes the key that determines the distinctive character of that level.

1) The first depth: the pious ascetics At the first depth, the character of the Qur'anic text is established by the description of it as the “Book that brings the Reminder” (wa’l-Qorâni dhî’l-dhikr, 38:1), the Book that is the great Reminder. This first inward meaning, the first stage in the spiritual landscape, corresponds to the inner life and religion of the “mystical wayfarer” (sâlik). Having responded to the Reminder, the wayfarer has set foot upon the Path in order to acquire the first elements of spiritual formation. These consist above all of the various forms of spiritual struggle (mojâhada).

Indeed, Sufism has sometimes understood itself as consisting essentially in this kind of discipline, as happened in early Mesopotamian Sufism during the first centuries of the Islamic era. At this initial level, then, the Qur'an—whose literal appearance presents it as the code of a religious Law—reveals itself as a guide to the individual's inner life. It is read and meditated upon as a practical handbook of spiritual struggle.

Interpretation discovers throughout the details of the text allusions to the states and trials through which entry onto the mystical path becomes possible: firm resolve, willing acceptance, trusting surrender, patience, inner tranquility, and so on. The people who put into practice this first inward meaning, corresponding to their spiritual capacity, are called the “pious ascetics” (ahl-e riyâza). 2) The second depth: the Sufis At the second depth, the character of the Qur'an is established by its designation as the “Noble Book” (Qorân karîm, 56:76). This second inward level expresses the way of being and spiritual dwelling place of the Sufis (ahl-e tasavvof).

Through their understanding of this meaning, they move beyond the mere asceticism of the preceding group and enter the states of spiritual experience: the stations (maqâmât), degrees (madârij), and successive stages (ma’ârij) familiar to those who practice Sufism. They learn to understand everything implied by the term mokâshafa, inward revelation or intuitive unveiling. They learn to distinguish the meaning of the moment (waqt), the passing spiritual state (hâl), ecstasy (wajd), mystical perception or taste (dhawq), mystical intoxication (sokr), wakefulness, the soul's contraction or anguish (qabz), expansion (bast), and so forth. They then interpret the whole Qur'an using the technical language of Sufism, because this second inward meaning reveals the Qur'an to them as a guide to the psychology of mystical experience. It is possible that our author had in mind mystical commentaries such as those of Sulami and Qushayri.

3) The third depth: the philosophers Descending one degree further, we reach a level of interpretation characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Wise Book” (Qorân hakîm, 36:1). This is the inward meaning that reveals itself to philosophers (ahl-e hikmat), shapes their inner being, and determines their spiritual place. By penetrating the meaning that belongs specifically to their level, they perceive the objects of philosophical knowledge (ma’qûlât) concealed beneath the literal appearance.

To write a Qur'anic commentary from this perspective is to show how the sacred text, beneath the veil of its allusions, answers to the demands of philosophical knowledge. Such matters include the affirmation of the First Principle (Mabda’ avval), the emanation of multiplicity from that First Principle through a hierarchy of intermediate hypostases, and related questions. We may think here of Avicenna's commentaries on certain surahs, his Epistle on the Angels, and other works. 4) The fourth depth: the gnostics and theosophers

At a higher—or deeper—level than that of the philosopher in the ordinary sense stands the spiritual seeker designated by the term ’ârif, usually translated as “gnostic.” This translation is technically accurate. It indicates a kinship with the kind of knowledge common to the various traditions of gnosis, without implying anything beyond that. More precisely, the distinction between philosopher and gnostic (hakîm and ’ârif) corresponds here to the distinction established by Suhrawardi, the master of Illumination (Ishrâq).

The preceding group consisted of philosophers in whom mystical experience was not yet assumed to be present. The present group consists of the theosophers (hakîm ilâhî), who unite philosophical knowledge with mystical experience. The Qur'an as these seekers read and understand it—the Qur'an whose meaning takes shape within them spiritually—is characterized by the designation “Luminous Book” or “Translucent Book” (Qorân mobîn, 15:1). By penetrating the inward meaning corresponding to their way of being, they perceive the divine secrets (asrâr-e ilâhî) and the higher teachings of spiritual knowledge (ma’ârif-e haqîqî) concealed within the text's outward appearance.

We may think here of certain monumental works still entirely unknown in the West: the mystical commentaries of Ibn Arabi and his disciples, Semnani, and Haydar Amoli; and the commentary later produced in seventeenth-century Iran by Mulla Sadra Shirazi, a student of Mir Damad, the great master of Illuminationist theosophy in the Safavid period.275 There would, admittedly, be just as much reason to associate these commentaries with the seventh inward level described below. Faced with works of such immense scale and doctrinal depth, one senses the presence of an extraordinary spiritual adventure, for which the Qur'an serves as both nourishment and guide.

Until we undertake their comparative study, the fundamental problems of interpretation raised throughout this work, as well as research into the nature of mystical experience more generally, will remain deprived of evidence of extraordinary importance and impressive scope. 5) The fifth depth: the faithful of love The fifth inward meaning is characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Glorious Book” (Qorân majîd, 85:21). The reference to the “Preserved Tablet” (85:22), upon which the Book has been inscribed since the very beginning, also directs us toward the heavenly archetype of that Book.

The spiritual group corresponding to this degree of inward understanding is that of the “mystical lovers” (’oshshâq). More precisely, they are those whom we have already called the “faithful of love,” because of their affinity with those in the West who, in the circle surrounding Dante, gave themselves that name: the Fedeli d'amore. It is important to notice that, according to our author, this name is by no means interchangeable with the simple designation “Sufis.” He placed the devout Sufis in general at the first two levels.

The faithful of love stand much higher: at the fifth degree of spiritual elevation or inward depth. In fact, Sufism had to struggle to gain acceptance for the term ’ishq—eros, passionate love—as a description of the believer's relationship with God. The very conception of divinity was at stake. To conceive and experience this divine eros, a person must open himself to an undivided, personal manifestation of God. The result is a mysticism of bridal love, toward which the communal and egalitarian religious consciousness of monotheism understood primarily as Law could feel only alarm and jealousy.

Hallaj, Suhrawardi, Attar, Ruzbihan, Jalal Rumi, Ibn Arabi, and so many others, together with all their disciples, were the heroes of this religion of love. They lived and read the Qur'an as though it were a version of the Song of Songs.276 Their interpretation discovers in every passage of the Book a sign of the Beloved. It comments upon the text by transforming all its words into symbols of love. Our author knows that the faithful of love do not shrink from any of the daring expressions technically known as shathîyât.

As we have explained (Book III above), this term corresponds etymologically to the Greek paradoxa: paradoxes, astonishing and incredible declarations, statements that overturn all received ideas. The Arabic root shth evokes the idea of falling backward in astonishment. For the rigidly orthodox believer, such paradoxical declarations are nothing but scandalous blasphemies and acts of unbelief. For the passionate mystic, who may declare, for example, “Without me, God could not exist for a single instant,” they are, at most, “pious blasphemies” or “beautiful acts of unbelief.”

Earlier (Book III), we mentioned the great work in which Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz collected and interpreted a large number of these paradoxical sayings—a major monument of Sufism.277 It is possible that our anonymous author was thinking of Ruzbihan here. 6) The sixth depth: those who realize divine Unity At the sixth depth, the distinctive character is established by the description of the Qur'an as the “Venerable Book” (Qorân ’azîz, 41:41).

Our author is rather reserved about identifying the spiritual group to which this level, and the following one, correspond. He describes this sixth group as those who have realized within themselves and through their own being the inward meaning of tawhîd, the affirmation of divine Unity. They are the Mowahhidân, whom we may call the “unifiers”: those who have experienced fanâ’ in its true sense. What they experience is the hidden absorption into divinity of everything that ordinary, naive, or merely literal knowledge imagines and treats as existence outside God. The path of these unifiers is marked by successive stations (maqâmât) in the inward realization of tawhîd. Its culmination is not the destruction or annihilation of the mystic as a person.

Rather, it is a fanâ’ that abolishes the opacity of a being who formerly existed only “for himself,” because his ego absorbed the whole of the being entrusted to him. The mode of heightened existence (baqâ’) that follows fanâ’ then gives him the transparency of a mirror. He acquires the capacity to become a place of divine manifestation (mazhar). 7) The seventh depth: the one who has arrived We are now prepared for the inward realization corresponding to the seventh meaning, characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm, 15:87).

Here lies the goal of every station along the mystical Path. It is the spiritual dwelling place of “the one who has arrived” (wâsil), the person who has attained union. His entire being gathers together the different ways in which the divine Attributes become manifest. He has become the mirror in which the radiance of pre-eternal Subsistence is reflected. And because he contemplates the divine manifestations (tajallî) in the mirror that he himself has become, he is truly their eyewitness. This seems to be the level at which the saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” has been realized so completely that its truth also makes the reverse true:

“Through knowing his Lord, he comes to know himself.”

For after fanâ’, the soul perceives itself at once as uncreated and as a creature.278 At this point, another saying becomes especially significant. Our author associates it with this mystical station:

“Whoever has seen me has seen God” (man ra’ânî faqad ra’a al-Haqq).

This declaration, which seems to be a transposition of a passage from the Gospel of John (14:7 and 19), was especially cherished and meditated upon in Shiite circles.279 It expresses the Shiite understanding of divine manifestation as something accomplished in the heavenly person of the Imam. The Imam is the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being, in whose person the invisible and unknowable God becomes visible to the eye of the heart. At the deepest level of inward interpretation, therefore, the operation we previously described as the necessary complement to the first is accomplished.

Following the example of the Prophet, the mystic's soul becomes a pure mirror. And what appears within that mirror is the heavenly Anthropos, the eternal Imam. The relationship is the same as that between the prophet who proclaims (Nâtiq) and the silent Imam (Sâmit). It is also the same as that between the letter of the sacred Book, transformed into a symbol, and the spiritual meaning that becomes manifest through it. Here we reach the final goal of both prophetic philosophy and the interpretation of inward meaning.

On the divine side, there is the taking of human form at the level of the Imam's heavenly humanity—the figure who, in Ismailism, bears the name Melchizedek. Corresponding to this, on the human side, is the taking on of divine form (ta’alloh, theôsis): the transformation of the human being through mystical experience. Here we should recall everything Haydar Amoli observed concerning the relationship between Shiism and Sufism.

Later we shall try to analyze the implications of Semnani's interpretive method. His extraordinary tafsîr, embracing all seven hidden meanings, properly belongs at this seventh inward level. Admittedly, the other Qur'anic commentaries mentioned earlier, in our discussion of the fourth level, could equally well be placed here. That a thinker who is explicitly Shiite should find the understanding of the Imam at the very end and summit of mystical experience is something another previously unpublished Persian treatise will now show us. We owe this next work to an eminent Iranian Shiite philosopher and mystic of the fifteenth century.

PreviousI. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of SufismNextIII. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)

Chapter III A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)

1. The Inner Meaning of the Splitting of the Moon

Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî belonged to a Shiite family originally from Turkestan that later settled in Isfahan. During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries (the eighth and ninth centuries of the Hijra), the family produced a distinguished succession of scholars.280

Sa’inoddin, who died in Herat in 830/1427, gives us an exceptionally revealing picture of the learning and intellectual interests of a mystical philosopher in Iran at that time. He was thoroughly familiar with Suhrawardî’s philosophy of Light (Ishrâq) and understood its deeper meaning. He wrote commentaries on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs and on the great Persian mystical poem by Mahmûd Shabestarî.281 He was a Shiite whose philosophical and mystical thinking drew nourishment from works of this kind. His own writings thus helped shape a specifically Shiite theosophy, close in spirit to the original inspiration from which Ismaili gnosis had itself emerged.

In Iran, meanwhile, following the fall of Alamût in 1257, Ismailism had reorganized itself while retreating, to varying degrees, into secrecy. Its influence was all the more active for being less visible. It can be felt throughout later Iranian Sufism and is especially apparent in the emergence, during the fourteenth century, of the school known as Hurufism. Its followers cultivated a mystical science of letters whose tradition reaches back to the beginnings of Shiism. Within Islam, they are the closest counterparts to the Kabbalists. Sa’inoddin himself was a Shiite hurufi, a practitioner of this letter mysticism, and that fact left a deep mark on his thought.

Among his writings is a short Persian treatise particularly well suited to helping us understand how meaning becomes inwardly realized. The anonymous author discussed in the preceding chapter showed us that this process of inward understanding determines the hierarchy and spiritual character of different kinds of seekers. Sa’inoddin’s treatise offers something like a practical exercise in the interpretation of a Quranic verse, designed to test the hierarchy of different forms of consciousness through the ways they understand it. His chosen text is the first verse of surah 54, the Surah of the Moon: The Hour drew near, and the Moon split apart.

Hence the title of his treatise: The Treatise on the Splitting of the Moon.282

Interpreters who insist on the literal meaning of the Quran have had considerable difficulty giving this verse a coherent explanation, particularly in establishing a connection between its two statements. They generally understand the approaching Hour as the final Resurrection, conceived as an entirely objective, outward event: something that will take place at the end of historical time and bring the entire sequence of worldly events to a close.

But what connection can there be between that final event and the splitting, or breaking open, of the Moon? The Arabic word shaqq suggests both a material object splitting in two and the breaking forth of dawn. If we remain with the outward, literal meaning alone, the problem is made still more difficult by the following verse, which seems to establish the context: “But when they [the unbelievers] see a Sign (âyat), they turn away and say: This is nothing but continuing magic” (54:2).

Literalist commentators have had no difficulty recognizing here an allusion to a miracle performed by the Prophet. According to the story, on a night of the full Moon, one of his relentless opponents from the Quraysh challenged him to produce a Sign proving the prophetic mission he claimed for himself. Those opponents, who denounced the Sign as magic, may actually have had a clearer sense than the devout literalists of the level of reality at which such a Sign can be perceived.

But the central difficulty remains. If the Hour means the final Resurrection, what bearing does a Sign once performed by the Prophet have upon it? How can the splitting of the Moon signify that the Hour is near? If it truly is such a Sign, then the event performed by the Prophet must be understood as a symbolic history, one whose setting is not the world of physical facts and whose meaning is not perceived through the bodily senses. It calls instead for a movement inward: a return (ta’wîl) from the outward event to its hidden, real meaning.

The truth of that meaning becomes apparent when the two parts of the verse acquire the coherence that literalist commentators have been unable to give them. It also means that the Sign of the Hour must be perceived not “on the horizons” (fi’l-âfâq)—not within the objective time of the world, measured by the movements of the stars and extending continuously onward (zamân âfâqî)—but within the soul’s own time. This is inward, subjective, qualitative time, distinguished not by measurable length but by intensity (zamân anfusî).

Literalist interpreters miss the eschatological event when they place it at the end of historical time, as though it were simply the last material occurrence in a series of similar occurrences. The event belongs instead to the soul’s own time. It is the growing intensity of that inward life that brings the event to birth, allowing it to break suddenly into consciousness.

Our philosopher-mystics therefore set aside the questions that modern philology would ordinarily ask about such a verse. Those questions seem to them to pass beside the matter that truly concerns them. They go directly to the issue they consider decisive: we can understand how the Sign appearing in the Moon announces the approaching Hour only by asking in which heaven that Sign occurs and within what kind of time it is true to say that the Hour is near. Their inquiry leads to a remarkable conclusion.

Whatever the moment in historical time, whatever our position beneath the “horizons” of world history, the meaning of the verse depends upon the kind of consciousness for which the Sign actually means something. It depends, therefore, upon the qualitative intensity of the inward time being lived—in other words, upon the depth at which the Sign is spiritually perceived. Sa’inoddin will distinguish seven kinds of spiritual seekers according to the different ways they understand the verse, whether their understanding is illusory or authentic. Each way of understanding reveals, without possibility of self-deception, the person’s inner mode of being. It thereby places that person within a hierarchy of forms of religious consciousness.

The anonymous Sufi’s treatise examined above was intended to illustrate a saying of the Prophet that speaks of seven inner meanings of the Quran. It described seven groups of spiritual seekers, each corresponding to one of those meanings, because the particular meaning accessible to a person reveals and determines that person's mystical rank.

We shall encounter these seven inner meanings again in ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî, though he relates them not to seven classes of people but to the seven subtle organs, or centers of consciousness, within the individual. Sa’inoddin Ispahânî’s treatise offers another variation. The seven forms of consciousness he identifies and describes in connection with a single Quranic verse do not correspond exactly to the seven levels of inner meaning.

The first two, the lowest ranks, belong to interpreters concerned with the outward, literal meaning. The remaining five belong to seekers of the inner meaning, but their grouping differs somewhat from that proposed by the earlier anonymous author. Philosophers are divided into two groups: the Peripatetics and the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light (corresponding to the third and fourth groups in the earlier treatise). This gives us another opportunity to recognize Suhrawardî’s influence on the Shiite theosophy of the period.

Here we should recall a view commonly held by the authors we are studying: the relationship of the Ishrâqiyûn to the Peripatetic philosophers is much like that of the Sufis to the theologians of Kalâm, the discipline of rational theology. The Sufis themselves are gathered into a single group; as described here, they are essentially disciples of Ibn ’Arabî.

Finally, since Sa’inoddin is himself a hurufi—that is, a practitioner of the mystical science of letters—and a Shiite, the two highest ranks of his mystical hierarchy are represented by figures corresponding to his own spiritual commitments.

His treatise has two distinct parts, each devoted to one of the two statements in the Quranic verse. For our purposes, it will be more illuminating to consider them together. There is something further. An indispensable supplement to this treatise is found in the Dabestân-e Madhâhib, the Persian encyclopedia of comparative religion that preserves so much otherwise unique information about religious communities and sects in seventeenth-century India.

One chapter reproduces word for word the section of Sa’inoddin’s treatise concerning the Peripatetics and the Ishrâqiyûn. It also contains an essential discussion missing from our manuscript. We may wonder whether that passage was omitted out of caution or whether it represents a personal addition by the author of the Dabestân, though the latter possibility seems unlikely. In any event, there can be little doubt that the author of the Dabestân had Sa’inoddin’s treatise before him.

2. The Jurists and the Traditionists

Those who adhere to the outward meaning fall into two groups. The first commands little respect from our philosopher-mystic. It consists of the doctors of religious law (foqahâ) and the Traditionists (Mohaddithûn), the specialists in hadîth, who appoint themselves guardians of the literal meaning of every text and every saying attributed to the Prophet. As Sa’inoddin puts it: “These are people who rest the back of their contentment upon the cushion of conformity (taqlîd).

“Having brought all serious inquiry to a halt once and for all, they are perfectly satisfied with themselves.” There is no point in asking them how the splitting or breaking open of the Moon should be understood. In their eyes, to question its literal truth, to doubt that it was a visible, material event, or even to ask how such a thing could have happened is already to surrender to forbidden innovation (bid’a) and commit heresy.

As for the approaching Hour, they see no difficulty if it refers to the great final Gathering of everything that has appeared from the beginning to the end of time, when all will be weighed in the Balance and the righteous separated from the condemned. That Gathering necessarily entails the resurrection of material bodies: every particle of every part of the human body, scattered by death, will come to life again at that supreme Hour. One must not ask how this will happen.

One must simply conform, strictly and literally, to the teaching of the prophets. Does the astronomical Sign refer to a miracle performed by the Prophet or to a prodigy at the end of time? Either way, how does it signify the Hour? It is impossible even to put the question to these interpreters. For the question can only be asked by entering a deeper level of meaning, one that transforms the literal facts themselves. And it is precisely that transformation which these literalist scholars reject with stubborn alarm.

3. The Philosophers of Islam

The second group of those concerned with the outward meaning deserves more consideration. These are the philosophers of Islam (Hokamâ-ye Islâm) and the orthodox scholastic theologians (Motakallimûn). At least they have gone beyond straightforward literalism. They have had the courage to reflect and reason, and have advanced as far as they could along the path of independent inquiry.

Although their fundamental beliefs (i’tiqâd) lead them to the same answers as the first group on the questions that concern us, they do not forbid themselves to ask how things happen. It is true, Sa’inoddin observes, that when they agree to ask the question, they do so with the firm intention of demonstrating that the material event is possible. Their reasoning rests on two premises.

First, they accept the absolute power of the divine Agent, who can freely bring about whatever he wishes, in any manner he chooses.

Second, they reject the celestial physics of the philosophers inspired by the Greeks, who maintain that the heavenly spheres are made of a subtle substance different from earthly matter and therefore cannot be torn or split apart. The Motakallimûn, by contrast, teach that the spheres and heavenly bodies are of the same nature as bodies composed of the earthly elements. They can consequently be torn or divided like anything else accessible to the senses.

From the standpoint of Greek-inspired cosmology, this amounts to an extraordinary physical paradox. It also prevents these theologians from moving beyond the realm of sensible things to an intermediate level of reality. They face a further difficulty in determining the status of a being that is genuinely real while existing outside the divine Being.

Nevertheless, once their premises are granted, it becomes possible to accept that the event in question occurred in the visible, astronomical heavens, as a Sign intended to establish the truth of the prophetic Message before those who denied it.

The same premises help them address the event that announces the approaching Hour. Philosophers object that something which has been completely annihilated cannot return to existence as the numerically identical individual it once was. The resurrection of material bodies as imagined by the Motakallimûn is therefore, they argue, absurd. The theologians reply that it is no more absurd than the original creation of that individual, who was brought into existence when previously he was nothing. Such an argument will convince only those who are already convinced.

Yet in Sa’inoddin’s eyes, this does not deprive the Motakallimûn of their achievement. Given their premises, their conclusions follow necessarily; and at least they have taken the trouble to construct those premises. With a touch of humor, he concludes that they represent a definite kind of consciousness: the person who works hard to extract arguments from the Book and the traditions in order to confirm an interpretation that remains entirely literal. If their powers of philosophical reflection went no further, it was because the wisdom of the Most Wise judged that, for their purposes, they had no need of a capacity exceeding what was required to argue about the letter and its outward meaning.

4. The Peripatetics

With the third group we enter the company of those who seek the inner meaning. Here we witness the first transformation of the literal facts. From that transformation emerges an esoteric meaning that makes it possible to understand what the splitting of the Moon may signify and how it announces the approaching Hour. Although this group gives us access to the first level of inner meaning, it is still described, in contrast to the Ishrâqiyûn of Suhrawardî’s school, as the group of “outward philosophers” (Hokamâ-ye zâhir). These are the thinkers commonly called Peripatetics (Mashshâ’ûn), whose master was Aristotle and whose leading representative in Islam was Avicenna, known as their chief (ra’îs) and shaykh.

Sa’inoddin tells us that an argument of compelling certainty has led these philosophers to the conviction that the Moon, although it is visible to the senses, cannot possibly be broken or split in any way. According to an axiom of their cosmology, the ethereal matter of the heavens is entirely incapable of undergoing the changes and accidents that affect earthly matter beneath the Moon.

Yet neither reason nor any authority in the world can legitimately compel us to accept an absurdity.

We must therefore acknowledge that the splitting of the Moon mentioned in the Quranic verse has another meaning. It must express a symbol (ramz), pointing toward an event whose true setting is not the visible heaven of astronomy. At the very outset, philosophy thus challenges religious reflection to turn away from the “horizons”—the outer world—and toward the inner world of the soul. The spiritual thinkers we are studying never imagined that a religious person must find either the home or the triumph of faith in absurdity. They accepted the shathîyât, those paradoxical mystical utterances that challenge conventional assumptions, and they sometimes delighted in their almost “divine-human” character.

But they were careful not to confuse what lies beyond ordinary reason with what contradicts reason altogether. To them, absurdity could only be an affront to the divine.

Another fundamental principle opens the way for these philosophers to enter the realm of inner reality—one of the basic ideas (osûl) to which they have devoted their most careful investigations. Every visible star (kawkab) and every heaven (falak) has a corresponding invisible, inward reality (bâtin): an Intelligence that they call the Angel of that star or heaven. Among these Intelligences, the inward reality of the Moon is identified as the “Agent” or “Active Intelligence” (’Aql fa’âl).

The highest degree of human perfection, its final seal, is reached when the spiritual seeker enters into conjunction with this Active Intelligence.283 The splitting of the Moon in the Quranic verse symbolizes precisely this conjunction with the Intelligence that is the Angel, the hidden reality of the Moon’s heaven. To acquire the stable disposition, or habitus, that makes frequent conjunction with the Active Intelligence possible is to attain the degree called the “acquired intellect,” intellectus adeptus (’aql mostafâd).

Whatever the sage who has reached this degree turns toward, he knows it immediately, without needing to work through a fresh sequence of mental arguments. Since this degree represents the highest limit and final seal of human perfection, the state symbolized by the “splitting of the Moon” must also have belonged to the person who was the Seal of the Prophets.

This interpretation already confirms the theme outlined in the preceding chapter. It reminds us that the intellectus sanctus, the “holy intellect” or highest degree of human intelligence, is a special gift shared by the prophet and the philosophical sage. Because they share that gift, it becomes the source of a prophetic wisdom—a prophetic philosophy.

The Angel of Knowledge is none other than the Angel of Revelation. What takes place is not a secularization of prophetic Revelation, but precisely the reverse: philosophical knowledge becomes sacred as it reaches the point where it surpasses its own ordinary limits. The spiritual state of the prophet thus becomes the model for the mystic’s experience, while mystical experience brings philosophy to completion in a metaphysics of ecstasy. It is in this sense that Suhrawardî’s Ishrâq fulfilled Avicenna’s project of an “Eastern wisdom.”

The coherence of the Quranic verse now becomes apparent. The splitting of the Moon is a Sign of the Hour—a connection that neither the devout literalists nor the theologians of Kalâm could establish, because they could not penetrate to the depth at which its meaning comes into view. As the author of the Dabestân will emphasize, the splitting of the Moon symbolizes the passage to the inner meaning. For that meaning to unfold, there must be a ta’wîl, a return to the hidden truth.

But this cannot merely be an operation performed upon a text; it must also be an event within the soul. The movement is from the Moon’s outward appearance—the astronomical body visible to everyone—to its inward reality, the Angel of the Moon’s heaven. In Avicennian cosmology, that Angel is the Active Intelligence, the Noûs poêtikos.284 The passage leads from a sensible reality to its Angel. This is why interpreting the text through ta’wîl cannot succeed unless the soul simultaneously undergoes its own ta’wîl, its own “return” to its source.

And this Return is precisely its resurrection. Resurrection does not mean an event that will take place one day at the far end of the series of events unfolding beneath the “horizons” of natural time. Nor does it mean the resurrection of material bodies, which these philosophers regard as both inconceivable and unnecessary. It means spiritual Resurrection: the soul’s return to its own world.

The orthodox theologians had imagined the final fulfillment of all things taking place within the time measured by the movements of the visible heavens. The philosophers understand the event as something inward. The human being has a twofold task. First, to serve as the mediator through whom things become manifest, since the human being contains a summary of them all—a microcosm.

Second, through acts of knowledge and contemplation, to lead those things back (ta’wîl) from their outward appearance to their inner reality, in a process that is at once an inward turning and an integration. Whenever a human being brings this process to perfection, that person becomes a world in himself (’âlam), an Aeon—what the Latin Avicennians would call a saeculum intelligibile, an intelligible world. He returns to the place of his Return (ma’âd), which is also the place of his origin: the world of pure, immaterial substances, untouched by the perishable matter of the world beneath the Moon. In that world, everything that exists possesses knowledge and perception, and neither ignorance nor anything harmful can exist.

This Return does not occur beneath the “horizons,” as an event belonging to the time of the world (zamân âfâqî), even if it were the final event of that time. It occurs when outward, worldly time—the time associated with literal, outward meaning—is transformed into the soul’s pure inward time (zamân anfusî), the time of inner meaning (see Book I, Chapter IV, §5). This, Sa’inoddin explains, is what is meant when we say that the Prophet “inaugurated the Cycle of the Moon.”

The expression refers to his conjunction with the Moon’s inward reality: the Angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, who is identified with the Active Intelligence, the Angel of the Moon’s heaven and the Angel of Knowledge. The Prophet thereby inaugurates a time that can no longer be measured by the movements of the astronomical heavens. It belongs instead to their hidden reality, to heavens invisible to the bodily eye.

There is, of course, a great difference between the Peripatetics presented here and those we ordinarily encounter in histories of philosophy.

We must never lose sight of that difference. Here, the theory of knowledge is governed by the figure and function of the Active Intelligence as the Angel of Knowledge. It is directed toward an inner level of reality, where its task is to provide the foundation for a prophetic kind of philosophy. The passage from the Dabestân that we shall examine below will show how far the implications of this understanding could be carried. Such a theory of knowledge does not have to struggle toward an artificial reconciliation between faith and knowledge, official dogma and philosophical understanding.

Instead, it makes possible both the experience and the philosophical grounding of one and the same supreme, profoundly personal encounter, appearing in two forms: that of the hero of prophecy and that of the hero of knowledge. Without some intuition of their underlying identity, no one could have recognized that the Angel of Revelation and the Active Intelligence are one and the same. And without that identity, the hidden meaning of the verse would remain unintelligible: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split apart.”

5. The Theosophers of Light (Ishrâqiyûn)

The preceding discussion has already brought us close to the method followed by a fourth family of spiritual seekers: the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light who follow Suhrawardî, in their search for the hidden meaning. At least in theory, we could distinguish their method from that of the Avicennian Peripatetics by recalling the distinction drawn in the introduction to Suhrawardî’s Hikmat al-Ishrâq. There, the Peripatetic sages are presented as outstanding philosophers who lack mystical experience, while the “Eastern sages”—above all, the sages of ancient Persia—are equally accomplished in philosophical reasoning and direct mystical experience.

As we saw in Book II, Suhrawardî called these ancient Persian sages the Khosrawâniyûn, the spiritual ancestors of the Ishrâqiyûn. In practice, however, the philosophy of Light established by Suhrawardî, with its deliberate aim of reviving the teachings of ancient Iran, so quickly overshadowed the pure Avicennism from which his metaphysics had begun that we can speak, to a considerable extent, of an Ishrâqî form of Avicennism in Iran. The philosophers discussed in the preceding group already bear witness to this in their own way.

As Sa’inoddin observes, the Avicennians and the Ishrâqiyûn begin by responding in the same way to the mysterious Quranic verse. According to celestial physics, the Moon belongs to a sphere composed of incorruptible matter and therefore cannot conceivably be split or torn apart. The verse cannot, then, be understood in terms of a physical phenomenon. Its real meaning must lie elsewhere.

Having established this, the specifically Ishrâqî interpreter brings in the principles of the metaphysics of Light. The Avicennians had already affirmed and described a passage from the Moon’s outward reality to its inward reality. Their interpretation of the text already presupposed an event taking place within the interpreter’s own soul. It is this event that the Ishrâqiyûn now undertake to examine, drawing upon principles that connect their teaching with Gnosis and Manichaeism.

To solve the riddle of the verse, they begin by recalling that Light is the very source of the world’s appearance (Persian: paydâ’i-e ’âlam). It is what makes it possible for anything to be manifest, revealed, or brought into view (paydâ, zâhir). Light is therefore the origin of everything that exists; indeed, light is identified with being itself.

Yet their understanding of beings of light distinguishes two categories. There is a Light that cannot, in any way or in any sense, become mixed with Darkness. And there is a Light that can enter into such a mixture. The first category consists of the angelic Intelligences.

The second consists of the celestial Souls, which move the heavenly spheres, and human souls, which have been entrusted with the task of governing material bodies.

The first category possesses complete and actual knowledge of realities separated from matter—that is, the archetypal Ideas—without needing to pass through the experience of particular things. Souls belonging to the second category, however, can come to know both the pure Ideas and concrete realities accessible to the senses. The light of their being shines in both directions.

Furthermore, if the entire order of beings is to reach completion and realize the fullest possible degree of perfection, every possible form of knowledge must become manifest: knowledge of pure Ideas no less than knowledge of concrete things. Nothing must remain merely potential. It is precisely this necessity that gives beings of light of the second category their particular task, and that determines their descent into matter and their temporary captivity within it. The Moon symbolizes these beings of light as they pass through a period of darkness and confinement.

This mixture with Darkness is the condition that makes it possible for all the forms of knowledge—all the lights—previously held in a merely potential state to become fully manifest. Light, by its very nature, is both visible and revealed to itself and through itself (zâhir li-nafsi-hi), and that which reveals everything other than itself (mozhir li-ghayri-hi).
