Its power to bring things into appearance is inseparable from what it is.

The rays it sends out return to it as reflections, multiplying without limit. In this way, Light eventually reaches the perfection of both its own manifestation (paydâ’î) and its power to reveal (paydâkunandagî). All the forms of knowledge, all the lights hidden within it in a state of potentiality, burst outward into manifestation.

The darkened Moon at the beginning of its cycle becomes the full Moon blazing in the night sky. This is the splitting to which the Quranic verse alludes: the soul’s triumphant emergence from the Darkness in which it was held captive, because it has filled that very Darkness with its own Light.

Yet for the soul to shine in Darkness in this way, the light hidden within it must first break forth. That emergence is the light of dawn: the soul’s knowledge rising into awareness. It is the soul’s own East, the place where its light rises—hence the expression “Eastern theosophy.” The soul’s state of manifestation reaches perfection because its power to reveal has reached its fullness. All the forms of knowledge contained within it have broken through the enclosure that held them captive and become manifest to the beings of every universe. This is why Light had to spend a time imprisoned in Darkness.

Here the interpretation converges once more with that of the Avicennians. The “splitting of the Moon,” whose meaning is now becoming clear, is indeed the Sign of the approaching Hour, because the two expressions refer to one and the same event. The literalists could not see their unity because they were unable to recognize the depth of reality at which the event takes place.

The Return, the Resurrection, the approaching Hour—these do not concern the scattered particles of an annihilated material body coming together again to reconstitute an individual who, in any case, could not be numerically identical to the original. They concern the Spirit, the eternally living being (zenda-ye jâvid), whose identity persists through every existence. This Spirit is the Light whose particular level of being required it to be joined for a time with the Darkness of the earthly body. Having completed its growth—as light itself can grow, as though there were a body composed entirely of light—it returns to its own world. That return is its resurrection.

The Ishrâqiyûn pay close attention to this growth of a being of light (see Book II, Chapter V, on the meaning of the Moon’s phases in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel). Whenever Light encounters an opaque object that it cannot penetrate or pass through, the object casts a shadow. The light is turned back upon itself, as though reflected by a mirror, and its brightness increases through that reflection.

In the same way, the living Light we call spirit, or the thinking soul, receives back the light that it projects, and grows accordingly. Certainly, what returns to the soul is its own light. What it perceives is the light reflected back to it by the screen—the body, the barzakh, or intermediate barrier—that intercepted it. The forms of knowledge that return to the soul are its own; the Image it projects upon things is its own Image.

But it must project them outward in this way, so that it may see itself in a mirror. That mirror reveals the soul to itself and increases its light by reflecting back what it has received.

For this to become possible, the soul had to descend into Darkness. Before its earthly existence, it was capable only of a comprehensive, undifferentiated kind of knowledge: knowledge of metaphysical universals. Once joined to a body, it became capable of grasping individual, concrete realities. To grasp them, to understand them, is to become conscious that the soul itself contains them, that they are present within it. This is how the complete manifestation of beings is achieved. When the soul reaches this perfection, not a single being in the upper world or the lower world remains absent from this being of light.

The approaching Hour, of which the splitting of the Moon is the Sign, is therefore “the day when all secrets shall be revealed,” as another Quranic verse declares (86:9). But the meaning of this revelation is made clear by the Persian poet’s lines quoted by Sa’inoddin:

“Everything that has been, everything that is, everything that will be—understand that it all exists within yourself.”285

At this degree, the movement inward is complete. The future and the past are no longer separate quantities of time scattered along the continuous extension of the world’s time, the time “of the horizons.” They are brought together into a single unity within the intensity of the “time of the soul.” At this degree, the entire chain of beings reaches its limit and perfection. It is the degree of the final Seal: both the state of manifestation and the power to reveal286 attain their fullness.

The splitting of the Moon thus signifies the attainment of the degree of the Seal. But who possesses this final Seal? Historically, within the “time of the horizons,” it is certainly the Prophet.

Yet according to the Ishrâqiyûn, the inner meaning of the verse becomes a reality in every spiritual seeker who reaches this degree. The conviction that the Prophet’s experience is the model for mystical experience is both the starting point and the outcome of an interpretation that takes the movement inward to its furthest depths. As we shall see, Semnânî carried it to the very limit.

Through this inward transformation, philosophical wisdom becomes, in lived experience, a prophetic philosophy. Correspondingly, the religion of Islam itself is transformed into a purely spiritual Islam. Its philosophy is this prophetic philosophy, leading toward a transcendent realization of individual personhood through conjunction with the Angel of the supreme Revelation—the approaching Hour. Why, then, is the daring passage that bestows the title “Seal of Prophecy” upon every spiritual seeker missing from our manuscript of Sa’inoddin’s treatise? We shall encounter it later, in the context of the Dabestân, where it will provide the conclusion to our discussion.

6. The Sufis

Sa’inoddin now presents three further ways of bringing meaning inward, corresponding to three spiritual families whose affinities may be more significant than their differences. We have deliberately spoken of different ways of going inward rather than of new depths to be reached. The interpretation developed by the Ishrâqiyûn already descends so deeply into the inner meaning of the Quranic verse that it would seem difficult to go further. What we encounter now are variations in the figures that become visible at a comparable depth of inward experience. Since these families of spiritual seekers are closely related, the figures that appear to their different forms of consciousness can be understood as corresponding to one another.

In the two spiritual worlds we have just visited—that of the Neoplatonically inclined Peripatetics and that of the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light—it was natural for the dominant figure to be the Active Intelligence. This Intelligence is identified with Gabriel, the Angel of Revelation, who among the Ishrâqiyûn is also identified with the archetypal Angel of humanity.

If we keep in mind this identity between the Angel Gabriel and the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being—an identity also found among the Mandaeans and the Ahl-e Haqq—we can recognize the corresponding figures that emerge at the horizon of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness. Sa’inoddin will now examine how these figures appear to the remaining three spiritual groups as they confront the same Quranic verse.

The sixth group in Sa’inoddin’s overall classification consists of the Sufis. They are no longer divided, as they were in the earlier anonymous treatise, into pious ascetics, Sufis in general, and the faithful of love. The Sufis discussed here possess a sophisticated spiritual and philosophical culture. They are deeply shaped by the spirituality of both Suhrawardî and Ibn ’Arabî.

Two terms describe them. First, they are Mohaqqiqûn: people who have personally verified the truth, both through philosophical reflection and through direct experience. They are, in the fullest sense, “those who have understood.”

This brings us back to the precise meaning we have given to the word hermeneutics: understanding is an act in which a person becomes conscious of what he himself contains and of the fact that he contains it. These Sufis are therefore also “speculative” thinkers in the original sense of the word. The speculative thinker becomes aware that he himself is the speculum, the mirror in which he sees all things, and that the Image appearing in this mirror is the image formed by his own understanding of them. The act of Understanding is thus inseparable from a personal realization.

This explains their second designation: Ahl-e shohûd, those who have witnessed directly, initiates admitted to the contemplation of the mystery. Perhaps the closest equivalent is a Greek word drawn from the ancient language of the mysteries: they are epoptes, initiates who have been admitted to direct vision. We should also recall that, since the thirteenth century, the philosophy of Light shared in Iran by Suhrawardî’s Ishrâqiyûn and the disciples of Ibn ’Arabî has dominated philosophical mysticism. The Sufis now under discussion and the theosophers of Light previously described share several fundamental themes. The transition from one group to the other is therefore scarcely noticeable.

We encounter here once again the idea of manifestation, understood in two related senses. First, there is the state of a being insofar as it is Light (Arabic zohûr, Persian paydâ’î).

Second, there is the power of manifestation—the power to reveal (Arabic izhâr, Persian paydâkunandagî)—that belongs to Light by virtue of its very being. Light illuminates from the instant it exists. It does not first come into existence and only afterward begin to shine. As soon as there exists something whose nature is to reveal, to bring something into view, there is already something revealed, something manifest—a “phenomenon” (zâhir).

Here, however, the question is no longer the destiny of the individual soul as a being of Light: the necessary drama of its descent into Darkness and its redemption. It is the fact of theophany in general—the appearance or manifestation of the divine—insofar as theophany is bound up with the Human Form. In a sense, we are now considering the prologue to the drama contemplated by the Ishrâqiyûn.

It is from this standpoint that the idea of theophany provides a solution to the riddle of the Quranic verse chosen by Sa’inoddin for his treatise. He begins with a brief reference to a hadîth familiar throughout Islamic theosophy, and especially fundamental to the teaching of Ibn ’Arabî:

“I was a Hidden Treasure, and I loved to be known. So I created creatures in order that I might be known.”

As Sa’inoddin reminds us, the whole of philosophical Sufism rests upon the idea that the “descents” (tanazzolât) of the primordial Source of being (asl-e wojûd)—from the levels of the Pleroma, the fullness of the higher spiritual world, down to creatures subject to becoming—have one ultimate purpose. The Source emerges in forms of infinite multiplicity so that it may reveal and manifest itself.287

There are two degrees corresponding to two aspects of this manifestation. The first is the resulting state of manifestation (martaba-ye zohûr o paydâ’î): the degree at which everything possible passes into actual, manifest existence. The fullness of this theophany is the “Human Form,” which the Sufis express through the personal symbol of Adam. In doing so, they too give expression to the Gnostic idea of the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being. This essence is perfect because it brings together every degree of being. It gathers all existence into itself, because in it and through it the whole of being attains the level of a form conscious of itself.

In its second aspect—the second degree of its perfection—this manifestation is considered no longer simply as the state brought about by the divine will to reveal itself, but as an active function inherent in that state. What has been revealed now itself reveals what is manifested within it. In this sense, the recipient of an action becomes its agent; what is revealed becomes what reveals.

Yet the two movements—acting and receiving—take place simultaneously and reciprocally.

Through the divine will to manifest itself, the Godhead reveals the Human Form by revealing itself within that Form. At the same moment, the Human Form reveals the Godhead precisely because the Godhead reveals the Form. Perfect theophany is a divine “anthropomorphosis,” a manifestation in human form. The Human Form assumes the highest power of revealing the divine. By serving as the bearer of the divine Attributes, it allows the Godhead in its own essence to remain free of every suggestion of “anthropomorphism,” or limitation to human shape.

In the philosophical terminology of Sufism, the Seal (khâtim) designates the person whose state of human perfection invests him, in the highest degree, with this power of divine manifestation. That investiture is the bursting into view of an inner meaning previously hidden beneath the perfected form. It is the manifestation, through that form, of the Forma Dei, the Form of God. This does not mean that the person incarnates the divine Form in the technical Christian sense of incarnation. Rather, he bears it within himself as a mirror bears an image. (We can recognize here the displacement of a Shiite doctrine of the Imams, an imamology that no longer speaks its own name.)

As in the symbolism of the Ishrâqiyûn, the Moon represents this perfected Form. The splitting of the Moon mentioned in the Quranic verse is the Hour of theophany: the moment when the divine becomes manifest in the mirror of the perfected Form, when the Human Form takes on the likeness of the divine. The initiated contemplative, the epoptes, beholds this directly, without needing to construct an argument or proceed through philosophical reasoning.

At once, the connection between the two parts of the Quranic verse becomes clear in a flash. Everything, every being, returns to its origin. For the Human Form, the return to its origin—the approaching Hour, the Resurrection—is the moment when it fully assumes its power to reveal the divine. It has become a pure, untarnished mirror, and the Forma Dei appears within it as an image appears in a mirror.

Now, the Perfect Human Being is the one in whom and through whom everything that was merely potential has become manifest. As a microcosm, this person thus performs the work of divine self-revelation. According to the Sufis discussed by Sa’inoddin, such a spiritual being is designated by the term nabî: prophet. (We shall see, in Semnânî’s teaching, the degree of inward realization corresponding to the birth of the nabî as an inner spiritual state.) Among the Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosopher’s vocation was already directed toward a “prophetic philosophy,” bringing him into relation with the prophet’s experience and calling. In the same way, the Sufi mystic is directed toward the archetype of the nabî.

At this point, the oppositions that our accustomed rational categories have taught us to make lose their force: philosophy itself is prophetic, mystical experience is a prophetic state, and the reverse is equally true. Spiritual life is centered entirely on the figure of the nabî, the prophet (just as Christian spiritual life is centered on Christology). Consequently, the very idea of the Seal is transformed by the mysterious event to which the Qur'anic verse alludes. The title borne on earth by the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets” is transferred to every spiritual seeker who, in turn, attains the state of nabî. For the state and calling of the nabî belong to the person to whom, and through whom, the Forma Dei, the divine Form, is revealed.

We shall soon see that this is the profound conviction of the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosophers of illumination. Both they and the Sufis whom Sâ'inoddîn has in mind express through this shared conception their belief that the prophetic gift continues.

But this brings us back to a serious question we have already encountered: what unspoken assumptions are these two groups making? Let us review the matter. We have just read that, for the Ishrâqiyûn and for the Sufis Sâ'inoddîn is discussing, every spiritual seeker reaches full inner perfection by attaining the state of nabî. The prophet thus remains the archetype that spiritual life seeks to realize. This is of the greatest interest, but some distinctions are essential. To begin with, there can be no question of repeating the role of the lawgiving prophet or the prophet sent on a mission. Only the state of the nabî in the simplest sense can serve as the model.

Yet to make this distinction is already to invoke the categories established by Shiite teachings on prophecy (see Book I, Chapter VI). Those teachings also tell us that, after the man who was the “Seal of the Prophets” in the absolute sense, the term nabî can no longer be used. Instead, for the period following Muhammad, the word is walî—a friend or beloved of God. In terms of the inner states experienced, the walî corresponds to what the simple term nabî designated throughout the pre-Muhammadan era.

So when we are told that the mystic's experience follows the model of the prophet's, this cannot possibly refer to the lawgiving mission of the Messenger invested with nobowwat al-tashrî', the authority to reveal a religious law. It can refer only to what, in the prophet-messenger himself, is the source of his prophetic status (nobowwat) and of his outward mission to others: his walâyat, his intimate spiritual nearness to God.

Are we therefore facing, in the Sufis described by Sâ'inoddîn, precisely the paradox denounced by Haydar Âmolî? Is this a Sufism that has forgotten its origins, one from which Shiite imamology has effectively been made to disappear, even though it is presupposed by the very notion of a distinctive prophetic gift continuing after the last prophet and the closing of the prophetic cycle? Or is this an instance of taqîyeh, esoteric discretion, deliberately concealing every sign of an openly acknowledged Shiism? Sâ'inoddîn gives us at least the beginnings of an answer in his final paragraph, where he places the spiritual schools he has described in relation to Shiism.

In comparison with Shiism, all of them have thus far been no more than the approaching Hour—or, more precisely, signs that the Hour is approaching. The “splitting of the Moon” does not take place—that is, its spiritual meaning cannot be perceived—unless one has learned from the “Pillars of the Prophet's House,” a reference to the line of the Twelve Imams.

Unfortunately, this final paragraph is deliberately brief and allusive (see §8 below). But perhaps we can make progress by studying the pages apparently lost from Sâ'inoddîn's text, which we have recovered in the Dabestân: the pages concerning the Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn.

We can then compare them with what we already know of Shiite spirituality founded on walâyat—what we have called its orientation around the Imam. Perhaps this will allow us to place the earlier degrees of esoteric understanding in relation to Shiism as the “seventh degree,” and to understand why Sâ'inoddîn regards all those earlier degrees as merely the “approach of the Hour.” The outlines of Sâ'inoddîn Torkeh's religious typology would then become clearer, helping us understand the spirituality of Iranian Islam as a whole. Before that, however, the author identifies one further spiritual group. It occupies the last stage before Shiite imamology, which is at once the source of all hidden meanings and the summit toward which they rise.

7. The Hurufis

This name designates those who practice the “science of letters” ('ilm-e horûf)288. In Islam, they carry forward a tradition dating to the beginnings of Ismaili Shiism in the eighth century. The techniques of their science correspond, even in their details, to those practiced by Kabbalists, although the science of letters is only one part of the immense spiritual tradition known as Kabbalah289. By training the initiate to see each letter as a symbol or an ideogram encoding a value, this science makes possible an immediate, intuitive perception that no longer needs the assistance of intellectual argument. It, too, is directed toward the prophetic model. As Sâ'inoddîn tells us: “Their contemplation proceeds through the same Forms that descended upon the prophets.”

The later religious community known in Iran by this name, for whom the science of letters was the defining doctrine, originated with a man whose fate was tragic: Fazlollah, a northern Iranian from Astarâbâd, executed as a martyr in 796 AH (1393–94 CE) on the orders of Mîrânshâh, one of Tamerlane's sons290. The emergence of his teaching and his tragic death mark an important stage in the history of Iranian Shiism.

The Hurufis' interpretation of the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon presupposes their entire metaphysics, because that metaphysics concentrates on the very phenomenon that most urgently calls for a conscious art of interpretation. It is not concerned with conceptual dialectic. Its essential concern is to interpret the Word: the spoken Word, in the form of sounding incantation, and the Word fixed—or, more precisely, symbolized—in writing. From this emerges the outline of an ontology of writing, an understanding of being through written forms. The shapes of letters are grasped intuitively as ideograms, since every stroke of the design can itself carry an ideographic value. Sâ'inoddîn, who died some thirty-five years after the movement's founder, knew the doctrine at first hand. He sketches it in a way we can summarize here, emphasizing a few of its characteristic features.

Being exists at many levels. The beings found on these levels differ in their capacity for existence and their receptivity to it. Because those capacities differ, we must first distinguish beings that can subsist in themselves and possess an independent existence: the Spirits at the various levels of their hierarchy, and bodies, whether heavenly, subtle, or material. Other beings cannot subsist independently. They exist only through something else—through the subject whose state or activity they are. Examples include actions, events, and words.

Now, among the very sources (ommohât) of the levels of being, one holds a privileged position: the Word (Kalâm). Everything that can exist in the divine worlds or in the worlds of becoming—and even everything that has been unable to achieve existence in either the world of universals or that of concrete individual things—can come into existence at this privileged level of the Word. There is more. One of its distinctive powers is that it makes manifest the meanings and significance of all actual and possible beings. Ideas, doctrines, theories, realities of every kind: they become manifest, enter the light, and acquire the status of meaningful “phenomena” only by reaching the level of the Word.

Yet the Word is not itself an autonomous level of being, subsisting on its own. The fullness of revelation that it confers on things by “uttering” them is borrowed from the one who utters it—the motakallim. Its existence depends on the existence of that speaker.

This brief account by Sâ'inoddîn brings into focus the guiding conviction of these Islamic Kabbalists. For them, interpretation—the passage from outward appearance to hidden meaning—is, in both the etymological and the deepest sense, an onto-logy: an understanding of being through the Word. For at the innermost depth of things, being itself is a Word, a Logos. That is why they say, for example, that sound does not originate outside the objects that strike one another.

Rather, it emerges from within them, from their hidden, inward reality291. The distinction between outward and inward meaning, on which the spiritual interpretation considered here depends, is also the condition of every being and every thing. The inward (bâtin)—what is hidden, unseen, unheard, and inaccessible to the senses—is each being's absolute essence (dhât motlaq), its energy from before eternity, its eternal and unchanging King, its constitutive Word.

Yet beings and things do not make that Word audible unless there is a collision. Until then, its sound remains a latent possibility buried within them. As long as the two things do not strike each other, the divine Word (Kalâm-e Haqq) remains submerged and entombed in them. The deepest secret of a being is thus understood as the sounding incantation that calls it into existence, a secret revealed only through that impact. Its sound is the manifestation of its innermost depth, its own distinctive rate of vibration.

To know a being, then, is to discern beneath its outward manifestation (zâhir) the hidden reality (bâtin) of the divine Word that uttered it and that it itself utters. This Word does not exist independently outside the being, for it is the being's very existence. The Word becomes manifest only through the manifestation of the one who speaks it, just as moonlight is nothing other than a revelation of the Sun's light. In a sense, the Sun “utters” that light; without it, the Moon would remain in the darkness of nonbeing. That is why, Sâ'inoddîn observes, the Moon can symbolize the level of being under discussion. Here we already glimpse the mystical meaning that will be found in the Qur'anic verse about the Moon's splitting: the bursting forth of the Word, a triumphant sounding incantation.

Unfortunately, sound is unstable and short-lived. Yet it can take a form more substantial and lasting than a momentary vibration, a form that is itself privileged because it reveals the effects, traces, and laws of being more clearly than any other. That form is the pattern traced by writing. On the one hand, the Word exists only through the one who utters it. On the other, this subtle and fragile mode of existence—existence as sound, the vibration produced by the impact that draws from beings the secret incantation of their existence—acquires a stable, lasting form in written signs, always ready to be awakened again into incantation.

Hence the fundamental importance of writing, whose reach is as universal as that of the Word itself. If the inward reality of a being is its secret Word, then its outward appearance, its visible features, become writing that conceals a secret, a code. Every being becomes an ideogram. Above all, the human face becomes an ideogram—or sacred inscription—of invisible divine beauty. The Divine Being is the Word immanent in every being. The Hurufi idea of creation, like Ibn 'Arabî's, does not involve some extra-divine existence being added to the being of the divine Creator.

The eternal Word becomes actual by taking on determinate, particular forms: it gives birth to the written letters. These are the twenty-eight letters of the Arabic alphabet (or twenty-nine if lâm-alef is counted), with which the Qur'an is written and which constitute the “Muhammadan Word” (Kalima mohammadiya); or the thirty-two letters of the Persian alphabet, which constitute the “Adamic Word” (Kalima âdamiya).

Letters here play a role analogous to the latent archetypes of beings, their eternally established individual realities (a'yân thâbita) in Ibn 'Arabî's thought. Everything we can imagine or conceive is expressed through the twenty-eight or thirty-two letters, corresponding to as many divine attributes. The sound, the audible Word encoded by the letters and spoken through them, is the divine Essence itself. That Essence is neither substance nor accident; it reveals itself through this sounding incantation. We have here a remarkable first outline of a phenomenology of music.

Hence the extraordinary complexity and precise rules governing the different ways of reading letters: simple numerical calculation, analysis of the letters composing a word, rules of permutation, and so on292. All these techniques are known in Kabbalah, and among the Hurufis they continue the practices of the Ismailis. As Sâ'inoddîn observes, such techniques allow an intuitive apprehension of the very Forms that descended on the prophets from the most holy Heaven, without constructing logical arguments or passing through the philosophers' conceptual dialectic.

Writing is thus as universal a phenomenon as the Word; its visible design fixes the sounding incantation in a lasting, encoded form. If one can hear the secret Word of each being, and hear each being as a Word, one must also be able to decipher its outward appearance as an ideogram—as the code of its own distinctive Word.

Hurufi interpretation, as an ontology in which being is Word, therefore also requires a science of the visible forms of beings, above all the study of the human face. Hurufi authors speak of the human being as a “Qur'an in human form.” As a microcosm, the human being is even the archetype of the holy Book, the “Mother of the Book” (omm al-Kitâb). A human face can be read like a Qur'an; the principles of spiritual interpretation, or ta'wîl, can be applied to it.

The beauty of a perfect human face then reveals the secret of theophany, the manifestation of God. This devotion to human beauty and to the beautiful face, already found in Iranian Sufism before the Hurufis, reaches among them an ecstatic worship of beauty (see above, Book III, on Rûzbehân's Sufism). What the initiate experiences before beauty has nothing to do with a frivolous, possessive, or merely worldly feeling. It belongs to the realm of the sacred and overwhelming. It brings exaltation and despair together, perhaps joy and terror as well. For to reach what beauty reveals, one would have to pass “through the other side of the mirror.”

The correspondences are carried very far, sometimes with a degree of artificiality. What matters is the result in which these mystics delight. The surah that opens the Qur'an, the Fâtiha, has seven verses—seven âyât, a word whose original sense is “signs.” The human face likewise bears seven lines or “seven signs.” Through these correspondences, the features and meaning of its beauty can be related to the meaning of Revelation, allowing the face of a beautiful person to be contemplated as the face of God.

The seven lines are the four lines of the eyelashes, the two lines of the eyebrows, and the line formed by the hair. They are the “maternal lines” (khotût ommîya), or “lines of Eve,” as opposed to the “paternal lines” that appear on a man's face only after puberty, where the beard begins to grow. The feminine lines are therefore the most essential, since they appear in every human being—in women and in men before adulthood. And it was under precisely these features, these feminine lines and seven divine inscriptions, that God showed his face to the Prophet in a vision on which the Sufis have meditated without end293.

For these mystics, the beauty of a face and the rapture it inspires were the highest manifestation of the divine in this world. It was in this sense that they spoke of the “paradise of the face” (jannat-e didâr). A Persian poem by 'Alî al-A'lâ, inspired by something very close to Rûzbehân's vision, goes so far as to ask: “Why, at the sight of beautiful faces, are you struck with bewilderment, intoxication, and madness? If these faces are not themselves the visible form of the divine … why do you let yourself die at the feet of the beauties you adore?”294

Beauty is the secret of God's will to reveal himself: the will that human beings should behold him. And what God reveals—the form through which they can begin to sense him—is human beauty as Forma Dei, the form of God (sûrat al-Haqq). From prophet to prophet, through the 124,000 nabîs spoken of in tradition, down to the ill-fated Fazlollah, the same Form has sought to disclose its mystery to humanity, only to be rejected, reviled, stoned, and crucified. Abraham sought the “signs” of divinity among the stars until he discovered them upon his own face. He read “his own Book”; then he broke every idol and bowed before the absolute Essence. So it was with Moses and with Muhammad295.

In short, there is a “silent Qur'an” (Qorân sâmit) and a “speaking Qur'an” (Qorân nâtiq). The speaking Qur'an is the human face, the Word made manifest. To read the true Qur'an, to decipher its hidden meaning completely, is to understand the essential “seven signs” revealed by the human-and-divine face.

But we must attend to a crucial point: in Shiite gnosis, the “Silent One” is a technical designation for the Imam, complementing the “Enunciator” (Nâtiq, the “Speaking One”), who is the prophet. As a theophany, beauty thus performs a prophetic function. The hidden meaning to which it points, like every spoken Word, is therefore the invisible Imam, in his state of heavenly humanity296.

This brief recollection of the Hurufi system is enough to place their interpretation of the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon among those of the related spiritual schools, and to understand how they turn its meaning inward. For them, too, the verse plainly does not describe an event in the visible heavens studied by astronomy. Its spiritual meaning emerges on two levels at once: the visual and the audible.

Consider first what the Moon symbolizes. Left to itself, it remains dark. The light of the Sun rises within it and gradually brings it to incandescence, until, gazing at itself reflected in itself, it may cry out, “I am the Sun.”

But the darkened Moon also symbolizes the original silence of a written line, an ideogram not yet deciphered. From that silence the Word is uttered, and suddenly its primordial, original meaning “bursts forth.” What bursts forth is the hidden being itself, the meaning of the existence within whose secret the Word had lain submerged—silent, not yet able to “speak itself.” Or again: from the face of beauty that has been misunderstood, profaned, and degraded, the overwhelming meaning of Beauty bursts forth as a divine manifestation. It fascinates and torments us with an unappeased longing: a longing like the expectation of an apotheosis that would lift the veil from the mystery momentarily glimpsed in the fleeting light of a beautiful face.

The Ishrâqiyûn and the Sufis have already helped us understand the “sign of the approaching Hour” in this way: Light breaks through the enclosing darkness, attains its perfect manifestation, and fully realizes its power to reveal. The masters of the science of letters are reflecting upon the same teaching: everything returns to its origin. The Form that makes this return is the primordial heavenly Form that existed before the stain of darkness and its mixture with material bodies. It is the divine Word taking a particular mode in the incantation uttered by each being; it is the perfect Form of the “twenty-nine letters” that descends in its fullness from prophet to prophet until it reaches the “Seal of the Prophets.”

From then on it can be perceived in the written signs of the Book—a code mute and unreadable to the uninitiated and the unawakened. This Book is both the holy volume whose pages bear written signs and the beautiful face marked with those same divine inscriptions. Whenever the meaning of the letters and signs emerges and shines through, the pure, primordial Word resounds. The Book—“your own Book,” as in Abraham's case—becomes, in the fullest sense, the “Speaking One” that reveals the Silent One. This is the signal of resurrection and return, and this is the meaning of the verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split.”

8. The Shiites

However deeply we have now entered the esoteric meaning of this verse, Sâ'inoddîn still reserves for us a final stage: a seventh spiritual group, “those endowed with strength and vision” (Qur'an 38:45). They are the Prophet's closest intimates, the heirs to his perfection. Brief as the indications are, they allow us to place the meaning that crowns all the others, the meaning properly disclosed by Shiite spiritual interpretation.

What is of exceptional interest here is that, for our author, the Shiite reading of the verse gathers together all the esoteric meanings previously examined. Each of them presupposes that reading because it brings their truth to completion.

We must therefore say: philosophy in its true sense, the theosophy of Light in its true sense, Sufism in its true sense—all of these are Shiism. The fundamental Shiite idea is that of theophany (zohûr, mazhar), the manifestation of God in the persons of the holy Imams. The ideas of the Ishrâqiyûn, the Sufis, and the Hurufis are therefore the “approaching Hour” of this central idea.

What these schools share is the thought of God taking human form on the plane of an angelic, more-than-human existence. It runs from Gabriel, the angelic archetype of humanity for the Ishrâqiyûn, to the human form whose ideal beauty reveals the Forma Dei. Throughout, the Shiite idea remains present as an intimation: the Imam, in his perfect heavenly humanity, is the mirror (mazhar), the eternal theophany in which human beings contemplate this divine Form, and to which the prophet's Word refers297.

Here again, the interpretation of the verse presupposes the “perfect Word” of the “Seal of Prophecy” (Kalâm-e kâmil-e khâtam al-nobowwa). This Word is called the “Perfection of the Form” (Kamâl-e sûrat). It conceals and contains the fullness of meaning, all spiritual meanings; within it is implied, brought to the highest perfection, the meaning of everything that was, is, and will be. Certainly, Sâ'inoddîn tells us, many spiritually perfected and realized people (Kâmilân o mohaqqiqân) have set out in the right direction to discover the true meaning of the Return (ma'âd). Many profound meanings have been unveiled to them in keeping with their capacity for mystical perception.

Yet the fullness of meaning, the deepest significance of what is meant by the “Word,” has not become wholly transparent to them298. For the key to spiritual meaning, the power to make meaning burst forth through this “perfect Form”—the divine assumption of form in the archetypal, heavenly humanity of the Imam—in short, the knowledge of ta'wîl in its fullness, must be learned from the “Pillars of the Prophet's Family” (Asâtîn-e Ahl-e Bayt), meaning the line of the Twelve Imams299.

Only then does the Qur'anic verse announcing the splitting of the Moon, and the event it signifies, “show the Way and give the signal, in a manner and in a sense well known to them and their followers. This short treatise cannot say more. Should an eager seeker taste a desire to know more of these mysteries, let him consult the longer treatises.”

9. An Imamology That Dares Not Speak Its Name

We can only regret Sâ'inoddîn's reserve in referring the seeker to other, more complete works.

Yet perhaps, without going beyond what we have tried to establish in this book, we can begin to glimpse what such a seeker might discover. What exactly does Sâ'inoddîn mean when he says that all these spiritual seekers have set out in the right direction, but that the fullness of meaning has nevertheless remained hidden from them? Is this really true of those who recognize in every spiritual seeker the status of nabî, and if so, why? These questions acquire their full force when we consider certain additional pages of Sâ'inoddîn's treatise dealing with the Ishrâqiyûn.

As noted earlier, these are pages apparently lost from Sâ'inoddîn's text in the version preserved by our manuscript. We find them again in the great Persian encyclopedia called Dabestân-e Madhâhib (literally, “The School of Religions”), already mentioned here, which was composed in India in the seventeenth century. One of its chapters begins by simply reproducing the Mi'râj-Nâmeh, a short Persian work attributed to Avicenna, which in any case offers an Avicennian spiritual interpretation of the Prophet's heavenly ascent. After this Avicennian text, the author of the Dabestân has inserted several pages copied literally from the sections of Sâ'inoddîn's treatise dealing with the philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn—the “theosophers of Light”—that we examined above.

Finally, these pages end with a number of remarks absent from our manuscript. Their great importance is that they show how the Ishrâqiyûn explain the transfer of the title “Seal of Prophecy” to all spiritual seekers who attain the state of nabî300. Here we should recall the significance of the proceedings brought against Sohrawardî by the religious scholars of Aleppo (Book II, Chapter I).

What makes the matter especially interesting is that the teaching on prophecy attributed to the Ishrâqiyûn by the author of the Dabestân begins by reproducing a characteristic feature of Ismaili prophetology. In the Ismaili account, prophecy and the prophetic mission begin “in Heaven,” before the visible universe appears, with the Call (da'wat) addressed by the First Intelligence to the entire angelic pleroma301. Here that call passes from one Intelligence to the next, until it reaches the Tenth, which then becomes the “Seal of Prophecy” in the pleroma. This Intelligence is none other than the “Active Intelligence” of Avicennian philosophy, identified by those philosophers with the Holy Spirit.

Avicenna's theory of knowledge is thereby integrated into a philosophy of prophecy. The Active Intelligence illuminating the philosopher is the same Holy Spirit that inspires the prophets; the Angel of Knowledge is identical with the Angel of Revelation. It thus becomes possible to speak of a calling shared by philosopher and prophet, and to account for the continuity of inspiration and the persistence of the prophetic vocation.

We have already observed that identifying the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit is not merely a theoretical construction. It is the intuitive perception of a perfectly real spiritual being, which can only be one and the same. This is in no sense a rationalization of the Holy Spirit. The Active Intelligence corresponds not to our calculating or discursive ratio, but to the Greek Nous, the spiritual intellect. Such rationalization may have occurred elsewhere. Here the movement goes in the opposite direction: the philosophers' calling is understood on the model of the prophets' calling. For in the conviction of Muslim thinkers, philosophers too receive their wisdom from the “Niche of the Lights of Prophecy” (Mishkât al-nobowwat).

The author of the Dabestân accordingly reminds us that these thinkers interpreted the term “Seal of Prophecy” as an allusion to the prophetic soul's union with the Active Intelligence ('Aql fa''âl). For whoever—the Persian says har ke—attains union with this Intelligence, and participates in the state it possesses in the angelic pleroma, thereby becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” Naturally, this cannot be an event taking place in the historical time of the external world (zamân âfâqî): the time in which events happen once and for all, the time in which the Prophet of Islam is said to have been the “Seal of Prophecy.”

At that level the event is irreversible, and no “repetition” is conceivable. When, therefore, the philosophers give the title “Seal of Prophecy” to every spiritual seeker who unites with the Active Intelligence, the event must occur in another kind of time. It must be a time without a closed and irreversible past, a time in which the event remains forever on the point of happening, ever able to take place “now.”

In short, it can only be existential time, the time of the soul (zamân anfosî, as Semnânî will call it), or the “time of the pleroma.” To apply the dates of our calendars and chronological systems to such time would plainly be absurd. We shall see, however, that not all difficulties disappear with this distinction.

Certainly, the foundations of a theory of prophecy must be sought at the level of angelology, as the Ishrâqiyûn described in the Dabestân do. We have just said that, in this respect, they are giving voice to an Ismaili understanding of prophecy. The case is remarkable enough to deserve emphasis, especially since we are not at present able to explain it.

Yet there is a fundamental difference. For the Ismailis, the “history” of prophecy—sacred history, or hierohistory—begins with a “prologue in Heaven”: the Call addressed by the First Intelligence, herald of prophecy, to all the Intelligences proceeding from it and to their respective angelic plenitudes.

But this prologue also includes a “drama in Heaven,” from which our world and the mystery of the earthly Adam originate. That drama does not appear in the doctrine of prophecy attributed to the Ishrâqiyûn in the Dabestân.

A few details will give substance to this outline. According to the Ishrâqiyûn as presented in the Dabestân, the first of the prophets, or nabîs, is the First Intelligence of the pleroma, the first of the Cherubim, also called the first spiritual Adam (Adam ma'nawî)302. This is the Intelligence Sohrawardî (see Book II above) names the “Nearest Light” (Nûr aqrab) to the Light of Lights. He identifies it with Bahman (Vohu-Manah), the first of the Zoroastrian Amahraspands, or Archangels, after Ohrmazd.

The “Seal of Prophecy” at the level of the pleroma is the Intelligence that marks its completion and fullness: the Tenth. The philosophers call it the Active Intelligence and identify it with Gabriel, the Holy Spirit. In Sohrawardî's terminology, it is the “Angel of the human race.” The prophetic cycle, the succession of prophets on the level of the pleroma, remains in an eternal present, like an annunciation passing from Angel to Angel. One may compare the heavenly existence of the True Prophet in Jewish-Christian prophetology: Christus aeternus, the eternal Christ, manifested at Jesus' baptism.

Thus prophecy has its original place, its source and true meaning, in the angelic pleroma. The recurring inspiration and prophetic gift “within souls” depend in no way upon the historical causality of the sublunar world. The event does not enter the sequence of material, visible, irreversible facts.

It occurs in a “heavenly place,” the pleroma, whose eternal coming-to-be is a prophetic annunciation from Angel to Angel. The Angel who is its perfect fruit, its Seal, may bear several names—the Active Intelligence, the Holy Spirit, Gabriel, the Angel of humanity, the spiritual Adam—but the figure is one and the same. Whether we speak of the prophetic soul's union with the Active Intelligence or of the descent of the “Supreme Nâmûs,” the Angel Gabriel, upon the prophets, we are speaking of one event. To unite with the luminous Aeon who is the “Seal of Prophecy” is to share that very title, because he invests everyone united with him with his own status. In the esoteric sense, he remains the true Seal of Prophecy.

But the possibility of union with him has no limit. The prophetic vocation will therefore never close; and the philosophy that explains this vocation, keeps its possibility open, and gives direct expression to it is raised, by that very fact, to the status of a “prophetic philosophy.” But is this “prophetic philosophy,” as it stands, complete? Does it contain everything essential? That is the question we shall ask alongside Sâ'inoddîn.

The Dabestân, at any rate, justifies raising philosophy to this status by showing how this theosophy can account for the many people called to the state of nabî and the title of Seal of Prophecy. The Active Intelligence—the Holy Spirit, the Angel of Knowledge—is the educator of the human race. When a human being becomes its willing pupil (parwarda), allowing it to teach and spiritually nourish him, his original human condition is gradually overcome. He takes on the mode of existence of this angelic Intelligence, its “heavenly humanity.” To unite with it is to make one's own Return, one's own resurrection, to the angelic archetype of humanity, the Holy Spirit.

Whoever (hâr ke!) accomplishes this Return becomes one of those nearest to it (moqarrab), its deputy or representative (qâ'im maqâm). For the Angel who is the “Seal of the Prophets” in the pleroma invests that person with his own mode of being, giving him his own name and title. That person in turn is the “Seal of the Prophets.” Even if a hundred thousand prophets were to assume this “identity” with the Active Intelligence, it would be true to say of every one of them that he is the “Seal of Prophecy”303. This does not mean that prophetic inspiration passes “into the past” after them.

The title names the status that each receives in the pleroma. This resurrection, this enthronement within the pleroma, is the complete esoteric meaning of the verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split.” And when all this has been said, the verse remains the only way to suggest an event so extraordinary and invisible. That is why it is a symbol, not an allegory.

It would be hard to push back the boundary any further or keep the door of prophetic inspiration open more boldly.

Yet this is possible because the investiture that makes each nabî a “Seal of Prophecy” is not an event whose occurrence can be recorded in a chronicle of external, “objective” facts. In terms of such external history, calling this nabî a “Seal of Prophecy” makes no sense. The title has meaning only in relation to another time: the time of the Malakût, the world of the Soul. In this earthly world, these nabîs are never “of their time,” because each is his own time. Their investiture is the fullness, the Seal, of their own time—that is, the Seal of their very being. It is the fullness that makes each an Aiôn, what the Latin Avicennians called a saeculum intelligibile, an intelligible age or eternity.

But literalists, by definition, can conceive of no time or history other than that of the visible events of the world below the Moon. To them, this multiplication of the “Seal” can only seem blasphemous or absurd.

Unfortunately, the literalists are not the only ones to find difficulties in the “prophetic philosophy” of the Ishrâqiyûn, at least as interpreted by the author of the Dabestân. Everything happens as though we really do have a prophetic philosophy here, but one deprived of an essential part. The result is something like an imamology that does not dare—or does not wish—to speak its own name. Sâ'inoddîn's reservation is therefore easy to understand: “They sensed what was at stake, but they failed to learn from the Pillars of the Prophet's House (Asâtîn al-Bayt).”

For among the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân, the idea that a prophetic spiritual gift continues after the “Seal of Prophecy” is nothing other than an application of the fundamental Shiite idea of walâyat. They sought the inward, hidden meaning (bâtin) of prophecy (nobowwat) and its message. But they overlooked the fact that this inward meaning of prophecy is precisely walâyat. Without the imamate of the Twelve Imams, which exists for the sake of this inward meaning, walâyat would be left hanging in the void.

Yet these thinkers do not even pronounce the word walâyat, although the esoteric dimension to which they appeal presupposes that the cycle of walâyat has succeeded the cycle of prophecy.

At the risk of repeating ourselves (see Book I, Chapter VI)—for these matters are rarely explained—let us summarize the situation.

First, by directing every spiritual seeker's vocation toward the state of nabî, the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân seem indeed to disregard the explicit words of the Prophet of Islam, the Seal of Prophecy: “There will be no nabî after me.” Throughout the period after Muhammad, therefore, the use of the word nabî is strictly excluded. The word employed is walî, plural awliyâ: the Friends of God, those close to him.

Of course, it is perfectly understood that, in terms of spiritual gifts—the divine graces actually experienced—the condition of one characterized by walâyat corresponds to that of the person called simply a nabî in the periods of the prophetic cycle before Muhammad. This simple nabî was neither a prophet sent to others (nabî morsal), still less a messenger (rasûl) commissioned to reveal a religious law (sharî'at). For this reason, post-Muhammadan walâyat is also called nobowwat bâtina: secret, inward, mystical, esoteric prophecy. Mollâ Sadrâ devoted several very substantial pages to this question in his commentary on Kolaynî's Kâfî.

We can therefore observe, with Sâ'inoddîn, that because they had failed to learn “from the Pillars of the Prophet's House”—in other words, because they had not embraced Shiism openly—the Ishrâqiyûn he describes, and those discussed later in the Dabestân, lacked a doctrine of prophecy capable of securing the foundations of their theory of knowledge. It is the task of such a doctrine to distinguish the various categories of prophets: the simple nabîs, contemplatives in a sense, and the prophets sent on missions, who themselves fall into several categories. These distinctions depend on the different modes of revelation and inspiration received. It is precisely the theory of inspiration (ilhâm) that allows us to recognize the equivalence between the nabî before Muhammad and the walî after Muhammad. Apparently unable to preserve the relations among walâyat, nobowwat (prophecy), and risâlat (the mission of a messenger), these thinkers have made every spiritual seeker a nabî, without qualification.

But they should have known that in every nabî, whether a simple nabî or a nabî morsal, the source of the prophetic gift was what is now called walâyat. This is precisely why walâyat is eternal, while the prophetic vocation and mission are temporary and passing. In every prophet, walâyat is his “face turned toward God,” while his prophetic work is his “face turned toward humanity,” his outward mission (ad extra). For him, walâyat remains both the point of departure and the point of return.

At exceptional moments, the Prophet of Islam himself experienced this return to walâyat, withdrawing, as it were, from his mission as Messenger. These are the moments evoked in a famous hadîth: “There are moments when I am in God's company and neither an angel of the highest rank nor a prophet sent on a mission could contain what I experience.” At such moments, his own walâyat became manifest to him.

Yet his mission as a prophet sent to others was not to reveal walâyat: it was to remain hidden within him. His mission concerned tanzîl, the “descent” of Revelation, and the sharî'at, the religious law. It did not concern ta'wîl, the return to hidden spiritual truth (haqîqat). That return is the manifestation of walâyat, and it takes place originally in the persons of the Twelve Imams, who together are one and the same Light.

Just as walâyat is the “sun” of the prophetic mission (nobowwat) in the person of the Prophet, so the Imams' walâyat, their spiritual gift as those near to God, is solar in relation to the “lunar” walâyat of their followers, their Shiites304. Here, too, we move toward the esoteric meaning of the splitting of the Moon. The Imam is thus the keystone of walâyat and of its entire cycle.

Without the Imam's walâyat, it would be impossible to speak of anything like an inward, “esoteric” prophecy after the Prophet, since such prophecy is simply another name for walâyat.

Hence the decisive importance of the question of the “Seal of walâyat,” which, as we have seen, Haydar Âmolî treated so masterfully. The First Imam is the “Seal of universal walâyat”: the walâyat of all the nabîs, with each of whom, until Muhammad, he had been sent secretly and invisibly. The Twelfth Imam, now in concealment, is the “Seal of Muhammadan walâyat.” For this reason it is said that the “Friends of God” belonging to the cycle of walâyat stand in relation to the Twelfth Imam, the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat, as the earlier nabîs stood in relation to the “Seal of Prophecy.”

With these points briefly recalled, we return to our two questions. What did Sâ'inoddîn mean when he said that the spiritual seekers—the Sufis and Ishrâqiyûn—had found the right direction, yet had not attained the full esoteric meaning of the splitting of the Moon? And, as we have also asked, is the prophetic philosophy of the Ishrâqiyûn described in the Dabestân truly complete? The foundations of the Shiite philosophy of prophecy, which we have just recalled, give us the elements of an answer.

By directing every spiritual seeker toward the state of nabî, achieved when the seeker unites with the Active Intelligence or Holy Spirit, the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân confront us with a dilemma. Either they know, in agreement with Shiite thinkers, that the walî of the post-Muhammadan period corresponds to the simple nabî of the earlier periods of the prophetic cycle. In that case, by retaining the term nabî while leaving the idea of walâyat unspoken, even though it is presupposed, they seem to offer a deliberately altered imamology, one that cannot or will not speak its own name.

Or they have failed, “because they did not learn from the Pillars of the Prophet's House,” to recognize that in every nabî, the state and gift of prophecy derive from walâyat. The word may not have been used during the pre-Muhammadan periods of prophecy, but the reality it names certainly existed. We recalled a few lines ago the hadîth according to which the Imam was sent secretly and invisibly with each nabî, whereas with Muhammad he was sent openly.

But after the “Seal of the Prophets,” how can one speak of the continuation of the prophetic vocation without giving that continuation its true name, walâyat, and explaining it through walâyat? To discuss either pre-Muhammadan nobowwat or a post-Muhammadan nobowwat without reference to walâyat and all that it means and implies is, in the end, to mutilate the philosophy of prophecy.

Since nobowwat concerns the outward dimension of revelation, while walâyat concerns its inward dimension, it is impossible to direct nobowwat toward the inward without referring to walâyat, which is precisely “the esoteric dimension of prophecy.” The Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn have indeed developed a philosophy of prophecy by identifying the Angel of Knowledge with the Angel of Revelation and by interpreting the callings of the philosopher and the prophet as two forms of a common vocation.

But by remaining silent about walâyat, they leave unanswered the question whether the Angel of ta'wîl, the Angel of spiritual interpretation, is the same as the Angel of Revelation. The full unveiling of esoteric meaning—symbolized by the splitting of the Moon—can in fact occur only through the intervention of the Imam. It is the Imam, through his solar walâyat, who reveals the hidden meaning to the initiate and makes it burst forth, just as the Angel reveals the outward message to the nabî. An angelology of knowledge must be brought to completion in an imamology of knowledge.

We find this imamology of knowledge clearly indicated in Haydar Âmolî, for example where it is linked to a transcendent teaching on Adam. It draws upon hadîths and upon statements made in certain sermons, in which the Imam declares, “I am the primordial Adam” (Adam al-awwal). This primordial or metaphysical Adam (Adam al-haqîqî), the “manifestation of the Merciful One,” in whose image the earthly Adam was created, is none other than the First Intelligence, the first Archangel of the cherubic pleroma. He is the archetype of the Book (omm al-Kitâb), the “speaking Qur'an,” the “supreme Word,” the “father of Lights” (abû'l-Anwâr).

All these names designate the Imam in his existence within the angelic pleroma, and in the rank that makes his Light the source of esoteric interpretation305. Gabriel, the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation, is the organ—the “tongue”—of this primordial Adam, the first Angel of the pleroma.

But the revealed utterance becomes nothing more than the silent Book unless the Imam in turn speaks its ta'wîl, its primordial hidden meanings. These brief indications already show how the imamology of knowledge completes the angelology of knowledge taught by our philosophers. They explain why Sâ'inoddîn could say that the philosophers had chosen the right direction, yet had not reached complete spiritual knowledge. The Hour is still approaching; it has not yet dawned. For the Hour is the Imam.

We can therefore begin to appreciate the importance of the fact that several Shiite thinkers identified the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John.

Such are the reflections prompted by Sâ'inoddîn's densely argued treatise. We do not believe we exaggerate its importance either for understanding Iranian Avicennism or for understanding imamism—and, consequently, for understanding the relation between the two. This also reminds us how different Avicennism's fate was in the East, specifically in Iran, from its fate in the West. Avicennism has remained an essential part of Iran's spiritual history, and its tradition has survived there into our own day.

At the same time, many thinkers absorbed Sohrawardî's work so thoroughly that we may speak, in their case, of an ishrâqî Avicennism shaped by Sohrawardî's philosophy of illumination. Sâ'inoddîn's treatise has drawn our attention to a shared theory of knowledge found in Avicennism, in Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy,” and in an entire branch of Sufism. From this understanding of knowledge comes the idea that prophet, philosopher, and mystic share a common calling.

At the heart of this prophetic philosophy we discover an imamology that does not recognize itself—or does not dare to speak its own name—but which is nevertheless presupposed as soon as one accepts that the prophetic spiritual gift continues and that it is directed toward the hidden dimension of revelation. For this orientation presupposes imamology: walâyat is, by its very nature, the esoteric dimension of prophecy.

We can thus conceive of Avicennian-Sohrawardian prophetic philosophy as being directed toward its completion in the prophetic philosophy of Shiism.

Since the Safavid Renaissance, a number of Iranian Shiite thinkers have written extensive commentaries on Avicenna's Shifâ, commentaries so substantial and original that they amount to independent works. Among them are that of Sayyed Ahmad 'Alawî, Mîr Dâmâd's student and son-in-law, and that of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. Mollâ Sadrâ also produced an equally personal commentary on Sohrawardî's Book of Oriental Theosophy. When imamology dares to speak its name, it appears in the great works characteristic of Shiite thought, those of Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, and others.

Yet when philosophers and theosophers openly acknowledge it, imamology provokes the hostility of those Shiites whose blindness Haydar Âmolî denounced with such force and insight. It was their hostility that compelled Mollâ Sadrâ to seek refuge far from Isfahan for several years (see below, Book V, Chapter II). These are the people who, forgetting Shiism's original spiritual calling and neglecting even the hadîths of their own Imams, shut themselves within a new literalism and seek to ban philosophy and spiritual knowledge (hikmat and 'irfân). That a Haydar Âmolî, and Shiite philosophers devoted to the Imams, should have had to confront such outward-looking literalists is one of the painful aspects of what we previously examined as Shiism's “spiritual struggle” (Book I, Chapter III).

Nevertheless, through philosophers such as Mîr Dâmâd and Mollâ Sadrâ, and through their students and successors down to our time, Avicennism enjoyed a remarkable flowering in Shiite Iran, sharply contrasting with its failure in the medieval Latin West. To analyze the reasons would make a fascinating and as yet unwritten chapter in comparative philosophy306. We have just seen the connection between Avicennian and ishrâqî theories of knowledge and the philosophy of prophecy—which means, in Sâ'inoddîn's language, imamology, “when the approaching Hour has finally dawned.” Seen from this perspective, Mollâ Sadrâ's monumental body of work contains a trilogy that is both a testimony and a symbol: his three major commentaries on Avicenna's Shifâ, Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy,” and Kolaynî's Kâfî, the great collection of Shiite hadîths. These three commentaries mark, as it were, the great streams from which Shiite thought draws nourishment.

In the medieval Latin West, Avicennism failed. Its theory of knowledge rested upon angelology, and that angelology provoked alarm. Was it all too clearly perceived that, by grounding the philosopher's prophetic calling, this teaching invested the individual philosopher with an independence and authority difficult to reconcile with the Church's teaching authority? Avicenna's theory of knowledge was criticized as though it undermined the very basis of divine prerogatives, because it made the human act of knowing depend upon illumination from an Angel—the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation.

By contrast, if Avicennism, whether in its original or its ishrâqî form, flourished in Iran, it was precisely because it led toward a philosophy of prophecy, in which the Angel is the intermediary through whom divine revelation reaches the prophets.

It has long been recognized that Islamic prophetology reproduces an essential feature of early Jewish-Christian teaching about prophecy, in which Christology was the completion of prophetology: the idea of the Verus Propheta, the True Prophet, “hastening from prophet to prophet until he reaches his place of rest.” The success of Avicennism in Shiite Iran and its failure in the medieval Latin West thus each acquire the value of a Sign—a Sign by which to measure the distance between an early, eschatological Christology, called by historians of theology the Christology of Christos Angelos, Christ as Angel, and the historical Christology that ultimately prevailed in the definitions of the Church councils.

When we say that imamology plays a role in Shiite theology analogous to the role Christology plays in Christian theology, the analogy holds only if we have in mind a Christology earlier than the one eventually adopted as official dogma. Avicennian or Avicennian-Sohrawardian theories of knowledge readily lent themselves to the formulation of a prophetic philosophy and to the idea of theophany (zohûr, tajallî), the divine manifestation that governs all imamology and Imam-centered spirituality. To precisely that extent, they could not serve a philosophy or theology of the Incarnation (tajassod) compatible with official dogma.

For theophany takes place “between Heaven and Earth,” in the Malakût, the imaginal world. It is transfiguration: it lifts beings out of time's becoming and frees them from the chain of historical causation. A perfect illustration is found in the “hadîth of the White Cloud,” masterfully interpreted by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî (see below, Book V, Chapter III). The Incarnation as understood by official dogma, on the other hand, brings God down into flesh and makes him “enter history.” Eventually some will conclude that God has died there, because everything that falls—or is made to fall—into historical time already carries death within itself.

The Prophet of Islam could say, “There will be no prophet after me.” But the cycle of walâyat remains open. The Hour is still approaching: this is the meaning of Shiism. Theophany is eschatological; it is the irruption of another world into this one. By comparison, we may say that earliest Christianity was itself essentially eschatological, before yielding to the “temptation of history” and becoming historical, indeed a historical power. That is why “God is dead.”

But with him every idea of the approaching Hour has also died. By contrast, the Twelfth Imam has not “entered history,” and yet he is already here, invisibly present within it. This is the meaning of the ghaybat, the Great Occultation. That is why Shiism remains eschatological: for each believer, in the believer's relationship with the Imam, the Hour is always near. Sâ'inoddîn has shown us that this is what ultimately gives the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon its esoteric meaning.

Yet our civilization has long known only the Moon's outward reality: the visible celestial body observed through our telescopes. The astronaut who in our own time became the first to set foot on its surface spoke words already becoming historic: “One small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.” Need we say that, for all the heroism of this “giant leap,” humanity has not advanced toward the Malakût by so much as a “small step”?

Of course, the destinies of humanity's religious and philosophical life are not decided in a single generation. Across several centuries, Avicennism may be taken as a symbol of the different destinies chosen by East and West.

But how can we speak of that distinction today? The East has become “Westernized.” The word “Orient” retains its spiritual meaning only if we understand it as the Ishrâqiyûn of Iran—the “Platonists of Persia”—have understood it since Sohrawardî. This is why there may still be much to learn by comparing the fate of Avicennism in Iran with its fate in the West. It was therefore necessary to dwell on Sâ'inoddîn Torkeh Ispahânî's treatise. Its final chapter suggests that everything changes when “the Hour is approaching,” when imamology dares to speak its name. The drama of Iranian spirituality then appears to us in a light consistent with the understanding of Haydar Âmolî, who summed it up in several striking pages of one of his major works307.

We shall encounter another aspect of this same situation when we turn to the work of one of the greatest masters of Iranian Sufism, 'Alâoddawleh Semnânî, who lived barely a century before Sâ'inoddîn. Here too we find a highly original application of the hadîth proclaiming that the Qur'an has seven levels of hidden meaning.

But unlike the anonymous Iranian author discussed earlier (Chapter II), Semnânî's genius for interpretation relates these mystical meanings not to the spiritual groups whose forms of consciousness they represent, but to the seven organs or centers in the subtle physiology of the individual's “subtle body.”

We shall see what amounts to a prophetic typology of these centers or organs take shape. The Ishrâqiyûn mentioned in the Dabestân grounded the common identity of the mystical philosopher's and the prophet's vocation in a theory of prophecy whose decisive event occurs in the pleroma. Its Seal is the last Angel of the pleroma, the Angel who is, for humanity, both the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation.

Here, by contrast, we shall be seeking to glimpse the identity of the latîfa jabrâ'eliya: the subtle organ named Gabriel, the “angel Gabriel of your being,” which becomes fully actual in each mystic on reaching the “Muhammad of his being.” In Semnânî's extraordinarily powerful work, Iranian Sufism pursues the effort to turn the meaning of Qur'anic Revelation inward, down to its deepest esoteric level, with the aim of a radical realization of the individual person.

This process therefore brings the whole teaching about prophecy within the individual: the state of nabî, the prophetic vocation, and the missions of successive prophets are all related to the organs or centers of the subtle body. We may thus say that the essential purpose and goal of spiritual interpretation is the inward meaning of prophecy, the bâtin al-nobowwat.

Yet, as the entire theosophical tradition of Shiism reminds us from its beginnings, this inward meaning of prophecy is the Imam's walâyat. Semnânî's allusions to it, however, will be discreet. Must we once again speak, in his case, of “an imamology that dares not speak its name”? In Iran, Semnânî is most often regarded as having been a Shiite, although some qualifications are necessary. What remains is that attaining the “seven prophets of your being,” as the inward meaning of prophecy, ought to mean attaining the “Imam of your being.” Perhaps the latîfa jabrâ'eliya already intimates this secret.

PreviousII. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'anNextIV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)

Chapter IV The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)

1. Semnani's Commentary on the Qur'an

The teaching that connects the seven inner meanings of the Qur'an with a mystical understanding of the human being, organized around seven subtle organs or centers (latîfa), appears to have been the personal achievement, early in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE), of a man of extraordinary importance in the history of Iranian Sufism: 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (659–736 AH/1261–1336 CE).

We have already encountered his name and thought (Book I, Chapter IV, §5) in discussing his account of different kinds of time and temporality, according to the levels of spiritual interpretation. He drew an admirable distinction between inner time—the soul's lived, existential time (zamân anfosî)—and the time of things, the objective time measured by chronology (zamân âfâqî).

His life, too, is of exceptional interest, even among the remarkable and original figures of Sufism. Born into a noble family in Semnan, a town some two hundred kilometers east of present-day Tehran, he entered the service of Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Iran, as a court page at fifteen. At twenty-four, while encamped with Arghun's army outside Qazvin, he underwent a sudden and decisive spiritual crisis—much as Haydar Amoli would—which stripped him of all interest in worldly affairs. He asked to be released from service.

Eventually, in Baghdad, he found the spiritual guide and master he had been seeking. He then returned to Semnan and founded an important Sufi khânaqâh, or lodge, whose memory remains alive in Iran today. His dargâh, or mausoleum, survived until quite recently, a few kilometers outside Semnan on the road from Tehran. Fragile, like so many buildings of the Mongol period, it collapsed some fifteen years ago.

Semnani's writings contain enough personal references to make up a Diarium spirituale, a spiritual diary: accounts of his inner trials, of his own experiences and those of his disciples. Several belong to what we would now call “extrasensory perceptions.” They are all the more valuable psychologically because the world of Iranian Sufism is still so little known to us.

Semnani wrote a considerable number of works. Only a few are accessible to us today, in relatively rare manuscripts; quite possibly many others survive unnoticed in private collections. For our purposes, one work stands out above all the rest: his commentary on the Qur'an, in which he develops a remarkably personal method of interpretation. It is usually called a tafsîr, a Qur'anic commentary, but ta'wîl would be the more accurate term. From beginning to end, it concerns itself strictly and exclusively with the inner, hidden meanings of the Qur'anic verses. It is an exemplary monument of spiritual interpretation.

Unfortunately, after a prologue summarizing the author's doctrine and an interpretation of the opening sura, the Fâtiha, the commentary proper begins only with the Sura of Sinai (Sura 52). The reason is that this tafsîr—or rather this ta'wîl—was intended to continue the unfinished commentary of one of Semnani's distinguished predecessors in the same Sufi path (tarîqat), Najm al-Din Daya Razi (d. 654 AH/1256 CE)308. Semnani belonged to the spiritual lineage of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 618 AH/1221 CE), the eminent shaykh of Khwarazm in Central Asia, celebrated for leading the resistance against the Mongols.

Kubra gave twelfth-century Sufism a direction markedly different from that taken by the devout ascetics of Mesopotamia during Islam's early centuries309. It would not be surprising if other religious influences, surviving or lying dormant in Central Asia, had also shaped Sufism there. It was in that same twelfth century, as we have seen, that Suhrawardi undertook to restore the philosophical and spiritual wisdom of ancient Iran. His teaching required anyone seeking the mystical path to acquire a solid philosophical education first: for although philosophical experience must bear fruit in mystical experience, mystical experience without that preparation risks going astray.

Under influences such as those of Najm al-Din Kubra and Suhrawardi, Sufism would rise to the level of what, in the West, we call speculative mysticism, as in the school of Meister Eckhart. Its encounter with the mystical theosophy of Ibn 'Arabi (d. 1240) would come naturally, since his teaching brought back toward Iran, from the far western reaches of Islam, an esoteric wisdom that had originally come to him from the East.

We can make out the broad outlines and structure of this coming together, but we remain far from understanding its details.

In any event, Semnani's Tafsîr is a work of exceptional importance among mystical writings inspired by reflection on the Qur'an. It carries the inward reading of scripture to what seems the furthest conceivable point.

Semnani himself understood how immense his commentary would have had to be if he had been able to treat the entire Qur'an in the same way: uncovering, step by step, its seven inner levels of meaning, not as an abstract exercise but by relating each level to the kind and degree of spiritual experience it indicates, and to the subtle organ that serves as its center and “place.” This may be a unique undertaking. It is a major witness for the comparative study of ta'wîl—spiritual interpretation across traditions—which we have long hoped to see developed, and which must take account of comparable works in Islam, Christianity, and Jewish mysticism310.

2. The Seven Prophets of Your Being

The prologue to Semnani's commentary tells us about his method of spiritual interpretation311.

But it is so brief and allusive that its statements become intelligible only when we turn to more explicit passages in his other works. From the opening lines, what strikes us is his insistence on terminology. So conscious is he of opening a new path that he urges his reader to master its technical language; otherwise, the reader will soon lose the way.

Semnani himself feels bound to offer at least a short explanation, knowing that without one his commentary might become unintelligible after his death. Here the terminology also governs the entire perspective of interpretation. Semnani's sevenfold reading of the Qur'an seeks to guide us through something like a world of seven dimensions. Its guiding law is the law of correspondences, the symbolism that connects different worlds. Outer events correspond to events within the soul—that is the governing principle of spiritual interpretation itself.

And the events spoken of in the divine teachings of the Book correspond to the seven organs, the seven subtle centers or regions, of mystical human nature (latâ'if insâniya). Since there are seven of these “subtle organs,” a prophet corresponds to each. In other words, every organ of the subtle human constitution embodies, within the human microcosm, the image and role of a particular prophet. Each is also marked by a colored light that the mystic can see in contemplation, and must learn to observe, for the light reveals the mystic's own spiritual condition.
