The first of these organs is called the subtle bodily organ, the subtle region of the bodily “mold” (latîfa qâlabîya; qâlab literally means “mold”). The human physical body, already regarded as the quintessence of Creation, is the product of a cosmic alchemy. This alchemy carries on its work as it descends through the successive planes of the universes, producing a kind of fermentation (takhmîr) that culminates in a human organism: a harmonious, well-proportioned distillation of all the influences of those worlds. This organism is the jism maj'ûl, the body “constituted” at our birth into the earthly world, a perishable mold formed by a mingling of influences from the celestial Spheres, the planets, and the Elements.

But the subtle organ called latîfa qâlabîya is described as arising from influences emanating from the Sphere of Spheres and the World Soul—that is, from the Korsî and the Throne ('Arsh)—without passing through the Spheres, planets, or Elements. It is therefore not the jism maj'ûl.

Indeed, it is an organ that can take shape only after the physical organism has been fully formed. This latîfa qâlabîya, the subtle bodily organ, has the form of the body but exists in a subtle state. It is, in a sense, the embryo or “mold” of a new body: the subtle body that is “acquired” (moktasab). That is why mystical anthropology calls it the “Adam of your being” (Adam wojûdî-ka).

The second organ or subtle center belongs to the soul (latîfa nafsîya). Here “soul” does not mean what may also be called Rûh (Spirit), the seat of spiritual activity in general. It means the soul in its particular role of giving life to a body: the anima sensitiva, vitalis, the vital and sensitive soul, where organic and vital functions take place.

For that reason it is also, within us, the “place” of unruly desires and destructive passions. For the seeker it is the very “place of trial” (dâr al-ibtilâ'), where, like Noah confronting his people, a human being confronts the contradictions of embodied, passionate existence. The subtle organ centered there is therefore the “Noah of your being” (Nûh wojûdî-ka).

The third subtle organ is that of the heart (latîfa qalbîya). Within it the embryo of a mystical offspring takes shape, like a pearl within its shell. This pearl, this offspring, is none other than the subtle organ that will become the True Self, the real person (latîfa anâ'îya), which we shall meet below as the “Muhammad of your being.” The reference to spiritual offspring—to the higher Self as a child conceived within the mystic's heart—immediately explains why the subtle center of the heart, destined to give birth to that child, is called the “Abraham of your being” (Ibrâhîm wojûdî-ka).

The fourth subtle organ (latîfa sirrîya) belongs to the center technically called the sirr: the “secret,” the innermost depth or higher consciousness, the threshold of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness. This is the place and organ of intimate conversation, secret communion, or confidential prayer (monâjât). It is the “Moses of your being” (Mûsâ wojûdî-ka).

The fifth subtle organ (latîfa rûhîya) belongs to the spirit (Rûh, pneûma). Because of the nobility of its rank, it is entrusted with divine vice-regency (khalîfa), the task of representing the divine. It is the “David of your being” (Dâwûd wojûdî-ka)312.

The sixth subtle organ (latîfa khafîya) belongs to the center technically called the “hidden mystery,” the innermost secret (al-khafî). Through this organ one receives the aid of the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods); within the hierarchy of spiritual states, it marks entry into the state of Nabî, or prophet. This is the “Jesus of your being” ('Isâ wojûdî-ka)313. It announces the Name to all the other subtle centers and to the “people” of their faculties, for it is their leader. The Name it announces is the prophetic figure of the seventh subtle organ, the seal of your being. Similarly, according to the Qur'an (61:6), Jesus, the next-to-last prophet of our Cycle, announced the final Prophet: the coming of the Paraclete314.

Finally, the seventh subtle organ (latîfa haqqîya) belongs to the divine center of your being, the eternal seal of your person. It is the “Muhammad of your being” (Mohammad wojûdî-ka). This divine subtle center conceals the “rare Muhammadan pearl”: the subtle organ that is the True Self (latîfa anâ'îya), whose embryo began forming in the subtle center of the heart, the “Abraham of your being,” as we saw above. Here is our first example of Semnani's remarkable way of making scriptural meaning an inward reality.

The point of departure is supplied by Qur'anic verses describing Muhammad's relationship to Abraham: “He follows the religion of Abraham as a pure believer (hanîf)” (4:124). “Those closest to Abraham are those who follow his faith; such is the Prophet, and such are those who believe, and God is the Friend of those who believe” (3:61). One may meditate on these verses as referring to persons who appeared “on the horizons” (fî'l-âfâq), that is, in the world's historical time.

But to meditate on them as signs (âyât) taking place “within the soul” is to experience and verify something else: the true Self coming to birth in the divine center of your being is the spiritual child of your “heart.” In other words, the “Muhammad of your being” is the spiritual offspring of the “Abraham of your being.”

Thus, within the person as microcosm, one realizes the truth of the claim that Muhammad's religion has its origin in Abraham's religion. For “Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian; he was a pure believer (hanîf), a moslim” (3:60). That is to say, the “Abraham of your being” is led through the subtle centers of higher consciousness and the hidden mystery—the Moses and Jesus of your being—avoiding the errors that threaten their people, meaning the faculties of each center, until he reaches the center that embodies his spiritual offspring: your true Self.

This is how every teaching and event of the Qur'an must be meditated upon, brought inward, and given its ta'wîl: its “return,” its exegesis, its turning from the “world of horizons” to the “world of the soul.” Every word addressed to one of the seven prophets, every word spoken by them, every event in which they act, must be understood as taking place within the “subtle centers” that each prophet embodies. This prophetic pattern of the centers or organs of the subtle human constitution opens up extraordinary possibilities for inward realization.

Semnani writes: “Whenever you hear in the Book the words addressed to Adam, hear them through the corresponding organ of your subtle body (latîfa qâlabîya) ... Meditate on what it symbolizes, and be certain that the inner meaning of the discourse concerns you, as a discourse about the world of the soul, just as its outer meaning concerns Adam in the world of horizons ... Only then will you be able to apply the teaching of the divine Word to yourself, and gather it like a branch still laden with flowers.”

“Whenever you hear or meditate on the verses concerning Noah, hear them through the subtle organ of your vital soul (latîfa nafsîya), so that you, too, will not be overwhelmed by the waters of the flood or held captive in the double hell of lust and violence315, and so that the people of your faculties will not be swallowed up in the depths of illusory desires. Whenever you hear the verses revealed about Abraham, hear them through the subtle organ of your heart (latîfa qalbîya).

“Attend to the words addressed to you by the divine Friend; take care not to become absorbed in anything else, so that, leading you from signs perceived by the senses to signs grasped by the understanding, he may become your only Guide as well. Whenever you hear the words addressed to Moses during his ‘secret conversations’ (monâjât), or anything concerning Moses' spiritual states, receive them through the subtle organ of your higher consciousness (latîfa sirrîya), the Moses of your being.

“Take care to fulfill what those words implicitly require, lest the Samaritan lead the people of your faculties astray with the golden calf of unruly passions316. And whenever you meditate on the verses that name David, on the divine visitations flowing from the Attribute of Love, perceive all of this through the subtle organ of your Spirit (latîfa rûhîya), the David of your being. He was taught the art of making coats of mail, which signify the gentle inspirations of love beneath the rigid appearance of servitude317.

“Then the people of your faculties will be protected from the sword of lies, the lance of conjecture, and the arrow of doubt; and you will make your body act through the action of the Spirit that uses it.”

“Whenever you meditate on what concerns the spiritual states of Jesus, hear it through the subtle organ of your ‘hidden mystery’ (latîfa khafîya), that is, through the Jesus of your being.” What we must understand here is profoundly serious. In a Qur'anic question addressed to Jesus, Semnani finds, at the level of the subtle organ embodied by Jesus, the reason why certain mystics in Islam and Christians in general have fallen into an illusion springing from the same source.

“Was it you,” Jesus is asked, “who ever said to the people: Take me and my mother as two gods apart from God?—By Your glory, no! [Jesus answers.] How could I say something unworthy of me?” (5:116). Neither Jesus son of Mary nor the “Jesus of your being,” then, is responsible for the failing of his people—a failing that Semnani understands with extraordinary insight, and for which he proposes an equally extraordinary spiritual remedy.

A study remains to be written of this criticism of Christianity as it appeared to one of Sufism's most profound masters. Needless to say, it differs entirely from the polemics of official apologists and scholars concerned only with outward doctrine. Its tone is impassioned, in keeping with the spiritual stakes as Semnani sees them. To understand it, we must turn to his commentary on Sura 112, one of the final suras of the Qur'an.

There he senses a striking connection between the temptation to which, in his view, Christian dogma succumbed when it proclaimed Christ, son of Mary, to be God, and the mystical intoxication in which Hallaj cried “I am God,” while Bastami declared “Glory be to me! How exalted is my state!” When the mystic emerges from this intoxication, horrified by a boldness for which the overwhelming experience of the divine affords some excuse, he seeks refuge in the desire to annihilate himself and thereby atone for the blasphemy: “Kill me, my companions!

“For to live is death to me, and to die is life”318. The mystic then faces an acutely dangerous situation. He needs the help of a shaykh of great experience to draw him out of the abyss into which his consciousness threatens to collapse, and to lead him to a higher station—the station that truly is the divine center of his being (latîfa haqqîya).

In Semnani's view, the Christian needs spiritual healing of the same kind. For beneath both manifestations of the same hybris, or spiritual overreaching, Semnani perceives an ending of Abraham's pilgrimage before its proper time: a premature birth, or even a miscarriage, of the spiritual offspring whose seed was placed in the subtle center of the heart, the “Abraham of your being.”

Indeed, the “mystery of the hidden mystery” (ghayb al-khafî—Semnani often calls the subtle organs, the latîfa, “mysteries,” ghayb) surrounds and encloses the five mysteries preceding it: spirit, higher consciousness, heart, vital soul, and body.

But this hidden mystery is itself surrounded and enclosed by the Mystery of Mysteries (ghayb al-ghoyûb), the mystery of the true divine center within you (ghayb al-latîfat al-haqqîya). What occurs in Christian dogma, as Semnani understands it, and in Hallaj's cry “I am God” (Anâ'l-Haqq), is a premature interruption of growth and maturation: an initiation that has failed (compare Book I, Chapter VII, §4, above).

That failed initiation is the one that should have led to the birth and recognition of the True Self: the person of your real Self as the organ of the divine within you (anâ'îyat haqqî-ka). The “Jesus of your being” is no more responsible for this failure than Jesus son of Mary is responsible for official Christology.

But the region of your being embodied by that subtle organ is precisely where the danger arises—the same danger confronting both the Sufi and the Christian.

Here Semnani offers an extended explanation. Every latîfa has its corresponding revelation, its unveiling of the self, from the self still bound to bodily life in the first two subtle centers up to the divine Self, the “Glorified One,” the “Muhammad of your being.” The danger arises when the Self “appears” (tajallî) at the level of the hidden mystery, the latîfat al-khafîya.

Conversely, it arises when the secret of this latîfa is unveiled to a self not yet entirely purified of intoxication—of the unconsciousness that clouds and distorts perception at the level of the first two latîfa, the subtle organ of the body and that of the vital soul319. A lower mode of perception is still at work, which is why we can speak of a failed initiation.

Christians, in Semnani's account, did not perceive at the level of the hidden mystery (latîfat al-khafîya) the mystery of the divine manifestation: the Holy Spirit appearing visibly to Mary as Gabriel, and breathing into her so that Jesus becomes Rûh Allah, the Spirit of God. They understood it instead on the level of the evidence available to the first two latîfa.

Or, to put it another way: their dogma makes the one God be born materially “on earth,” whereas the “Jesus of your being” is the mystery of your spiritual birth, your heavenly ascent. They spoke of fatherhood, motherhood, and sonship; they asserted a “third of three” (5:77), bringing the relationships of three persons into the mystery of the One who is essentially one. They remained within the kinds of relationship that ordinary consciousness can grasp in the outer world.

They did not penetrate to the sea of the Jabarût, where the points or centers of Knowledge, Will, and Power emerge. (In Semnani's thought these three names designate aspects of a cosmology to which we shall return.) Christians made the first the essence of the Creator, the second his Son, and the third the Holy Spirit320. There are, of course, intermediaries (wasâ'it) in the world of Mystery, for divine action always takes place through mediations.

But to conceive those mediations on the model of generation in the sensory world is to see nothing beyond that world. It is, as the old proverb says, to believe that “beyond 'Abadan there is no other town.”

Thus one declares Jesus to be the son of God, just as the Jews had come to declare 'Uzayr (Ezra) the son of God (9:30). According to Semnani, the same illusion threatens anyone who, while still spiritually imperfect, reaches the degrees corresponding to the subtle center of the secret (the fourth latîfa, the “Moses of your being”) and the center of the hidden mystery (the fifth latîfa, the “Jesus of your being”).

To save the mystic who, by proclaiming “I am God,” brings divinity down to the level of an earthly human being, Semnani believes the mystic must be “lifted” to a higher spiritual station.

There the nature of the true Self is revealed: a self of which divinity is not an attribute, but which serves as the organ of divine manifestation, because it can become the mirror in which that manifestation occurs and can be filled with it entirely. This is the secret of being “beloved of God”—the state of which God says, concerning the one he loves, “I am the eye with which he sees, the hand with which he touches,” and so forth321.

That is the true meaning of the spiritual perspective overturned by the illusion of Anâ'l-Haqq, “I am God”: the illusion of a Moon brought to incandescence by the Sun's light and crying, “I am the sun!” (We have encountered this image before, both in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Crimson Archangel and among the Hurufis.) Here again is the contrast between a way of thinking centered on divine manifestations and a way of thinking centered on incarnation; between an event experienced in vision and one that enters material history and belongs to the past.

This contrast inspires Semnani's extraordinary reading of the Qur'anic verse (4:156) that contains, as we know, the most explicitly “docetist” claim in Qur'anic Christology: “They did not kill him, they did not crucify him ... God raised him to Himself.” This “raising to God” presents the same contrast as Enoch's ascent—when he is invested as the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal human being, in the divine fullness or Pleroma—set against an Incarnation entering the material reality of earthly history.

The question is plain: does divine humanity come to fulfillment on earth, or rather “in Heaven”? Semnani in effect prescribes a radical cure of “docetism” for the Christian and the misguided Sufi alike, because both, in his judgment, misunderstand what divine manifestations mean: one declares that Jesus is God; the other cries “I am God.”

Just as the Gnostic Christology echoed by the Qur'anic verse makes any claim that “God is dead” meaningless and harmless in advance, so the “Jesus of your being” must be raised to the level of the latîfat al-haqqîya, if your initiation is to be completed and you are to be saved from error.

Just as Jesus had to be “raised to God”—lifted, like Enoch, out of the history of the outer, visible world, thereby depriving any worldly power claiming his authority of its foundation—and just as, from the heavenly place to which he was raised, he must return with the Mahdi, the Imam who is the flower of the prophetic lineage, to summon his people to the pure hanîfî religion: so too the “Jesus of your being” must be “raised” by the attraction of divine ecstasy to your latîfat al-haqqîya, until the Friend in the absolute sense makes you a confidant of the mysteries of his essence.

“Until then, do not yield to the illusion that you have arrived and been made perfect through the Manifestation (tajallî) of the subtle reality or mystery of your Self, as it appears to the subtle organ of your hidden mystery.”

Abraham's journey must be completed. That is what it means to hear the Qur'anic verses “through the Jesus of your being.” It allows you, when the most holy Light reveals itself, to banish all empty self-glorification from your mind and answer, as Jesus himself answers in the Qur'an: “You know what is within me, but I do not know what is within You. For You are the One who knows the mysteries” (5:116).

“From now on, whenever you hear anything God says to his friend the Prophet, or any allusion concerning him, hear and perceive it through the subtle organ of the divine within you (latîfat al-haqqîya)”—that is, through the “Muhammad of your being.” To understand this designation, we must recall how Semnani imagines the psycho-cosmic formation of the subtle organs, and the sources and influences from which arises the one that realizes the perfect humanity of the Nabî, the prophet, within the spiritual seeker's person. It is in this subtle center that the heavenly human being takes full shape.

Here, too, the subtle body “acquired” through the mystic's spiritual practice reaches its full stature. This “acquired body” (jism moktasab) is essential to Semnani's understanding of the human being; we shall return to it later. It develops like an embryo inside the physical body, which is destined to perish and serves, as it were, as its surrounding membrane.

In turn, this subtle body is like a womb containing the “essential heart” (qalb haqîqî, the Abraham of your being). That heart is the shell cast upon the waves of the human sea, yet it shelters the subtle reality of your true person, capable of serving as the mirror (al-mir'âya) in which the divine becomes manifest.

Two themes of fundamental importance for Semnani's entire spirituality are thus stated.

First, the “spiritual body,” whose formation requires the participation of every organ of the subtle centers, and which surrounds the spiritual child born as the offspring of the “Abraham of your being.”

Second, the “mirror,” the speculum: a favored image of this speculative mysticism, because in the mirror the true appearance of divine manifestations is preserved from premature materialization, which betrays a failed initiation. Together, these themes express the concern of a spiritual school whose whole expectation is shaped by the idea of heavenly ascent. Its aim is not to give God a human body of flesh in which God himself would suffer death, but to ensure the birth and growth of the subtle body: the transformation of the human being into a likeness of the divine.

For this school, it is unthinkable that the One should have to annihilate himself in the human condition of flesh so that a human being might be “raised” to the unseen realm of heavenly existence. If the mystic never awakened from the intoxication of “I am God,” that cry would reverse the direction of the ascent and merely foreshadow the tragedy of “God is dead.”

By contrast, the mystery of the speculum, the image in the mirror, offers the only way to recognize identity within difference and difference within identity without reducing the one to the other.

And so our shaykh contemplates this subtle body, crowned by the organ of the Self in which the divine appears, as a mystical Sinai322: a mountain radiant with purity and the brilliance of divine flashes, a mountain that is the substance of this latîfa. This subtle organ is at once knower and known, contemplator and contemplated, because its nature is that of a Mirror. It is also the “heart” (qalb), the “land of safety” (al-balad al-amîn), protected from demonic incursions and seductions. Here stands the most holy Temple (Bayt Allah al-harâm), of which the Book says: “Whoever enters it is henceforth safe.”

Summing up this part of the prologue to his Qur'anic commentary, Semnani insists: “Be certain that each of the seven centers or subtle organs of your being has a people composed of the faculties belonging specifically to that center. All the faculties that are well balanced and established in harmony form the believing people ... All the disordered faculties that persist in their disorder form the unbelieving people.”

Through this inner imagery, our shaykh can draw a correspondence between the prophets' roles in the “world of horizons” and their roles in the inner world of the individual person. It also enables him to describe, in moving terms, his experience of the rebellions of “his own unbelieving people” against the message brought to them by the “Muhammad of his being.”

“Each subtle center or organ is one of the prophets who appeared upon the horizons after Adam and called humanity to the religion of their father Adam, until the turn of prophecy came to Noah”323. So it continues from prophet to prophet, until the coming of Ahmad (Paracletos–Periclytos), the Seal of the Prophets, beloved of the Lord of the Worlds, whose sharî'at, or revealed Law, supersedes the other Laws.

The same is true of the soul's inner world. The spiritual organism grows through the seven latîfa, each corresponding to one of the seven prophets. The mystic recognizes the stages of that growth through visions of colored lights, each belonging to one subtle center—visions that Semnani studied with particular care. All spiritual wayfarers (sâlikân) see these lights at the successive stations of their journey. They are the delicate veils enveloping each latîfa; their characteristic colors reveal to the wayfarer the stage reached in spiritual growth and travel.

The light of the body (the Adam of your being) is smoky gray, shading toward black; that of the vital soul (Noah) is blue; that of the heart (Abraham) is red; that of higher consciousness (Moses) is white; that of the spirit (David) is yellow; that of the hidden mystery (Jesus) is luminous black, or black light (aswad nûrânî); that of the divine center (Muhammad) is a brilliant green (emerald)324, for green is the color best suited to the secret of the Mystery of Mysteries (sirr ghayb al-ghoyûb)325. The following table summarizes the correspondences among the organs of the subtle human constitution, the prophets whose names embody them, and the colored lights by which they are recognized.

Subtle organProphetColor
Latîfa qâlabîyaAdam of your beingSmoky gray
Latîfa nafsîyaNoah of your beingBlue
Latîfa qalbîyaAbraham of your beingRed
Latîfa sirrîyaMoses of your beingWhite
Latîfa rûhîyaDavid of your beingYellow
Latîfa khafîyaJesus of your beingBlack light
Latîfa haqqîyaMuhammad of your beingEmerald green

Elsewhere we have dealt at much greater length with “colored light-visions” in Najm al-Din Kubra and his school, particularly in Najm Daya Razi. The “luminous black” that here symbolizes the subtle center or organ embodied by Jesus is equivalent to the “black light” (Persian nûr-e siyâh) characteristic of certain visions described by Shams al-Din Lahiji, the commentator on Mahmud Shabestari's Rose Garden of Mystery. Unfortunately, we cannot return to this subject in detail here326.

3. “The Angel Gabriel of Your Being”

We have now reached the decisive point on which Semnani's whole doctrine of spiritual interpretation depends. On the one hand, we know that in the “world of horizons”—in the historical time of events beneath the moon—the Prophet Muhammad is the “Seal of Prophecy.” On the other, the seeker is instructed to perceive the meaning of the revelations “in the world of the soul” through the “prophets of his being,” and on the “Sinai of his being” through the “Muhammad of his being.”

The passage from the “Muhammad of history” to the “Muhammad of the soul” therefore determines the whole spirituality founded on drawing the Qur'anic revelations inward. Those revelations have seven depths of inner meaning, corresponding to the seven subtle organs or centers of mystical human nature. And once again, the process of bringing them inward confronts us with the question we have met before.

We have seen what this meant in the doctrine of the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosophers of illumination, as described by Sa'in al-Din Turka and developed further in the Dabestân. There, too, prophecy was brought entirely into the inner life, though by a path different from Semnani's seven subtle organs. We were reminded that the Active Intelligence, identical with the Holy Spirit and with Gabriel, the Angel of Revelation, is—as the Tenth Intelligence—the “Seal of Prophecy” at the level of the angelic fullness, or Pleroma.

Consequently, according to the theory of knowledge shared by Avicenna and Suhrawardi, every spiritual seeker who unites with this Intelligence acquires through that union the quality of nabî, prophet, and in turn becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” The event occurs invisibly in the angelic world. It is a purely spiritual event, not a material fact belonging to historical time (zamân âfâqî). It therefore does nothing to invalidate the title “Seal of Prophecy” belonging to the final prophet in the cycle of prophecy in this world.

But a question then arose. The Ishrâqiyûn realize and make actual the inner meaning of prophecy and the prophetic mission.

Yet it was originally Shiism that defined that inner meaning and determined its content, by declaring the Imam's walâyat—his spiritual guardianship and authority—to be the inner meaning of prophecy. What, then, becomes of walâyat, and of a walâyat without an Imam, when the Ishrâqiyûn reach the reality itself without speaking the name of walâyat or of the Imam? Sa'in al-Din offered a restrained answer: all seekers whose spiritual degree falls short of Shiism live in and represent the imminence of the Hour, but the Hour has not yet dawned.

Semnani's inward approach likewise brings the whole understanding of prophecy into the soul. It would be impossible to realize prophecy's inner meaning more radically than by tracing its different aspects back to the “prophets of your being.”

Yet because of his personal formation, Semnani's horizon is not dominated by the questions about knowledge that opened the way for the Ishrâqiyûn. The Active Intelligence, under its various names and in its prophetic function, does not occupy the center of his inner journey as it does for the mystical wayfarer in Suhrawardi's visionary narratives.

Nevertheless, beyond the seven latîfa, or subtle organs, whose prophetic figures together encompass the whole cycle of prophecy by corresponding to each of the seven great prophets sent to reveal a Book, a sharî'at—beyond these seven latîfa, Semnani mentions another, mysterious latîfa that he never explains systematically. He calls it the latîfa jabrâ'eliya. It is a subtle center or organ that, at the summit of prophetic anthropology and by analogy with the other seven latîfa, must be understood as the “Angel Gabriel of your being.”

Yet Gabriel, who is the Holy Spirit, is precisely the figure identified by the Ishrâqiyûn and the spiritual knowers ('orafâ) with the philosophers' Active Intelligence, and vice versa. He is the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation. This identification illuminates a familiar hadîth: “The learned [or the sages] of Muhammad's community play a role among it analogous to that of the prophets among the people of Israel”327. We thus encounter a situation parallel to the one Sa'in al-Din enabled us to examine among the Ishrâqiyûn. Gabriel, the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation, made each of them a nabî.

Yet in the traditional understanding of prophecy, the Angel's role is to reveal the outward meaning to the prophet. The prophetic teaching of the Ishrâqiyûn, by contrast, leads every spiritual seeker into the inward meaning of prophecy. Is the Angel of Revelation, then, the same as the angel of ta'wîl, of inward interpretation? Or should we say that an angelic understanding of knowledge necessarily calls for a corresponding understanding of the Imam's role in knowledge, because the outward (zâhir) calls for the inward (bâtin), and prophecy (nobowwat) calls for spiritual guardianship (walâyat)?

Now Semnani carries the inward interpretation of prophecy through to its conclusion by making Gabriel himself a latîfa, a subtle organ of mystical human nature. The “Gabriel of your being” is the angel of ta'wîl. And so the earlier question returns: does this also give us the inner meaning of prophecy—that is, the Imam's walâyat—without the Imam? The answer promises to be extraordinarily important for the history of spirituality.

Let us note briefly that this latîfa jabrâ'eliya is also what Semnani calls, with a telling expression, the ostâd ghaybî: the invisible master, the personal master within. When we sense in Semnani an understanding of the Imam that does not speak its own name, the reason may simply be that he has brought the role of the Imam, like that of prophecy, radically into the inner life.

But this inward experience is common to all the spiritual knowers ('orafâ). We already know that in certain meditations on the saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord,” the figure of the Imam comes to overlap with that of the self (“whoever knows his Imam”). The lived devotion to the Twelfth Imam, “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful,” is eo ipso, by that very fact, a relationship with the ostâd ghaybî.

There is no shortage of testimony to this. Why, then, by leaving unspoken the understanding of the Imam presupposed by his own esoteric teaching, does Semnani seem only to deepen the ambiguity between Shiism and Sufism—an ambiguity that Haydar Amoli would denounce so forcefully a generation later?

The elements of an answer—or rather, the lines along which we must investigate—are to be sought, first, in Semnani's own religious convictions. What are we to make of the Sunnism he professed? And, at the same time, what are we to make of the devotion he professed toward the Imam? Second, we must look to what constitutes the very essence of the ostâd ghaybî, and to the way this invisible master intervenes within a strictly inward, esoteric perspective—that is, within Semnani's understanding of prophecy as an inner reality.

In short, how is the “Angel Gabriel of your being,” as inward master and invisible guide, also the “Imam of your being,” even though Semnani does not use that term? For “Imam of your being” is precisely the expression that corresponds to bringing the Imam's role inward in Ismaili mysticism and in Twelver Shiism328. The comparison would be illuminating.

Although many people in Iran today regard Semnâni as having been a Shiite, the matter is not so simple. Certainly, it would be difficult to exclude him altogether from Shiism, if only because he shared Haydar Âmolî’s conviction that “the Sufis are the true Shiites.”

But there is more to it than that. The testimony of Qâzî Nûrollâh Shoshtarî may not be conclusive. Some scholars believe that this devout historian, later honored as Shiism’s “Third Martyr,” sometimes allowed his Shiite fervor to carry him away, claiming certain great figures of the past for the cause of the Imams.

Yet Qâzî Nûrollâh seems in fact to have recognized a “Shiism that dares not speak its name,” and to have judged Semnâni’s case with sensitivity and insight.329 Among other things, he refers to a treatise by Semnâni of which, unfortunately, we have not yet found a manuscript. On one point of doctrine, however, its teaching agrees perfectly with a passage in the prologue to Semnâni’s Tafsîr: the passage in which he acknowledges that Imam Ali alone possessed the fullness of the Imamate (khilâfat, wirâthat, walâyat).

We shall return to this. It is also striking that when Semnâni quotes a saying of the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-Âbidîn, he follows the Imam’s name with a solemn blessing (taslîm) of the kind customarily used only by Shiites. His position concerning the Twelfth Imam is not that of a Twelver Shiite, but he does accept that the Mahdi must be a descendant of Fâtima and that, after the First Imam, he alone will unite in himself the fullness of the Imamate.

Indeed, as we shall recall later, Semnâni draws from this belief a spirituality entirely consistent with his method of turning religious realities inward: the mystic must bring the spiritual power of the awaited Imam to life within himself. He must not simply wait for the Imam’s coming, but must bring it closer, make it happen. Many spiritual teachers have expressed this same feeling. No less significant is another detail. Throughout a short treatise devoted to the First Imam, published some years ago, Semnâni refers to Imam Ali as “our Imam”330—a phrase that comes naturally only to a Shiite.

Finally, as a master of Sufism, Semnâni understands perfectly well what the cycle of walâyat means. If the Qur’an contains every perfection, he tells us, it is because God has established within it both an “outer center” (al-noqtat al-zâhira) and an “inner center” (al-noqtat al-bâtina). Around the latter revolves the cycle of walâyat, once the cycle of prophecy has come to an end. This is why Semnâni repeatedly recalls the solemn words addressed by the Prophet to Ali ibn Abî-Tâlib.

Here—and this is the full significance the tradition acquires among Twelver Shiites and Ismailis alike—the name Ali (the “Exalted,” Excelsus) refers not merely to the historical individual who was Imam, but to the very reality of the Imamate: the eternal Imam. (In the Ismaili writings of the Alamût tradition, this eternal figure is called Melchizedek during the first two periods of the cycle.) The person of the visible Imam is the earthly pole of that reality, its manifestation in this world.

“God Most High said to me: O Mohammad! I sent Ali secretly [invisibly] with the other prophets; with you I have sent him openly [visibly].” The Prophet himself explained these words when he said to Ali: “You stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses.”331 He also said: “There will be no prophet after me”—so that it might be understood that the door of prophecy is, and remains, closed, whereas the door of walâyat is, and remains, open.

These traditions (hadîth) have an immense and quite definite significance in Shiism. They confirm other traditions proclaiming that a single Light gave rise to both the prophetic mission and the Imamate. These are the outward and inward aspects of the “eternal Muhammadan Reality” (Haqîqat mohammadîya): outwardly, the Prophet’s nobowwat, his prophetic mission; inwardly, the Imam’s walâyat, his spiritual authority and power of initiation. They are, respectively, the proclamation of Revelation and the unveiling of its hidden meaning.

What in “Paraclete” Christianity takes the form of a continuing inspiration destined to disclose the hidden meaning of earlier revelations and religions, appears in Shiite language as the meaning, function, and spiritual gift of the Imam. The idea of walâyat goes back to the earliest traditions recorded in the collections of Kolaynî and Saffâr. To speak of walâyat while saying nothing of the Imam’s spiritual gift is more than a paradox: it tears apart what belongs together.

Walâyat is then left hanging in empty space. It cannot be attached to the prophetic mission, for that mission was strictly limited to the tanzîl, the outward communication of Revelation. The initiative of the “return,” the ta’wîl that leads back to its inner meaning, must arise from the very heart of the Muhammadan Reality—from the Imam’s walâyat. That is what walâyat means as Imamate. Did a Sufi master such as Semnâni, every bit as conscious of his Sufism as Haydar Âmolî, consent to tear this unity apart?

Some scattered statements in his writings seem to suggest that he did. In them, he declares that he chose Sunnism as the “middle way.” His position on the Twelfth Imam, the son of Imam Hasan al-Askarî, is equally explicit.

Like the eleven Imams before him, he considers the Twelfth Imam to have been the spiritual “pole” of his age, during the nineteen years preceding “his death”; the “poles” of Sufism then succeeded him. It is as though the succession of the Imams had passed to the Sufi shaykhs who became the spiritual poles, so that Sufism would indeed be the “true Shiism.” This may well be the conception held by a certain kind of Sufism, but it is easy to see why Shiites reject it so firmly. It cannot be reconciled with their understanding of the Twelfth Imam and the Great Occultation (ghaybat).

For them, the Imam of the present age already exists, having appeared briefly in the past; yet he is also still to come, since his return—his parousia, or final manifestation—is awaited. The Hour of his coming is forever imminent, lending meaning to every present moment, every now. There is another, no less serious difficulty.

In a few lines, Semnâni condemns the “error” of two groups of Shiites. The first supposedly treats Imam Ali as a god, through incarnation (holûl) and a union of divine and human natures (ittihâd). (No Twelver Shiite has ever professed this doctrine. They never tire of insisting that, although the Imams are bearers of the divine Attributes, they remain created beings. Twelver Shiites understand themselves to be following precisely the straight path, sirât mostaqîm, the “middle way” between extremism and Sunnism.) The second group, Semnâni tells us, maintains that prophecy (nobowwat) is the outward aspect of walâyat, and walâyat the inward aspect of prophecy.332

Yet to condemn this fundamental teaching of Shiite spiritual knowledge is not merely to put himself at odds with Shiism. It is to put Semnâni at odds with himself—with his entire Tafsîr, and with the very idea of walâyat that enables him, throughout that commentary, to bring the meaning of prophecy into the inner life.

Confronted with these clashing assertions, one’s first reaction is bewilderment.

But it soon becomes clear that we are facing precisely the situation that Haydar Âmolî denounced so forcefully during that same eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century. Sayyed Haydar, like Semnâni, embraced the paradox that the Sufis are “the true Shiites.”

But he did so while professing Twelver Shiism in its entirety, laying claim to the full tradition of its spiritual knowledge and writing, alongside his Jâmi’ al-asrâr, a monumental Shiite commentary on Ibn Arabî’s Fosûs. What, then, was Semnâni’s secret? We must never forget the importance of ketmân, or taqîyeh: the “discipline of the secret,” prescribed by the Imams and practiced by Shiites over so many centuries.

Shiite esotericism is no empty expression; one may often encounter a Shiite without suspecting it. This discipline meant, on the one hand, respect for a truth that should be given only to those worthy and capable of receiving it, and, on the other, the need to protect oneself against persecution. We may therefore ask to what extent Semnâni himself made use of this protection.

But to stop at that question, whatever the answer, would be to travel only halfway along the spiritual path on which he invites his reader. At the end of that path stands the idea of the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.”

Ultimately this is none other than the invisible master, the ostâd ghaybî, who discloses the hidden meaning of Qur’anic verses to the mystic and thereby makes it possible to discover the entire prophetic tradition within oneself. Perhaps this is where we should seek Semnâni’s secret: a secret of his spiritual teaching that was destined to bear further fruit.

The idea of an invisible master, a personal guide within, is especially alive in the spirituality of Najmoddîn Kobrâ’s school, the spiritual lineage to which Semnâni belongs.

Najm Kobrâ even described in detail how this Figure, this person of light, appears as an imaginal vision to the inner sight (basîra). (The expression shakhs nûrânî, “person of light,” is precisely the one Shiite theosophers use, in the plural ashkhâs nûrânîya, for the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in their existence within the divine fullness.) “It is this person of light before you,” Najm Kobrâ writes, “who is called, in the terminology of Sufism, the Guide of the unseen world (moqaddam al-ghayb). He is also called the personal master of the unseen world (shaykh al-ghayb), or the spiritual Balance of the unseen world (mîzân al-ghayb).”

Still other names are bestowed on him: Guide of Light, like the Sun of the Heart; Sun of Certainty; Sun of Faith; Spiritual Sun of the Spirit. And Najm Kobrâ declares even more explicitly: “Know that the mystic has a witness (shâhid). He is the one called the personal Master in the unseen world. He lifts the mystic toward heaven, and so it is in heaven that he appears.” He is the “Witness in Heaven.”333

All these names point us back toward the spiritual being whom Suhrawardî, drawing on the Hermetic tradition, called the “Perfect Nature” (see above, Book II, chapter III, §5, and chapter VI, in the discussion of “the angel of the gnostic”).

Equally revealing is the fact that a profound Shiite theosopher such as Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, in his commentary on Ibn Bâbûyeh’s Tawhîd, identifies the Imam’s function with that of the Angel of the Human Species (rabb al-nû’ al-insânî) in the philosophy of the Master of Illumination, Suhrawardî. This figure of the Perfect Nature had earlier led us back to the Zoroastrian Fravarti, the heavenly archetype and counterpart of a being of light who has come into this world.

Najm Kobrâ says essentially the same thing when he calls the “Witness in Heaven” the mîzân al-ghayb, the “balance,” the counterpart of the earthly self in the spiritual world. Taken together, these facts further strengthen what we have already established about this figure.

All this, then, also lies behind Semnâni’s idea of the ostâd ghaybî, the invisible master and guide. He is indeed the shaykh al-ghayb revealed in Najm Kobrâ’s visions. Just as the visible, outward master teaches tafsîr, the interpretation of the revealed text, so the invisible, inward master discloses ta’wîl, its hidden meaning, to the person who has received spiritual inspiration.

We shall read Semnâni’s text in a few pages; it is extraordinarily rich in suggestion. The inspired mystic stands in relation to his ostâd ghaybî as the Prophet Mohammad stood in relation to the angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit. This is why the highest latîfa, or subtle organ, is also associated with the “Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary,” where the Prophet saw Gabriel standing in Paradise (53:14).

Hence the preeminence of the color green, which the Prophet saw covering the whole horizon of heaven in his first vision of the Angel.

We can now understand immediately why the ostâd ghaybî is also called the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” We might equally say that this inner Gabriel stands in relation to the Angel of Revelation as the Perfect Nature stands in relation to the Angel of the Human Species in Suhrawardî’s Hermetic philosophy.

We can also understand why so many mystics, from Jalâl Rûmî to Mîr Dâmâd, have contemplated the Annunciation of Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, to Mary as a message addressed to every mystic.

There is something more. The Angel who, in the study of prophecy, is the Angel of Revelation, and who, in the “Eastern theosophy” of the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn), is the Angel of Knowledge, appears here as the Angel of ta’wîl, of spiritual interpretation. He reveals the hidden meaning of earlier revelations, provided that the mystic possesses the hearing of the heart, the “heavenly” (malakûtî) sense of hearing.

To this extent, he takes on the spiritual function that belongs to the Imam in Shiism. For by initiating the believer into hidden meaning, the Imam imparts walâyat, which is a spiritual birth for the person who receives it. We may therefore say that Semnâni’s complete inward transformation of the doctrine of prophecy goes hand in hand with an equally complete inward transformation of the doctrine of the Imamate. The Imam becomes the personal, invisible, inward master.

Hence, in Semnâni’s vocabulary, we might call the latîfa jabrâ’eliya—the “angel Gabriel of your being,” who presides over all the other latîfa and reveals the inner meaning of each “prophet of your being”—the “Imam of your being” (Imâm wojûdî-ka). Such a way of experiencing the Imam would be perfectly in tune with the lived devotion of Shiite mystics, the orafâ. I am reminded of a distinguished Shiite shaykh in present-day Iran. A disciple asked him: “Where is the Hidden Imam?” He answered: “Within you, if you can discover him.” One does not say such things from the pulpit or in the public square.

Yet throughout the ghaybat, the Great Occultation, the Imam, as personal guide, is above all—and exclusively—the ostâd ghaybî: the hidden, invisible personal master, whose presence is sometimes disclosed in fleeting appearances, without the person to whom he appears realizing who he is until afterward (see below, Book VII).

We shall therefore leave Semnâni in possession of his secret. Perhaps he sincerely declared himself a Sunni, having chosen Sufism within Sunnism because he believed that the Sufis were “the true Shiites.” Or perhaps he made the declaration in obedience to ketmân, the “discipline of the secret.” In either case, his work can lead a Shiite seeker who knows how to read it all the way to the sanctuary of the Hidden Imam. That sanctuary is not reached through an outward faith, a fides historica, but as one enters a liturgical mystery celebrated in the innermost heart.

We shall regard Semnâni as a great spiritual master, whose surviving works in Arabic and Persian alike ought to be published for their exceptional riches of speculative spiritual philosophy and lived spiritual experience. Even if a Shiite reader sees in his work “a doctrine of the Imamate that dares not speak its name”—because perhaps only someone with Haydar Âmolî’s courage could have given it that name—it remains true that Semnâni, by revealing the seeker’s invisible guide, the “angel Gabriel of his being,” opens the way to the highest organ of the subtle body: the latîfa haqqîya, the “Mohammad of his being.”

Only on reaching this summit of the hidden meaning of prophecy, this visio smaragdina, or emerald vision, does one become fully “Muhammadan.” For no one can change the fact that this hidden meaning is what it is: walâyat. Later on (§7), perhaps we shall gain an even deeper sense of what this latîfa, the “angel Gabriel of your being,” signifies. Semnâni writes: “This subtle divine sense of one’s being is, for every seeker, the supreme horizon (al-ofq al-mobîn). The reality of our essential Self (li-anâ’îyati-nâ) cannot pass beyond it (tajâwoz, transgress that horizon).

“And so, whoever reaches this point—whether by traveling the path, walking, flying, or entering ecstasy334—whoever brings the powers of all his subtle organs out from the stains of illusion and relativity and allows them to appear as they should appear in their purity: that person, truly, is Muhammadan in the fullest sense. Otherwise, do not deceive yourself. Do not imagine that merely pronouncing the words, ‘I bear witness that Mohammad is the Messenger of God,’ is enough to make you Muhammadan.”

4. The Four Modes of Being of the Revealed Book

Semnâni thus insists with particular force that a faith limited to acknowledging a historical event, and related only to that outward event, is utterly powerless. In Luther’s language, this is fides historica seu mortua: historical, or dead, faith. For faith to have any transforming power, the event must become an inner reality. This requires an organic connection between the method of interpretation that penetrates ever deeper into hidden meanings and the spiritual states that arise within the mystic.

The link between interpretation and mystical anthropology means that understanding of these meanings can advance only as the subtle organism concealed within the human being grows. This subtle body develops “from prophet to prophet,” each prophet representing one of its members or “centers,” until it reaches the Muhammadan organ that supports the Self in which God becomes manifest.

An interpretation grounded in the prophets must therefore correspond to an understanding of the human being grounded in those same prophets. We are about to encounter a structure even more complex than the sevenfold account of inner meaning presented in the short work by the anonymous Iranian author discussed earlier (chapter II). Although that structure could already be related to Semnâni’s seven latîfa, here there is something further.

The seven hidden meanings of the Qur’an do indeed correspond to the seven centers of the subtle organism concealed within the human being. That organism develops as a person comes to understand the hidden meanings proper to each center. Seen in this light, the interpretation of scripture is inseparable from mystical anthropology—an understanding of the human being’s spiritual constitution.

But these hidden meanings also correspond to different modes of being of the Holy Book itself, which in turn correspond to the stages of creation. Here we must return to a profound idea: the cosmic text and the written text of the Book, the creative Word and the Word fixed in writing, are two aspects of one and the same process. Seen in this light, the interpretation of scripture is inseparable from cosmology and cosmogony, from the structure and unfolding of the universe.

To understand the different states of the “eternal Book,” we must therefore turn to Semnâni’s cosmological scheme, which we can only sketch here. For it is this account of creation and the cosmos that ultimately explains how the organs of the subtle body are formed: the substantial influences and cosmic energies that give birth to them and determine their capacity for knowledge. We already know that the seven organs or centers of the subtle body are represented by seven prophets, the “prophets of your inner being.”

We can thus begin to glimpse the extraordinary complexity of the doctrine.

The four modes of being of the Book rise in order from the lowest to the highest.

First is its outward state: the Word set down in ink on paper, conveying the literal meaning understood by the overwhelming majority of people.

But this outward form is the body that supports everything else. Even the deepest interpretation of hidden meanings can never dispense with it or abolish it. (This, precisely, is what distinguishes a symbol from an allegory.) Above this outward form, the material appearance of the Book, come three further levels.

Each is represented by a designation of the Book taken from the Qur’an itself, as in the work of our anonymous Sufi discussed earlier (chapter II). Semnâni does not assign precisely the same meanings to these designations, but the difference is of little consequence here. Everything that follows should also be compared with our earlier discussion of the “successive manifestations of the Book” (Book I, chapter V, §2).

Semnâni puts it this way: “Be on your guard. Flee the demonic suggestion that the stories [hikâyât] related in the Qur’an are incoherent accounts. Do not go astray or become one of the condemned. Be certain that anyone who rejects the tafsîr of the Qur’an’s outward meaning (zâhir) in the world of external human events (’âlam al-âfâq al-nâsûtî) is a heretical Bâtini.335

“Conversely, anyone who rejects the interpretation—that is, the ta’wîl—of the Qur’an’s inner meaning (bâtin) in the heavenly inner world of the soul (’âlam al-anfos al-malakûtî) is a denier, an enemy of enlightenment, and a fool.” (His terms are severe.) “But whoever brings the outward and inward meanings together—the visible and the hidden—is a true moslim, one of the Chosen. Whoever knows the ‘limit,’ or essential Idea, of the Qur’an in the world of the Jabarût [the world of the divine Attributes and angelic Intelligences] is a mu’min, a true believer,336 a knower of spiritual realities (’ârif) who follows the Straight Path.

“Finally, whoever knows the summit of the Qur’an’s upward, inward path of interpretation (mottala’) in the world of the Lâhût [the divine realm] is one of the excellent, a Perfect One, a witness before humanity, an initiate into the mysteries, a noble and glorious being.”

We are thus shown the Book’s different modes of being—what we might call the “cosmogony of the Book”—and how each corresponds to the spiritual standing of someone able to understand the Book at that “cosmic” level, through the gradual growth of the subtle organs, or latîfa. In practice, we see throughout Semnâni’s Tafsîr that he readily explains the hidden meanings belonging to the “Glorious Book” at the level of the Malakût, where interpretation falls within the domain of walâyat.

But whenever an interpretation would require him to disclose a meaning at the level of the Jabarût or the Lâhût, he draws back, invoking the discipline of the secret, which forbids him to reveal it. The same reserve can be observed in many Shiite authors.

There is a further correspondence. The spiritual standing produced by understanding the Book at a particular level also corresponds to the kind of interpretive authority appropriate to that mode of being. This will show us just how deeply we are within a Shiite sphere of influence. As noted earlier, Semnâni analyzes the matter with great precision. In its ideal and perfect fullness, the Imam’s function has three aspects.

Khilâfat is succession to the outward government of the community: its temporal affairs. Walâyat is the Imam’s status as a “Friend of God,” investing him with the initiatory function of a purely “spiritual priesthood”; in this respect the Imam stands in relation to the Prophet as Aaron stood to Moses. Wasâyat is the status of spiritual heir.

In historical fact, the union of these three aspects was always exceptional. (The other eleven Imams did not in practice exercise the khilâfat.) It was realized uniquely, and with incomparable perfection, in the person of the First Imam, Ali ibn Abî-Tâlib, who was thus Imam in a “threefold” sense (fî’l-marâtib al-thalâtha). In him, the light of spiritual authority (walâyat) prevailed over the other two aspects.

Semnâni’s emphatic affirmation of this is all the more significant from the Shiite point of view because he then allows that this ideal perfection may be united again at the end of time in a child descended from Fâtima: the awaited Imam, or Mahdi in the Shiite understanding.337 Now, Semnâni specifies that the caliphal function—succession to temporal government—belongs properly to the outward aspect of the Book, the text of religious Law. This is entirely consistent with the way someone devoted to inner meaning should understand the workings of society.

Walâyat, the initiatory function, belongs properly to the inward meaning of the Book (and therefore corresponds to the true moslim). Wasâyat, the status of spiritual heir, belongs properly to the Book’s “limit”—the Book in its essential reality or Idea, as it exists in the world of the Jabarût. Here, then, the Imam’s threefold function is understood in relation to the interpretation of the Book’s hidden meaning.

The three technical terms are used in precisely their Shiite theological sense. This use does not occur, and cannot occur, in the framework of Sunni Islam, where what constitutes the scriptural foundation of Shiism is absent: the affirmation of a hidden spiritual meaning and its corollary, the Imamate.338 (The Sunni understanding of the Imam is purely secular, social, and temporal; the Shiite understanding is essentially metaphysical and “hieratic,” in the Neoplatonic sense of that word.) When the ideas of the Imam and the Imamate are organically linked to the interpretation of hidden meaning, we are, by that very fact, within the sphere of Shiite influence.

We have already suggested how complex the connections are between what openly belongs to Shiism and what belongs to it more discreetly—connections that still need to be investigated. Semnâni’s case seems particularly revealing.

Be that as it may, we are now in a position to follow the outline of his theory of interpretation up to the point where the spiritual seeker, by realizing the “Mohammad of his being,” realizes what we may call the “Imam of his being.”

  1. At the lowest level stands the literal, outward meaning (zâhir), perceived by the physical sense of hearing, the outward hearing (sam’ zâhir). Correspondingly, the tafsîr of this outward meaning belongs to the caliphal function, whose concern is solely temporal succession—the outward level of reality. Its validity depends on properly historical testimony, which confirms what is visible and external. This is why anyone who offers his own interpretation of the Qur’an’s outward meaning without having heard it from an interpreter whose chain of transmission leads back to the Prophet’s Companions risks falsifying most of its statements and misunderstanding the reasons and circumstances that prompted the revelation—the “descent” (nozûl)—of its verses.
  2. If we now survey the structure rising above this lowest level, we see three successive heights. Each is represented by a Qur’anic title that establishes the metaphysical character of the text to be understood.339 First comes the “Glorious Book” (Qorân majîd), read by those who seek its inner meaning in proportion to the growth of their subtle organs (latîfa). This Glorious Book is inscribed on the “Preserved Tablet.” It is the manifestation, or revealed form, of the “August Book” (Qorân karîm), which is concealed in a hidden Book that only the utterly pure may touch—those whom God has already purified of every trace of the world of coming-to-be and passing-away, through the living streams that nourish their subtle organs. The August Book is itself a manifestation of the “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm), concealed in the divine archetype, the “Mother of the Book.” Immediately above the common outward level, then, we encounter the Glorious Book. This is the Book as understood by those who advance through its seven inward meanings, its seven depths (batn). As inner meaning, it is perceived through inward hearing, through the angelic hearing of the heart (al-sam’ al-bâtin al-malakûtî)—that is, through the subtle organ of the heart, the “Abraham of your being.” This suggests that the Book’s mode of being here is the one it possesses in the world of the Malakût, the realm of angelic souls: the heavenly souls of the spheres and human souls. The organs that perceive it therefore belong to the Malakût and are themselves angelic in nature (malakûtî). Its tafsîr, or rather its ta’wîl, comes under walâyat: in Shiite language, the Imam’s spiritual gift of interpretation. Here, significantly, as we anticipated, this function of the Imam is performed by the “invisible inner master.” Anyone who tried to interpret the Qur’an’s inner meaning without divine inspiration (ilhâm) being given to the subtle organs of his higher consciousness, spirit, and innermost secret (sirr, rûh, and khafî—the Moses, David, and Jesus of his being) would betray and profane the inspirations that flash upon those angelic organs (latâ’if malakûtîya) from the realm of divine lordship (Hazrat al-Robûbîya), coming as sudden illuminations (wârida). Just as a healthy physical sense of hearing is necessary for someone to hear the outward Qur’an and receive its tafsîr from an “outward, visible master” (ostâd shahâdî), so an unimpaired hearing of the heart is necessary for the inspired seeker (molham) to hear the Qur’an’s inner meaning and receive its interpretation—its ta’wîl—from an “invisible master” (ostâd ghaybî). The person whose heavenly hearing of the heart is impaired is one of the deaf to whom the verse refers: “Deaf, mute, blind: they understand nothing” (2:166). Here, then, the “invisible and secret” master who teaches ta’wîl to his disciple does indeed appear as the “Imam of his being.”
  3. The “August Book” (Qorân karîm) is the Book at its “limit” (hadd), in its essential Idea or reality (haqîqat), as it exists in the world of the Jabarût—the world of the divine Attributes and cherubic Intelligences. It is perceived through a sense of hearing that itself belongs to the Jabarût (al-sam’ al-jabarûtî), and the interpretation (tafsîr, or ta’wîl) of this metaphysical Book belongs to the status of spiritual heir (wasâyat). Anyone who interpreted its “limit,” or haqîqat, without authorization issuing from the secret Temple, the Kaaba of the divine realm (Ka’bat al-olâhîya), would commit a sacrilege against the higher teachings concerning the divine Attributes. Much may lie behind this restriction: a Shiite or an Ismaili could certainly recognize something of his own tradition in it. And indeed, at certain decisive points in his commentary, we see Semnâni draw back and declare that he is not permitted to reveal the interpretation. The health or integrity of the jabarûtî hearing—the capacity to hear in the cherubic world of the divine Attributes—is required in order to receive this interpretation without the mediation of the three subtle organs that still played a part at the preceding level (sirr, rûh, and khafî). Here it is received through the latîfat al-haqqîya alone, the “Mohammad of your being.”
  4. The “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm) is the Book preserved in the archetype, the “Mother of the Book.” It stands at the summit of the upward path of interpretation (mottala’), the “Orient” (matla’) where the Book eternally rises. It is perceived through divine hearing (al-sam’ al-lâhûtî). Anyone who attempted to interpret this “Orient” of the Book by that upward path before receiving authorization through admission to the Sublime Presence (Hazrat ’ozmâ),340 before attaining supreme purity and penetrating to the innermost depth of the divine subtle organ (latîfa haqîqîya) that nourishes and brings to maturity his true spiritual Self (latîfa anâ’îya), would commit a sacrilege against the metaphysical Realities (haqâ’iq) of the Qur’an. Just as healthy, unimpaired cherubic hearing in the world of the Jabarût made it unnecessary to call upon the three intermediaries still needed at the preceding level, so healthy, unimpaired divine hearing is the power to perceive the Book at its “eternal Orient” and receive its interpretation directly from God, without the mediation of the latîfat al-haqqîya. This means that a seeker who reaches this degree of mystical realization no longer needs the “Mohammad of his being” as an intermediary, for he has become that Mohammad himself. (This refers to the formation of that latîfa at the third degree of its perfection.) In other words, the higher Self, which this subtle organ had been nurturing, is now fully formed. The Self, having become a perfect mirror, is itself the organ in which God becomes manifest—the organ of the theophany—and contemplates that manifestation without an intermediary.

At this final point we can fully appreciate the significance of the “invisible inner master,” whom Semnâni described earlier as the one who grants ta’wîl to the inspired mystic. Having become the “Mohammad of his being,” the mystic now occupies a position exactly corresponding to that assigned by the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn) to the spiritual seeker who, through union with the “Active Intelligence,” the Holy Spirit, is invested as the “Seal of Prophecy.” In the teaching of the Illuminationists, the Active Intelligence—or the Perfect Nature—assumes the role of the “invisible master.” In Semnâni’s teaching, the invisible master assumes the Imam’s role and spiritual gift of interpretation.

Moreover, the very word used to describe him (ghaybî, invisible, hidden) gives him a quality that, in one way or another, associates him with the Hidden Imam, who is in a state of occultation (ghaybat) according to Twelver Shiism. The invisible master fulfills the Imam’s function by inspiring the inner meaning, the ta’wîl, in the “prophets of your being.”

Thus we may indeed say that the invisible master is none other than the “Imam of your being,” the “inner Imam,” the “Hidden Imam.”

We may therefore conclude that the complete inward transformation of the doctrine of prophecy occurs together with an equally complete inward transformation of the doctrine of the Imamate. This helps us understand the relationship between Sufism and Shiism. The Imam is the invisible, inward master who guides the seeker from one hidden meaning to another (see Book I, chapter VII, §4). Here we meet once more the conception of the Imamate formulated by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî: “a heavenly and uncreated thing within the human being, which is the Imamate.”

But unlike the Illuminationists described in the Dabestân, Mollâ Sadrâ was both a Shiite and an Illuminationist—or, more exactly, a Shiite Illuminationist. His own terminology (in his commentary on Kolaynî) includes explicit references to the “inner Imam” (Imâm dâkhilî, Hojjat bâtina). These various names bring us back to the figure Semnâni sometimes calls outright the “secret personal master,” the invisible inner master, and sometimes evokes indirectly as the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.”341

And the circle closes when we return to the Illuminationists’ Active Intelligence or Perfect Nature. All these expressions bear witness to one and the same spiritual experience, one and the same encounter at the threshold of the Unseen. We have observed in another setting that this does not mean casting aside the teaching about prophecy. It means realizing its deepest truth in the very heart of the most undeniable personal experience.

Yet this fulfillment of prophecy through a transcendent interpretation that makes its meaning inwardly real could never take place without the doctrine of the Imamate, which is the key to that interpretation. Sufi inwardness is not the enemy of the Shiite Imamate; whether it knows it or not, it is rather the Imamate’s work. Viewed in this way, these matters seem to come into focus as Haydar Âmolî and Mollâ Sadrâ themselves understood them.

All these indications seem to converge toward a final view that brings together what we have already gathered and developed. We have seen that Semnâni accepts that the threefold perfection of the complete Imamate will one day be repeated, at the end of time, in a descendant of Fâtima. This does not mean, as we have said, that he thereby accepts the Twelver Shiite doctrine, according to which the Twelfth Imam is the son of the Eleventh, Hasan al-Askarî, and believers await not his future birth but his return, his final manifestation as the Mahdi.

Nevertheless, it brings Semnâni’s spirituality into harmony with the Shiite spiritual outlook toward the end of time—and does so through a striking transformation of that very expectation into an inward reality. In Semnâni’s eyes, merely sitting and waiting for the Mahdi to appear is the attitude of an ignorant, lazy, irresponsible person. If the blessing spoken whenever the awaited Imam is mentioned—“May God hasten the joy of his coming”—is to be sincere and effective, that coming must take place each time, here and now, invisibly, within the person who utters it.

Semnâni insists: it is within yourself that you must realize the power of the Guided One who is himself the Guide (al-qowwat al-hâdîya al-mahdîya). For it is also within yourself that the forces of the Antichrist (Dajjâl) are present, and it is these forces that the manifestation of the “Mahdi of your being” must drive back and dispel.342

We have thus reached the complete inward realization of a Shiism whose presence can hardly be missed wherever the hidden meaning of scripture is interpreted. Perhaps its secret and its surest triumph lie precisely here: in an inward realization that brings Shiism itself to fulfillment at the end of the stages of inward understanding into which it initiates the seeker.

The person who reaches this degree unites within himself the light of the Imamate and the light of prophecy: the light of his “invisible guide” and that of the “Mohammad of his being.” His Self, in which God becomes manifest, takes on the quality of “beloved of God.” It becomes a pure mirror of the divine, and the divine presence moves and animates the Image of itself contemplated in that mirror.343

We have surely reached the essential point, and this first outline has given us a glimpse of the supreme goal toward which Semnâni’s method of interpretation seeks to lead us.

Yet even after setting out the main lines that connect the seven subtle organs of the human being with the hierarchy of the Qur’an’s “cosmic” modes of being, many technical details remain to be worked out. In particular, we must account for the actual multiplicity of hidden meanings through which a complete spiritual education must lead the mystic before the goal is reached. The complexity only increases.

Each of the seven centers or organs of the subtle body is itself made up of ten subtle coverings, or latîfa, corresponding to the ten latîfa that develop within the physical organism through the stages of its growth and perfection.344 Each of these latîfa has its own way of judging and understanding the Book.

We must therefore reckon not simply with seven hidden meanings corresponding to the seven subtle organs, but with seventy. (Seventy is, moreover, a known variant of the number in the celebrated tradition concerning the seven hidden meanings.) And there is a still more distant prospect: each of these subtle coverings or layers, marking a stage in the growth of the original seed, can itself be regarded as possessing ten organs of outward and inward perception, whether potentially or actually.

Thus, in the end, the possibility of seven hundred hidden meanings comes into view. We may be forgiven for feeling dizzy at the thought. Even a master of spiritual experience such as Semnâni can be forgiven for shrinking from the task of carrying out the entire plan. “For my part,” he says, “I have dug down to the water and opened a passage for those who are gifted.

“Now it is for you, O seeker, to descend to the waters of these Mysteries, so that you may deserve the stream flowing from each of the seven subtle centers. Let your outward being be purified by the water of the wisdoms which, descending from the divine Presence, run through the streams of the Qur’anic verses. Renounce the intoxications produced by outward, visible forms, so that you may become capable of intimate converse (monâjât).” By way of experiment and example, Semnâni undertook to give a sevenfold ta’wîl of one verse among many.

We cannot even offer an analysis of this extensive lesson here: it would need to be set out in a comparative table, with the interpretations of the seven meanings advancing in parallel.

Yet it is enough to give us a sense of the ideal task as he conceived it—a task that would have produced a monumental work unlike any other.345

The verse chosen for this exercise in interpretation is identified as verse 4 of surah XLVI: “O you who believe, do not approach the Prayer while you are intoxicated; wait until you understand what you are reciting. Nor approach it when you have incurred an impurity other than those one incurs in passing, until you have performed your ablutions.”346

The verse is perceived and understood, contemplated and fully drawn out in turn at the level of each of the seven subtle centers, through the organ of perception belonging to that center. At every stage, the effort is directed toward bringing about in that center the state that will enable the mystic to move to a higher or deeper degree and to draw nearer to the person of his true Self, leaving behind the illusory self of the bodily soul.

Each time, the people to whom the command is addressed are different: they are the faculties belonging to that subtle center, the “people” of the “prophet” whom the center represents within the world of the soul. Each time, the Prayer that must not be approached in a state of intoxication corresponds to a different degree or form of the divine Presence.

Each time, intoxication—the unconsciousness and ignorance from which these “people” must awaken—brings different dangers, ever more hidden and subtle. Each time, the impurity one might incur is different; but the command remains the same: pass only through the sanctuary (masjad) of each subtle center. For then, however unavoidable contact with appearances may be for those merely passing through, the forms that appear according to the properties of each organ can no longer halt the ascent.

In short, the aim is to escape the danger of what we earlier called a failed initiation, to prevent the illness that makes the “angelic hearing of the heart,” the organs of inward hearing, go deaf. To this end, Semnâni lays out various forms of dhikr, the remembrance of God, ascending through seven degrees from ritual dhikr (rasmî) to the supreme dhikr (a’zam).347

It is impossible to mistake what is meant here: these are neither allegories nor edifying metaphors.

What is at stake is attaining a way of understanding that, each time, brings a particular way of being into existence. Interpretation and mystical anthropology are inseparable—a point Semnânî insists on emphatically. This is a truth that must be lived: whichever subtle center, or latîfa, one reaches and inhabits, one becomes the human being proper to that latîfa.

Every way of understanding reveals an inner spiritual state. In examining these states, mystical anthropology naturally arrives at the categories of Gnostic anthropology: those of the first latîfa are the material, or hylic, human beings; those of the second are the psychic, or soul-centered, human beings; and those of the remaining five are the pneumatic, or spiritual, human beings at successive stages of their development.

At each stage, the faculties belonging to that latîfa form, as it were, its own “peoples.” They enjoy all the delights appropriate to its maturity and health, or suffer the disasters that follow its decline, when it can no longer lead the “pilgrim” onward into the latîfa above it. Of course our shaykh knows what his claims demand: “No one will believe what I have just said until he has himself traveled the mystical Way, and has seen with a vision belonging to his own eyes the things that my explanations have enabled him to hear about.”

5. The Three Bodies of the Human Being

Because these are not allegories but something real and substantial that must be brought into being, the interpretation of meaning at its seven depths translates directly into mystical anthropology. We have seen Semnânî describe the “subtle center of the heart” as the “Abraham of your being,” because it holds the pearl of a spiritual offspring that the mystic must bring to birth. This child is the true Self in its divine reality: the theophanic Self, capable of reflecting the divine Face.

Yet the child can grow only if it is surrounded and protected by a subtle membrane to whose formation all the latîfa contribute. This protective envelope is the body of spiritual fruition: the subtle body acquired (jism moktasab) through spiritual practice. Semnânî returns repeatedly to this imperishable, acquired subtle body, sometimes in direct teaching, sometimes through a symbol—the microcosmic egg. The theme stands at the heart of his account of the cosmos and the soul.

Indeed, it provides the point of connection, the transition, at which his cosmology joins his prophetic psychology: the point where the latter's seven latîfa meet the cosmic influences or energies of which they are formed.348

The human being has three bodies: (a) the original body, the perishable earthly body studied by biology (jism maj’ûl, donyâwî); (b) the acquired body, or body of spiritual fruition (jism moktasab), which is imperishable and corresponds to some extent to the Neoplatonists' okhêma, the soul's subtle vehicle, and which belongs to mystical anthropology; and (c) the resurrection body, literally the “gathered body” (jism mahshûr), assembled on the day of the Great Resurrection (Qiyâmat kobrâ).

Our shaykh likes to point out that a similar power of attraction forms each of these three bodies. The original material particle placed in Adam's loins—that is, in the human being—draws to itself every kindred particle of the element Earth, until the physical organism reaches its full growth and becomes the protective casing, or womb, of the acquired body.

In the same way, an influence proceeding both from the universal Soul and from the individual soul that governs the physical body draws to itself, by a law of affinity, all the subtle substances belonging to the world of the divine Command (’âlam al-Amr), the world of creative creation. These are the latâ’if amrîya, the subtle substances that enter into the formation of the subtle organs. Even when dispersed or hidden in the world of the Elements (’âlam al-khalq, the world of created creation), the soul draws them together into an enduring subtle body that will forever envelop the true spiritual Self.

Finally, on the day of the Great Resurrection, the Rûh, the Spirit, will attract and gather the scattered atoms of the vanished physical body. This “gathered body” will become the eternal garment of the “body of fruition,” just as the latter is already the subtle and imperishable garment of the subtle substance of the true Self (latîfat al-anâ’îya).
