7. Spiritual Diary (Diarium spirituale)

We use this term again, as we did for Rûzbehân in Book III, because the material is both remarkably similar and, in another sense, quite different. Here too we have a “spiritual diary” recording a series of visionary experiences (earlier we also mentioned Swedenborg's).

Yet Rûzbehân, at a friend's request, gathered the contents of his diary into a single book. Semnâni did not. His accounts are scattered throughout his writings, and someone would have to bring them together to reconstruct his Diarium spirituale—a task we cannot undertake here.

We can at least offer a glimpse of some of its contents. We may expect them to provide the confirmation of experience for the account just given. They concern the growth of the subtle body's organs, the ascent from one latîfa to another, and the awareness of what occurs at each level: above all, the perception of an aura whose color reveals to the visionary how far his true Self has grown within its imperishable subtle body. Semnâni confides his trials and doubts, his visions of lights, and his many experiences of perception beyond the ordinary senses.

Yet when the moment comes to disclose the “ultimate secret,” he holds back; he “rolls up the carpet.” He does not consider himself entitled to say more, leaving us to approach the experience only from some distance.

We have just used the word “event” (wâqi’a), a characteristic term in Semnâni's technical vocabulary. It must be understood in the very sense his Qur'anic commentary, or Tafsîr, gives it when interpreting the surah that bears this title: surah 56, al-Wâqi’a. It is generally translated “the Event.” But the ordinary word lacks sufficient force.

What is meant is a visionary event, an encounter with the unseen through every form of mystical perception. At each turning point in the mystic's inner life, the event carries the full eschatological meaning associated with it in the Qur'an, for each such event contains the idea of a resurrection. This becomes entirely clear from Semnâni's commentary on two neighboring surahs: surah 54, on the splitting of the Moon, which we saw earlier allowed Sâ’inoddîn ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî to sketch his own hierarchy and typology of spiritual seekers; and surah 56, the Event. In his Tafsîr, Semnâni relates the “approaching Hour” (al-sâ’at, 54:1) and the visionary Event to two different latîfas, according to the depth of the hidden meaning that each can reach. For each subtle organ has its own resurrection, designated by a particular Qur'anic term.

The resurrection announced by surah 54—“The Hour drew near and the Moon was split” (54:1)—concerns the center of the heart (latîfa qalbîya). It is the third center in the ascending order, the “Abraham of your being,” because it carries the embryo of your spiritual posterity: your own child, your true Self. Struck by a flash of divine inspiration, the mystic now finds himself, in the “world of his soul,” in the Prophet's own situation: his people rise against him.

“If they see a Sign, they turn away and exclaim: This is an unending spell of magic.” Here the rebellious people are the psychic faculties belonging to the first two subtle organs—the people of the “Adam of your being” and the “Noah of your being,” enveloped respectively in dark black and blue fluorescence. These faculties represent unbelievers and deniers who use rationally established knowledge to demonstrate the impossibility of what their prophet announces. “They call him a liar. Before them, Noah's people had already cried imposture” (54:3, 9).

In the inner reading, this refers to the time when the latîfa nafsîya, purified of its stains, was sent to those lower powers of your being with “manifest Signs.” “So turn away from them” (54:6). Through ta’wîl, the inward interpretation, this command is addressed to the “Muhammad of your being”: turn away from those who cannot die before their bodily death, and who therefore remain strangers to the conditions of spiritual resurrection. Semnâni even coins a term made possible by Arabic.

Since the angel Isrâfîl, or Seraphiel, is the angel of resurrection, the call to the “Seraphiel-like power” (isrâfîlîyat) of the “prophets of your being” inevitably makes the doubting, calculating, denying faculties recoil in helpless terror. Surah 56 then sounds the answering note of a resurrection belonging to the center of the Spirit (latîfa rûhîya), the fifth latîfa, the “David of your being.” “When it comes, the mountains shake, and the earth trembles like the surface of a sea stirred by waves; the fires of desire and Eros blaze beneath the victorious breath of grace, brought by the north wind of beauty.”

The event is decisive. Once it occurs, nothing and no one can cast doubt on it. When the mystic opens his eyes again upon the world accessible to the senses, he understands that, compared with this visionary event, everything he had previously seen in the visible world was seen as though in a dream. Hence the Prophet's saying: “Human beings are asleep; when they die, they awaken.”

With the resurrection of the latîfa rûhîya, the eyes are opened to visions in which the divine becomes manifest. Reading the commentaries on these two surahs together allows us to understand the full meaning of wâqi’a in Semnâni. “The wâqi’a,” he writes, “the event or encounter, consists in your vision perceiving something in the supersensible world (al-ghayb). Your vision means this: that when you open your eyes, you see something in the sensory world, certainly, but as though you were seeing it in the supersensible world (nahwa mâ tarâ-ho fi’l ghayb).”381

These words express with exceptional clarity the very secret of theophanic perception: a vision that apprehends sensible things while simultaneously “seeing” them in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, as they truly are in their spiritual state, invisible to our outward senses. For a sensible form is true only when its spiritual counterpart is perceived. This is the very process of visionary experience, and we could cite converging testimonies here, from Ibn ’Arabî as well as Swedenborg. For Semnâni, the wâqi’a is a compelling confirmation through experience of the great principle underlying his ta’wîl, his esoteric interpretation: that meaning must be discovered inwardly.

All visible forms in the “outer or exoteric world of the horizons” (’âlam al-âfâq) are, at the same time, forms of the soul's attributes or modes of being in the “inner or esoteric world of souls” (’âlam al-anfos). Otherwise, we could know nothing of the soul's modes of being and could not rise from one mystical station (maqâm) to another.382 The inward discovery of meaning must therefore occur as the growth of the subtle body, an ascent from latîfa to latîfa, and the mystic must be able to see his inner states. Semnâni experienced this throughout his life, yet he does not conceal the doubts he had to overcome. That candor is surely one of his most valuable lessons.

Something perceived by a visionary in the “world of mystery” (’âlam al-ghayb), he explains, may become manifest in the visible world. The visible and the invisible belong together “as one sandal matches another.” The problem is the same when an inner state is given an imaginal form within an aura of a particular color. The spiritual masters want to verify that what appears to them—not through the outward senses, but through inward imaginative perception—is indeed the outward Form, the apparentia realis, the real manifestation of an invisible or “hidden” spiritual reality (sûrat al-ma’nâ al-ghaybî), and that this Figure bears truthful witness to what exists in the “world of mystery.”383

We are therefore not dealing with idle fancy or empty fantasies. His interpretation of verse 8:12—“When God said to the Angels: I shall be with you. Strengthen those who believe”—discovers in every detail of the verse an allusion to the wâqi’a taking place in “each mystery of the seven mysteries,” that is, in each subtle organ or latîfa. Spiritual realities and lived states undoubtedly take shape in images or in lights whose particular qualities vary from one mystic to another. This is because everyone has a spiritual countenance of his own, distinguishing him in the “world of mystery,” just as his individual face distinguishes him in the sensory world.384

Yet the essential visionary event is shared by all. Semnâni records both findings repeatedly in the scattered passages of his Spiritual Diary:

“Often, at the beginning of my spiritual life, I had this thought: perhaps what you behold during the wâqi’a belongs to you alone. How, then, can you claim that it has value for everyone? My shaykh directed me to the spiritual guidance of those traveling the mystical path (irshâd al-sâlikîn). He instructed me to keep them company in retreat and to interpret their visions.

“I then learned that at every mystical station (maqâm) through which I myself had passed, they too had undergone encounters with the supersensible (wâqi’ât) and direct visions (moshâhadât) corresponding to mine exactly, as closely as the feathers of an arrow resemble one another. Through them I thus acquired complete certainty that this path (tarîqat) is true, and that whoever travels it arrives at what all the mystics have reached.”385

Ideally, we would gather here every fragment of the Spiritual Diary scattered through Semnâni's works, including all the visions reported by spiritual seekers. The veils change in opacity and transparency as the colored lights appear: the “colors of the veils of the seven mysteries,” the seven subtle centers. Semnâni never ceases to attend to them, faithfully continuing the Central Asian Sufi tradition inherited from Najmoddîn Kobrâ.386

  1. In the latîfa qâlabîya, the mystic sees a dark blackness—not an indistinguishable void, but “a light the color of black smoke.” Depending on whether the element of Earth, Water, or Air predominates within him, he sees mountain peaks either clouded or clear.387
  2. In the latîfa nafsîya, the light is blue. As he progresses from the nafs ammâra, the state of the flesh-bound, commanding soul, toward the nafs motma’yanna, the soul at peace and purified, the clouds obstructing the sky break apart. He sees a star-filled heaven; the stars seem to descend toward him, acting upon him as they will, and temptations recede.
  3. In the latîfa qalbîya, the light is red. Seven phases correspond to the seven degrees of the heart, each with its own visionary encounters (wâqi’ât) and symbols. The bond with the flesh-bound soul is broken; the heart is free. The light of pre-eternal Eros now predominates within the mystic, at the very center where his “spiritual child,” his true Self, begins to form.
  4. In the latîfa sirrîya, the light is white. The realities of the “world of mystery” begin to appear, together with fragrances subtler than anything the senses can smell.
  5. In the latîfa rûhîya, the light is yellow. According to the mystic's capacity to receive them, Angels and the Spirits of prophets become manifest. When he is firmly established at this station (maqâm), his own Spirit, his own “Angel,” manifests itself to him (tajallî al-rûh). From this we must begin to sense what the latîfa jabra’îlîya might be: the “Gabriel of your being,” as he appears in the pure mirror of the latîfat al-anâ’îya, the subtle center of your true Self.

Each of the five stations marked by these first five latîfas has its own paradise, with castles, houris, and angels. Entry into them depends on the efforts of the disciple (morîd) under the direction of his shaykh. But the disciple cannot rise beyond them without the aid of divine attraction.

  1. The latîfa khafîya is the place and organ of the theophanies—manifestations—of the divine Names and Attributes. They are already so numerous for each mystic that no one could count them. The lights of the preceding five centers may appear here with heightened intensity, but the light peculiar to the circle of this latîfa is luminous black (aswad nûrânî).388
  2. Finally, the latîfa haqqîya, the “mystery of mysteries,” is the place and organ of the theophanies of the divine Essence. In its existence before this world, in the world of Spirits before descending into the world of bodies, the soul contemplated what it now contemplates at this mystical station. That is why the Sufis say that the color of this “station of mystery” is a brilliant green: visio smaragdina, the emerald vision. “From it we departed [in our pre-existence], and to it we finally return.” We should add that devotional acts, intuitive perceptions, and contemplative stations also each have their own color.389

The growth of the subtle body, announced by a supersensible perception of the aura or colored Light belonging to each latîfa, corresponds to a penetration into the depths of the seven hidden meanings of the Qur'an—a penetration Semnâni pursues in his Tafsîr. The celebrated saying (hadîth) of the Prophet speaks of seven esoteric depths, or even seventy, seventy thousand, and so on: amid these multiplications, the number seven retains its qualitative significance. This recalls another, equally famous saying attributed to the Prophet: “God has seventy thousand veils of light and darkness.”

Semnâni confirms that the saying refers to the veils encountered (wâqi’a) within the seven latîfas. Each has ten thousand veils of light. Beyond them is the supreme Veil, which is Light itself, as the Prophet indicates when he says: “His Veil is light,” or “His Veil is fire.” These successive veils are attributes of the soul, forms of its mode of being through which, from one latîfa to another, it perceives minerals, plants, animals, the celestial Spheres, houris, and Angels, until it reaches the Pen, the destination of its heavenly ascent, its mi’râj.

The mystic's own effort can carry him no farther; what is needed now is the attractive force of theophanic ecstasy (jadhba tajallîya). Semnâni deliberately uses the word mi’râj390, for the Prophet's ecstatic ascent is precisely the model for the mystic rising through the successive heavens of his own being. And this brings us again to the question of the relationship between the subtle center Semnâni calls the “angel Gabriel of your being” (latîfa jabra’îlîya) and the “Muhammad of your being.”

Is this Gabriel to the inward Muhammad what the angel Gabriel was to the historical Muhammad? Or what walâyat, spiritual guardianship or intimacy with God, was to the Prophet's prophetic charisma (nobowwat)? Can we hope to find among the scattered passages of Semnâni's Spiritual Diary some indication that would let us go beyond what we suggested earlier (§3): namely, that the “Gabriel of your being” might be identical with the personal, supersensible guide (ostâd-e ghaybî), the “witness in Heaven” described by Najm Kobrâ and his school? Although Semnâni holds back just when we hope for a decisive statement, we can glean a few clues by reading certain passages together.

In one group, he asserts that he has seen his Rûh, his “Angel,” in language similar to Najm Kobrâ's account of seeing his shaykh al-ghayb, his unseen spiritual guide. These passages must then be read alongside those in which Semnâni interprets the Qur'anic surahs describing the Prophet's first visions of the angel Gabriel. We find that whenever Semnâni recounts his own vision in his Diarium, and acknowledges how deeply it disturbed him, he appeals to the Prophet's example, since the Prophet's vision of the Angel had caused the same disturbance.

Semnâni's “inner prophetology” thus identifies the two experiences. This identification brings us into contact with the hidden meaning of the prophetic gift itself, for the “Muhammad of your being” is the inner reality of outward prophecy. To reach that hidden meaning would, by that very fact, mean reaching walâyat, the “Imam of your being.” Yet Semnâni's reserve allows us to do no more than ask these questions.

First, there are the passages in which our shaykh's interpretation finds an inner meaning in the Qur'anic account of the Prophet's vision of Gabriel. Above all, these are his commentaries on surah 53, the Star, and surah 81, the Folding Up of the Sun. The Book “is nothing but a revelation given to him; the One mighty in power taught it to him” (53:4–5)—that is, the angel Gabriel, the trustworthy Angel who serves as the organ of Revelation (amîn al-wahy).

Semnâni comments: “Your portion of this in the world of your soul, O traveler of the mystical path”—that is, your personal share in the Angel's revelation, the hidden meaning of that revelation for you—“is to understand that God has placed within you the divine subtle organ, the ‘Muhammad of your being,’ and that this latîfa is the prophet within you who summons to God all the other subtle organs of your being: those at the level of the body, the vital soul, the heart, the innermost heart, the spirit, and the hidden mystery, together with all their faculties.”391

The following verses of the surah, by indicating the height of the horizon where the Angel stands, allow the inward interpretation to take a decisive step forward: within you there is a latîfa higher than the “Muhammad of your being.” “The Angel stood at the highest horizon” (53:7), when he paused, upright and still. For each latîfa, Semnâni explains, has two horizons: one facing what is above it and the other facing what is below it. This corresponds exactly to the teaching of Shiite theosophy concerning the Haqîqat mohammadîya, the Muhammadan Reality, with its two “dimensions”: the one turned toward created beings is nobowwat, prophecy; the one turned toward God is walâyat.

Thus each “prophet of your being” has a double horizon: below him, toward the prophet he succeeds; above him, toward the prophet who succeeds him. In the same way, minerals open onto the horizon of plants, plants onto that of animals, and animals onto that of human beings. The “Muhammad of your being” is therefore the supreme height of the horizon for the six preceding latîfas: their highest horizon.

But his own highest horizon lies above him. It is the horizon at which the Angel is seen, a vision evoked first in surah 53 and then in surah 81: “The Qur'an is the word of the noble Messenger, obeyed and trustworthy. No, your companion is not mad. He saw him at the clear, translucent horizon (al-ofq al-mobîn)” (81:19–23). The “Muhammad of your being” beholds the Angel appearing at the “translucent horizon”—a horizon higher than himself, although he is the highest horizon of the six other latîfas.

Unfortunately, on at least three occasions, we find Semnâni observing ketmân, the discipline of concealing a secret, at precisely this decisive point. In his commentary on surah 81, he writes: “Within the inner reality (haqîqat) of the horizon is a secret suspended at the boundary (hadd) of the Qur'an, something it is not permitted to disclose.” Earlier, commenting on surah 53:7, he had written: “Examine the two horizons. Strive to receive directly from the divine Being at the translucent horizon, without an intermediary. Do not be content with leftovers. Do not seek nourishment beneath your own level.

“Yet no one can be nourished from his own self (min dhâti-hi) until he has reached the Self of the primordial Unity of unities (al-dhât al-wâhida, the Intelligence) and plunged into it. To understand this secret, one would have to knock at a door I have been ordered to keep closed. So pass on, and meditate.”

A third passage speaks more plainly of the latîfa jabra’îlîya, only to refuse just as firmly to say more. Verse 53:8 declares: “Then he drew near and remained suspended. He was at the distance of two bows.” For Semnâni, we should emphasize, the subject of the sentence is not the Angel, as almost all commentators suppose, but the Prophet—and thereby the “Muhammad of your being.” He accordingly writes:

“Understand, O mystic, that the divine subtle organ within you, your latîfa haqqîya, draws near to the divine Being. It remains suspended, stretching from the horizon of pre-eternity to that of eternity-to-come, until the latter meets the former. I mean that the expression ‘at the distance of two bows’ alludes to the two notches of the bow meeting when the archer draws it to its utmost tension. The words, and what they hint at, refer here to the latîfa haqqîya reaching the divine Being, at a boundary no one may cross. Everything the mofassirûn, the commentators, explain about the Prophet seeing Gabriel, the Angel's form covering the whole horizon, is entirely correct and true.

“But then we must understand properly what the latîfa jabra’îlîya, the angel Gabriel of your being, is; what the horizon is; how the Angel's form covered the horizon; and what ‘covering the horizon’ means. The inner realities (haqâ’iq) of all this are suspended at the boundary (haqq) of the Qur'an. This is something that may not be explained explicitly in a commentary.”

“To understand what the latîfa jabra’îlîya is”: that is indeed the question on which the meaning and substance of this mystical experience depend.

But since Semnâni refuses to answer it directly, we can only try to glimpse his secret in other remarks. They suggest how a vision in which the divine becomes manifest must, as such, be an angelophany: an appearance of the Angel, when what had previously disclosed itself to the mystic only invisibly takes on the reality of a visible face. And they suggest how the appearance of the Angel compels an inward interpretation through ta’wîl to posit a subtle center higher than the other seven latîfas. “The heart cannot deny what it saw” (53:11), and the Angel of Revelation had already been seen by Muhammad “another time, at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary, where the Garden of Abiding is” (53:13–15). Our shaykh comments:

“Here again, everything the exoteric interpreters (ahl al-zâhir) say about the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary is true. Every mystic, in the course of his mi’râj, therefore contemplates something resembling what they describe.

“Yet you must understand this: the Garden of Abiding certainly exists already, today, but it is with you. If you cultivate it and sow the seeds of paradise there, it will become your supreme Refuge. Hell exists, too, but it is with you; if you cultivate it and sow hell's seeds there, it will become your Gehenna.

“Paradise and hell are at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary. Every human being has a Lotus of the Utmost Boundary, because it is the outermost limit of the heart's secret (sirr), and he cannot go beyond it. Those seized by ecstasy, however, are drawn beyond the Lotus by the magnetic force of grace. For it is impossible for a human being to pass beyond the Lotus by his own action: every action is conditioned by the one who performs it.

“Thus no one reaches God by his works, but only through divine assistance, and by being carried away through that assistance.”

“Every human being has a Lotus of the Utmost Boundary.” Perhaps that is the best and most discreet answer to the question, “What is the latîfa jabra’îlîya?” For every human being there is an Angel appearing at that Lotus, appearing to the “Muhammad of his being,” just as the Angel appeared to the Prophet. To pass beyond this Lotus, this boundary, is therefore to pass beyond the Angel of the theophany “who covers the whole horizon.” It is to pass beyond one's own paradise, to go beyond oneself.

No human being can accomplish that by his own power. The Angel standing at the Lotus of the Utmost Boundary announces, by his very presence, something about which the mystic must remain silent. That is why the first vision, or the first few visions, of the Angel may so profoundly shake the visionary that he believes himself to have gone mad. We find an admission of this kind in Semnâni's Diarium. By identifying his own vision of “his Angel” with the Prophet's vision, he helps us sense more clearly what the latîfa jabra’îlîya is.

Here we meet once more concepts and mystical images that have appeared throughout this book. For the gnostics, ubique et semper—everywhere and always—have sought and experienced one and the same reality: the transcendent archetypal Image, the heavenly Self, the divine alter ego, the companion who has existed since before time, and so on. All these themes are brought together and recalled in Semnâni's pages on the Rûh, the Spirit, and on the visionary experience of his own Rûh, his “Angel.” The Rûh, he explains,392 is a “subtle luminous substance” (jawhar nûrânî latîf) shaped in human form (mosawwar bi-sûrat âdamîya).

Each person's Rûh is shaped like that person's body—or rather, to put it more precisely, the reverse is true: the Spirit is the archetype in whose image the body is formed. Semnâni understands the famous saying “God created Adam in His image” (’alâ sûrati-hi, “according to his form”) to mean that God created Adam's material body in the image, or according to the form, of Adam's Rûh. We might say that the Rûh, the personal spirit or angel, corresponds here to the Mazdean idea of the fravarti (forûhar). The Rûh, however, belongs to the “world of the immediate divine Command” (’âlam al-Amr), not to the world of mediated creation (’âlam al-khalq).

Its first manifestation (tajallî) blossoms at the level of the subtle organ bearing its very name: the latîfa rûhîya, the “David of your being.” But there is more. The Rûh reveals itself differently at each of the higher latîfas. It then appears as the alter ego that “dwells in heaven” and acts directly upon its earthly self. At the sixth latîfa, the “Jesus of your being,” there is a distinct unveiling393 in which God manifests Himself through His attributes of Majesty and Beauty.

The arcanum, or latîfa khafîya, is a luminous, transcendent, personal rûh, a special gift from God to those servants of whom He says: “In their hearts He has inscribed faith, and He supports them with a Spirit from Himself (bi-rûh min-ho)” (58:22). Semnâni understands this to mean: “He supports them with a Spirit that belongs to this faith. That is the hidden Spirit (rûh khafî),” meaning the Spirit of the latîfa khafîya. Elsewhere Semnâni adds394: “In the words ‘with a Spirit from Himself’ lie sublime secrets that inspire sacred awe.

“Let the believer fear for his faith, lest it be left without the help of a Spirit from Him—or the Spirit of that faith. If the faith inscribed in each soul”—the sacred inscription of faith from the beginning, the original religious disposition or fitra—“does not come to that soul's aid through a Spirit from Him, or through the Spirit of that faith, then its life beyond this life will be impossible.

“So, believer, guard your faith carefully. Hold fast to the Friend of God”—the “Muhammad of your being,” the latîfa haqqîya—“so that the faith inscribed within you may be supported by a Spirit from Him.” This “Spirit from Him” is generally understood to mean the angel Gabriel. But there is more. In his Diarium, Semnâni bears witness to having seen this Spirit; and he immediately connects his experience with the Prophet's vision of the angel Gabriel and the distress the Prophet felt before gaining certainty.

“Know with certainty,” he writes, “O seeker who aspires to certain knowledge, that for twenty-five years I have seen—I have been an eyewitness (ashâhido) to—my Rûh, my ‘Angel,’ in my visionary encounters (wâqi’ât), always in the same form. It never exchanges that form for another; it never changes. Sometimes, certainly, its form appears weaker, sometimes more intense; at times it seems to be suffering, at others to shine with strength. Its beauty increases as my actions become purer, and diminishes if some impurity casts a shadow over them.

“Sometimes it reproaches me, and I too reproach it. When it is pleased with me, it receives me kindly, and I welcome it joyfully in return. If it were only a product of imagination, it would not persist so faithfully in one and the same form.”395

During those twenty-five years, Semnâni had, of course, had time to become familiar with this spiritual companionship—for that is exactly what it was. These pages of the Diarium echo what we read in Najmoddîn Kobrâ and his disciples about the “witness in heaven,” the supersensible guide and companion (ostâd-e ghaybî).

But at the beginning he had been seriously alarmed. That alarm is precisely why he appeals to the Prophet's experience: the Prophet, too, was profoundly shaken after seeing the Angel in his majestic form, “covering the whole horizon,” before becoming accustomed to his companionship in a form of human proportions.

“When I first began to have this vision,” writes Semnâni, “the thought came to me that it was an imaginary fantasy brought on by strain upon the brain, the consequence of excessive spiritual practices and efforts. And who is safe from such a temptation? It came even to the prince of prophets himself, the beloved of God, at the beginning of his mission, so much so that he said to Khadija, his wife: ‘I am afraid I am going mad!’”

Semnâni then recalls the famous episode. Khadija comforts the Prophet with the certainty of her own feminine intuition and takes him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nûfal, the aged Christian Arab, the “great shaykh,” of whom tradition says that he had translated the Gospel into Arabic. Muhammad tells him of his vision, and Waraqa confirms that the being who came to him was indeed the “Supreme Nâmûs,” the one who had descended upon the earlier prophets, upon Moses and Jesus: that Nâmûs who is Gabriel, “the one who knows the secrets of the king.”396

The word Nâmûs is a transcription of the Greek nomos, borrowed directly into Arabic. It occurs in an Arabic version of the Gospel of John, in verse 15:25, immediately before the reference to the coming of the Paraclete announced by Jesus. For Waraqa, Khadija's cousin and the “great shaykh,” Nâmûs is indeed the angel Gabriel. Islamic theology identifies Gabriel with the Holy Spirit, who descended upon Muhammad to invest him as the Paraclete foretold by Jesus, upon whom he had already descended.

In Arabic the name Nâmûs acquires an additional resonance through its possible connection with the root n-m-s, “to keep a secret.” It means the confidant, “the one who knows the secrets of the king,” as Semnâni has just written, recalling Gabriel's traditional title, Rûh al-Amîn, the Faithful Spirit. The Ismaili encyclopedia of the “Brethren of Purity” (Ikhwân al-Safâ’) developed the notion of Nâmûs at considerable length.397 Nâmûs comes to mean the kingdom of the Spirit, the spiritual kingdom (mamlaka rûhânîya).

Likewise, in its psychology, it denotes the highest of five categories of souls. Above the soul associated with philosophical wisdom, the soul of the intellect, stands the angelic or nâmûsian—that is, “Gabriel-like”—soul, the organ of prophetic wisdom. Here we are very close to what Semnâni calls the latîfa jabra’îlîya, the “Gabriel of your being,” who initiates the “Muhammad of your being.”

We can now understand why, when Semnâni describes seeing his Rûh, he is led to recall the Prophet's vision of the Angel: in both cases, the first alarm gives way to unshakable certainty. “Often, when I had first entered the spiritual path,” he says, “that same thought”—the thought that shook the Prophet—“came back to me, pressing upon me day after day, until my Lord favored me with inspiration and gave me the strength to drive it away by persevering in the dhikr, the remembrance of God. I waited until my soul found peace in contemplating Him and became like the first brightness of dawn.

“Then there was no longer any room for doubt within me. If anyone wishes to be initiated into the events of the world of Mystery (’âlam al-ghayb), to contemplate them and perceive them intuitively, let him enter the way of the mystical travelers. Through sustained concentration of the heart (himma), they have crossed the deserts of existence, until ecstatic rapture has carried them into the tabernacles of glory. There they have tasted the drink of true spiritual knowledge, poured into the cup of love.”398

We had asked whether Semnâni's Spiritual Diary could tell us more about what he calls the “angel Gabriel of your being,” the latîfa jabra’îlîya. We have seen him keep the secret at the decisive moment.

Yet the indications brought together here confirm what we glimpsed earlier (§3). It does not seem possible to say more. We would, however, like to close these pages on the eminent visionary mystic ’Alâoddawleh Semnâni with a passage that sums up his Diarium. It appears at the end of his commentary on surah 54—the very surah that, a few pages back, opened our inquiry into the Diarium. This is one of the passages that best traces the course of his spiritual experience, expressed in the language of the latîfas and the “prophets of your being.” Every mystic inevitably experiences the rebellion of the people of each of these prophets: the natural faculties refusing to accept their prophet's message.

“I myself experienced this state”—the rebellion of the “people of Noah”—“at the beginning of my spiritual life, when my father, my uncle, all my relatives, and my friends attributed to madness what they saw happening to me. For when I began practicing the effective and secret dhikr399, then, on the very first night, there appeared to me blazing, radiant sparks, as though they were rising out of my chest to join the heavens.400

“When I lifted my eyelids and looked with my own eyes, I said to myself: ‘So everything they say about me is true!’ For a vision of sparks in the darkness of the night, inside a house plunged in darkness, surely could only come from a disorder of my brain. And my psychic faculties”—those belonging to the “Noah of my being”—“cried out that it was an imposture. They frightened me, trying to turn me away from the dhikr; the satanic powers inspired doubts in me about this vision of manifest Signs.

“But my heart”—the “Abraham of my being”—“paid them no attention, and remained wholly absorbed in the dhikr until morning came.”

At dawn, then, the young man goes to the mosque. Yet when he takes his place on his prayer mat, brilliant stars appear before him and to his right, “in the direction of his qibla,” the direction of prayer. He is afraid, although inwardly he rejoices.

But the satanic powers of his lower being trouble him, urging him to give up the dhikr. “I was so afraid of people's gossip,” he says, “that I did not dare breathe a word to anyone about what I had seen and contemplated with my own eyes.”

Until then, Semnâni had practiced the many traditional devotions customary in Sufism. Never before had he experienced these visions of light whose importance for his spiritual teaching we have now seen.

But as soon as he received the secret of the dhikr from one of his brothers in religion (min akh lî fi’l-dîn), a disciple of the same shaykh, the visionary encounter occurred: the wâqi’a, the “Event,” which is the “approaching Hour” announced in the first verse of surah 54. At first he dares tell no one except his spiritual brother, Sharafoddîn Semnâni. Sharafoddîn then plays a role similar to that played for the Prophet by Khadija and the wise Waraqa. He rejoices and says with a smile:

“Glory to God, who has brought you to this secret vision, to the Signs that appear in the world of the Soul! I myself had to make pilgrimage for a whole year in the sanctuary of the Sacred Temple before these sparkling stars appeared to me on Mount ’Arafat. God has been generous to you in granting you the sight of these Signs after so short a time. Your duty now is to show gratitude to the divine Being: withdraw from ordinary company, and practice the dhikr according to the method you have now learned. For it will open the door of the heart to you, in sha’Allah—God willing.”

“Then I freed myself from the faculties that cried imposture and sought to raise doubts within me, and I devoted myself wholly to this dhikr. I chose solitude and retreat for two consecutive years, so that by the end of that time I had completed the full course of Moses' forty-day retreat. And behold, by His grace God opened to my heart what no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what has never entered the heart of any human being.”401

This gives us some sense of the importance of the symbolic visions in which the young Rûzbehân began to realize that he himself was one of the Awliyâ’ (friends of God). On the same page of the Ighâna, Rûzbehân also reports another tradition from Shaykh Abû Bakr al-Kattânî: 300 Noqabâ’ residing in the West, 70 Nojabâ’ residing in the East, 40 Bodalâ’ (= Abdâl), seven Abhyâr who are continually travelling, three ’Omadâ’, and finally the Pole (Ghawth), in Mecca. There is also mention of the 124,000 Walis corresponding to the 124,000 prophets. The structure of their hierarchy mirrors the configurations of the stars: the same imago mundi, or image of the world, is embodied in both. The key to this conception very probably lies in Central Asian Sufism, while the source of its astronomical symbolism—with the special prominence of Ursa Major—may be sought in Taoist and Buddhist cosmologies. This hierarchy remains a living idea in Shiism today, notably in the Shaykhi school, where it sustains the conception of a purely spiritual Church, an Ecclesia spiritualis. It differs, however, from the hierarchy of Sunni Sufism by reserving walâyat (spiritual guardianship) to the holy Imams alone. Beneath them, the Noqabâ’ and Nojabâ’ are mirrors (mazâhir) of the Imam. This esoteric hierarchy has already been mentioned here (vol. I, Chapter III, § 4); see also below, vol. IV, Books VI and VII. Bringing together the different traditions on this subject would take an entire book. See L’Homme de lumière, index. ↩

  26. “Because you are my organ, my tongue.” We can hear an echo here of the famous hadith: “My faithful servant never ceases to draw near to me ... and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he touches ...” See Introduction au Jasmin, p. 113, note 152. ↩

  27. Ighâna, fol. 19a. It is highly significant that, in one of the visions recorded in his spiritual diary, Rûzbehân saw Sarî al-Saqatî (Kashf al-asrâr, § 85 of the edition in preparation). ↩

See also below, notes 50 and 54. ↩

But it should be noted that, for him, these attributes correspond to variations in a quite specific visual form. See below, p. 49, note 35, on the vision “in the most beautiful of forms.” The attributes of Jalâl and Jamâl correspond respectively to the fourth and fifth sefirot in Jewish Kabbalah: Gebura and Hesed. ↩

  31. Af’âl: divine activities or operations, each of which manifests a divine Attribute in a form suited to the nature of the person to whom it appears. See Introduction au Jasmin, p. 114, and below, Chapter V and p. 120, note 170. ↩

  32. On these two “earthly Angels” (the Angels “of the right and the left,” “who dictate and write”), see our Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire, vol. I (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 4), Paris, 1954, index, p. 327. ↩

  33. See below, Book IV, Chapter III, § 7 (the precedence given to “maternal lines” or “lines of Eve” among the Hurufis). It is because of this precedence that God shows his face to the Prophet with these features, in a vision on which the Sufis meditate tirelessly; see below, p. 49, note 35. ↩

  34. Jalâl and Jamâl: see above, p. 46, note 30. We should also think here of Rudolf Otto’s categories, tremendum and fascinans, with all the qualifications required by the different forms taken by the sacred. In one sense, they may be translated, as Fritz Meier does (op. cit.), by Erhabenheit (sublimity) and Freundlichkeit (kindliness). Yet these are merely aspects and consequences flowing from the primordial Image. Better to keep the primary meanings: Majesty (awe-inspiring severity) and Beauty (which fascinates). Otherwise, we break the unity of the language characteristic of this mystical worship of Beauty (jamâl-parastî), and lose sight of the fact that the primordial Image presses itself upon the visionary as an entirely specific, visible form (see the following note). ↩

  35. These are the characteristic words of the famous “hadith of the vision,” in which the Prophet declares: “I saw my Lord in the most beautiful of forms, as a youth with abundant hair, seated upon the Throne of grace. He wore a green robe, with a golden headdress upon his hair and golden sandals upon his feet.” On this hadith, its variants, and its use as a theme of meditation, see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 203 ff.; above, pp. 46 and 48, notes 30 and 34; and below, p. 93, notes 112 and 114. In Rûzbehân’s time, even within Iran, Central Asian Turkic beauty was regarded as the ideal of beauty, among both young women and young male pages. Rûzbehân’s visions and his vocabulary both bear its imprint. Perhaps a link should be drawn between the extraordinary beauty for which the inhabitants of certain towns in what is now Turkestan were renowned and the testimony of Abû Shakûr Sâlimî (5th/10th century), according to whom the Manichaeans of Central Asia distinguished themselves by their reverence for every beautiful being. See our Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 100 ff. This makes it clear why, when the occasion arises, it would be quite impossible to translate the expression simply as “young Turks”! See below, notes 40, 44–45, and 49, and our study Manichéisme et religion de la beauté, in Cahiers du Sud, April 1963. ↩

Michael, as the universal divine Soul, the lower right-hand pillar of the Throne and the highest summit of the Malakût (spiritual kingdom), is red. In Iranian Shiism of the preceding century, one of the leaders of the Shaykhi school, Shaykh Mohammad Karîm Khân Kermânî (whose brilliant work is vast almost beyond reckoning; see below, vol. IV, Book VI, Chapter II), wrote, among other things, an entire treatise on red light, ranging from the optical phenomenon to the colour’s esoteric meaning (Risâlat al-yâqûtat al-hamrâ’).   58. We see no reason to doubt the authenticity of this anecdote. Rûzbehân’s stay in Mecca is firmly attested by our sources, among them the biography written by his great-grandson, Shaykh Sharafoddîn Ibrahim, son of Rûzbehân II, and is confirmed by the setting of several of his visions. As for its psychological credibility, his experience in Mecca accords with the whole teaching of the Jasmin. It was certainly not some sordid, commonplace adventure—an episode in which he “threw off his monk’s habit.” His purity matched the sincerity that Ibn ’Arabî recognizes in him. Rûzbehân remained faithful to the teaching of the famous hadith: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies without betraying his secret, dies as a truthful Witness.” His conduct was that of a true “faithful lover”: the young woman whose beauty had awakened his love knew nothing of it until others told her. See Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 108–111. Compare the answer Rûzbehân gave Emir Sa’d of Shiraz, preserved in a long poem by Fakhroddîn ’Erâqî: “Before Abraham the fire bloomed harmlessly like a rose, and Moses’ body was not consumed by the theophany of the Burning Bush. To your eyes my contemplation may seem sensual; but what is born of my heart’s inclination is purely spiritual.” See ibid., p. 110, note 149. ↩

  59. Ibn ’Arabî first came to Mecca in AD 1201. By then, Rûzbehân had long been settled in Shiraz, where he died in 1209. There is no reason to transfer the story to his namesake Rûzbehân Kazrûnî Misrî, from whom he must be carefully distinguished, and who was the master of Najm Kobrâ.   61. The contemplative gaze (nazar) that takes the beloved’s beauty as its witness of contemplation (shâhid) is a gaze that transforms. Otherwise, as they grow older, the light of their outward beauty gradually fades through the accidents of nature. No longer held in the contemplative gaze of the mystics, their being is invaded by Darkness” (Jasmin, Chapter VII, § 103). ↩

For Rûzbehân, this is certainly not a matter of reasoning from the beauty of a creature to the beauty of the Creator as its cause; it is a matter of seeing the Creator’s beauty in the creature itself, because the creature is its only mirror, its unique manifestation. The theophanic vision is immediate and has nothing to do with reasoning via eminentiae, by ascending from finite perfections to a higher, divine perfection. See also below on the shâhid, the “witness of contemplation.” ↩

  69. Jasmin, §§ 19–20, pp. 120–121. He especially recalls the famous master Ibn Khaff, who at first opposed this language but completely changed his negative judgment after Jonayd put a question to him. ↩

See above, Chapter III, on the idea of the shâhid, the witness of contemplation, arising within the divine mystery itself: the Divine Being longs for a Witness to contemplate him, yet can be contemplated by no one other than himself. His longing is only stilled when the one who contemplates him (shâhid) is, in the very act of contemplation, also his own Contemplated (mashhûd), one with himself. The French expression quelqu’un que Dieu regarde (“someone whom God looks at,” as opposed to someone for whom “it is none of his concern”) has a double sense—regarder means both “to look at” and “to concern”—which can suggest this simultaneity. ↩

But he also knows that, to rediscover the secret of the uncreated within a creature in this way, the “daring adventurers of tawhîd” must first have travelled the Path of Trial, crossing the bridge suspended above the hell of sensual nature (see Introduction, p. 18). ↩

II, p. 466: “A Contemplator (a witness, shâhid) whom no one knows, whose measure no one can measure but God, because he is annihilated in Him. When the forms and figures that are so many theophanies (ashkâl-e f’il) appeared in the gallery of images belonging to the creative Command, the form of Adam was the quintessence of Being and of beings, because it was the most subtle of the substances of the angelic pleroma (malakût). It was God himself who had put on the garment of Being, and whose Attributes were no longer veiled from the world.” Compare the opening of Suhrawardî’s Vade-mecum of the Faithful in Love. ↩

  87. Jasmin, Chapter VII, §§ 98–101, interpreting the famous “Verse of Light” (Âyat al-Nûr, Qur’an 24:35) as an image of the veils of theophanies. The Intelligence then reveals itself in the Spirit, the Spirit in the Heart, and from the Niche of the Heart its light is cast into the world of Nature. As for the substance called Intelligence, it receives its beauty directly from the Being of God; consequently, it is itself the cause of the world’s existence (as a manifestation of divine Beauty). It is also the Guide who leads to discovery, to gnostic knowledge, to the lifting of the veil of created existence before the Face of true Reality.” Intelligence, Spirit, Heart: compare Suhrawardî’s triad of Beauty, Love, and Sorrow (here, Book II, Chapter VII, § 3). ↩

  88. Jasmin, Chapter V, § 60. Compare §§ 66–67: the divine Attributes “enter” (dar-âmad) the human form, but only as an image “enters” a mirror. The unity of mirror and reflected image has nothing in common with the disturbance, change, and “constriction” associated with an Incarnation (be-surat-e holûl). Adam is clothed in the lights of uncreated Beauty (jamâl-e qidam). This clothing necessarily involves an ambiguity of appearance (iltibâs), a dokesis or seeming; without it, Adam could not possess the transparency of a mirror. It is this theophany in the person of Adam, on the plane of paradisal humanity, that the Prophet Muhammad recognized, and this is why he proclaimed the religion of love. When he said, “God created Adam as the image of his own form,” he was echoing the verse revealed to him: “I breathed my Spirit into him” (38:72 and 75). “From his person, original Beauty presents itself again in his descendants until the hour of Resurrection”—as a recurring theophany (tajallî), not as an incarnatio continuata, or continuing incarnation. See also Chapter I, § 10. ↩

  91. Gloss 151. See also below, p. 103, note 137, and earlier, Book II, Chapter VII, § 3, at the end. ↩

  92. Muslim writers on heresy were not “historians of doctrine” (see also below, p. 111, note 147). Although they could distinguish Melkites, Jacobites, and Nestorians, their accounts of the Christologies attributed to these groups lacked technical precision. They did not have enough information to grapple with the difficulties of ittihâd (unio, union) and holûl (enoikesis, indwelling), or to distinguish technically between docetic Christology, monophysite Christology, and the Christology of the Councils. They used the term holûl on every occasion (for examples, see H. Ritter, Das Meer der Seele, pp. 449 ff.). That is why we have just seen Rûzbehân and his commentator vigorously reject the notion of holûl. Their opponents could all the more easily accuse them of it because the relation Rûzbehân understood as that between mirror and image counted, in his opponents’ eyes, as holûl. The misunderstanding seems impossible to dispel. These heresiographers were adept—and for good reason—at recognizing the recurrence of a Christological pattern in every Shia teaching concerning the Imams. Their mistake, which we must avoid, was failing to recognize which Christology was involved. Without that distinction, one is liable to make the gravest errors in speaking of the “divinity of the Imams.” ↩

This soul governs it in accordance with the corresponding Attribute and the theophany of the Essence, and this is especially true of the things we admire for their beauty. Only the eye whose very seeing is certainty can truly see. The nearer one draws to the source of Beauty, the nearer one draws to the covenant of love.” ↩

  103. Ibid., § 49. The prophetic meaning of beauty, and thus also the ambiguity of its appearance (iltibâs); the theophanic function that the lover confers upon the beautiful person; that person’s power to lead the lover back to the archetypal source—all these “articles of faith” of the religion of beauty (jamâl-parastî) rest on the primary premise that love existed before creation. “The force that moves (moharrik) the lover is a pre-eternal love (’ishq azalî).” See below, Chapter VI, § 4, where the Platonic and prophetic themes meet, in the texts referred to in note 142. ↩

  104. Ibid., § 50: the elevation of the shâhid (witness) to the rank of shahîd (“martyr”). Compare Mogholta’l’s book “in memory of those faithful in love who have borne true Witness” (ed. O. Spies, Bonner Orient. Stud., 18, 1936). Yet, as we have already stressed, the literal death from love suffered by the heroes of ’odhrîte love gives way here to a mystical meaning. The elevation of the shâhid to shahîd signifies attainment of the esoteric tawhîd: the oneness of lover and beloved, of Contemplator (shâhid) and Contemplated (mashhûd). See also below, p. 92, note 108. ↩

  105. Ibid., § 50. ↩

  106. We have briefly discussed elsewhere (Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 7–12) the difference between, on the one hand, ’odhrîte love, which embodies the ideal of Platonic love and is celebrated in Ibn Dâwûd Ispahânî’s masterpiece, the Kitâb al-Zahra (d. 297/909), and, on the other, the theophanic love experienced by Rûzbehân. Compare (ibid., p. 10) Ibn Dâwûd’s lived understanding of the hadith of the “martyrs of love,” which he followed even to death. Wherever the dominant theme of theophany is missing, the “esoteric meaning” of love and the contemplation of a beautiful being is missing too. Without that theme, love—Eros—cannot take on the essential role of initiation into theophany that Rûzbehân’s spirituality gives it. The difference appears equally clearly in Rûzbehân’s understanding of Majnûn (see below, Chapter VI, § 6, and p. 138, note 200). Of course, mystical meaning does not exclude a collapse that may end in physical death. Popular preachers sometimes sent their devout listeners into trances by speaking about the divinity as they did, using the feminine names of heroines from Arabic courtly poetry (see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, p. 275, note 322, and above, p. 75, note 72). In the Jasmin, Chapter X, § 118, Rûzbehân relates, on the authority of Yûsof Hoseyn Râzî, an account of a gathering at which the celebrated master Zû’l-Nûn Misrî spoke of the love of God. Eleven people died. When the gathering was nearly over, a kind of wanderer stood up: “O Abû’l-Fayz,” he said, “you have spoken enough of love for the Creator. Tell us something now about the love of one creature for another.” Zû’l-Nûn cried out, tore his robe, and fell prostrate. His face became crimson as he murmured in Arabic: “Their pledges have not been released, and their eyes know only tears.” ↩

  119. It is here that the commentator distinguishes three mirrors in which the divine Invisible, God’s visible Form, and the eternal divine Face may respectively be contemplated. Abraham contemplated the first; the power to contemplate the other two was reserved for Muhammad. A translation of this Gloss appears below, in the passage connected with note 111. In Chapter XXIX, § 262, Rûzbehân examines the same theme in relation to mystical states: the state of certain lucidity (sahw), which can grasp the ambiguity of appearance; the state of spiritual intoxication (sokr); and the state in which the ego is effaced (mahw), which combines the previous two and is spiritual intoxication multiplied by itself (sokr dar sokr). Abraham experienced the first state when he prayed: “Lord, show me how you raise the dead” (2:262). Moses experienced the second when he cried: “Lord, show yourself to me, so that I may contemplate you” (7:139), expressing his desire for an absolute vision. Muhammad, finally, was granted both mystical states at once. In the first he asked, “Show me things as they are.” In the second he declared, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” “For God came from Sinai” (the place of Moses’ theophany); “he rose from Seir” (the place of Jesus’ theophany); “and his light shone forth from Mount Paran” (at Mecca, the place of Muhammad’s theophany, as the Seal of the Prophets) (compare Deuteronomy 33:2–3). Compare also Chapter V, § 60, on the difference between Abraham and Joseph. When Abraham saw the stars, he exclaimed, “This is my Lord.” With Joseph it was the reverse: the stars (the eleven stars) acknowledged him as their Lord (12:4), just as the angels prostrated themselves before the beauty of the heavenly Adam. ↩

  137. Jasmin, Chapter X, § 122 and Gloss 155; see also above, p. 57, note 47, and p. 86, note 91. Rûzbehân’s allusion to zend and pâzend belongs entirely to the tradition of “closed language” characteristic of Iranian Sufism. His anonymous follower and commentator expands it in this way: “The fire of Beauty blazing upon your face is the radiance of the Burning Bush; and I, a new Moses beholding this theophany, hear the secret meaning of these words: ‘It is I who am God’ (Qur’an 28:30).” The commentator is thereby practising ta’wîl, a spiritual interpretation of symbols that “leads back” the outward appearance of the religion of Fire (âtesh-parastî) to its inner meaning: the worship of Beauty (jamâl-parastî). Whether Sufis or orthodox believers, everyone in Islam knows that the ancient Iranians used the terms zend and pâzend for commentary on their sacred book, the Avesta. Zend and pâzend are thus equated with ta’wîl. Hence the name zendîq applied to anyone who insists upon the necessity and practice of ta’wîl. Yet this was the scriptural foundation of Shiism and, after it, of Sufism. Every outward statement or appearance (both how something looks and how it appears) presupposes an esoteric meaning. To those who understand religion only outwardly, this claim seemed to destroy the very letter of Revelation. Without troubling over distinctions, therefore, they described Shia Muslims, Ismailis, and Sufis as “survivors of the Mazdean Magi within Islam” (Hujwîrî). Iranian Sufis, meanwhile, practised with equal enthusiasm a symbolic “closed language,” with key expressions such as sons of Magi, priest of the Magi, wine of the Magi, Fire Temple, and so on. It was probably within such spiritual circles that the hadith quoted earlier (Book II, Chapter VII, § 3) arose: “Never speak ill of Zoroaster, for Zoroaster was the prophet sent to Iran by the Lord of love” (see our introduction to Moh. Mo’in’s Le Mazdéisme et son influence dans la littérature persane, Tehran, 1948, p. 36; also everything said here about Xvarnah in Suhrawardî’s doctrine, above, Book II, Chapters III and IV). This gives rise to the idea already noted (p. 86, note 91), and still needing fuller examination: in practising ta’wîl, one follows the example of the Zoroastrian religion, and by applying ta’wîl to that religion itself—interpreting the worship of Fire as a symbol of the religion of love—one escapes two related dangers: idolatry and belief in incarnation, anthropomorphism (tashbîh) and abstract monotheism (ta’til). Rûzbehân is constantly on guard against precisely these dangers, into which those who accuse his Sufism of them themselves fall. What the religion of the Magi symbolizes through its dualism, and what forms the basis of its interpretation (ta’wîl) in Sufism (see Latîfa-ye ghaybîya, Moh. Dârâb’s commentary on Hâfez), is both the duality of Lover and Beloved and the apparent duality of the earthly and heavenly Beloved. Both dualities must be led back to the unity of the esoteric tawhîd. In either case, to perceive duality as calling for ta’wîl is to be initiated into theophanic perception: the theophanic contemplation in which the shâhid (contemplating witness) becomes the mashhûd (one contemplated). The very idea of the shâhid presupposes this ta’wîl, which is less a constructed interpretation than a spontaneous act, an inborn capacity. As for the beauty that qualifies this shâhid as a Witness of Contemplation, we must think both of Xvarnah, the Mazdean Light of Glory, and of Abû Shakûr’s testimony that the Manichaeans of Central Asia were particularly devoted to the worship of every beautiful being (see the study cited at the end of note 35 above). These are simply variations of the same experience. One variation is the theophanic perception of a beautiful face: to stand before the blaze of its beauty as Moses stood before the Burning Bush. Another is musical perception. Sufis who, like Rûzbehân, regularly took part in the spiritual concert (samâ’) clearly distinguished two kinds of listening, one sensual and the other spiritual. The latter presupposes a ta’wîl that is, so to speak, a priori: it occurs at the very moment of hearing. Yet puritans again denounce this as the practice of a zendîq. What is at stake, however, is listening to the inaudible, perceiving once again the ambiguity of appearance, the iltibâs. Toward the end of his life, Rûzbehân himself abstained from the samâ’, from gatherings of spiritual oratorio, and listened only to the sounds of a purely inward music. This long note aims at nothing more than suggesting the almost inexhaustible richness of the theme touched upon in Rûzbehân’s passing allusion. ↩

  143. Javânmard (§ 270) means not simply vir juvenis, a young man or adolescent, but a “knight of the soul,” a “spiritual knight.” The word expresses a characteristic Sufi ideal (Arabic fotowwat = Persian javânmardî). The ancient Iranians called themselves mard, in contrast to the Turanians: the man in the fullest sense, the hero, the superman. The term entered Iranian Sufism as a designation for the “spiritual hero,” the whole person, the free human being whom only Sufi spirituality can bring into being. In this sense, javân-mard is equivalent to mard, with the additional idea of youthfulness. See our Introduction au Jasmin, p. 119, note 164; earlier, Book II, Chapters IV and V; and below, vol. IV, Book VII, Chapter III. ↩

II, p. 18). “When He enveloped them in his light and clothed their innermost consciousness (asrâr) with the radiance of his love, they became adorned with every beauty, inwardly and outwardly. They are contemplated as a mirror of divine beauty; whoever sees them loves them. For God loves them, and they love him with his love. And creatures love them with the love God bears them, just as they love the lights of divine Beauty that they see within them” (on 20:39, vol. II, p. 31). ↩

  145. Jasmin, Chapter XVIII, § 199. Just as Rûzbehân distinguished the faithful lovers from pious devotees in Chapter VIII, so throughout this chapter (§§ 194–201) he forcefully refutes the pretensions of libertine Sufis. They imagine that the condition of a faithful lover who is a malâmatî (one who accepts blame) is equivalent to simple rejection of religious and moral restraints, although they themselves cannot attain even the faintest theophanic perception. “Their inclination is nothing more than the stirring of their sensual passions. When they look at the outward form of beautiful beings, their eyes see nothing beyond that appearance. They see nothing of the beauty that results from a divine Operation, the colour that manifests a divine Attribute, the theophany of the Essence—all taking place in the cage of the human body without even coming from the Bird, the Spirit, that inhabits it. In short, they see none of these magnificent gifts that blossom at the outer limits of human existence ... They no longer distinguish the archetype from the idol. Yet they dare to claim: We are the daring men of our age, the men of paradoxes (Tammatîyân = Shattâhîyân; compare Hâfez, Dîwân, p. 257, no. 279: Tâmmat = shath), because we have made our home in the world of Omnipotence ... Beware of being seduced by the eloquence of these madmen (§§ 195–197).” Here, following certain autobiographical recollections, Rûzbehân reminds the faithful lovers that they must first pass through the Path of Trial and cross the bridge suspended over the hell of sensual nature (§ 201). Notice also that, for him, it is the perception of love’s pre-existent origin that lifts the veil before the Witness of Contemplation of the Uncreated (shâhid-e qidam). ↩

  147. This final stage of vision is esoteric tawhîd. Far from dissolving into the formless, it brings forth before the mystic the form of the theophany suited to his particular experience—the prophetic vision “in the most beautiful of forms” (see above, p. 49, note 35). Rûzbehân’s Diwân bears witness to this by specifying each time the form in which the divine Friend appears to him. For “each divine Attribute has an eye, which is part of that Attribute itself, and it is through the Attribute’s own eye that the mystic contemplates that Attribute” (Risâla-ye Qodsîya, fol. 167b). We have already recalled (notes 91, 92, and 137) Rûzbehân’s care to place his theophanic understanding at an equal distance from belief in incarnation and abstract monotheism. Muslim writers on heresies and doctrines were far from sharing either his sensitivity to nuance or his sense of the necessary distinctions. An entire investigation remains to be made of those whom they indiscriminately placed in the category of holâliyân, believers in indwelling. ↩

  153. Ibid., § 145. See above, p. 95, note 116, and p. 97, note 121. The point is therefore this: Abraham’s experience was still one of inward theophany; the time had not yet come for the prophet who would announce the theophany within created beauty. Rûzbehân has told us (§ 146) that if the eternal Bride had appeared to this spiritual prince in the features of human beauty, he would have suffered the fate of Moses on the mountain. Because Muhammad proclaimed the prophetic meaning of human beauty, he was the prophet of the religion of the faithful lovers: Sufism. “The masters of mystical gnosis know that a creature cannot bear the Uncreated in its pure state (§ 147).” Yet a creature could no more bear its vision within created beauty without the very discipline of the faithful lovers, which “initiates the disciple into discovering the rules of divine love through the experience of human love.” Only this path makes ultimate access possible to the highest and absolute vision, that of the elite of the elite. The circle closes: the theophanic perception of human beauty is no easy path. It is no more within a creature’s unaided powers than the pure vision of the Uncreated. Yet through the discipline of the faithful lovers, it opens as the only path leading toward that vision. ↩

  171. Jasmin, Chapter XVII, §§ 187–188. The latter paragraph develops an astronomical symbolism related to Abraham’s experience (see above, p. 95, note 119, and p. 114, note 153). Mystics must eventually leave behind the planetary heavens. Like planets, they remain wanderers until they recognize the essence of the theophany. They must reach the Heaven of the Fixed Stars, which is the heaven of the divine Attribute, its constellations being the manifestations that determine the visible figures of the Attributes (see the preceding note). These forms are no longer experienced as something other than the One, but as the One’s own manifestation. Only the process of theophany, as the One’s multiplication by itself (1 × 1), saves us from shirk, the association of something else with the One (1 + 1). “Being then within God’s gaze”—that is, beings upon whom God looks, whose own gaze is God’s gaze (see Chapter III above)—“they repent of having associated these theophanies with Him [as though they were something other]. Their vision is so beautiful that they whisper in astonishment: Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:22). From these planetary stages, marked by Abraham’s cry, ‘This is my Lord’ (6:76–78), the Spirit journeys to the fixed constellations, to the theophanic manifestations that stud the Heaven of the divine Attributes. At the Orients of tawhîd, the rising stars of mystical experience point toward the world of the Uncreated and mark the path of initiation for the prisoners of what passes away. The theophany has nourished them, like a mother, with the milk of the divine Attribute in the world of divine election. For at the spiritual station designated by the verse, ‘It is toward you that I turn’ (7:142), the intelligence of the microcosm repeats in turn: ‘I am free from what you associate [with God]’ (6:19 and 78).” ↩

But this refers to a privilege belonging, among all created and time-bound beings, to the holy Spirits and the most sacred Intelligence (’Aql-e jalâlî = ’Aql-e qodsî), as it is written: God guides to his Light whom he wills (24:35) ... For since the beginning of beginnings, love has been united with beauty.” Compare the statement Rûzbehân made in Shiraz during his first sermon, at the end of Chapter II above, and Suhrawardî’s Vade-mecum of the Faithful in Love (above, p. 84, note 87). ↩

In this final passage of his book, Rûzbehân unmistakably establishes a connection between the divine assumption of human form, the primordial theophany in angelic humanity, Adam’s heavenly form, and the beautiful face that has become his personal mystical Qibla—the direction toward which he turns. We need only weigh the words of the supreme “theophanic greeting” he addresses to the beautiful woman to whom his book is dedicated, a greeting that introduces the quotation from Hallâj. Besides an allusion to the Sura of the Star (the Prophet’s vision, in which the Angel of Revelation remains suspended at the horizon he fills), there are technical expressions such as ’ayn-e fi’l, literally “the eye of the divine Operation.” This means the eye of the theophanic process manifesting the Attribute. For, as we learned above, every Attribute is a divine eye, and it is through that divine eye itself, and no other, that the mystic contemplates the Attribute.   238. Truth and falsehood: for some, these consist in acknowledging the esoteric (bâtin) while rejecting the outward (zâhir); for others, conversely, they consist in accepting only the outward letter while rejecting the esoteric. The first position is that of a whole group of Sufis, of certain extremist Shia groups, and of the Ismailis of Alamût (hence the latter’s insistence that the Imamate takes essential precedence over the prophetic mission). The “Straight Path” consists in maintaining the balance. Haydar Âmolî is so conscious of this that he declares—calmly, without the slightest denunciation—that this, and this alone, is what separates him, a Twelver Shia, from the Ismailis. The second position is that of Shia Muslims who, while Shia in name, have forgotten what constitutes Shiism’s very essence. ↩

  241. These remarks do not concern the Prophet and Imams as empirical persons, but their eternal, pre-cosmic reality: the “Muhammadan Light” (the Perfect Human Being). The “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” form the pleroma of the lâhût (the divine world) as primordial theophanies. See also our Terre céleste et corps de résurrection, pp. 108 ff. As a rule, we translate al-Tâhirûn as “the Most Pure Imams,” and al-Ma’sûmûn as “the Immaculate Ones” or “the holy Imams.” ↩

Recall that the meaning conveyed by this term—Friend or Intimate of God, and hence protector of human beings—has no easy everyday equivalent in our languages (though one may think of the fourteenth-century Gottesfreunde, the “Friends of God”; see Book VII below). Shia theosophy reserves its proper meaning for the Imams (“solar” walâyat). It also applies to followers whose hearts have undergone trial (“lunar” walâyat). The Friends of God and those known by God (gnostics and theognostoi, people who know God) initiate others into divine knowledge and guide them toward it. The cycle of the prophetic mission (nobowwat) has been succeeded by the cycle of spiritual initiation (dâ’irat al-walâyat). ↩

  243. An entire investigation is needed into this sermon attributed to the First Imam. See Shaykh Âghâ Bozorg, Dharî’a, VII, pp. 198 ff. The famous Khotbat al-Bayân (Sermon of the Great Declaration) and the Khotbat al-Iftikhâr belong to the same genre, although it is uncertain whether they are the same sermon under two different titles, even though Haydar Âmolî quotes the same passage again in Book III, this time explicitly referring to the Khotbat al-Bayân. The Khotbat al-Iftikhâr was already known to Ibn Shahr-Âshûb (d. 588 AH); it cannot therefore have been invented by Rajab Borsî (8th/14th century), as some have insinuated. It is possible that Sayyed Râzî omitted the Khotbat al-Bayân from his great collection of the First Imam’s writings, letters, sermons, and conversations (Nahj al-Balâgha) because the teaching about the Imam implied in this sermon has certain affinities with Ismaili imamology. Indeed, the Kalâm-e Pîr cites a commentary on it by Hasan Sabbâh. Two other commentaries are presently known: one by Mohammad ibn Mahmûd Dehdâr (Bibliothèque Sepahsâlâr II, 139–140), and the other by Mîrzâ Abû’l-Qâsim Shîrâzî (a shaykh dhahabî, d. 1286 AH), ed. Shiraz, 1343 AH. Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî quotes it frequently and explains why he accepts its authenticity (below, vol. IV, Book V, Chapter III). Sermons of this kind, attributed to the First Imam but actually expressing the eternal Imam as Shia consciousness perceives his words, form a whole group to which we shall return elsewhere. On the Khotbat al-tatanjiya (= al-khalfîya, the sermon “between the two gulfs”), see our report in Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses, 1969–70, pp. 235 ff. ↩

In one who lends an ear while present and being guided, it is the wisdom of the Stoa, because this is hearing from behind a veil.” Compare Ibn ’Arabî’s interpretation of the same verse in our L’Imagination créatrice dans le soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 171 ff. ↩

  270. Inna li’l-Qorân zahran wa bâtinan, wa li-bâtinihi bâtinan ilâ sab’at abton. This is the hadith already quoted many times here because our authors constantly refer to it. Its significance is so fundamental that even the slightest attempt to unfold its meaning brings the whole of Shia thought into view. See Majlisî, Bihâr al-Anwâr, Tehran, 1307, vol. XIX, Part I, pp. 21–28, Bâb VIII; and the Safîna of ’Abbâs Qommî, vol. II, p. 44. Recall again that ta’lîm, the work of spiritual initiation entrusted to the Imam, must not be confused with the teaching authority of the ecclesiastical institution familiar in Christianity (the Roman See, councils, pontifical commissions, and so forth). This ta’lîm essentially concerns esoteric meaning and therefore has no equivalent within the framework of an official Church. It may be communicated personally in a private conversation with the Imam (as in the conversations between Jâbir Jo’fî and the Fifth Imam, Mohammad Bâqir), through one of the Imam’s representatives (one of the hodâd in Ismailism), or even in a dream (as in Mîr Dâmâd’s visions). For in Twelver Shiism the present age is the age of the Hidden Imam, the “Great Occultation.” ↩

  271. This alludes to the great controversy sparked by the Mu’tazilite doctrine that the Qur’an is not eternal but created. In AD 833, Caliph Ma’mûn imposed this doctrine as an article of faith. A period of fanatical inquisition followed, during which the “orthodox”—including the “old believer” Ibn Hanbal—suffered persecution. About fifteen years later, Caliph Motawakkil, Ma’mûn’s third successor, reversed the situation in favour of the orthodox theologians for reasons of high politics. The arguments for and against the Qur’an’s eternity have sometimes been compared to arguments about Christ’s two natures in the Christological controversies. Yet even if one invokes al-Ash’arî’s reconciliation (the Qur’an as eternal Word, its letters and ink as human productions), we must not forget that the question raised by the esoteric interpretation of Sufism and Shiism is not of the same kind as the questions addressed by the orthodox Christology of the Councils. The relation of zâhir to bâtin—outward to hidden, earthly to heavenly, Nâtiq to Sâmit (Speaking Prophet to Silent Imam), literal meaning to prophetic spiritual meaning—reflects an entirely different conception and concern. Its distinctive expression is ultimately found in the doctrine of the Imams, in the language of theophany, and it follows the pattern of a Christology other than the orthodox one: in broad outline, rather the Christology of the Ebionites or the Melchizedekians, with the pre-eminent significance of Christ’s baptism, its interpretation through the idea of Christos Angelos, and so on. See also below, p. 302, note 117, and our edition of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques, index under “Word” and “Book.” ↩

  284. In fact, the structure of this angelology varies.   289. On the foundations of this method, see Gershom Scholem, Die Bedeutung der Thora in der jüdischen Mystik (Diogenes 14/15, 1957), and, for detailed applications, C. D. Ginsburg, The Kabbalah, reprinted 1956, pp. 131 ff. We should not forget that the earliest systematic attempts to explore the symbolic values of the alphabet’s letters appear in the Greek Gnosis of Asia. As early as the eighth century, the Shia Gnostic Moghîra (d. 737 at Kufa) spoke of “the twenty-eight Arabic letters that came from the fall of God’s Supreme Name upon his Crown” (see our Avicenne ..., vol. I, p. 321). On Hurufi interpretation, see Clément Huart, Textes persans relatifs à la secte des Houroufis (Gibb Memorial Series IX), London, 1909, pp. 284 ff., concerning abjad-e hisâbî (gematria, the practice of assigning numerical values to the letters of a word and explaining the word by comparison with another of equal value). There is a simple or abbreviated calculation (hisâb jomlî): treat each letter of a word as an arithmetic unit and add the values. There is also an analytic calculation (hisâb tafsîlî): break each word down into letters, write out the sound-name of each letter, count every resulting letter as one unit, remove repetitions, and add them together. The Gnostic Marcus already proceeded in exactly this way. We cannot trace in detail here the correspondence between the rules used by Kabbalistic interpretation and those of the Ismailis and Hurufis, but a study of them would be well worth undertaking. ↩

  302. The idea attributed here to Suhrawardî’s Ishrâqiyûn is typically Ismaili. The Cycle of Prophecy begins with the First Intelligence of the Pleroma (or Archangel Logos), which summons the other Intelligences emanating from it to tawhîd, the affirmation of divine unity. By undertaking this summons (da’wat), it becomes the first Nabî, or prophet. Although it is called the spiritual Adam (Adam ma’nawî) here, we must remember that in Ismailism the designation Adam rûhânî (the “pneumatic” or spiritual Adam) is reserved for the Third Intelligence. It was the protagonist of the drama that brought it down from the third rank to the tenth, where it is henceforth functionally identified with the Archangel Gabriel as the Active Intelligence of Illuminationist Avicennism. Yet the pair formed by the First and Second Intelligences, from which the Third proceeded, is also called the Adam-and-Eve of the Pleroma. This explains the designation found in the Dabestân. We still need to analyse further, within Ismailism, the intimate relation between the Angel-Anthropos and the Angel-Logos from which it proceeds, the latter being invested with the divine Name above all names (Al-Lâh). Ismaili metaphysics has perceived the drama of humanity as a drama within the divine world. See our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Intelligence. ↩

If henceforth I wish to see myself, my Beloved stands before me as my mirror.” This implies a connection of ideas resembling that established by the Fedeli d’amore between the Active Intelligence and Madonna Intelligenza. As for the idea of parwarda (a being nurtured or reared), compare Avicenna’s gloss in the margin of the so-called Theology of Aristotle, which speaks of the care with which the angelic Intelligences adorn and perfect the soul, treating it as their child. See our Avicenne ..., p. 88. ↩

  308. Recall once again the relationship among three great mystical Tafsîrs (Qur’anic commentaries; see above, p. 176, note 19). Najm Kobrâ began a Tafsîr but could not finish it. Najm Râzî sought to continue it, while starting again from the beginning of the Qur’an, but got no further than the Sura of the Star. Semnânî then took up the commentary and completed it, adding a prologue and an interpretation of the Fâtiha. Semnânî’s work has a depth and inwardness beyond comparison with that of his predecessors. It is in his commentary on Sura 54 (fol. 12) that Semnânî tells us how Najm Râzî had begun his commentary at the start of the Qur’an and carried it forward. When he reached the Sura of the Star he exclaimed, “How wonderful it would be if God allowed me to undertake the Sura of the Star and bring it to completion!” “But on reaching this sura, he fell ill, and his shining star bore him from the earth of men into the Heaven of divinity.” Semnânî was then inspired to continue and complete the Tafsîr. In it, as in his other writings, he scattered many allusions from which his autobiography can be reconstructed. A short book on his life and works recently appeared in Tehran (Sharh-e ahwâl o afkâr o âthâr-e Shaykh A. S., by Sayyed Mozaffer Sadr). His mystical chain of affiliation (silsila) passes through ’Abdorrahmân Esfarâ’inî ... Najmoddin Kobrâ ... Abû’l-Najîb Sohrawardî, Ahmad Ghazâlî ... and Jonayd Bâghdâdî, back to the Eighth Shia Imam, ’Alî Rezâ (Sadr, op. cit., p. 43). A work by Najm Râzî, Mirsâd al-’Ibâd, is still widely read in Iran today. Chapter XVII deals with visions of coloured lights, the theory of which Semnânî would develop further. ↩
